eps.t: The Future of China's Quantitative Investment Through the Eyes of a Coder
eps.ot: 一名程序员眼里中国量化投资的未来
eps.ol: China Securities Journal 10th Private Fund Golden Bull Awards, Quantitative Investment & FinTech Forum (中国证券报·第十届私募金牛奖)
eps.s: In 2019, while running a quant hedge fund, Liang Wenfeng used the US as a guide to predict how far Chinese quant investing could grow. He defines quant simply: a program, not a person, makes the call. The most striking idea is his Moore's Law observation: quant ability doubles every 18 months, yet returns stay flat because the market keeps getting more efficient.
g: Founder of quant hedge fund High-Flyer, speaking as its head; later founded DeepSeek

eps.t: Surprise! LatePost is doing a podcast
eps.ot: EP 0: 没想到吧，晚点做播客了！
eps.s: The first episode of LatePost Chat (LateTalk). Hosts Honghao Gao, Jing Chen and Hanyang introduce LatePost's new podcast: stories beyond the written page that are worth passing on by word of mouth, told from many angles on today's business world and the people in it. Based on the show's description.

eps.t: After the tutoring crackdown, my home filled up with Moutai and cash
eps.ot: 1: 教培行业被打压后，我家堆满了茅台酒和现金
eps.s: After China's "double reduction" policy cut homework and after-school tutoring, LatePost reporter Jing Chen, who covered education for two years, and new host Hanyang trade strange stories from the crushed tutoring industry: what the policy really cut, big companies' odd pivots, who stayed and who left, an illegal tutoring scene and how CEOs handled angry parents. Based on the show notes, which list only topics.
g: LatePost reporter who covered the education industry for two years

eps.t: Depression inside China's big tech companies
eps.ot: 2: 互联网大厂中抑郁的人
eps.s: Ren Youbing, head of the Depression Research Institute, starts from his own experience with depression and talks with Hanyang about depression among big-tech employees: whether they're more prone to it, what to do if you're worried or diagnosed, and how companies and coworkers can help. Based on the show notes, which list only topics.
g: Head of the Depression Research Institute, who has lived with depression himself

eps.t: I ran a do-anything shop in North Korea
eps.ot: 3: 我在朝鲜开「万事屋」
eps.s: Terry, from Guangxi, trades with North Korea from China's northeast and lived in Pyongyang before the pandemic. His company also runs North Korea tours. As trader, observer and tour guide, he describes North Korea's market economy and its companies, the tricks and traps of the trade, the long lockdown after sanctions and COVID, and shopping and cooking in Pyongyang. Based on the show notes, which list only topics.
g: Trader with North Korea based in northeast China; writes for the WeChat account "in North Korea"

eps.t: Fixing toilets while finding new stories for Chinese food: a talk with Penguin Guide founder Zhiwei Wang
eps.ot: 4: 在为中国食物寻找新叙事的间隙，修厕所：与企鹅吃喝指南创始人王志伟的对谈
eps.s: Zhiwei Wang, founder of the food content brand Penguin Guide, talks with Hanyang about content, China's new consumer brands and how Chinese food is presented: whether the boom makes sense, why some brands never take hold, whether the key metrics are wrong, his views on Saturnbird, coffee, WeChat, Douyin, Alibaba and Freshippo, and new stories for Chinese food, with rice wine and sake as examples. Based on the show notes.
g: Founder and CEO of Penguin Guide, a food WeChat account that also sells products

eps.t: When games and technology spiral upward (bonus episode)
eps.ot: 当游戏与技术螺旋上升【番外】
eps.s: A bonus episode in which Honghao Gao and Hanyang discuss games and technology. The usual view is that technology drives games, but Hanyang argues games also push technology forward. Starting from how he learned to code through games, they cover games' pursuit of realism, the generation raised on games, self-driving simulation and game engines, the game industry, and what players mean by "faith." Based on the show notes.

eps.t: A Bilibili creator looks back and reflects: making things harder for Lao Jiang (Part 1)
eps.ot: 6: 一位脖部 UP 主的回顾与省思：给老蒋添点堵（上）
eps.s: Part one of a two-part conversation. Lao Jiang, who makes educational videos on Bilibili, talks with Hanyang about what he has learned as a creator: long videos versus long articles, whether Bilibili is a "hot" or "cool" medium, public reach versus a loyal following, handling floods of comments, whether video can carry deep discussion, and a creator's loneliness. Based on the show notes.
g: Educational video creator on Bilibili, under the account "Lao Jiang Ju Kaopu"

eps.t: Can I love Zhihu more than Zhihu itself? A crossover with Sspai
eps.ot: 7: 「我可以比知乎更爱知乎吗？」× 少数派
eps.s: After Hanyang published a LatePost essay about Zhihu, China's big Q&A site, he recorded a crossover episode with Lao Mai, founder of the content community Sspai, and Nick, host of Yipai Podcast. They discuss how the essay came about and its reception, Zhihu's dealings with Sspai, whether knowledge platforms must fail or change, whether speed and depth can coexist, and where the Chinese internet should go. Based on the show notes.
g: Founder of Sspai, a digital-lifestyle content community; calls himself "chief odd-jobber"
LatePost writer and host of LatePost Chat

eps.t: Inside Bilibili's creator economy: making things harder for Lao Jiang (Part 2)
eps.ot: 8: UP 主生态面面观：给老蒋添点堵（下）
eps.s: The second half of the conversation with Bilibili creator Lao Jiang turns to the platform's creator ecosystem: where a beginner's first money should go, whether growth paths can be learned, how his style formed, misunderstandings about Bilibili, whether creators make money, what followers on different platforms are worth, running multiple accounts and cross-posting, and how traffic, editors and site sections work. Based on the show notes, which list only questions.
g: Educational video creator on Bilibili, under the account "Lao Jiang Ju Kaopu"

eps.t: The metaverse begins in Hegang: a chat with a Hegang construction worker
eps.ot: 9: 元宇宙开端在鹤岗：与一位鹤岗打灰人的交流
eps.s: Beifang Li, a Hegang native, took a COVID test and rushed to Beijing to talk with Hanyang and JT Sunwalker about his small northeastern city of 890,000: the misconception that it's a resource-exhausted town, local food and work, whether outsiders and digital nomads could live there, why few people come though Hegang isn't bad, its quiet young people and the northeastern countryside. Based on the show notes.
g: Hegang native who works in construction (the show calls him a "concrete guy")

eps.t: How I caught your fake résumé: two headhunters on background checks
eps.ot: 10: 我是如何发现你简历造假的：与两位猎头聊背景调查
eps.s: In job-hopping season, LatePost host Jing Chen talks background checks with Mo Zhou, co-founder of headhunting firm Cailu, and Cailu headhunter Xiangang Hao: where checks came from, how they work, how fake résumés get caught, where polishing ends, what talent is always in demand, and how hiring changed after the education crackdown. The show page doesn't separate the guests' views, so all points are listed under Mo Zhou.
g: Co-founder of headhunting firm Cailu, joined by Cailu headhunter Xiangang Hao

eps.t: Sealed-off tech, cyber-theology and vaporwave: technology in an age of vanishing consensus, with Degang Kong
eps.ot: 11: 封装、赛博神学与蒸汽波音乐：共识消逝年代的技术 × 孔德罡
eps.s: Artist and tech commentator Degang Kong and Hanyang start from Hanyang's essay "A Sealed-Off Future" to discuss modernity, postmodernity and today's technology: the collapse of shared consensus, from how people found music and media in the early internet era to "retro-futurism," vaporwave's copyright tension, a "cyber-theology" to set rules for the digital world, and whether cyborg feminism gives reason for tech optimism. Based on the show notes.
g: Artist and commentator on technology news

eps.t: Can the internet still get better? The hacker spirit and Web 3
eps.ot: 12: 互联网还会变好吗？极客精神与 Web 3
eps.s: A special episode: host Hanyang reads aloud his LatePost essay "Can the Internet Still Get Better? The Hacker Spirit and Web 3," adding material the written version left out. His question is whether the internet can still improve, and what that has to do with the hacker spirit and Web 3.
g: Host of the LatePost Chat podcast and a writer at LatePost

eps.t: Can you live a non-technological life today? Ruyi Li on packaging and Japan
eps.ot: 13: 是否在现代社会过非技术式生活：和李如一聊聊封装与日本
eps.s: Ruyi Li, creator of One Day World, talks with Hanyang about "packaging" and Japan: can you live a non-technological life today, and how does packaging relate to shipping, local life and globalization? They also cover why original versions matter, how the Beatles guard their image, eating local, a thousand-day Buddhist mountain pilgrimage, and whether a foreign language can reach native level.
g: Writer and creator of One Day World, Mechakucha and Mujigen

eps.t: Would you take 10% off a car's price to skip the lidar? A talk with a lidar industry veteran
eps.ot: 14: 如果不要激光雷达车价打九折，你接受吗？与激光雷达资深从业者的对谈
eps.s: Lichen of Tanway Technology has watched China's lidar industry almost from its start. With Hanyang and LatePost tech reporter Manqi, he explains lidar: starting with the US company Velodyne, why it's expensive, when it actually starts helping on cars, how the 905nm and 1550nm wavelengths differ, eye safety, and why Chinese carmakers are the most aggressive adopters.
g: Lidar industry veteran at Tanway Technology, author of a LatePost history of lidar in cars

eps.t: Making peace with your emotions during the pandemic: a talk with clinical psychologist Kaiwen Xu
eps.ot: 15: 疫情中，如何与情绪和平相处：与临床心理学博士徐凯文对谈
eps.s: Clinical psychologist and psychiatrist Kaiwen Xu talks with LatePost host Jing Chen about mental health during the pandemic: why teenagers are most vulnerable, how people stuck at home can cope, when to seek professional help, and how front-line workers can protect themselves. They also discuss hiring discrimination against people with anxiety or depression, and whether therapy is worth it.
g: Clinical psychologist with a PhD, and a psychiatrist

eps.t: What is a DAO? A founder and a seasoned member explain
eps.ot: 16: 什么是 DAO？与创始人和资深参与者聊聊 DAO
eps.s: Wendy, founder of DAOrayaki, and Chao Wang, an active member of several DAOs, talk with Hanyang about DAOs: groups run by rules on a blockchain and member votes, without a traditional boss. What is a DAO, how does it work, how is it different from open source, how do you join, and how does it make money? The episode page lists only the questions.
g: Founder of DAOrayaki, former core founder of DAOONE, researcher of how DAOs govern themselves
Self-described DAO learner, deeply involved in Bankless, fwb, Seed Club and others

eps.t: Would you pay 2,000 yuan a jin for crickets to feed your lizard? Reptile keepers in the pandemic
eps.ot: 17: 2000 一斤的蟋蟀，你会买回家喂蜥蜴吗？疫情与那些养爬行动物的人【特别音频实录节目】
eps.s: An audio documentary cut from interview recordings, adapted from the LatePost article "The Pandemic and the People Who Keep Reptiles." Hanyang weaves together voices including YY, founder of Pahun TS, Xianggu of the CG reptile shop, and Fengjian and Eason of Paxiange. It explores a niche hobby outsiders rarely understand, and how keepers worked to care for their animals during lockdowns.

eps.t: Do camera-brand phones really take better photos? Tianxi on how makers quietly alter your pictures
eps.ot: 18: 和相机公司合作的手机，能让我拍照更好看吗？和影像工作者 Tianxi 聊聊厂家对照片动了哪些「手脚」
eps.s: Prompted by Xiaomi's partnership with Leica, photographer Tianxi and Hanyang take phone photography apart: what camera brands have actually built up, what besides the lens shapes image quality, how photos are processed before you see them, and how color, filters and the "film look" relate to taste. The episode page lists only the questions.
g: Photographer and visual artist, known online as Zhengdian Shutiao

eps.t: Overcome imposter syndrome and accelerate your career | Julie Zhuo (Sundial, Facebook)
eps.s: Former Facebook design lead Julie Zhuo looks back on going from intern to manager to founder. She talks about living with imposter syndrome, using writing to force her own thinking, how product sense is built, and how intuition and data work together. The second half covers running design reviews, giving feedback that helps, moving from individual contributor to manager, and how small companies can attract designers.
g: Cofounder of Sundial, former VP of product design at Facebook, author of The Making of a Manager

eps.t: The art of product management | Shreyas Doshi (Stripe, Twitter, Google, Yahoo)
eps.s: Veteran product leader Shreyas Doshi recalls what he learned at Yahoo, Google, Twitter and Stripe and from their founders, then unpacks his best-known ideas on product management: the pre-mortem, the LNO framework for sorting tasks, the three levels of product work, why execution problems are usually strategy or culture problems, prioritizing by opportunity cost instead of ROI, and why high agency is what sets great PMs apart.
g: Former product lead at Stripe, Twitter, Google and Yahoo; now writes and advises on product

eps.t: How to nail your product positioning | April Dunford (Obviously Awesome)
eps.s: B2B positioning consultant April Dunford explains how to tell from your funnel and your sales calls that positioning is off, why most positioning problems are really the team telling different stories, and her five-step method that starts with what customers would use instead of you. She also covers turning positioning into a sales narrative, keeping it loose at an early-stage company, and the difference between segmentation and personas in B2B sales.
g: B2B product positioning consultant, author of Obviously Awesome, former VP of marketing at several startups

eps.t: Gokul Rajaram on designing your product development process, when and how to hire your first PM, a playbook for hiring leaders, getting ahead in you career, how to get started angel investing, more
eps.s: Drawing on his years at Google, Facebook, Square and DoorDash, Gokul Rajaram talks about career luck and how to pick a company, how simple a startup's product process should be, when to hire a first PM and who should fill the role, a playbook for recruiting executives, why titles should come late, and his founder-first approach to angel investing. Great companies take many paths, he says, but the product must be good enough to grow by word of mouth.
g: Product and business executive at DoorDash, board member at Coinbase and Pinterest, angel investor

eps.t: Why must tech companies innovate, and why believe humanity progresses? Peter Thiel's convictions and faith
eps.ot: 19: 为什么科技公司要创新？为什么相信人类会进步？彼得·蒂尔（Peter Thiel）的信念与信仰
eps.s: Hanyang goes solo on the topic he most wanted to cover before launching the show: the faith of Silicon Valley investor Peter Thiel. Through Thiel's eyes, he tackles two questions. Why do companies have to innovate? And why should people who build technology believe it pushes humanity forward?
g: Host of the LatePost Chat podcast and a writer at LatePost

eps.t: Jackie Bavaro on getting better at product strategy, what exactly is strategy, PM pitfalls to avoid, advancing your career, getting into management, and much more
eps.s: Jackie Bavaro went from Google's new-grad PM program to Asana's first product manager and later its head of product management. She breaks strategy into three parts, shows how a good strategy connects company goals to specific features, and explains when and how PMs should practice it. She also covers asking for a promotion, choosing between management and staying hands-on, early-career mistakes, and her PEARL framework for telling project stories.
g: Asana's first PM and former head of product; author of two books on PM careers

eps.t: Gibson Biddle on his DHM product strategy framework, GEM roadmap prioritization framework, 5 Netflix strategy mini case studies, building a personal board of directors, and much more
eps.s: Former Netflix product VP Gibson Biddle walks through his DHM model for product strategy: delight customers in ways that are hard to copy and improve margins. He shows it in action with real Netflix cases, from testing faster DVD delivery and Netflix Party to auto-cancelling inactive members during the pandemic, an ad tier, and password sharing. He also explains the GEM ranking for aligning executives, building a personal board of directors, and treating your career like a product.
g: Former VP of product at Netflix and Chegg; teaches product strategy and writes the Ask Gib newsletter

eps.t: Why product-led growth is the future | Elena Verna (Amplitude, Miro, Surveymonkey)
eps.s: Growth expert Elena Verna explains how B2B growth is changing: buying power is shifting from procurement to the people who actually use the software. Product-led growth has to be built in order: retention first, then acquisition, then monetization. She also explains why product-led companies sabotage themselves when moving upmarket, why freemium beats time-limited trials, which features belong in the free tier, and how to hire and build a growth team.
g: Growth advisor; former head of growth at SurveyMonkey, interim CMO at Miro, interim growth lead at Amplitude

eps.t: Brandon Chu on building product at Shopify, how writing changed the trajectory of his career, the habits that make you a great PM, pros and cons of being a platform PM, how Shopify got through Covid
eps.s: Shopify product VP Brandon Chu describes how Shopify builds product: set direction once a year, leave the how to teams, and tear up plans when the world changes. When Covid hit, they cut a quarter's forty projects down to three, and after going remote they made in-person meetups extremely easy. He also explains how writing accelerated his career by a decade, how PMs should ration decision energy, what's different about platform work, and why every PM needs a side project.
g: VP of product at Shopify, long in charge of the platform and developer ecosystem; angel investor

eps.t: Build better products with continuous product discovery | Teresa Torres
eps.s: Teresa Torres, author of Continuous Discovery Habits, explains the opportunity solution tree: how to work from a business outcome down to what to build, and how to map user needs and pain points into an opportunity space. She also covers why discovery and delivery should run at the same time, how to automate interview scheduling, why interviews should collect stories rather than ask direct questions, how product trios decide together, and why small samples and assumption tests are enough.
g: Product discovery coach, founder of Product Talk, and author of Continuous Discovery Habits

eps.t: Sanchan Saxena (VP of Product at Coinbase) on the inside story of how Airbnb made it through Covid; what he's learned from Brian Chesky, Brian Armstrong, and Kevin Systrom; much more
eps.s: Sanchan Saxena tells the inside story of how Airbnb went from preparing an IPO to fighting for survival during Covid, and shares product lessons from Kevin Systrom and Brian Chesky: set the intent before you A/B test, and design the ideal experience before worrying about constraints. He also explains Coinbase's single-owner written decision process, who is suited to Web3, why to hire for substance over process, and running a career on small bets.
g: VP of Product at Coinbase; previously led product at Airbnb and ads and shopping at Instagram

eps.t: Merci Grace (ex-Head of Growth at Slack) on PLG, interviewing, storytelling, building a diverse team, hiring salespeople, building a growth team, and much more
eps.s: Former Slack head of growth Merci Grace draws on her game design and venture background to explain how founders should tell their story, how Slack's "tool for work" positioning and a single activation metric drove product-led growth, why onboarding must be designed into the product from day one, and how to tell whether a product can grow on its own and when to hire a first salesperson. She also shares how she hires PMs with work samples and builds growth and diverse teams.
g: Co-founder of Panobi, former head of growth at Slack, co-founder of Women in Product

eps.t: Investor Mengqiu Wang on California, the funding winter, and Lin Daiyu from Dream of the Red Chamber
eps.ot: 和投资人梦秋聊聊加州、投资寒潮和林黛玉
eps.s: Mengqiu Wang, founding partner of Qingliu Capital, starts with graduating into the dot-com crash in 2001 and explains why she joined a tiny, unloved Baidu. She walks through three economic cycles in twenty years and how markets heal after a slump, then covers what really has investors stuck in 2022, how founders should ride out the winter, and which Dream of the Red Chamber character would make the best founder.
g: Founding partner of the VC firm Qingliu Capital; former VP of technology at Baidu

eps.t: Manik Gupta (ex-CPO Uber, Google Maps) on how to build consumer apps, why it's useful to be optimistic about technology, creating inflections in your PM career, the changing CPO role, and more
eps.s: Manik Gupta, former Google Maps product director and Uber CPO, lays out the two repeatable patterns behind his career, why consumer products are harder and slower than people expect, the "company-product fit" question big companies should answer before starting anything, and his five-part consumer capability stack. He also discusses how the CPO role is turning into a GM role, how he decides a PM is ready for promotion, and the product cultures of Google, Uber and Microsoft.
g: Former Uber CPO and Google Maps product director, now corporate VP of consumer at Microsoft

eps.t: Nickey Skarstad (Airbnb, Etsy, Shopify, Duolingo) on translating vision into goals, operationalizing product quality, second-order decisions, brainstorming, influence, and much more
eps.s: Nickey Skarstad went from Etsy forum moderator to product director, then built zero-to-one products at Airbnb Experiences and Duolingo. She explains how to balance growth with a quality metric, how to judge whether a job fits by the energy each meeting gives you, and how to choose between functional and GM org structures. The core is her method for turning vision into quarterly goals, spotting one-way-door decisions, running cross-functional product reviews, and keeping remote teams aligned.
g: Product director at Duolingo; formerly product director at Etsy and product lead for Airbnb Experiences

eps.t: Not going gently into the crypto winter: Yang Li of Orange Book on two years of blockchain
eps.ot: 20: 不温和地走入区块链寒冬：与橙皮书李阳聊聊区块链这两年
eps.s: Yang Li, founder of the crypto media outlet Orange Book, planned to explain blockchain's recent years to outsiders with Hanyang. The recording kept getting delayed and landed right in a new market crash. So they start with this latest winter, then cover DeFi, smart contracts, choosing a blockchain, whether insiders really made money, and how to find useful information amid the noise.
g: Founder of the crypto media outlet Orange Book and writer of Prophet Weekly

eps.t: How to sell your ideas and rise within your company | Casey Winters, Eventbrite
eps.s: Casey Winters, Chief Product Officer at Eventbrite, explains how to brief executives clearly, how to prepare for high-stakes meetings, and how to keep a product feeling simple as features pile up. He also covers winning resources for hard-to-measure work like performance, why operations roles should aim to make themselves unnecessary, where product managers get stuck on the way up, and his two-stage "kindling and fire" view of growth.
g: Chief Product Officer at Eventbrite; formerly led growth product at Pinterest and advised Greylock startups on growth

eps.t: How to unlock your product leadership skills | Ken Norton, Ex-Google
eps.s: Ken Norton built Docs, Calendar and Maps at Google, then became a full-time executive coach. He explains how coaching differs from giving advice, and why senior leaders need to rework the beliefs running in their heads rather than learn another framework. He also covers fear-driven versus curiosity-driven leadership, treating communication as a hard skill, handling impostor feelings, and building teams that dare to aim for 10x.
g: Executive coach for product leaders; spent 14 years leading products at Google and worked at GV

eps.t: How to create a winning product strategy | Melissa Perri
eps.s: Melissa Perri has trained thousands of product managers and led product turnarounds at dozens of companies. She diagnoses the most common disease of scaling companies: strategy that was never written down, prioritized or communicated. She covers when to hire a chief product officer, what a company without strategy looks like, how to link strategy with a two-page document at each level, what makes a good vision, and what product operations should own.
g: Product management consultant and educator; founder of Produx Labs, Harvard Business School lecturer, author of Escaping the Build Trap

eps.t: How to scrappily hire for, measure, and unlock growth | Crystal Widjaja, Gojek and Kumu
eps.s: Crystal Widjaja built the data, risk and growth teams at Gojek from scratch and is now chief product officer at Kumu. She shares Gojek's scrappy growth playbook: fake a feature by hand before writing code, fix the step right before the decision rather than chasing "retention," and learn the physics of your growth before pulling levers. She also gives retention benchmarks, explains why most analytics fail, and describes how to build and hire an early growth team.
g: Chief product officer at Kumu; previously built and led data, risk and growth teams at Gojek

eps.t: How to own your career growth and become a powerful product leader | Deb Liu, Ancestry (ex-Facebook, PayPal)
eps.s: Ancestry CEO Deb Liu starts with the messy integration after eBay bought PayPal and what it taught her: systems and incentives shape behavior more than individuals do. She argues a product manager's real output is communication, and that you should plan a career the way you'd plan a product. She also shares how peer circles work, the hiring changes she made to diversify product teams, and lessons from incubating Facebook Marketplace from scratch.
g: CEO of Ancestry; former Facebook VP of product who led Marketplace, ex-PayPal, cofounder of Women in Product

eps.t: How to launch and grow your product | Ryan Hoover of Product Hunt and Weekend Fund
eps.s: Ryan Hoover founded Product Hunt and now runs the early-stage Weekend Fund. He talks about what to ask yourself before starting a company and before raising money, what a launch is really for, and how to write a launch page. He revisits his regrets from Product Hunt, explains why consumer startups are much harder than B2B, where good ideas come from, why to start narrow, and why momentum feeds on itself in early companies.
g: Founder of Product Hunt and of the early-stage investment firm Weekend Fund

eps.t: The rituals of great teams | Shishir Mehrotra, Coda, YouTube, Microsoft
eps.s: Shishir Mehrotra, co-founder and CEO of Coda and former head of product and engineering at YouTube, explains Coda's two growth loops, its pricing that charges only document makers, and why platform companies can't control the conversation with users. The heart of the episode is the rituals of great teams he collected for his book, how to make rituals stick, his "eigenquestion" method, his PSHE framework for assessing talent, and how he runs reference checks.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Coda; formerly ran product and engineering at YouTube; Spotify board member

eps.t: The art of building legendary brands | Arielle Jackson (Google, Square, First Round Capital)
eps.s: Arielle Jackson launched Gmail at Google, ran product marketing at Square, and is now marketing expert in residence at First Round Capital. She walks through how early-stage companies should pick a name, how to build a brand from three pieces (purpose, positioning and personality), and how a seed-stage startup can land its first press coverage.
g: Marketing expert in residence at First Round Capital; formerly product marketing at Google (Gmail) and Square

eps.t: The nature of product | Marty Cagan, Silicon Valley Product Group
eps.s: Marty Cagan of Silicon Valley Product Group explains why the gap between good and bad product companies is so wide and so persistent: the difference between feature teams and empowered product teams, which risks a product manager owns, and why companies lose their product DNA as they grow. He also covers discovery versus optimization, how to do user research properly, the three channels a PM must never give up, and why scaling by process goes wrong.
g: Founding partner of Silicon Valley Product Group and author of Inspired and Empowered

eps.t: Persuasive communication and managing up | Wes Kao (Maven, altMBA, Section4)
eps.s: Maven cofounder Wes Kao shares a toolkit for persuasive communication: writing and teaching should go deep on the specific how, different content formats leave different room for fluff, and talks and meetings need a state change every few minutes to hold attention. She also explains how to read someone's real interest from their body language, how to calibrate managing up by whether a decision is reversible, why to lead with the conclusion, and how to say no by naming the trade-off.
g: Cofounder of Maven, a platform for cohort-based courses; cofounded altMBA with Seth Godin

eps.t: How to grow a subscription business | Yuriy Timen (Grammarly, Canva, Airtable)
eps.s: Yuriy Timen, former head of growth at Grammarly and now an advisor to Canva, Airtable and others, breaks down whether a subscription product should bet on virality, SEO or paid acquisition. He explains how the 2022 capital pullback changed paid acquisition, attribution and channel choice, offers conversion-rate benchmarks, and says when to focus on a single channel and when to diversify.
g: Growth advisor to Canva, Airtable and others; formerly head of growth and marketing at Grammarly

eps.t: To make electricity, you first need electricity: a chief engineer's story of building dams in China and Africa
eps.ot: 21: 想要发电，要先有电：一个总工在中国和非洲修水电站的故事
eps.s: Power cuts across China put "hydropower plants without water" in the news. Hanyang retells the experience of a chief engineer who built plants in China and Africa (credited as Fengze here, later as Engineer Cao), through two stories: Fengman in Jilin and Kafue Gorge Lower in Zambia. The aim is to show the hidden parts of modern life. Network problems ruled out a live conversation.
g: Chief engineer with a PhD who has built hydropower plants in China and Africa

eps.t: The role of AI in new product development | Ryan J. Salva (VP of Product at GitHub)
eps.s: Ryan J. Salva, VP of Product at GitHub, retraces how GitHub Copilot went from a flood of clone requests that looked like an attack to a research prototype, a technical preview and a paid product. He explains how a large company isolates moonshot projects, how researchers hand their work to product teams, and the ethics, compute and community-trust questions an AI coding assistant raises.
g: VP of Product at GitHub, responsible for productizing and launching Copilot; spent about ten years at Microsoft

eps.t: How to build a powerful marketing machine | Emily Kramer (Asana, Carta, MKT1)
eps.s: Emily Kramer built marketing teams from scratch at Asana and Carta and now runs MKT1, a marketing newsletter and early-stage fund. Using her "fuel and engine" framework, she explains what kind of first marketer a B2B startup should hire and when. She also covers how product and marketing should divide work, how to tell whether a marketing team is making real impact, and how functional experts can angel invest.
g: Founder of MKT1, a marketing newsletter and early-stage fund; formerly led marketing at Asana and Carta

eps.t: When to invest in new acquisition channels | Adam Grenier (Uber, MasterClass)
eps.s: Adam Grenier ran growth marketing at Uber and marketing at MasterClass. He lays out a simple way to decide whether a new channel like TikTok, Clubhouse or influencers is worth trying: check three things for overlap, put half a person on it for a month, and give it at most a quarter. He argues product-led companies need a "growth CMO." He also talks openly about burning out at Uber, telling exhaustion from depression, and what improv taught him.
g: Growth and marketing advisor and investor; formerly marketing VP at MasterClass and growth marketing lead at Uber

eps.t: Building a meaningful career | Jason Shah (Airbnb, Amazon, Microsoft, Alchemy)
eps.s: Jason Shah is a serial founder who built products at Yammer, Amazon and Airbnb and now works at Alchemy, a blockchain infrastructure company. He talks about leading a team through the crypto winter, Amazon's "working backwards" press-release documents, what the best leaders have in common, and how to turn "pushing back on the CEO" into alignment. Later: careers as maps rather than ladders, treating hiring like a business, and why defining the problem is the core skill.
g: Works at blockchain infrastructure company Alchemy; former PM at Airbnb, Amazon and Yammer; founder of do.com

eps.t: Growth tactics, retention strategies, and becoming a better writer | Julian Shapiro (Demand Curve, Hyper, Webflow, TechCrunch)
eps.s: Julian Shapiro founded the growth training company Demand Curve and is a partner at Hyper. He shares two growth ideas: products that bring in new users just by being used, and retention that comes from users building up something they can't take with them. Then he turns to writing: how to create novelty, his formula for writing quality, how to pick topics, and the "creativity faucet" he spotted in several prolific creators.
g: Founder of growth training company Demand Curve, partner at Hyper, former marketing VP at Webflow

eps.t: Customer-led growth | Georgiana Laudi (Forget The Funnel)
eps.s: Georgiana Laudi (Gia) co-founded the SaaS growth consultancy Forget The Funnel and previously led marketing at Unbounce. She walks through her full "customer-led growth" process: research your best customers, pick one job they hire you for, map the journey by value milestones with a KPI at each step, then rewrite messaging and onboarding around it. Using SparkToro as the running example, she explains why funnel thinking is out of date.
g: Co-founder of SaaS growth consultancy Forget The Funnel; former head of marketing at Unbounce

eps.t: Using behavioral science to improve your product | Kristen Berman (Irrational Labs)
eps.s: Kristen Berman, co-founder of the behavioral science consultancy Irrational Labs, explains how to apply behavioral economics to product design: define the behavior you want to change in extreme detail, then remove barriers and add immediate benefits. Using a fintech app, TikTok and One Medical, she shows which intuitive tactics fail, and how team incentives decide whether these techniques help users or exploit them.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Irrational Labs, a consultancy that applies behavioral science to products

eps.t: Wei Cao on Elon Musk, the robot uncanny valley, and Westworld
eps.ot: 和曹巍聊聊马斯克、机器人恐怖谷和《西部世界》
eps.s: With Elon Musk unveiling Tesla's Optimus humanoid robot, BlueRun Ventures partner Wei Cao explains what makes humanoids so hard: walking like a person, controlling force precisely, how much of Tesla's self-driving work carries over, and which jobs actually need a human shape. He also covers the uncanny valley trap, Musk's motives, and why China has a broad opening in robotics.
g: Partner at BlueRun Ventures who has long studied the robotics industry

eps.t: Developing a growth model + marketplace growth strategy | Dan Hockenmaier(Faire, Thumbtack, Reforge)
eps.s: Dan Hockenmaier, head of strategy and analytics at Faire, first explains how to build a growth model, how to use it to allocate resources, and why retention is the biggest lever. He then goes deep on marketplaces: which metrics show one is healthy, how to balance supply and demand, how to expand, and where the marketplace model is heading.
g: Head of strategy and analytics at Faire; early Thumbtack employee; founded the consultancy Basis One

eps.t: Astronauts and robots: a relaxed chat about the deep, romantic world of robots
eps.ot: 宇航员与机器人：漫谈深邃浪漫的ROBOT新知
eps.s: The CEO of a robotics unicorn, who returned to China to start his company in 2016, talks robots: why humanoids are like the Moon landing, how Musk sells near-term work with grand visions, and why home robots are harder than self-driving cars. He compares today's robots to computers in 1980, says hardware founders often get only one shot, and names which entrepreneurs are worth learning from.
g: Tsinghua and TU Munich graduate who returned to China in 2016 to start a robotics company

eps.t: How to build a high-performing growth team | Adam Fishman (Patreon, Lyft, Imperfect Foods)
eps.s: Adam Fishman, Lyft's first growth marketing hire and former head of product and growth at Patreon, covers three things: how to hire and evaluate growth talent with a growth skills model, why onboarding is an underrated growth lever (using Patreon as the example), and how to pick a company when job hunting using his people, mission and financials framework, including doing due diligence on your future team.
g: Growth and product advisor; formerly CPO at Imperfect Foods, head of product and growth at Patreon, and Lyft's first growth marketer

eps.t: How do we find joy? A primer on the video game industry with Zhongqing
eps.ot: 22: 如何获得快乐：与重轻唠唠游戏产业的科普
eps.s: Zhongqing, host of the podcast Bu Zai Chang and a regular on the gaming site Gcores, joins Hanyang's co-host Xu Huan for a primer on video games: a short history for business people, big tech firms' gaming dreams, why games are addictive, esports and game aesthetics. In a bonus segment, the two old-school gamers vent about industry giants and mobile games. The page lists only topics.
g: Host of the podcast Bu Zai Chang and a regular guest on the gaming site Gcores

eps.t: Building better roadmaps | Janna Bastow (Mind the Product, ProdPad)
eps.s: Janna Bastow co-founded the product community Mind the Product and the roadmapping tool ProdPad. She talks about growing a community, running conferences, and learning to speak on stage. Then she explains why she rejects timeline roadmaps, how to use Now/Next/Later, how to handle dates and launches, and how to change product culture inside a big company one small team at a time.
g: Co-founder of the roadmapping tool ProdPad and of the product community Mind the Product

eps.t: Starting up and living abroad: visiting Vietnam, the last untapped Confucian society
eps.ot: 【到全世界创业生活】寻访越南：最后一个待开掘的儒家社会
eps.s: Fan Yang, a former lawyer and investor in Hong Kong and Shanghai who moved to Vietnam in 2021, talks about Vietnam's economic opportunities and limits, its business climate, the gap between north and south, and daily life there, plus what Chinese companies should watch out for. Having missed China's golden decade, he feels he is watching it replay in Vietnam.
g: Former lawyer and investor who has lived in Vietnam since 2021

eps.t: Humanizing product development | Adriel Frederick (Reddit, Lyft, Facebook)
eps.s: Adriel Frederick is VP of Product at Reddit, previously ran pricing and marketplace products at Lyft, and was an early growth PM at Facebook. He explains how incubation teams avoid being rejected by the rest of the company, why diverse teams understand global users faster, what a PM should do amid public controversy, how to split work between people and algorithms, and how Facebook's early growth really worked: relentless focus on a few core actions and on the marginal user.
g: VP of Product at Reddit; formerly Lyft's marketplace and pricing product lead and an early Facebook growth PM

eps.t: How to build trust and grow as a product leader | Fareed Mosavat (Reforge, Slack, Instacart, Pixar)
eps.s: Fareed Mosavat is chief development officer at Reforge, previously ran growth at Slack and Instacart, and started out building effects tools at Pixar. He explains how product managers grow: a loop of doing real work, distilling lessons, and talking about them, plus sponsors who hand you bigger problems. He also covers the jump from individual contributor to manager, and the pros and cons of portfolio careers for senior operators.
g: Chief development officer at Reforge; former growth lead at Slack and Instacart, ex-Pixar engineer

eps.t: The months around Steve Jobs's return to Apple [Big Company Moments S1E1]
eps.ot: 23: 乔布斯回归苹果前后几个月的故事 【大公司的瞬间 S1E1】
eps.s: The first episode of a new series, Big Company Moments. Hanyang goes solo on the few months around Steve Jobs's move from NeXT back to Apple. He skips the well-known ending and focuses on what Jobs actually did in the days he decided to return. The episode page lists only the sources.
g: Host of the LatePost Chat podcast and a writer at LatePost

eps.t: Category creation and brand building | Barbra Gago (Pando, Miro, Greenhouse, Culture Amp)
eps.s: Barbra Gago was Miro's chief marketing officer and earlier ran marketing at Greenhouse and CultureAmp. She covers three things: when to create a new product category, how to do it, and what to do when it doesn't work. She also tells the story of renaming RealtimeBoard to Miro and building values into the brand. Finally, why her new company Pando is building opinionated software to replace performance reviews.
g: Founder of Pando; former CMO of Miro, marketing lead at Greenhouse and CultureAmp

eps.t: Building Substack | Sachin Monga (Substack, Facebook)
eps.s: Sachin Monga leads product at Substack, after years at Facebook working on growth and sharing products and co-founding Cocoon. He explains why Substack bets on direct subscriptions instead of ads, how the product team was built, and how to work alongside a product-minded founder. The highlight is the story of Recommendations, the feature Lenny calls legendary, and how principles shaped it. He closes with his view on the future for writers.
g: Head of product at Substack; co-founded Cocoon (acquired by Substack), ex-Facebook PM

eps.t: Lessons from one of the world’s top executive recruiters | Lauren Ipsen (Daversa Partners, GC)
eps.s: Lauren Ipsen is a veteran executive recruiter, now a talent partner at General Catalyst. She looks at product hiring from three angles: how founders should define and find their first senior product leader, how product people should manage their careers and show up in resumes and interviews, and the mistakes recruiters make. The thread through it all: treat people as people, build relationships early, and play the long game.
g: Talent partner at General Catalyst for consumer and crypto; former executive recruiter at Daversa Partners

eps.t: Meituan's massive expansion, the war with Ele.me, and how a company views talent [Big Company Moments S1E2]
eps.ot: 24: 美团大扩张、饿了么之战与公司的人才观【大公司的瞬间 S1E2】
eps.s: The second episode of Big Company Moments. Drawing on a 2021 LatePost story, "Meituan's Management Test: Hiring 60,000 Is Only the Beginning," and the reporter's notes, Hanyang covers the problems Meituan faced while growing explosively: office space, how it views talent, the war with rival Ele.me as insiders saw it, and company culture.
g: Host of the LatePost Chat podcast and a writer at LatePost

eps.t: How Snyk built a product-led growth juggernaut | Ben Williams (VP of Product at Snyk)
eps.s: Snyk makes security tools for developers. VP of Product Ben Williams walks through how it started in the Node.js community, built growth loops into the product itself, stumbled when early self-serve monetization failed, and then shifted to product-led sales. The second half covers how growth teams are organized, how weekly experiments turn into company-wide learning, where to draw the free/paid line, and how to define activation.
g: VP of Product at Snyk, leading developer journey and growth; formerly head of product and growth at CloudBees

eps.t: How to work through fear, give hard feedback, and doing layoffs with grace | Matt Mochary
eps.s: Matt Mochary coaches CEOs, including the founders of Coinbase and OpenAI. He explains how leaders can spot the bad decisions that fear and anger produce, why smaller teams work better, and how to fire someone or run a layoff with grace. He also shares three levels of making people feel heard, how big companies should structure new-product teams, and how an "energy audit" can reshape your calendar.
g: CEO coach and author of The Great CEO Within; has coached founders at Coinbase, OpenAI, and others

eps.t: Yuxiang Huang on six Southeast Asian countries: politics, killings, and founding fathers
eps.ot: 和黄宇翔聊东南亚6国：政治、杀戮和国父
eps.s: Yuxiang Huang, an editor at the newsmagazine Yazhou Zhoukan, uses politics and conflict as a lens on Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand, Vietnam, and Singapore: how their politics evolved, the key episodes of violence, and their founding fathers. His larger point is how a country's politics shapes its economic potential.
g: Planning editor at the newsmagazine Yazhou Zhoukan (Asia Weekly)

eps.t: An inside look at how the New York Times builds product | Alex Hardiman (CPO, the New York Times)
eps.s: Alex Hardiman is Chief Product Officer at the New York Times. She describes what's different about building product inside a newsroom: from running news products at Facebook after the 2016 election to tearing up the roadmap when COVID hit, from a subscription bundle with journalism at the center to teams with editors embedded, and how the Times absorbed Wordle. She also contrasts how tech platforms and news organizations think about algorithms and impact.
g: Chief Product Officer at the New York Times; formerly led news products at Facebook and was CPO of The Atlantic

eps.t: Betting big to win big: the Tencent empire and Genshin Impact [Big Company Moments S1E3]
eps.ot: 25: 以大博大：腾讯帝国与原神 【大公司的瞬间 S1E3】
eps.s: The third episode of Big Company Moments. Starting from the LatePost story "Tencent Games Missed Genshin Impact," Hanyang looks at how big companies judge a game's worth and how to seize a chance like Genshin when it appears. He also asks: after three breakout opportunities in the past decade, where will the fourth come from?
g: Host of the LatePost Chat podcast and a writer at LatePost

eps.t: Leaving big tech to build the #1 technology newsletter | Gergely Orosz (The Pragmatic Engineer)
eps.s: Gergely Orosz left his job as an engineering manager at Uber and built The Pragmatic Engineer into the top paid technology newsletter on Substack. He explains why he quit big tech and how a blog became a business that out-earns his old salary. Lenny, a full-time writer himself, joins him to discuss the income, daily rhythm, loneliness, and pressure of this life, and what actually determines whether it works.
g: Author of the paid newsletter The Pragmatic Engineer; formerly an engineering manager at Uber and principal engineer at Skyscanner

eps.t: What it takes to become a top 1% PM | Ian McAllister (Uber, Amazon, Airbnb)
eps.s: Ian McAllister spent 12 years at Amazon and has managed over a hundred PMs. He breaks down what separates the best product managers: which skills new PMs should practice first, what senior PMs still need to add, and why trust is the currency of product leaders. He also shares the operating habits he learned from Jeff Bezos and Jeff Wilke, and the most common way Amazon's working-backwards method gets misused.
g: Senior director at Uber; created Amazon Smile and led Alexa's international expansion; previously at Airbnb

eps.t: Silicon Valley's mass layoffs under a microscope: doing the real math
eps.ot: 显微镜下的硅谷大裁员：一笔笔现实经济账
eps.s: On the night Meta's mass layoff was finalized, Meta product manager Neal Zhang walks through the week and does the math on severance pay. He also compares workplaces, pay, and living costs in China and the U.S., and talks about the position of Chinese professionals in Silicon Valley.
g: Meta product manager who lived through Meta's 2022 mass layoff

eps.t: Jing Tan on freezing her eggs in Silicon Valley and traveling the world to explore Web3
eps.ot: 和谈婧聊：硅谷冻卵历险记和Web3环球旅行
eps.s: Investor Jing Tan shares two adventures. Freezing her eggs in Silicon Valley in 2019 unexpectedly changed how she sees marriage. And after six months traveling the world to visit Web3 projects, blockchain-based efforts to move money and assets directly online, she shares her views on globalization, what Web3 really is, and where to invest.
g: Investor who visited more than ten places worldwide in six months to study Web3

eps.t: How to be the best coach to product people | Petra Wille (Strong Product People)
eps.s: Product leadership coach Petra Wille talks to the managers who manage product managers. She lays out five steps for coaching your reports, how to define what a good PM looks like on your team, and why storytelling and public speaking decide whether a PM gets promoted. She closes on internal product communities: why they are the cheapest, highest-return way to grow people, and how to run one well.
g: Independent product leadership coach, author of Strong Product People, organizer of a Hamburg product conference

eps.t: The ultimate guide to SEO | Ethan Smith (Graphite)
eps.s: Graphite founder Ethan Smith walks through SEO from the ground up: first check whether the market is big enough and your site has enough standing, then plan pages around topics rather than single keywords, and get growth from database-generated pages and human-written articles. He also explains why SEO is slow, why it keeps getting cut from roadmaps, and where AI-written content helps or hurts.
g: Founder of Graphite, an SEO and content strategy firm; led growth for Thumbtack and MasterClass

eps.t: How to hit revenue targets in a recession | Sahil Mansuri (Bravado)
eps.s: Sahil Mansuri, founder of the sales community Bravado, has live quota data from hundreds of thousands of salespeople. He uses it to explain how founders should adjust in a downturn: plan conservatively with checkpoints, redesign commission plans that only reward new deals, move your best sellers to protect existing customers, and close through warm introductions and genuinely useful insights. He also tells how one cold email landed Facebook, and how he launched a new business in a bad market.
g: Founder and CEO of Bravado, a B2B sales community of about 300,000 members; formerly ran enterprise sales at Glassdoor

eps.t: The art and science of pricing | Madhavan Ramanujam (Monetizing Innovation, Simon-Kucher)
eps.s: Pricing expert Madhavan Ramanujam explains how to price scientifically: test what people will pay before you build the product, and let that decide the roadmap. He covers how to interview customers about willingness to pay, how to segment by needs, three pricing strategies, the three roles features play in a bundle, subscription versus usage-based billing, behavioral tricks like decoy tiers, and how to price in a downturn.
g: Senior partner at pricing consultancy Simon-Kucher and co-author of Monetizing Innovation

eps.t: How Notion leveraged community to build a $10B business | Camille Ricketts
eps.s: Camille Ricketts was Notion's first marketer and previously started First Round Review. She breaks down how Notion used community to become visible everywhere, then rode that into the enterprise market. The second half covers content marketing, why you need to find "content-market fit" first, and why press coverage is still worth pursuing when anyone can publish directly.
g: Notion's first marketing hire and former head of marketing; previously led content and marketing at First Round Capital

eps.t: We're too obsessed with creating: Xia Zhao and Gcores' boundless imagination
eps.ot: 26: 我们太沉迷创作了：赵夏与机核的无疆想象
eps.s: Xia Zhao, founder of the gaming media company Gcores, has just closed a new funding round. Instead of games and subculture, Hanyang and Honghao talk business: why Gcores needed to reintroduce itself, how content, expos and retail grew, how it picks topics and keeps staff, when it decided to raise money, and how to make more good content. The page lists only the questions.
g: Founder of Gcores, a Chinese media company covering games and subculture

eps.t: Founder-led sales | Pete Kazanjy (Founding Sales, Atrium)
eps.s: Pete Kazanjy, author of Founding Sales and founder of Atrium, explains why B2B founders have to sell themselves first, when to hire the first salespeople, who to hire, and how to use leading indicators to tell whether the sales process and new reps are working. His core stance: sales isn't talent, it's a set of behaviors you can iterate on like software.
g: Founder and CEO of Atrium, author of Founding Sales, and founder of the Modern Sales Pros community

eps.t: 97.2 million medicine boxes and no ibuprofen to buy: a printing plant's pandemic crunch [Bonus episode]
eps.ot: 27: 9720 万个药盒与买不到的布洛芬：一家印刷厂在疫情下的挑战【临时加更】
eps.s: As fever medicine ran short across China in late 2022, Hanyang called up his friend Hongjian, who works at a medicine-box printing plant in Changchun. Workers ran 24-hour shifts and machines ran flat out, yet supply still fell short. They discuss why printing medicine boxes is its own business, whether drugmakers saw the surge coming, when it might ease, and why drugmakers cluster in China's northeast.
g: Works at a medicine-box printing plant in Changchun; a friend of Hanyang

eps.t: Launching and growing a podcast | Chris Hutchins (All the Hacks, Wealthfront, Google)
eps.s: Chris Hutchins hosts the podcast All the Hacks and previously led new product strategy at Wealthfront. He first looks back on what worked and what didn't when he pushed a big bet, autopilot money management, inside the company. Then he lays out how to start a podcast from scratch: whether to do it at all, how to pick topics, how to launch onto the charts, which metrics matter, and how to find listeners when no algorithm will do it for you.
g: Host of the podcast All the Hacks; formerly head of new product strategy at Wealthfront and an investor at Google Ventures

eps.t: I quit VC: Minghao Zhuang quietly shares what investing taught him
eps.ot: 28: 我不做 VC 了：庄明浩低调分享做投资的感悟
eps.s: Minghao Zhuang, a former vice president at Matrix Partners China and a popular writer on Zhihu, talks with Hanyang after leaving venture capital. Topics include what early-stage investing is, whether VC pays, how yuan and dollar funds have changed, what "investing is betting on people" means, why he quit, and whether VC suits young people as a first job. The page lists only the questions.
g: Ex-Matrix Partners China VP, now strategy head at an internet company, popular Zhihu writer on startups

eps.t: Bestselling author Sebastian Mallaby on The Power Law: the origins, secrets, and big personalities of Silicon Valley venture capital
eps.ot: 和畅销书作家马拉比聊《The Power Law》：硅谷风投的起源、秘密和大人物肖像
eps.s: British writer Sebastian Mallaby draws on his book The Power Law to explain Silicon Valley venture capital: why the power law is the key to the business, and how VC was born from an act of rebellion and reshaped the Valley's culture. He also explains why Sequoia thrived while Kleiner Perkins faded, the risks of giant checks, what top VCs share, and why weak ties matter.
g: British journalist and author of The Power Law, a history of venture capital

eps.t: Two and a half stories [Year-end special]
eps.ot: 29: 两个半故事【年终特别节目】
eps.s: LatePost Chat's 2022 year-end special tells "two and a half stories," threaded through a snake, a person and the internet, and ends by wishing listeners a happy new year. No speaker is listed, but it is likely Hanyang. The page says only that the episode can't be summarized, since it's all in the stories, and adds further reading, including books by Japanese thinker Yoshimi Takeuchi.
g: Host of the LatePost Chat podcast and a writer at LatePost

eps.t: Bonus episode in English: an oral history of Silicon Valley venture capital
eps.ot: 加更英文原声版：口述一部硅谷风投史
eps.s: The extended English-language version of Sebastian Mallaby's interview from episode 8, in which he narrates a history of Silicon Valley venture capital. These notes cover what episode 8 didn't: why so many VC legends came from the margins, the inventions that shaped the industry, how VC lowers the cost of risk-taking, Sequoia's handoffs and teamwork, China's path, and his view of downturns.
g: British journalist and author of The Power Law, a history of venture capital

eps.t: A California native on the Silicon Valley spirit and work culture: You can be totally weird!
eps.ot: 加州土著谈硅谷精神与职场：You can be totally weird!
eps.s: Huiping Xiao, who has lived in California for 35 years, gives an insider's view of Silicon Valley work culture and career planning, why Chinese founders often struggle to raise money in the U.S., and how Americans see Chinese companies expanding abroad. Her big message: in Silicon Valley, you can be totally weird.
g: California native who has worked at IBM, Box, Twitch, and an investment firm

eps.t: Leveraging mentors to uplevel your career | Jules Walter (YouTube, Slack)
eps.s: Jules Walter leads product at YouTube and was Slack's first growth PM. He explains which skills product managers should practice at each career stage, how to learn a new skill fast by working backward from a provable result, how to get honest feedback, and how to find your real strengths. In the second half he breaks down how to approach a mentor with the smallest possible ask and turn it into a lasting relationship.
g: Product lead at YouTube; Slack's first growth PM; co-founder of Black PMs and CodePath

eps.t: An inside look at how Figma builds product | Yuhki Yamashita (CPO of Figma)
eps.s: Figma's chief product officer Yuhki Yamashita explains how Figma builds product. He argues a product manager's main job is storytelling and owning the "why," that staying close to users must not mean being steered by a loud few, and that quality comes from the whole company using its own product daily. He also admits the team still hasn't cracked goal-setting, and describes what he looks for when hiring PMs. The twist: Figma's famous product-led growth is really community-led.
g: Chief product officer at Figma; previously led product and design at Uber

eps.t: Singapore's gold rushes and its business and political climate
eps.ot: 新加坡的淘金热和政商环境
eps.s: Neil Han, a serial entrepreneur who has lived in Singapore for 16 years, describes the rise and fall of the city's gold rushes, including the Web3 boom. He also shares local insight into how the government backs startups, how it manages officials, and how Temasek, its state investment company, operates.
g: Peking University graduate and serial entrepreneur who has lived in Singapore for 16 years

eps.t: How to price your product | Naomi Ionita (Menlo Ventures)
eps.s: Naomi Ionita, a partner at Menlo Ventures who previously ran growth at Evernote and Invoice2go, walks through pricing from start to finish: the three most common monetization mistakes startups make, where to draw the line between free and paid, how to tie price to value and build tiers, and how to research and test prices. She closes with her investing theme, the "modern growth stack": new software that saves growth teams from building internal tools.
g: Partner at Menlo Ventures; formerly head of growth product at Evernote and VP of growth at Invoice2go

eps.t: What differentiates the highest-performing product teams | John Cutler (The Beautiful Mess)
eps.s: John Cutler, formerly product evangelist at the analytics company Amplitude, draws on four years with hundreds of product teams. He explains what high-performing teams share and how they differ, whether people or systems matter more, and how big companies outside Silicon Valley should read the product advice online. Later he covers how to keep learning in a constrained company, how to break "product sense" into teachable skills, and what measurement is really for.
g: Former product evangelist at Amplitude, author of The Beautiful Mess newsletter, about to join Toast

eps.t: Conflicts of nation and race still exist in blockchain: Mable on topics the industry usually avoids
eps.ot: 30: 区块链里国家和种族的矛盾依然存在：与 Mable 唠唠一般这行不聊的话题
eps.s: Mable, a prominent Chinese figure in the blockchain industry, skips the basics with Hanyang to discuss what insiders rarely talk about: national and racial conflicts persist in a supposedly borderless blockchain world, and tokens meant to help people cooperate are used mostly to speculate. She also shares insider perspectives and the industry figures she respects. The page lists only the questions.
g: Chinese blockchain industry insider and host of the podcasts HODLong and Paipaizuo

eps.t: Yuxiang Huang on five more Southeast Asian countries: how small states pick a side or hedge
eps.ot: 和黄宇翔聊东南亚另5国：小国的扈从和对冲
eps.s: A sequel to episode 5. Yuxiang Huang moves outward through Myanmar, Laos, Cambodia, Brunei, and East Timor, using two strategies, siding with one big power or hedging among several, to explain how small countries survive great-power rivalry.
g: Planning editor at the newsmagazine Yazhou Zhoukan (Asia Weekly)

eps.t: How to build your product strategy stack | Ravi Mehta (Tinder, Facebook, Tripadvisor, Outpace)
eps.s: Ravi Mehta, former Chief Product Officer at Tinder and founder of Outpace, starts with how building product differs between big companies and startups. He then walks through his five-layer "product strategy stack," explains why goals should come after the roadmap, and how to pick goals based on what a team actually understands. The second half covers his twelve-skill framework for product managers, using it for feedback that compounds, and how new managers should practice "selective micromanagement."
g: Co-founder and CEO of Outpace, former Chief Product Officer at Tinder, ex-Facebook and Tripadvisor product leader

eps.t: A short history of cruise ships: searching for a utopia at sea
eps.ot: 邮轮小史，去寻找海面上的乌托邦
eps.s: Jianbin, who has been aboard more than 100 cruise ships, covers a short history of cruising, the feuds between the big cruise groups, how ships are classified and judged, and the sights he has seen on board and in Antarctica.
g: Cruise industry veteran who has boarded over 100 ships in a decade-plus

eps.t: China is basically at alien-tech level in hydropower: catching up with Engineer Cao, back from Africa
eps.ot: 31: 中国在水电站方面基本上处于天顶星级别存在：和非洲回来的曹工唠唠
eps.s: A Spring Festival special. In episode 21, network trouble meant Hanyang could only retell Engineer Cao's story. Now Cao is home on leave from Tanzania, and they finally talk face to face about hydropower, how good China is at it, the difficulties of projects in Africa, "debt traps" and spreading technology, and why Africa shouldn't be lumped together. The page lists only the questions.
g: Hydropower chief engineer with a PhD, has built plants in China and Africa, lately in Tanzania

eps.t: Is ChatGPT A Step Toward Human-Level AI? — With Yann LeCun
eps.s: As ChatGPT took off, Yann LeCun poured cold water on it: well engineered, but not new science and not a big step toward human-level AI. He uses a falling sheet of paper to show that text-only models don't understand the physical world, lays out his alternative of world models that predict and plan, and ends on machine emotions, AI art and copyright.
g: Meta's chief AI scientist, NYU professor and deep learning pioneer

eps.t: An inside look at Mixpanel’s product journey | Vijay Iyengar
eps.s: Vijay Iyengar, head of product at Mixpanel, looks back on how the company expanded into several products and then retreated to a single analytics product: why it cut messaging and data infrastructure, how it rebuilt the roadmap around reasons customers left, and how design then reshaped the product's architecture. He also covers how Mixpanel plans, prioritizes and estimates work, how engineers get raw customer feedback directly, and why event tracking belongs on the server side.
g: Head of product at Mixpanel, previously an engineering manager there and an engineer at Uber

eps.t: Lessons from Airtable’s unconventional growth strategy | Zoelle Egner
eps.s: Zoelle Egner, an early Airtable employee, starts with three organizing lessons from VaccinateCA, the volunteer effort she joined during the pandemic. She then breaks down how Airtable punched above its weight: building trust through details and billboards, cultivating internal champions at scale, and treating customer success as marketing. She is blunt about which marketing spend is mostly wasted, including sponsorships, category creation and PR for its own sake, and what templates and launches are really for.
g: Airtable's 11th employee and former head of marketing and customer success, now leading marketing and growth at Block Party

eps.t: Hong Kong's language policy, its ambiguity, and the myths facing its young people
eps.ot: 香港的语言政策、暧昧和青年迷思
eps.s: Hong Konger Yuxiang Huang starts from the city's "two written, three spoken languages" policy and compares it with Singapore's language reforms. He talks about Hong Kong's mix and ambiguity, the myths around its economic repositioning, and the disillusionment of its young people, whose top exam scorers no longer pick finance or law.
g: Hong Kong-born features editor at the magazine Yazhou Zhoukan (Asiaweek)

eps.t: How to foster innovation and big thinking | Eeke de Milliano (Retool, Stripe)
eps.s: Eeke de Milliano, head of product at Retool and an early product manager at Stripe, explains why Stripe kept making good decisions, why teams struggle to think big and how to fix it, and how Retool incubated three new products in a year. She also covers the cost of process and "minimum viable process," the three documents every level of a company needs, a few mental models for building product, and how to assemble a complementary PM team.
g: Head of product at Retool, previously an early product manager at Stripe

eps.t: This is "No Priors"
eps.s: A one-minute trailer: hosts Sarah Guo and Elad Gil introduce themselves and the show. Each week they sit down with leading AI engineers, researchers and founders to talk about where the technology really is, what it means for business, and where it's heading. They also tease their first guest, Noam Brown.
g: Co-hosts of No Priors; both invest in AI companies

eps.t: The bot Cicero can collaborate, scheme and build trust with humans. What does this mean for the next frontier of AI? With Noam Brown, Research Scientist at Meta
eps.s: Noam Brown, a research scientist at Meta's FAIR lab, traces his path from poker-playing AI to Cicero, an AI that plays the negotiation game Diplomacy. His key finding: letting a model search and plan at test time beat simply scaling up training. He explains how Cicero negotiated with people without being spotted, and discusses scaling costs, sample efficiency and general reasoning as the next frontier.
g: Research scientist at Meta FAIR; built poker-playing AIs and the Diplomacy AI Cicero

eps.t: AI and product management | Marily Nika (Meta, Google)
eps.s: Shortly after ChatGPT took off, Marily Nika, a product lead at Meta who teaches a course on AI product management, discusses how product managers should approach AI. She argues every PM will soon be an AI PM, but warns against doing AI for its own sake. She covers when not to train a model, how much data you really need, how ChatGPT can help PMs work, how non-technical people can get started, and the particular challenges of being an AI PM.
g: Product lead for avatars and identity at Meta, former Google PM, teaches AI product management

eps.t: Leading with empathy | Keith Yandell (DoorDash, Uber)
eps.s: Keith Yandell has led legal, HR, marketing, support and business development at DoorDash. He explains how DoorDash turns its customer-first culture into actual rules, how a generalist without the specialist background can lead expert teams, and his management habits: a "how to work with me" doc, promising to help reports find their next job, using empathy to unblock decisions, and asking for feedback. He also covers why adversity helps companies, fundraising trade-offs, and how BD should work with product.
g: Head of business and corporate development at DoorDash; former chief legal officer who also ran HR, marketing and support; ex-Uber litigation lead

eps.t: What does AI-powered content creation look like? with Runway ML's Cristobal Valenzuela
eps.s: Cristóbal Valenzuela, co-founder and CEO of Runway, describes his path from business and design into media art, and how Runway went from a platform hosting other people's models to a creative tools company building its own. He covers human-in-the-loop product design, why film and TV professionals find value in it, and why AI art is at its "paint tube moment."
g: Co-founder and CEO of Runway, which makes AI video and creative tools

eps.t: Mastering onboarding | Lauryn Isford (Head of Growth at Airtable)
eps.s: Lauryn Isford, head of growth at Airtable, uses the story of Airtable's onboarding redesign, which lifted activation by about 20%, to explain how to design onboarding, segment users, define and break down an activation metric, and when to change a north star. She also argues you don't need to A/B test everything, makes the case for "reverse trial" pricing, and describes organizing a product-led growth team around a join, evaluate, upgrade, expand funnel.
g: Head of growth at Airtable; previously led product growth at Facebook

eps.t: Go to America and build your startup there
eps.ot: 到美利坚去创业吧
eps.s: Three Chinese women who moved to the U.S. at different stages of life, and now help foreign companies enter the American market, talk about "globalization 3.0" and why even startups can target the U.S. from day one. The best part is their list of traps Chinese founders fall into when America is their first overseas market, from copying habits that work at home to underestimating storytelling and cultural details.
g: A Chinese professional in the U.S. who helps foreign companies enter the American market
Chinese professional in the U.S. who has visited 100+ countries and helps foreign firms enter America

eps.t: Understanding the role of product ops | Christine Itwaru (Pendo)
eps.s: Christine Itwaru moved from product management into product operations and now leads it at Pendo. She explains what product ops actually is, why it took off around 2019, what the job involves, and how it divides work with product managers and product marketing. She answers the charge that ops roles signal inefficiency, tells how a bad launch led Pendo to create product ops, and offers advice for people considering the switch and companies building a team.
g: Head of product operations at Pendo; previously a product director there

eps.t: How can we make sure that everyone has access to AI? Can small models outperform large models? With Stability AI's Emad Mostaque
eps.s: Stability AI founder Emad Mostaque traces his path from hedge funds, to researching treatments for his autistic son, to building an open-source AI company. He explains why base models should be open, why data quality beats sheer parameter count, how selling to nations and big companies works, and how emerging markets could leapfrog in education and health. He also proposes registering large models and labeling AI in ads.
g: Founder and CEO of Stability AI, the company behind Stable Diffusion

eps.t: Trends 2023: Where did the internet managers who made their money and vanished go?
eps.ot: 【趋势2023】那些挣到钱、消失的互联网中高层去哪了
eps.s: Kelin (Colin) Li, a former Baidu VP who also ran Midea's president's office, explains why so many internet managers are leaving and where they go. He revisits four good moments to join the industry over 20 years, and uses SHEIN and Midea to show internet thinking reaching traditional industries and founders choosing successors. His boldest call: now, while people are still doubtful, may be a fresh chance to get on board.
g: Former Baidu vice president and Midea president's office director; now CEO of Aibo Xingchen

eps.t: 10 lessons on bootstrapping a $200m business | Patrick Campbell (ProfitWell)
eps.s: Patrick Campbell bootstrapped ProfitWell, a subscription analytics company, to a sale of more than $200 million without raising venture money. He runs through ten topics: team and values, bootstrapping versus fundraising, pricing, retention, release tempo, first-principles thinking, customer research, competitive intelligence, in-person meetings, and the middle of the funnel. He leans on cross-company data his firm collected, speaks bluntly, and often contradicts conventional wisdom.
g: Founder and CEO of ProfitWell, sold for more than $200 million without raising funding

eps.t: Founder Stories: What's behind the largest commercial autonomous system on earth? With Zipline's Keller Rinaudo Cliffton
eps.s: Keller Rinaudo Cliffton, co-founder and CEO of Zipline, explains how the company went from toy robots to delivering medical supplies by drone, starting with blood in Rwanda. He reflects on the full-stack complexity and early naivety, describes its acoustic detect-and-avoid system, and argues that hardware and infrastructure companies are underrated, and that serving billions takes a sustainable business, not charity.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Zipline, which delivers medical supplies by drone

eps.t: An inside look at how CNN builds product | Upasna Gautam
eps.s: Upasna Gautam is the product manager behind the publishing platform that CNN's journalists and editors use every day. She explains how to build product when breaking news can interrupt anything: working with editors who may be pulled away at any moment, four standing touchpoints for gathering requests, and breaking-news rehearsals that stress-test the platform. A longtime meditation teacher, she also talks about calm, listening, and where product management in journalism stands today.
g: Product manager for CNN Digital's publishing platform, News Product Alliance member, and meditation teacher

eps.t: Why the Future of Machine Learning is Open Source with Huggingface's Clem Delangue
eps.s: Clem Delangue, co-founder and CEO of Hugging Face, explains how the company pivoted from a companion chatbot to the open-source hub where developers share machine learning models. He argues open and closed models will coexist and specialized models each have their place. His key point: the fast loop from research to production and back is what drives ML progress. He also explains Hugging Face's freemium business model.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Hugging Face, the open-source hub for AI models

eps.t: Behind the scenes of Calendly's rapid growth | Annie Pearl (CPO)
eps.s: Annie Pearl, Chief Product Officer at Calendly, explains how she broke into product from a non-technical background and how Calendly builds product: narrowing the target customer, using the Playing to Win framework for strategy, shifting resources across three horizons year by year, and committing only to dates the team can control. She also traces Calendly's first users and viral loop, and what has to change when a product-led company adds a sales team.
g: Chief Product Officer at Calendly; formerly CPO at Glassdoor and a product manager at Box

eps.t: Lessons from working with 600+ YC startups | Gustaf Alströmer (Y Combinator, Airbnb)
eps.s: Y Combinator partner Gustaf Alströmer, a founding member of Airbnb's growth team, draws on advising more than 600 startups to explain why startups really fail, how to get over the fear of rejection and talk to customers, why you need a technical co-founder, what successful founders have in common, and how YC office hours work. The second half turns to climate tech: why it is now a huge business opportunity, and the companies he is excited about.
g: Partner at Y Combinator; previously founding lead of Airbnb's growth team

eps.t: How AI can make drug discovery fail less, with Daphne Koller from Insitro
eps.s: Daphne Koller, founder and CEO of insitro, traces her path from Stanford to Coursera and Calico to founding insitro. She explains why about 95% of drug programs fail, and how human genetics and stem cell experiments can generate the data machine learning needs. She also covers patient selection, the limits set by regulators and by biology itself, and building a team culture across computing and biology.
g: Founder and CEO of AI drug discovery company insitro; Coursera co-founder

eps.t: Trends 2023: Will sluggish Hong Kong stocks recover? Plus the family offices and worries of the rich
eps.ot: 【趋势2023】沉闷的港股会好吗、富豪的家办与苦恼
eps.s: Na Tian of Harvest International, a longtime Hong Kong resident, draws on the Hang Seng Index swings she has lived through to explain why Hong Kong stocks move with money flows, and predicts 2023 will mostly trade in a range. She traces the eras of Hong Kong capital, then explains the boom and the mess in family offices, and how trusts plus insurance can shield wealth and pass down values.
g: Deputy GM of Harvest International Securities and GM of its family office business

eps.t: Lessons from scaling Stripe | Claire Hughes Johnson (ex-COO of Stripe)
eps.s: Former Stripe COO Claire Hughes Johnson, drawing on her book Scaling People, explains how to build the company once you've found product-market fit: foundational documents, operating systems and cadence. She shares her personal operating principles, including self-awareness, saying the unsaid, and telling management apart from leadership. She closes with when a company needs a COO, how to judge whether one is working out, and practical habits for meetings and decisions.
g: Former COO of Stripe, former Google vice president, author of Scaling People

eps.t: Career frameworks, A/B testing, onboarding tips, selling to engineers | Laura Schaffer (Amplitude)
eps.s: Laura Schaffer has just taken over growth at Amplitude after running growth at Twilio. She explains how being "the person who knows the customer best" opened new roles for her, and shares counterintuitive lessons from Twilio: adding questions to sign-up raised conversion, and hiding the scary step inside something familiar got users to keep going. She also covers why most growth ideas fail, when to relax 95% confidence, how to start product-led growth, and why developers are such unusual buyers.
g: Head of growth at Amplitude; previously led growth at Twilio and product and growth at Rapid

eps.t: What is the role of academia in modern AI research? With Stanford Professor Dr. Percy Liang
eps.s: Stanford professor Percy Liang explains why in-context learning in GPT-3 changed the field, what academia should do when industry has the compute, and why foundation models are becoming less open. He describes the HELM benchmark, Together's distributed compute and BioMedLM, and discusses transparency in governance and how his views on AGI have shifted.
g: Stanford professor; director of the Center for Research on Foundation Models (CRFM)

eps.t: Hot takes and techno-optimism from tech's top power couple | Sriram and Aarthi
eps.s: Sriram Krishnan, a partner at a16z, and serial founder Aarthi Ramamurthy are married. Starting from the night they got Elon Musk onto Clubhouse, they talk techno-optimism, how to build a network and a personal brand, how to run a community, impostor syndrome, and products each of them got wrong. Sriram also shares how Mark Zuckerberg runs executive reviews, and closes with a takedown of the Jobs-to-be-Done framework.
g: Partner at a16z; former product leader at Twitter, Meta and Microsoft; co-host of The Good Time Show
