Serial founder and YC alum; former product leader at Clubhouse, Facebook and Netflix; co-host of The Good Time Show

eps.t: An oral business history: from life in America to Google losing round one to OpenAI
eps.ot: 商业口述史：从美国往事，到Google输掉OpenAI第一局
eps.s: Huainan Wang, Google's former CMO for Asia, tells his story from Tsinghua, Columbia, McKinsey and P&G to Yahoo and Google. He explains why Yahoo "had no soul," how Google approaches acquisitions, and why Google fell behind in the first round set off by ChatGPT. He also discusses Meta's organizational problems and argues this AI revolution is at least as big as the internet.
g: Former Google CMO for Asia, now a partner at MiraclePlus, Qi Lu's startup accelerator

eps.t: The Silicon Valley Bank crisis isn't over: three ways the risk could spread
eps.ot: 硅谷银行危机未结束：未来风险传导的3个可能
eps.s: A few days after Silicon Valley Bank collapsed, Huainan Wang walks through why the bank run happened, why the Fed chose to protect depositors but not shareholders, and what it all means for China's startup and venture world. He also warns that the risk could keep spreading.
g: Former Google CMO for Asia, now a partner at MiraclePlus, Qi Lu's startup accelerator

eps.t: The ultimate guide to OKRs | Christina Wodtke (Stanford)
eps.s: Stanford lecturer and "Radical Focus" author Christina Wodtke walks through OKRs end to end: what they can and can't do, how to get from mission down to this quarter's goals and this week's actions, how to write objectives and key results, how to run the weekly rhythm, and where to look when OKRs stop working. She also explains why stories and sketches work so well, and argues that PMs serve the business first and that young PMs lack product sense.
g: Stanford lecturer and author of "Radical Focus"; former product leader at LinkedIn, MySpace, Zynga and Yahoo

eps.t: What is the future of search? With Neeva's Sridhar Ramaswamy
eps.s: Neeva co-founder and CEO Sridhar Ramaswamy explains how large language models push search from a list of links to direct answers, and runs numbers suggesting those answers may cost more than search earns. He also lays out how Microsoft and Google fight over search traffic, and why user habits, ad models and publishers all face hard problems once search gives answers.
g: Co-founder and CEO of the search engine Neeva, former Google executive

eps.t: The industry most afraid of customer visits: a close look at chips with Tan Sanquan
eps.ot: 32: 最怕客户来参观的行业：和谈三圈仔细谈谈芯片
eps.s: Tan Sanquan, an engineer just back from a major German auto-chip maker and a Bilibili science creator, talks with hosts Manqi and Hanyang about why Chinese carmakers now design their own chips. They cover the shifting division of labor, auto safety standards, car versus phone chips, ultra-clean fabs and the cost. Notes are based on the episode description, so his reasoning is only sketched.
g: Bilibili science creator; engineer just back from a major German auto-chip maker

eps.t: Competing with giants: An inside look at how The Browser Company builds product | Josh Miller (CEO)
eps.s: Josh Miller is co-founder and CEO of The Browser Company, maker of the Arc browser. He explains why they design for how users feel rather than for metrics, how their values grew out of the team itself, why they treat the team as a product, and experiments like building in public, a membership team, a storytelling team, and having no PM department. He also explains why experience decides winners in browsers, and the long-term vision of an "internet computer."
g: Co-founder and CEO of The Browser Company (Arc); former Facebook PM and Thrive Capital investor

eps.t: A former reporter for The Information lands in Brazil: her Latin American business travelogue
eps.ot: The Information前记者空降巴西，她的拉美商业游记
eps.s: Yunan, a former reporter for the U.S. tech outlet The Information, spent a stretch living in Brazil. In a relaxed chat she covers Brazil's food delivery and ride-hailing, its startup and investment scene, what Chinese companies are doing there, and the politics, economies and national character of Brazil and Argentina.
g: Former reporter at the U.S. tech outlet The Information, now living in Brazil

eps.t: Navigating comms and PR | Lulu Cheng Meservey (Substack, Activision Blizzard)
eps.s: Lulu Cheng Meservey is chief communications officer at Activision Blizzard and formerly led comms at Substack. She lays out how a startup gets an idea to spread: say it in a way people want to repeat, attach your message to what the audience already cares about, move outward in concentric circles, concentrate limited firepower on a few people using a "pressure formula," and have founders speak directly to the public in their own voice.
g: EVP and chief communications officer at Activision Blizzard; former head of comms at Substack; writes the newsletter Flack

eps.t: How do we go from search engines to answer engines? With Perplexity AI's Aravind Srinivas and Denis Yarats
eps.s: Perplexity co-founders Aravind Srinivas (CEO) and Denis Yarats (CTO) trace their winding path from visual search to an "answer engine." They cover the rule that every sentence needs a citation, the errors that creep in when blending many sources, a lightweight form of reinforcement learning, hiring and focus, and what answer engines mean for Google's ad model and for publishers.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Perplexity, an AI answer engine
Co-founder and CTO of Perplexity

eps.t: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman on GPT-4 & the A.I. Arms Race
eps.s: Days after GPT-4's launch, Sam Altman talks with Kara Swisher about OpenAI's ties to Microsoft, its capped-profit structure, the race with rivals and how AI should be regulated. The striking part is his double view: he still thinks superhuman AI may be humanity's biggest threat, yet insists on releasing models step by step, because society can only adapt through real use.
g: CEO of OpenAI, days after launching GPT-4

eps.t: An Interview with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang About AI's iPhone Moment
eps.s: Right after Nvidia's GTC conference, Jensen Huang tells Ben Thompson why ChatGPT woke up the whole industry. He covers LLMs as a new computing platform, surging demand for both training and inference, the slowed-down chips sold in China, and why DGX Cloud is not a bid to become a fifth cloud. His boldest call: Moore's law is fading, yet AI can get another million times faster in ten years.
g: Nvidia co-founder and CEO, just after launching DGX Cloud and new inference platforms

eps.t: Sam Altman: OpenAI CEO on GPT-4, ChatGPT, and the Future of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #367
eps.s: Shortly after GPT-4 launched, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman spent over two hours with Lex Fridman on why ChatGPT took off, how GPT-4 was built from many small gains, how to handle bias and safety, OpenAI's odd capped-profit structure, and what AI means for jobs. The most striking parts: he calls GPT-4 definitely not AGI, and a sudden takeoff is what he fears most.
g: Co-founder and CEO of OpenAI, just after launching GPT-4

eps.t: Taxi mafias, cash vaults & 100% MoM growth: The story of SEA's biggest startup | Kevin Aluwi (Gojek)
eps.s: Kevin Aluwi, co-founder and former CEO of Gojek, tells how a company that began with motorbike taxis in Indonesia grew to roughly 3 billion orders a year while having far less money than its rivals. The answer: brand, a willingness to do hard things, and a lot of hands-on operations. He also pours cold water on the "super app" idea and shares lessons on building outside Silicon Valley and on who should make decisions.
g: Co-founder and former CEO of Gojek, Indonesia's biggest ride-hailing and delivery company

eps.t: Humans are imprecise parrots: a casual chat about ChatGPT with Ruyi Li and Zhongqing
eps.ot: 33: 人类本质是不精确的复读机：与李如一和重轻闲聊 ChatGPT
eps.s: Ruyi Li, host of the podcast Yitian Shijie, and Zhongqing, creator of Buzaichang, chat with Hanyang about ChatGPT-style chatbots and what human language and mistakes are worth. Topics include where humans and AI differ, ChatGPT's flat prose, data and time, creativity, and OpenAI no longer being open. The standout idea: humans are imprecise parrots. Based on the episode description.
g: Host of the podcast Yitian Shijie; author of the books Miecha Kucha and Wu Ciyuan
Creator and editor of Buzaichang

eps.t: Thinking beyond frameworks | Casey Winters (Pinterest, Eventbrite, Airbnb, Tinder, Reddit, Grubhub)
eps.s: Casey Winters returns for a second visit. He starts with why the chief product officer job is so hard, criticizes "zero interest rate PMs" who lean too heavily on process and research, and explains when to spend on user research and when founder intuition should give way to the team. Then he lays out three kinds of network effects, what Grubhub got wrong against DoorDash, why SaaS and marketplaces struggle to grow into each other, and why consumer subscriptions are so hard.
g: Former chief product officer at Eventbrite, ex-growth lead at Grubhub and Pinterest, adviser to Whatnot and others

eps.t: What's Beyond GitHub Copilot? With Copilot's Chief Architect and founder of Minion.AI Alex Graveley
eps.s: Alex Graveley, chief architect of GitHub Copilot and founder of Minion.AI, traces his path from open source and the assistant company Magic to building Copilot. He explains how homemade evaluations drove Copilot's progress, why speed decides how much people use it and how it was priced, then discusses Minion, an AI that does tasks for you, and risks like AI impersonation scams.
g: Chief architect of GitHub Copilot; founder and CEO of Minion.AI

eps.t: The ultimate guide to adding a PLG motion | Hila Qu (Reforge, GitLab)
eps.s: Hila Qu, former head of growth at GitLab, gives a step-by-step guide to adding product-led growth (PLG) to a company: why PLG and sales end up coexisting, why PLG is really data-led growth, what you need in place first, and the common traps. She then covers mapping the funnel, auditing it end to end, defining the aha moment, handling retention and expansion, and how to set up the data stack and the team.
g: Growth adviser, former head of growth at GitLab and growth lead at Acorns

eps.t: Driving alignment within teams, work-life balance, and the changing PM landscape | Nikita Miller
eps.s: Nikita Miller leads product at The Knot Worldwide and previously ran growth and retention at Trello. She explains how Trello grew from a personal tool into a team tool by starting simple and adding complexity as users needed it, how a written "roles and responsibilities" agreement keeps product, design, engineering and data aligned, why focusing only on outcomes neglects shipping speed, how the PM role is changing, how remote teams work well, and her guiding question: what are you optimizing for?
g: SVP and head of product at The Knot Worldwide; formerly led growth and retention at Trello

eps.t: The Future is Small Models, with Matei Zaharia, CTO of Databricks
eps.s: Databricks co-founder and CTO Matei Zaharia tells how the company grew out of Berkeley's Spark project just as data, cloud and machine learning converged. He explains why Dolly shows small models can follow instructions, argues for retrieval and outside data rather than ever more parameters to fix stale knowledge and hallucinations, and covers the infrastructure companies need to put large language models to work.
g: Co-founder and CTO of Databricks, Stanford computer science professor

eps.t: Large AI models and how hot the market really is, from an investor's view: talking ChatGPT with Mengqiu Wang
eps.ot: 投资人视角下的大模型和市场真实水温｜和梦秋聊ChatGPT
eps.s: Mengqiu Wang, founding partner of Qingliu Capital, looks at ChatGPT through an investor's eyes: why OpenAI won, who should build large AI models, where startups still have room, and how hot or cold private-market investing really is in 2023.
g: Founding partner of Qingliu Capital and a former Baidu vice president

eps.t: Product lessons from Waymo | Shweta Shrivastava (Waymo, Amazon, Cisco)
eps.s: Shweta Shrivastava is senior director of product management at Waymo. She explains how building product at a self-driving company differs from ordinary software: the car must drive like a human yet more safely, rider trust comes from many small designed details, the safety bar for an MVP is far higher, and progress is tracked through both business and driving metrics. She also shares lessons from Amazon and Cisco: work backwards from customer problems, disrupt yourself, listen well, and how to think about promotion.
g: Senior director of product management at Waymo; former CPO at Nauto and product lead for AWS database services

eps.t: Artists who've started using AI: Tianxi and Yixuan Xie on text-to-image
eps.ot: 34: 开始用上 AIGC 的艺术家：和 Tianxi/轶轩一起聊文生图
eps.s: Hanyang talks with two tech-savvy visual artists, Tianxi (who goes by Tim) and Yixuan Xie, about text-to-image AI, where you type a sentence and get a picture. They should be first in line to be disrupted, yet both already use it in their work. The talk moves to randomness, how photographers work, the changing idea of a photo, and whether photography is about truth.
g: Visual artist known as Tim; author of the photo book Anonymous Landscapes
Visual artist

eps.t: How to build a cult-like brand | Laura Modi (Bobbie)
eps.s: Laura Modi founded the organic infant formula brand Bobbie after running hospitality at Airbnb. She shares what she took from Airbnb about culture and storytelling, why she shut her website during the 2022 formula shortage to protect existing customers, and how to build a brand people are devoted to: branding internal processes, hiring "optimistic doers" with a dash of naivety, and putting content and community before commerce. She also explains how leaders manufacture momentum and how systems let her run three kids and a company.
g: Founder and CEO of the infant formula brand Bobbie; former director of hospitality at Airbnb

eps.t: Your AI Friends Have Awoken, With Noam Shazeer
eps.s: Noam Shazeer, a co-author of the Transformer paper, recounts learning neural networks from scratch at Google Brain, working on the Transformer and LaMDA, and then leaving to found Character.AI. He explains why language modeling is the main road to intelligence, why scaling is nowhere near its limit, and why letting users create AI characters with personality beats big companies' play-it-safe assistants.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Character.AI, co-author of the Transformer paper

eps.t: How to make better decisions and build a joyful career | Ada Chen Rekhi (Notejoy, LinkedIn)
eps.s: Executive coach and Notejoy co-founder Ada Chen Rekhi shares a toolkit for making decisions and shaping a career: run a "curiosity loop" to gather structured advice before big decisions, build an inner scorecard with a values exercise, explore early and exploit later, and don't be the frog in slowly heating water. She also covers when you actually need a coach, how to handle Silicon Valley's unspoken rules, and what she's learned co-founding companies with her husband.
g: Executive coach and Notejoy co-founder; former SVP of marketing at SurveyMonkey and growth marketing lead at LinkedIn

eps.t: Building China's OpenAI? Zhifei Li urges his peers to calm down
eps.ot: 要做中国OpenAI？李志飞劝各位同仁冷静点
eps.s: A month ago, Mobvoi founder Zhifei Li wanted to build "China's OpenAI." After a trip through Silicon Valley, he has cooled off. He traces how language AI evolved toward one model that handles every task, explains why OpenAI rather than Google built ChatGPT and what protects it, estimates how crowded China's model race will get, and urges peers to work out use cases and business models first.
g: Founder and CEO of Mobvoi and a former Google scientist

eps.t: An inside look at how Miro builds product | Varun Parmar (CPO of Miro)
eps.s: Varun Parmar, chief product officer at Miro, the online whiteboard company, explains how Miro builds product: teams organized around user types, with product marketing sitting inside the product org. The most interesting parts are his views on competition (how fast you grow is largely what rivals allow) and speed (in a new market, be the first to hit the wall). He also covers Miro's one-line product motto, its rolling six-month roadmap, and its mix of product-led growth and enterprise sales.
g: Chief product officer at Miro; previously SVP and chief product officer at Box

eps.t: The Computing Platform Underlying AI, with Jensen Huang, Founder & CEO of NVIDIA
eps.s: Jensen Huang tells how NVIDIA started in graphics acceleration, bet everything on accelerated computing, rode out years of unprofitable CUDA investment and caught deep learning around 2012. He explains why NVIDIA stays a platform rather than a model company, shares his views on organization and running a business, and names the next "impossible problems": robotics, drug discovery and climate simulation.
g: Founder and CEO of NVIDIA

eps.t: From the great AI shift to startups, old feuds and temperament: a conversation with Fu Sheng
eps.ot: 和傅盛从这场伟大的AI变革，谈到创业、恩怨和心性
eps.s: Fu Sheng of Cheetah Mobile talks about how large AI models will go from a cutting-edge tool for the few to something everyone can use, when robots will enter homes, and why this shift rivals the steam engine. He also looks back on his hardest moments as a founder and his old history with Zhou Hongyi, founder of 360.
g: Chairman and CEO of Cheetah Mobile and founder of OrionStar

eps.t: The ultimate guide to product-led sales | Elena Verna
eps.s: Growth expert Elena Verna returns for a whole episode on product-led sales: letting users adopt a product on their own, then using sales to turn that usage into large company-wide contracts. She explains which companies should do it, how to tell from usage data when a sales conversation makes sense, and what data and people you need to start. Her sharpest point: product teams must own pipeline and revenue, and handing PLS to marketing fails within six months.
g: Growth advisor and Reforge instructor; former interim growth lead at Amplitude, ran marketing at Miro and growth at SurveyMonkey

eps.t: Listener Q&A: AI Investment Hype, Foundation Models, Regulation, Opportunity Areas, and More
eps.s: The two hosts take listener questions: how fast open-source models can catch OpenAI, what autonomous agents really are, whether AI should be regulated now, whether AI investing is overheated and which applications deserve attention, and where the real opportunities lie in healthcare and drug development. They largely agree on the timing of regulation but disagree on where AI adds value in drug development.
g: No Priors co-host and founder of the venture firm Conviction
No Priors co-host, serial entrepreneur and investor

eps.t: How to achieve hypergrowth in your business and career | Carilu Dietrich (Atlassian)
eps.s: Carilu Dietrich ran marketing at Atlassian through its IPO and now advises fast-growing B2B companies. She talks about how to reach the executive level, how to pick a company with momentum, and how to handle a downturn. Her sharpest point: hypergrowth comes from a product people love and word of mouth, not from ad spend. She also covers brand ads, why Atlassian hired salespeople late, and why big growth shifts are a company-wide strategy question.
g: Former Atlassian marketing head through its IPO; now advises CEOs and CMOs at fast-growing B2B companies

eps.t: Geoffrey Hinton at MIT Technology Review's EmTech Digital (published as "Q&A: Google's Geoffrey Hinton — humanity just a 'passing phase' in the evolution of intelligence")
eps.ol: MIT Technology Review EmTech Digital (text via Computerworld)
eps.s: Soon after leaving Google, Geoffrey Hinton explains at EmTech why he suddenly fears AI (text is excerpts). He says he changed his mind in recent months: digital models may learn better than brains, and what one copy learns all copies know. Smarter AI could manipulate people and seek control, and humanity may be just a passing phase in the evolution of intelligence.
g: Deep learning pioneer and Turing Award winner who had just left Google

eps.t: Building a culture of excellence | David Singleton (CTO of Stripe)
eps.s: Stripe CTO David Singleton explains how Stripe hires and why engineers long doubled as product managers. The most interesting part is how he turns "care about craft" into concrete habits: friction logs, group walkthroughs of the product, and executives shipping code themselves. He also covers how Stripe stays highly reliable while deploying constantly, early uses of AI inside and outside the company, and his approach to delegation, time, and energy.
g: Stripe's CTO, running engineering and design; previously a VP of engineering at Google

eps.t: Personalizing AI Models with Kelvin Guu, Senior Staff Research Scientist, Google Brain
eps.s: Google Brain research scientist Kelvin Guu walks through research directions for making large models customizable and traceable: the retrieval-augmented model REALM, mixture of experts, FLAN instruction tuning, training data attribution and "model surgery." He also analyzes where autonomous agents fell short at the time on memory, error correction and continual learning.
g: Senior staff research scientist at Google Brain

eps.t: 'Godfather of AI' discusses dangers the developing technologies pose to society
eps.s: Soon after leaving Google, Geoffrey Hinton tells PBS NewsHour what worries him: AI smarter than us could seek control and manipulate people, and digital systems may already learn better than brains. He doesn't want AI halted; he wants roughly as much effort spent on controlling it as on improving it, and thinks nations can cooperate as they did on nuclear war.
g: Deep learning pioneer called the "Godfather of AI," just after leaving Google

eps.t: Mastering paid growth | Jonathan Becker (Thrive Digital)
eps.s: Jonathan Becker founded Thrive Digital, a performance marketing agency that manages roughly $500 million in ad spend a year. He lays out paid growth from end to end: why it can become an addiction, which companies should do it, why ad creative is now the biggest lever, and how to test it. He also covers the state of each ad platform, attribution after Apple's privacy changes, B2B lead scoring, and how AI has already changed agency work.
g: Founder of Thrive Digital, a performance marketing agency

eps.t: Godfather of AI Warns of the Existential Threat of AI
eps.s: Soon after leaving Google, Geoffrey Hinton explains on Amanpour and Company why he changed his mind: digital systems know more with fewer connections, learn as 10,000 sharing copies, and, he is confident, really think. He proposes punishing undisclosed AI fakes like counterfeit money, wants safety spending raised from about 1% to near half, and likens forecasting AI to looking into fog.
g: Deep learning pioneer called the "Godfather of AI," just after leaving Google

eps.t: Will Everyone Have a Personal AI? With Mustafa Suleyman, Founder of DeepMind and Inflection
eps.s: Mustafa Suleyman, co-founder of DeepMind and Inflection, starts with his early work on a counseling helpline and in conflict resolution, then revisits DeepMind's early bets and AlphaFold. He explains why he came to believe conversation is the future interface and that everyone will have a personal AI aligned with their own interests, and discusses platform governance, how Inflection is organized and the growth of compute.
g: Co-founder of DeepMind; co-founder and CEO of Inflection AI

eps.t: Trends 2023: What Beisen's IPO says about two tough years for China's business software
eps.ot: 【趋势2023】从北森IPO看充满挑战的中国企服这两年
eps.s: Fei Xiong, a partner at Matrix Partners China, was an early investor in Beisen, the first Chinese business software company to go public after the pandemic, whose stock then halved. He uses it to look back on two roller-coaster years for enterprise software, covering falling valuations, the path to profit, and how open source could shape the AI landscape.
g: Partner at Matrix Partners China and an early investor in Beisen

eps.t: Frameworks for product differentiation, team building, and first principles thinking | Ayo Omojola
eps.s: Ayo Omojola helped build Cash Card and Cash App at Square and is now chief product officer at Carbon Health. He looks back at why Cash App worked, what real differentiation means, and what it takes to incubate a new business inside a big company. The most interesting parts are his personal rules: hiring former founders, building relationships years ahead of need, and chasing every question to the bottom. He closes with advice on health tech startups.
g: Chief product officer at Carbon Health; helped build Cash Card and Cash App at Square

eps.t: Yann LeCun: Meta's New AI Model LLaMA; Why Elon is Wrong about AI; Open-source AI Models | E1014
eps.s: Harry Stebbings and Yann LeCun start with his early years in AI and the long winter for neural networks, then cover why word-by-word language models will soon be obsolete, what AI doomers get wrong, why open source wins, jobs, research ecosystems and Elon Musk's call for a pause. Only a written summary of the episode was available.
g: Meta VP and chief AI scientist, NYU professor, 2018 Turing Award winner

eps.t: Oversight of A.I.: Rules for Artificial Intelligence (Senate Judiciary Subcommittee hearing)
eps.ol: U.S. Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Privacy, Technology, and the Law
eps.ho: Sen. Richard Blumenthal (chair), Sen. Josh Hawley and senators
eps.s: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman testifies alongside Gary Marcus and IBM's Christina Montgomery on how AI should be governed. The striking part: the company being regulated asks for regulation, proposing a new agency to license the most capable models, mandatory pre-release tests and outside audits. He also covers election manipulation, jobs, creators' rights and who should be liable when things go wrong.
g: OpenAI CEO, testifying to the Senate and calling for licensing of powerful AI

eps.t: CNBC Transcript: Elon Musk Sits Down with CNBC's David Faber Live on CNBC Tonight
eps.s: An hour with Musk after his Twitter takeover. He walks through the robotaxi math, how Tesla sets prices as rates rise, China and Taiwan risk, Twitter's layoffs and new CEO, and why he opposes remote work. Most striking is his account of OpenAI: he says it exists because of him, yet it now resembles a rainforest charity turned logging company.
g: Tesla and SpaceX CEO; Twitter owner handing day-to-day control to new CEO Linda Yaccarino

eps.t: OpenAI going open source and Amazon's new moves: where is the global AI model race headed?
eps.ot: OpenAI开源、亚马逊新动作，全球大模型格局走向何方
eps.s: Huainan Wang returns. He argues the race for general-purpose foundation models is already over, and the real business lies in industry "copilots," AI assistants that help professionals work. Companies focused on one industry, he says, are protected by data and relationships. He also discusses how OpenAI open-sourcing a model and Amazon's entry could reshape the field.
g: Former Google CMO for Asia, now a partner at MiraclePlus, Qi Lu's startup accelerator

eps.t: Lessons on product sense, AI, the first mile experience, and the messy middle | Scott Belsky (Adobe)
eps.s: Scott Belsky founded the designer community Behance, became Adobe's chief product officer, and is now its chief strategy officer. He talks about how to build product sense, why a user's first 30 seconds deserve the most investment, why hot consumer apps rarely last, his rule of building only half the features, and how AI will change product teams and creative work. He closes with how to survive the "messy middle" of a startup and when to walk away.
g: Chief strategy officer at Adobe, also running design and emerging products; former CPO; founder of Behance

eps.t: The AI Will See You Now: Exploring Biomedical AI and Google's Med-PaLM2 With Karan Singhal
eps.s: Google researcher Karan Singhal explains how the medical models Med-PaLM and Med-PaLM 2 were built: aligning a general base model to medicine and evaluating it mainly through physician review. He also covers choosing adaptation methods by data volume, patient privacy and HIPAA, why medicine is a testbed for AI safety, and the near-term path into clinical use.
g: Google Research scientist and core member of the Med-PaLM project

eps.t: Skip eye surgery, dry eye has no cure, pricey glasses are a waste: a chat with a UK optometrist
eps.ot: 35: 别做近视手术、干眼症没救、给眼镜多花钱没用：和英国视光医生聊聊天
eps.s: Hanyang asks Xiao Tan, an optometrist working in the UK, the questions glasses-wearers most want answered: how eye tests differ between the UK and China, eye-test basics, which eyewear selling points are gimmicks, laser surgery, contacts and colored lenses, and everyday eye care. The overall message: stop wasting money on your eyes. Based on the episode description, so his reasons aren't spelled out.
g: Optometrist working in the UK

eps.t: The science of product, big bets, and how AI is impacting the future of music | Gustav Söderström
eps.s: Gustav Söderström, Spotify's co-president and head of product and technology, walks through the internet's three eras, from curation to recommendation to generation, and the design principles behind Spotify's AI DJ. He discusses what generative AI means for music and copyright, why Spotify abandoned its famous squad model and put autonomy at the VP level, the trade-off between centralized and decentralized organizations, and what went wrong with a home-screen redesign. His credo: product is 100 percent science, and every decision must be explainable.
g: Co-president of Spotify, also its chief product officer and chief technology officer

eps.t: The Shanghai auto show that shocked the Germans: a portrait of today's car industry
eps.ot: 令德国人惊吓的上海车展：一幅当代汽车众生图
eps.s: Junyi Zhang, an auto consultant and investor, unpacks the 2023 Shanghai auto show that rattled his German colleagues: how the relationship between Chinese and German carmakers has changed, the price war Tesla set off, foreign carmakers' struggle over who makes decisions in China, and how many Chinese automakers will survive the shakeout.
g: Head of automotive and industrial at Oliver Wyman, and co-founder of NIO Capital

eps.t: Going Full Send on AI, and the (Positive) Impact of AI on Jobs, with Kevin Scott, CTO of Microsoft
eps.s: Microsoft CTO Kevin Scott explains why Microsoft went all in on AI: pooling its GPU budget, partnering with OpenAI, building its own AI supercomputers, and creating a platform centered on Copilot. He also covers the open versus closed source debate, how to build real AI products, and why he's optimistic about AI's effect on jobs and about regulation.
g: Microsoft's chief technology officer, who led its big bet on AI

eps.t: OPPO suddenly stops making chips: an ambition born at the wrong time
eps.ot: 36: OPPO 突然中止造芯，生不逢时的雄心
eps.s: LatePost's Manqi Cheng and Jiahao Zhang, with business reporter Hao Qiu, look back at OPPO's chip unit ZEKU, shut down suddenly on May 12, 2023. They cover how abrupt it was, the pressure on OPPO's phone business, four years of ambition and missteps, the rise and fall of a chip talent boom, and the odd position of Chinese chip companies. Views are combined under Manqi Cheng.
g: Head of tech coverage at LatePost; views here also include Jiahao Zhang and Hao Qiu

eps.t: The Madness of High-Flyer: A Hidden AI Giant's Road to Large Models
eps.ot: 疯狂的幻方：一家隐形AI巨头的大模型之路
eps.s: In his first long interview, as DeepSeek was being founded in 2023, Liang Wenfeng explains why a quant fund is chasing general AI. He covers how High-Flyer grew from one GPU to 10,000, why it can fund research without venture capital, and why he hires for ability over experience. Most memorable is his take on being crazy: like a 50 km hike, body wrecked, mind satisfied.
g: Founder of quant fund High-Flyer, just launching its AI research company DeepSeek

eps.t: The power of strategic narrative | Andy Raskin
eps.s: Andy Raskin helps CEOs at companies like Gong, Zuora, and 360Learning craft a strategic narrative. Instead of starting from customer pain, his story opens with a shift from an old game to a new one, then the stakes, the new goal, the obstacles, and finally the product as a "magic gift." He also covers how the narrative filters product decisions, why category names matter less than people think, and why the CEO must lead the process.
g: Strategic narrative consultant who has worked with CEOs at Gong, Dropbox, Uber, and Salesforce

eps.t: Storytelling with Nancy Duarte: How to craft compelling presentations and tell a story that sticks
eps.s: Nancy Duarte, CEO of the presentation firm Duarte, has built slides for Apple and for Al Gore's An Inconvenient Truth. She offers three rules for a great talk: the audience is the hero; tell the story by moving between "what is" and "what could be," ending in a "new bliss"; and let people see what you mean. She also covers slide design, beating stage fright, the five acts of leading change, and why product managers need storytelling too.
g: CEO of the presentation firm Duarte, an expert on presentations and storytelling, and bestselling author

eps.t: AI & Defense Technology with Anduril CEO Brian Schimpf
eps.s: Anduril co-founder and CEO Brian Schimpf explains why future defense needs large numbers of cheap, software-driven autonomous systems rather than a few expensive platforms. He covers the Lattice software, unmanned submarines and counter-drone systems, keeping humans accountable for autonomous weapons, what LLMs can do for defense, and what the war in Ukraine teaches about deterrence in the Pacific.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Anduril, a defense company building software and autonomous systems

eps.t: English episode: talking brains, models and human love with a founder of deep learning
eps.ot: 英文播客：和深度学习奠基人聊聊大脑、模型和人类的爱
eps.s: Xiaojun Zhang talks in English with deep learning pioneer Terrence Sejnowski. Starting from his work with Geoffrey Hinton on Boltzmann machines, they cover what the brain teaches AI, his feud with Marvin Minsky's rule-based school, large models as an "alien" intelligence, how to regulate AI risk, and missing pieces like emotion and long-term memory. His theme: humanity has just taken off, and everything will change in our lifetime.
g: Deep learning pioneer and author of The Deep Learning Revolution

eps.t: Moving fast and navigating uncertainty | Jeremy Henrickson (Rippling, Coinbase)
eps.s: Jeremy Henrickson, head of product at Rippling, recalls leading a team through Coinbase's 40x usage explosion in 2017, then explains how Rippling, the HR and IT software company, stays fast at scale: tiny teams incubating new products, designing for the hardest case instead of an MVP, one employee record under every product, deciding in the room, and leaders going to see the work. He also covers sequencing international expansion, process frameworks, and hiring PMs.
g: Senior VP of product at Rippling; previously chief product officer at Coinbase

eps.t: Listener Q&A: AI Misconceptions, The Reality of Regulation, Infinite Context, Incumbent AI Execution and Startup Ideas
eps.s: Sarah and Elad answer listener questions: the biggest misconception about generative AI, whether the industry is naive to welcome regulation, whether context windows can grow without limit, China's homegrown models and chip sanctions, how well big incumbents are executing on AI, and the startup ideas they like.
g: Co-hosts of No Priors, both tech investors

eps.t: Lots of hype, little investment? Kai Qu of 42zhangjing on the temperature of AI venture capital
eps.ot: 37: 热度很高，投资很少？与 42 章经曲凯聊聊 AI 创投水温
eps.s: Kai Qu, founder of 42zhangjing, is helping several large-model and generative AI startups raise money. He tells Manqi Cheng about the gap between buzz and actual deals in China's 2023 AI boom: which layer gets the money, why app companies are underrated, and what AI-native apps might look like. His most surprising claim: the AI bubble isn't big enough yet. Based on the episode description.
g: Founder of 42zhangjing; nearly ten years in venture capital and startups

eps.t: ZhenFund's Yuan Liu on the hackathon revival, and a faint sadness amid the AI frenzy
eps.ot: 和真格刘元聊聊，黑客松复兴、AI狂欢中，怎么夹杂着一丝朦胧的忧伤
eps.s: ZhenFund partner Yuan Liu starts from an AI hackathon run by the social app Jike, then talks about why investors are unsure how to back AI apps, the kinds of founders China and the US each produce, and why AI startups are splitting into two extremes. Most striking: amid the frenzy, he senses a twilight of the human era.
g: Partner at ZhenFund, an early-stage venture capital firm

eps.t: Building a long and meaningful career | Nikhyl Singhal (Meta, Google)
eps.s: Meta product leader and career coach Nikhyl Singhal walks through a product manager's career in three stages. He covers planning backward from the job after next, leaving highly valued companies that still lack a product people truly want, the four reasons promotions stall, how new managers earn their team's trust, the rise of the senior individual-contributor path, and why executives' biggest weaknesses hide behind their strengths. He closes on finding a new purpose for a career's third act.
g: Product lead for Meta's Facebook app, former Credit Karma CPO and Google product executive, founder of The Skip

eps.t: With anti-globalization on the rise, why are foreign CEOs flocking to China?
eps.ot: 逆全球化思潮来势汹汹，外企CEO何故密集访华？
eps.s: Using Elon Musk's 44-hour whirlwind trip to China as a starting point, Wei Wang explains why so many foreign CEOs visited China in the first half of 2023, and what that signals in a fracturing world. His most interesting point: who these leaders shake hands and pose with is planned, and meant to be read.
g: VP and board secretary at a Fortune Global 500 company; former CFO of Meihua Bio

eps.t: Leveraging growth advisors, mastering SEO, and honing your craft | Luc Levesque (Shopify, Meta)
eps.s: Shopify's chief growth officer Luc Levesque opens with Mark Zuckerberg asking him point-blank when results would show up, then explains an impact-first culture and how he hires. The core is growth advisors: when to bring one in, how to tell the real ones apart, and how to structure the deal with equity and a three-month cliff. He also covers which products suit SEO, why one keyword can carry a business, how AI search will shake things up, and his daily hour of structured reflection.
g: Chief growth officer at Shopify, former growth lead at Meta and VP of growth and GM at Tripadvisor

eps.t: What happens to Observability If Code is AI-Generated? The Potential for AI in DevOps, with Datadog Co-founder/CEO Olivier Pomel
eps.s: Datadog co-founder and CEO Olivier Pomel explains why observability matters more once AI writes code, what new monitoring needs LLM apps create, and why statistical methods still beat LLMs at anomaly detection while automated operations remain far off. He also talks about the capital efficiency of building in New York and growing through a platform plus acquisitions.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Datadog, which makes monitoring tools for cloud software

eps.t: Infighting? Investor pressure? Why he stepped down as CEO after five years and a valuation above 2 billion yuan
eps.ot: 38: 内斗？投资人逼宫？创业 5 年后公司估值超过 20 亿元，他为什么辞任 CEO？
eps.s: Guangyao Liu, founder of the gender-neutral clothing brand bosie, publicly stepped down as CEO after the company was valued at over 2 billion yuan. With host Jing Chen he discusses why he quit and how people reacted, losses and layoffs after COVID, lessons and his biggest regret, how ofo founder Dai Wei influenced him, and running a business after the consumer-brand boom faded.
g: Founder of gender-neutral clothing brand bosie; stepped down as CEO in 2023

eps.t: Building high-performing teams | Melissa Tan (Webflow, Dropbox, Canva)
eps.s: Melissa Tan, Dropbox's first growth PM and later head of growth at Webflow, starts with what Dropbox got right and wrong as it moved into business customers, and when to shift from product-led growth to sales. She then explains how to become a manager people follow between companies, what high-performing teams share, and her PM interview process that coaches candidates before their final presentation. She closes with common growth-team mistakes and who to hire first.
g: Former head of growth at Webflow, Dropbox's first growth PM, and growth advisor to Canva, Grammarly, and Miro

eps.t: What's for Dinner? AI-Driven Commerce with Instacart CEO Fidji Simo
eps.s: Instacart CEO Fidji Simo talks about her leadership style, how Instacart uses generative AI to let its search box answer questions and connect early intent to real-world delivery, why automated warehouses don't pencil out, and the future of smart carts and ads. She also explains why, after founding Metrodora, she's both hopeful and cautious about AI in healthcare.
g: CEO of Instacart, the grocery delivery company

eps.t: Lessons from scaling Ramp | Sri Batchu (Ramp, Instacart, Opendoor)
eps.s: Ramp's head of growth Sri Batchu explains how the company reached $100 million in annualized revenue in two years: founders were brought in as shareholders early and their companies became the first customers, then engineering and data were applied to every channel. He also covers Ramp's count-the-days speed culture, converting team metrics into one north star, payback period instead of CAC, the order to invest in B2B channels, experiments that fail conclusively, and paying top talent far more.
g: Head of growth at Ramp, former head of growth at Instacart and VP of operations at Opendoor

eps.t: Bringing AI to the Data Cloud, with Snowflake's CEO Frank Slootman
eps.s: Snowflake CEO Frank Slootman describes the operating philosophy he has carried from Data Domain to Snowflake: drive the organization with urgency and high standards. He explains Snowflake's cloud-native architecture and the idea of a data cloud, and covers natural-language queries, the Neeva and Streamlit acquisitions, data governance, usage-based pricing, and steady pruning instead of mass layoffs.
g: Chairman and CEO of Snowflake, the cloud data platform company

eps.t: Does a company full of high-EQ people end up mediocre?
eps.ot: 【职场人性】情商含量越高，公司越平庸？
eps.s: Yajun Wang, former chief strategy officer of property developer Longfor Group, looks at the role of emotional intelligence at work: whether it's a ticket to promotion, and whether executives should have as much of it as possible. His counterintuitive claim: the more a company runs on reading the room and leaving things unsaid, the more mediocre it becomes.
g: Founder of Jingmen Management; former chief strategy officer of Longfor Group

eps.t: Building minimum lovable products, stories from WeWork & Airbnb, and thriving as a PM | Jiaona Zhang
eps.s: Jiaona Zhang (JZ), senior VP of product at Webflow and a Stanford PM lecturer, starts with the classic mistake of jumping straight to a solution and what went wrong with Airbnb Plus. She covers thinking big while validating in stages, talking a founder out of a bad idea, the "minimum lovable product," roadmaps and OKRs, building an early reputation, and leadership lessons from WeWork and Webflow. Her closing lesson: know why users love you and double down.
g: Senior VP of product at Webflow and Stanford PM lecturer; previously led product at WeWork and Airbnb

eps.t: Trends 2023: Investor Weifeng Fan on the ebbing tide of content investing
eps.ot: 【趋势2023】和老范从退潮的内容投资谈起
eps.s: Weifeng Fan, an investor who made his name backing content companies, looks at why content investing has ebbed: whether content is still a good business in 2023, who should be doing it, and why investors are switching from funding content to making their own. His memorable image: content is the saddle and whip, but investors are looking for the horse.
g: Founding partner of Gaozhang Capital; host of the podcast Lao Fan on Startups

eps.t: How to ask the right questions, project confidence, and win over skeptics | Paige Costello (Asana)
eps.s: Paige Costello leads core product at Asana, the work-management software company. She walks through Asana's nested planning system and its "double diamond" product process: pick the customer, then the problem, then the solution. She then explains how a young PM earns the trust of senior colleagues by bringing insight rather than faking seniority, how to project confidence, and how to help people grow. She closes with mistakes she made as a new manager and three ways to evaluate a job.
g: Head of core product at Asana; previously product director at Intercom and PM at Intuit

eps.t: The man who first brought Charlie Munger to China, and his years in publishing
eps.ot: 第一个把查理·芒格引入中国的人和出版风云
eps.s: Publisher Hongjun Shi looks back on twenty years in publishing and tells how he brought Charlie Munger and Poor Charlie's Almanack to China. The twist: Munger's ideas then changed Shi's own life, giving him the courage to leave CITIC Press.
g: Publisher of the Chinese editions of Poor Charlie's Almanack and The Munger Way

eps.t: From Meituan buying Light Years Beyond: how tech mergers and acquisitions really work
eps.ot: 39: 从美团收购光年之外，聊聊科技公司收并购的操作与故事
eps.s: Starting from Meituan's purchase of Light Years Beyond, the AI model startup founded by Wang Huiwen, Lanqiao Capital founder Chao Wang and partner Shaotao Zou talk with Manqi Cheng about what Meituan really paid, how tech acquisitions work and how each side plays, and the state of China's M&A market. The key line: deals full of conflict get done by facing reality and compromising together.
g: Founder of Lanqiao Capital
Partner at Lanqiao Capital

eps.t: M&A, competition, pricing, and investing | Julia Schottenstein (dbt Labs)
eps.s: Julia Schottenstein left venture firm NEA to run product at dbt Labs. She explains how she picked a startup the way an investor picks a deal, how she led the acquisition of Transform, and what founders should know about selling a company. She also breaks down how dbt thinks about competition, open source and pricing, why shipping something slightly worse is often better, and what investor habits help a product manager.
g: Head of product at dbt Labs, running dbt Cloud; previously an investor at NEA

eps.t: LinkedIn’s product evolution and the art of building complex systems | Hari Srinivasan (LinkedIn)
eps.s: Hari Srinivasan runs product for LinkedIn's hiring and learning businesses. He explains how one guiding goal, connecting people to economic opportunity, keeps decisions simple across a tangle of interlocking marketplaces. He also covers how skills-first hiring has reshaped the job market, how job seekers should present themselves, how a complex organization breaks ties fast, and what makes a great product manager.
g: VP of product at LinkedIn, leading hiring products and LinkedIn Learning

eps.t: Office human nature: What are company power struggles really about?
eps.ot: 【职场人性】企业内斗，究竟在斗什么？
eps.s: Kelin Li (Colin), a former Baidu vice president, uses organizational behavior to take apart office infighting: how open fights differ from hidden friction, how people at each level fight, why infighting surges when markets shrink, and how to avoid getting dragged in. His sharpest point: the friction you can't see is deadlier than the fights you can.
g: CEO of Aibo Xingchen; former Baidu vice president and director of Midea's president's office

eps.t: The Timeline for Realistic 4-D: Devi Parikh from Meta on Research Hurdles for Generative AI in Video and Multimodality
eps.s: Meta's generative AI research director Devi Parikh breaks down the idea behind Make-A-Video: learn what things look like from image-text data, and how they move from video. She explains why video generation lags well behind images, why control and multimodal inputs are key for creative tools, and looks ahead to audio generation and AI content on social networks.
g: Research director for generative AI at Meta and associate professor at Georgia Tech

eps.t: The 10 traits of great PMs, AI, and Slack’s approach to product | Noah Weiss (Slack, Google)
eps.s: Slack chief product officer Noah Weiss on how to work with a strong product-minded founder, the old principles that still apply to building AI products, and how Slack uses rituals like complaint storms to see its product through a newcomer's eyes. He also explains how Slack restarted self-serve growth after it stalled in 2019, and lays out his ten traits of great product managers and which matter at each career stage.
g: Chief product officer at Slack; previously led product at Foursquare and was a PM at Google

eps.t: The ultimate guide to A/B testing | Ronny Kohavi (Airbnb, Microsoft, Amazon)
eps.s: Ronny Kohavi is one of the world's foremost experts on A/B testing. Drawing on his years at Amazon, Microsoft's Bing and Airbnb, he explains a humbling fact: most ideas fail. He also covers how to pick a single metric that protects long-term value, when a company is big enough to start experimenting, and the traps that make results untrustworthy: sample ratio mismatch, too-good-to-be-true wins and misreading p-values.
g: A/B testing expert; former Airbnb VP, head of Microsoft's experimentation platform, Amazon personalization director

eps.t: How Palantir's AI Bet is Revolutionizing Defense and Beyond, with CTO Shyam Sankar
eps.s: Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar explains where the forward deployed engineer model came from and why Foundry's ontology is the foundation for bringing LLMs into the enterprise. He argues LLMs should be treated as statistical systems that need evals and tools, that structured outputs should drive application state instead of chat, and that human-AI teaming should start from a single state transition.
g: CTO of Palantir, which builds data software for governments and companies

eps.t: Are general-purpose robots the next wave of AI?
eps.ot: 40: 通用机器人，AI 的下一个浪潮？
eps.s: With the large-model boom, Tesla, OpenAI, Nvidia and ByteDance are all exploring general-purpose robots. Mech-Mind founder and CEO Tianlan Shao talks with Hanyang and Manqi Cheng about where the hype comes from, how robots really work today, what large models can and can't give them, and the future of people, machines and the world. The striking point: AI can beat Go champions but not replace assembly-line workers.
g: Founder and CEO of Mech-Mind

eps.t: How to measure and improve developer productivity | Nicole Forsgren (Microsoft Research, Github)
eps.s: Nicole Forsgren, creator of the DORA and SPACE frameworks, explains how to measure and improve software team productivity. Why speed and stability move together, how to use DORA's four metrics and benchmarks, how SPACE picks metrics that keep each other honest, and why surveys beat telemetry when they disagree. She also covers the biggest trap in rolling out metrics and how AI coding tools are changing developers' work.
g: Leads developer productivity research at Microsoft Research; DORA co-founder and co-author of Accelerate

eps.t: How are overlooked mid-tier companies doing? Their ambitions, struggles and fate
eps.ot: 被忽视的中腰部公司活得还好吗？他们的欲望、挣扎与天命
eps.s: Shanshan Wu, former chief strategy officer at Vipshop and TAL Education, describes life for mid-tier companies that are neither leaders nor small. They're often stuck in a niche of a big market, their founders restless and struggling, and many end up chalking it up to timing and fate. A highlight: TAL deliberately avoided star teachers, while New Oriental built around them.
g: Managing director at a global consulting firm; former chief strategy officer at Vipshop and TAL

eps.t: Eradicating Machine Learning Pain Points with Weights & Biases CEO Lukas Biewald
eps.s: Weights & Biases founder Lukas Biewald looks back on academic machine learning, search at Yahoo and his data-labeling company Figure Eight, and explains why researchers need simple tools. He admits that LLMs, by letting prompts replace training, are the first existential threat W&B has faced, and talks about how fast enterprises adopt AI and what he learned starting a second company.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Weights & Biases, which makes tools for machine learning developers

eps.t: Dream city: what has Xiaohongshu shaped, and who is shaping Xiaohongshu?
eps.ot: 41: 造梦都市：小红书塑造了什么？而又是谁在塑造小红书？
eps.s: Hanyang and Yixuan Xie spent nearly a year on a long article about Xiaohongshu (RedNote), interviewing at its headquarters many times. After it ran, they kept talking with Zhongqing, creator of Buzaichang, about what the app has shaped and who shapes it, with about half the material not in the article. The sharpest point: an app urging you to record life can make you skip living it.
g: LatePost Chat host; co-wrote the Xiaohongshu feature with Yixuan Xie; views here combined

eps.t: Velocity over everything: How Ramp became the fastest-growing SaaS startup ever | Geoff Charles
eps.s: Ramp, which makes corporate cards and expense software, is one of the fastest-growing SaaS startups ever. Its VP of Product, Geoff Charles, breaks down how Ramp puts velocity above almost everything: small single-threaded teams, context instead of control, guardrails around fast shipping, and planning precision only where it matters. He also covers first-principles thinking, why support reports to product, how a few PMs steer a large team, and what Ramp hires for.
g: VP of Product at Ramp, the corporate card and expense management startup

eps.t: Why 200 Chinese fund managers flew to the Middle East: sovereign funds and a kingdom of money
eps.ot: 200位GP赶去中东募资？聊聊沙漠上的白袍、主权基金和金钱王国
eps.s: Recorded in Dubai, this episode features Bill Qian, an investor based there, on the 2023 rush of Chinese fund managers to raise money in the Middle East. He explains how the region's capital is structured, how its sovereign wealth funds behave, and why most visitors left empty-handed. Key takeaway: big local investors often take 18 months or more to back a new fund.
g: Partner at Phoenix Group; former global head of investments at Binance

eps.t: Relentless curiosity, radical accountability, and HubSpot’s winning growth formula | Chris Miller
eps.s: Chris Miller, VP of Growth and AI Products at HubSpot, explains how he went from an ordinary PM to a seat at the leadership table, what he looks for when hiring PMs, and how to break into the job and find a sponsor. He then breaks down how HubSpot bakes customer-first thinking into its processes, how the early growth team pushed the company toward product-led growth, where PLG differs from pure self-serve, the common mistakes, and the "give value before you extract value" flywheel.
g: VP of Growth and AI Products at HubSpot; operator in residence at OpenView

eps.t: Listener Q&A: 2024 Tech Market Predictions, Long Term Implications of Today's GPU Crunch, and Will AI Agents Bring Us Happiness?
eps.s: Sarah and Elad answer listener questions: why GPUs are scarce and what the shortage means long term, when big enterprises will really deploy AI, whether agents should be general or vertical, and what happens in 2024 to startups that raised at high valuations in 2021.
g: Co-hosts of No Priors, both tech investors

eps.t: The ultimate guide to Martech | Austin Hay (Reforge, Ramp, Runway)
eps.s: Austin Hay runs marketing technology at Ramp, meaning the software and data systems marketing teams run on. He explains what the job is, when a company needs a dedicated person and where that person should sit, how consumer and business tool stacks evolved from customer data platforms to the warehouse plus reverse ETL, how to collect data from day one for multi-touch attribution, why precise tracking is over, and how he hires.
g: Head of marketing technology at Ramp and Reforge instructor; formerly VP at Runway and mParticle

eps.t: Let's start a business: young people leaping into Houhai, alcohol, and a sinking era
eps.ot: 【做个生意吧！】跳向后海的年轻人、酒精和下沉年代
eps.s: Ergou, founder of the Tiaohai bar, tells the ups and downs of a serial entrepreneur born in the 1990s. One of his startups sold for 200 million yuan on paper, yet he never saw a cent. Then, amid nights of drinking, drumming and jumping into Beijing's Houhai lake, he built an internet-famous bar. His bigger theme: an era that feels like it's sinking.
g: Founder of the Tiaohai bar; a serial entrepreneur born in the 1990s

eps.t: Xiaoice's Di Li speaks frankly: an AI model company without a business model will struggle to survive
eps.ot: 小冰李笛讲点真心话：只做大模型不追求商业模式是很难生存的
eps.s: Di Li, CEO of Xiaoice, stayed quiet during the AI model frenzy of early 2023. Here he lays out his contrarian views: don't have illusions about how AI models will make money, and bigger models aren't always better. His sharpest warning: companies that only build models, without a real business model, will struggle to survive.
g: CEO of Xiaoice; former vice president of Microsoft's Asia internet engineering institute

eps.t: The AI Tutor For Every Child and the Next Frontier of Education, From Khan Academy's Creator Sal Khan
eps.s: Khan Academy founder Sal Khan traces his path from tutoring cousins remotely to building free online education, and explains why mastery learning beats schools that move students along by age. He describes Khanmigo, the AI tutor built with OpenAI, and its guardrails, predicts AI tutors will be common within three to five years, and discusses the trouble facing colleges and the basics people need in the AI era.
g: Founder of Khan Academy, the free online learning platform

eps.t: Monetizing passions, scaling marketplaces, and stories from a creator economy vet | Camille Hearst
eps.s: Camille Hearst has worked the supply side of two-sided marketplaces from iTunes and YouTube to Patreon and now Spotify, where she leads fan monetization. She explains why creators are shy about charging, what platforms should do about it, and what makes creators succeed. She also shares lessons from selling her startup to Patreon, running supply at ride-hailing company Hailo, and why the riskiest big bets should be tested first.
g: Leads fan monetization at Spotify; formerly head of creator product at Patreon and founder of Kit

eps.t: A former SoftBank Vision Fund partner on where AI goes after the hype around large models cools
eps.ot: 和软银愿景原GP聊聊，大模型全球降温后，人工智能何去何从
eps.s: Eric Chen, a former managing partner at SoftBank Vision Fund, looks at the sudden boom and cool-down of large AI models through the lens of technology cycles. He covers what changes from AI 2.0 to AI 3.0, whether OpenAI can hold its lead, and the "aesthetics of business models" that later-stage investors cultivate. His key point: the cool-down is the best time to build.
g: Former managing partner at SoftBank Vision Fund; chairman of Yifang Jianshu

eps.t: A decade of ups and downs for product managers: Shaonan and Fei Liu look back
eps.ot: 42: 产品经理十年沉浮：和少楠、刘飞一起聊聊这个职业这些年
eps.s: Shaonan, co-founder of flomo and Xiaobaotong, and Fei Liu, who now runs a podcast and a cold-brew tea business, both became product managers when the job was brand new in China. With Hanyang they look back on a decade of highs and lows: doing the job well, common myths, whether PM courses help, whether young people should still join, and why so many are going independent.
g: Co-founder of note app flomo and paid-newsletter platform Xiaobaotong
Former product manager; now a podcast host starting a cold-brew tea business

eps.t: The ultimate guide to JTBD | Bob Moesta (co-creator of the framework)
eps.s: Bob Moesta co-created the Jobs to Be Done framework, the idea that people hire products to make progress in their lives. He explains where demand really comes from (moments of struggle), what makes people switch (four forces), and how to design sales around where the buyer is. He also shares concrete interviewing techniques, how to cluster conflicting jobs, how his approach differs from Christensen's and Ulwick's, and where the framework doesn't apply.
g: Co-creator of the Jobs to Be Done framework; co-founder and CEO of The Rewired Group

eps.t: AI-Powered Biological Software with Jakob Uszkoreit, CEO of Inceptive
eps.s: Jakob Uszkoreit co-wrote the Transformer paper and now runs the biotech startup Inceptive. He looks back at why attention won: it happened to fit the parallel chips of the day. He argues today's models spend compute by text length rather than problem difficulty, and explains how Inceptive uses deep learning to design mRNA as programmable "biological software."
g: Co-founder and CEO of Inceptive; co-author of the Transformer paper

eps.t: Are US dollar funds saying goodbye to Chinese tech? A former lawyer turned AI founder on Biden's new executive order
eps.ot: 43: 美元基金与中国科技说再见？和前律师、现 AI 创业者聊聊拜登最新行政禁令改变了什么
eps.s: In August 2023, President Biden signed an executive order limiting "U.S. persons" from investing in Chinese chips, quantum computing and AI. Yiwei Wang, a former transactional lawyer and now co-founder and COO of Mita Technology, walks Manqi Cheng through the order and the Treasury's draft-rule notice, and what his own startup's experience shows. The surprise: AI, defined by use, is hit hardest.
g: Co-founder and COO of Mita Technology; former transactional lawyer

eps.t: An inside look at Deel's unprecedented growth | Meltem Kuran Berkowitz (Head of Growth)
eps.s: Deel helps companies hire and pay people anywhere in the world. Head of growth Meltem Kuran Berkowitz walks through how annual recurring revenue went from under $1 million to nearly $300 million in about two and a half years while staying profitable. Early growth came from answering questions on Reddit and from SEO, with paid and long-tail channels added later. She also covers her traffic-light method for picking content, choosing partners, hiring a growth team, and Deel's culture.
g: Head of growth at Deel; previously led marketing at Bench Accounting

eps.t: AI Superpowers for Frontend Developers, with Vercel Founder/CEO Guillermo Rauch
eps.s: Vercel founder Guillermo Rauch sees foundation models as "cloud 2.0": AI-native apps will be built on models the way SaaS was built on AWS. He covers what AI apps newly need, from streaming and abuse prevention to observability, how answer engines are shaking up SEO and crawling, and how AI is changing frontend development and dependency management.
g: Founder and CEO of Vercel, a cloud platform for deploying web apps

eps.t: Inside Etsy's product, growth, and marketplace evolution | Tim Holley (VP of Product)
eps.s: Tim Holley has spent more than a decade at Etsy and is now its VP of product. He traces how gross sales grew from about $500 million to over $13 billion: the 2017 culture shift around a single north-star metric, the overnight surge in mask demand during the pandemic, the move from a seller focus to a buyer focus, and specific tactics for conversion, acquisition and retention. He also covers how the brand defines what can be sold, validation beyond A/B tests, and team leadership.
g: VP of product at Etsy; briefly head of product at SoulCycle

eps.t: An inside look at Figma's unique GTM motion | Claire Butler (first GTM hire)
eps.s: Claire Butler was Figma's tenth employee and first marketing hire. She breaks down Figma's bottom-up go-to-market: first make individual designers love the product, through technical credibility, building with users, long-term relationships on Twitter and radical transparency; then let it spread inside companies through a shareable free tier, designer advocates, design systems as an upgrade reason, and internal champions. She also recalls launching before multiplayer was ready, and when this playbook works.
g: Figma's tenth employee and first marketing hire; now leads go-to-market and bottom-up growth

eps.t: The World's Largest AI Processor with Cerebras CEO Andrew Feldman
eps.s: Cerebras CEO Andrew Feldman explains why the company bet on wafer-scale chips and how its dataflow design works. He argues performance should be measured by how long a customer takes to go from model to finished training, not by benchmarks. He also covers the cost of mistakes in chipmaking, GPU shortages caused by TSMC's rigid supply, and why companies will train smaller models on their own data.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Cerebras, which makes wafer-sized AI chips

eps.t: When enough is enough | Andy Johns (ex-FB, Twitter, Quora)
eps.s: Andy Johns ran growth at Facebook, Twitter and Quora, then became president of Wealthfront. At the peak of his career, severe burnout and buried childhood trauma pushed him out of tech and into mental health advocacy. He talks about the body's burnout signals, the four steps of deep change, how to dig for your own truth, daily practice for rewriting old inner stories, and how society trades our individuality for acceptance.
g: Former growth lead at Facebook, Twitter and Quora, ex-Wealthfront president, now a mental health advocate

eps.t: Picking sharp problems, increasing virality, and unique product frameworks | Oji Udezue (Typeform)
eps.s: Oji Udezue is chief product officer at Typeform and previously built products at Microsoft, Atlassian, Calendly and Twitter. He shares a four-box map for picking B2B software ideas based on how many teams a workflow touches and how often it runs. He also explains "sharp problems" and the 3x improvement bar, how to keep listening to customers, onboarding and tiered activation, what virality and network effects really are, his monthly "forest time," and how Bridgewater taught him to read people.
g: Chief product officer at Typeform; previously led product at Calendly, Twitter and Atlassian

eps.t: From Guomao finance bros to a generation's fate: a chat with Wendy, whose memes you've surely seen
eps.ot: 44: 从国贸金融男到一代人的一代命：与你肯定看过她梗图的 Wendy 聊聊
eps.s: Wendy runs Finance Bro, a comedy account on Xiaohongshu (RedNote) whose memes poke fun at finance workers in Beijing, Shanghai and Hong Kong. She talks with Hanyang and Manqi Cheng about the all-out push before she lost her job, finding calm, fighting anxiety and discovering new joys afterward, and how to get by as opportunities shrink. The tagline: we overrate ourselves and underrate the times.
g: Creator of the Xiaohongshu comedy account Finance Bro; former finance professional

eps.t: The Intersection of AI and Blockchain, with Transformers author and NEAR founder Illia Polosukhin
eps.s: Transformer co-author and NEAR founder Illia Polosukhin explains how NEAR pivoted from teaching machines to code to blockchain. He imagines AIs with on-chain accounts becoming economic actors that might even run organizations. He argues the real problem is aligning humans, backs cryptographic signatures and identity to fight AI fakes, and discusses decentralized inference, data-labeling marketplaces and the future of SaaS.
g: Co-founder of the NEAR blockchain and co-author of the Transformer paper

eps.t: How to become a category pirate | Christopher Lochhead (Author of Play Bigger, Niche Down, more)
eps.s: Christopher Lochhead, often called the godfather of category design, argues that legendary companies don't out-compete in existing markets; they design and dominate new categories, and in tech the leader takes roughly three quarters of the value. He explains the "better trap," why product-market fit and positioning are dangerous ideas, how to design a category by reframing the problem and inventing its language, how to think backward from the future, and how lightning-strike marketing and superconsumers drive word of mouth.
g: Category design expert, co-author of Play Bigger and Niche Down, Category Pirates co-founder, three-time public company CMO

eps.t: 50 questions for Kevin Kelly: monopolists and borders, billionaires and life
eps.ot: 对凯文·凯利的50问：垄断者与国界、大富翁与人生
eps.s: Kevin Kelly, author of Out of Control, answers 50 questions during a visit to China: why the next tech monopolist will be an AI company from outside today's giants, when the "mirror world" arrives, whether technology has borders, and whether AI is overrated or underrated. Best of all is his life advice: skip the billion dollars, learn faster, and stay young by changing your mind.
g: Founding executive editor of Wired; author of Out of Control and The Inevitable

eps.t: Becoming evidence-guided | Itamar Gilad (Gmail, YouTube, Microsoft)
eps.s: Former Google PM Itamar Gilad opens with a tale of two products, Google+ and Gmail's tabbed inbox, to show how organizations move from opinion-driven decisions to evidence-guided product work. Following the GIST model from his new book (Goals, Ideas, Steps, Tasks), he walks through North Star metrics and metric trees, ICE scoring and the confidence meter, a ladder of validation methods, and the GIST board, and suggests starting wherever the pain is greatest.
g: Product coach, author of Evidence-Guided, former Google PM on Gmail and YouTube

eps.t: How Replit's AI Tools are Changing Software Development with Co-founder and CEO Amjad Masad
eps.s: Replit CEO Amjad Masad thinks today's AI coding tools are still primitive, and the opportunity lies around the model: context, tool use and agents. He explains why Replit trained and open-sourced its own 3B code model, calls for more backers to follow Meta in funding open-source models, and imagines bounty markets and a built-in currency that let people and AIs earn money by coding.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Replit, a browser-based platform for writing and deploying code

eps.t: NIO, XPeng and Li Auto land on Zhihu, Bilibili and Xiaohongshu: carmakers' content marketing battles
eps.ot: 45: “蔚小理”登陆知乎 /B 站 / 小红书，车企们的内容社区营销战事
eps.s: Sean Yang, CMO of auto marketing agency Indigo Social, talks with Manqi Cheng and Haining Sun about how carmakers market on Zhihu, Bilibili and Xiaohongshu. He covers how his firm started on Zhihu, how community content ads differ from traditional ads, what each platform is good for, and why carmaker budgets make brand-building hard. Best image: good community ads give endorphins, not dopamine.
g: CMO of auto marketing agency Indigo Social; host of the BB Business & Brand podcast

eps.t: How to drive word of mouth | Nilan Peiris (CPO of Wise)
eps.s: About 70% of Wise's new customers come from friends. Chief Product Officer Nilan Peiris explains how: use customer scores to find what drives referrals, make price, speed and ease ten times better, price each transfer on its real cost, let a sincere mission turn customers into helpers, and show people inside the product how much they saved. He also covers building on conviction rather than A/B tests, and running one global codebase with local teams.
g: Chief Product Officer at Wise, the money-transfer company; joined early and has stayed over 11 years

eps.t: Building Anchor, selling to Spotify, and lessons learned | Maya Prohovnik (Head of Podcast Product)
eps.s: Maya Prohovnik was Anchor's first employee and now runs podcast product at Spotify. She walks through Anchor's two big pivots, from voice social app to podcast platform, the early days when college interns submitted users' shows by hand, and what it took to fit into Spotify after the acquisition. She also covers why product teams should make their own podcasts, how gut feel and data work together, and the rarely discussed slump founders hit after selling.
g: Head of podcast product at Spotify; the first employee at podcast tool Anchor

eps.t: If DNA is Code, Can AI Help Write It? Scaling Cell Programming and Synthetic Biology, with Ginkgo Bioworks Co-founder and CEO Jason Kelly
eps.s: Ginkgo Bioworks CEO Jason Kelly probes where the "DNA is code" analogy holds and where it breaks, and describes Ginkgo's model of separating an automated lab "foundry" from DNA programmers, plus the data edge it creates. He argues AI will surpass experts faster in biology than in language, calls for biosurveillance that works like antivirus software, and explains an experiment giving all employees super-voting shares.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Ginkgo Bioworks, a cell-programming and synthetic biology company

eps.t: Working in Africa without a visa: Fengze on construction jobs across different African countries
eps.ot: 46: 没有签证怎么去非洲干活：和丰泽聊聊在非洲不同国家打灰的体验
eps.s: Fengze, an engineer building hydropower projects in Africa, returns to tell Hanyang about two years working in Tanzania, Zambia, Lesotho, South Africa, DR Congo, Zimbabwe, Mozambique and Eswatini. He covers how different each country is, absurd visa and legal rules, the resource curse, birth rates, farming and travel. Most striking: DR Congo's leftover mining waste holds more copper than China's best ore.
g: Engineer working on hydropower and construction projects across Africa

eps.t: Silicon Valley's AI highs and lows, with US tech insiders: the second wave begins
eps.ot: 和美国科技界人士聊硅谷AI的冷与热：第二波浪潮拉开帷幕
eps.s: 309 days after ChatGPT launched, two Chinese-American tech professionals share Silicon Valley's new consensus on AI: a second wave has begun, models alone are no moat, and money is moving into hardware. The most striking shift: tech companies that once kept their distance from Washington are now moving closer.
g: Investor at a top-five US venture capital firm; Chinese immigrant
Works at GitHub; previously on Barack Obama's campaign team

eps.t: What sets great teams apart | Lane Shackleton (CPO of Coda)
eps.s: Lane Shackleton, Chief Product Officer at Coda, boils product work down to turning ambiguity into clarity. He shares the principles he has collected for PMs: systems over goals, cathedrals over bricks, make things instead of talking about them. He also walks through team rituals from Coda and elsewhere, such as labeling how strongly you mean a piece of feedback, parallel review sessions called Catalyst, and two-way docs, plus lessons from his path from AdWords reviewer to CPO.
g: Chief Product Officer at Coda for over eight years; previously a product manager at YouTube

eps.t: Brian Balfour: 10 lessons on career, growth, and life
eps.s: Reforge founder Brian Balfour distills years at HubSpot and Reforge into ten lessons: hire and promote on work, not conversations; plan by picturing the end state; let senior individual contributors stay on the field as captains; treat growth as a connected system; look for white space by doing the opposite; build around use cases, not personas; find sparring partners; and give new bets far more sustained investment than feels natural.
g: Founder and CEO of Reforge; former VP of Growth at HubSpot

eps.t: Inside Linear: Building with taste, craft, and focus | Karri Saarinen (co-founder, designer, CEO)
eps.s: Karri Saarinen, co-founder and CEO of Linear, explains the project-management company's unusual approach: a focus on craft and taste, no A/B tests, no metrics on individual features, a single PM in the whole company, and projects led by engineers and designers. He also covers opinionated software and cycles, staying on the main quest, paid work trials for hiring, and growing through a waitlist, one customer segment at a time.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Linear; formerly principal designer at Airbnb and founding designer at Coinbase

eps.t: "Godfather of Artificial Intelligence" Geoffrey Hinton on the promise, risks of advanced AI
eps.s: On 60 Minutes, Geoffrey Hinton says humanity may be creating something smarter than itself for the first time: these systems really understand, yet we don't truly know how they work. He describes GPT-4 solving a house-painting riddle, weighs medical benefits against job losses, and admits he can't see a path that guarantees safety.
g: Deep learning pioneer and co-winner of the 2019 Turing Award

eps.t: Model Quality, Fine Tuning & Meta Sponsoring Open Source Ecosystem
eps.s: The hosts discuss how today's models could get 10 to 100 times more useful without waiting for bigger ones, and compare what fine-tuning and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) each do. They look at why Meta sponsors open-source models and whether generative AI opens a new window for consumer social, then advise founders to tackle easy, high-value problems first.
g: The two No Priors hosts, both investors

eps.t: VC's big dreams: Minghao Zhuang on the hard times for funds and founders (a crossover episode)
eps.ot: 47: VC的春秋大梦：和明浩聊聊基金和创业的困境 ｜ 串台《屠龙之术》
eps.s: Minghao Zhuang, who left venture capital and started his own podcast, talks again with host Hanyang: why investors keep starting podcasts, what was unusual about GGV splitting up two days before taping, how markets and companies changed, how the view differs from inside a company, and what dollar funds should do. Notes come only from the episode page, which lists questions but not his answers.
g: Former venture capital investor; host of the podcast "Tulong Zhi Shu"

eps.t: How to get press for your product | Jason Feifer (editor in chief of Entrepreneur magazine)
eps.s: Jason Feifer, editor in chief of Entrepreneur magazine, explains from the receiving end how startups get press: decide what the coverage is for, study the publication's mission and the specific writer covering your area, then send a short, clearly personalized pitch. He also covers how to pick a PR firm, why coverage is often worth more as an endorsement than for its readers, ways into a story without being its subject, and his career idea of "opportunity set B."
g: Editor in chief of Entrepreneur magazine, formerly senior editor at Fast Company; author and podcast host

eps.t: From App to Suite to Platform, with HubSpot's Co-Founder Brian Halligan
eps.s: HubSpot co-founder Brian Halligan looks back on the origins of inbound marketing, the bet on small businesses, and the move from a single product to a suite and a platform, along with hiring a COO, handing over the CEO job and building culture. He then explains why AI favors incumbents this time and introduces Propeller, his ocean-climate investment fund.
g: HubSpot co-founder and former CEO; co-founder of ocean-climate fund Propeller Ventures

eps.t: Building beautiful products with Stripe's Head of Design | Katie Dill (Stripe, Airbnb, Lyft)
eps.s: Katie Dill, Head of Design at Stripe, opens with the day her Airbnb team confronted her as a group, and what it taught her about earning trust as a new leader. She argues that quality and beauty drive growth, explains how Stripe walks through and scores its key user journeys, and shares her formula "performance = potential minus interference," plus views on where designers should sit, bold visions, and hiring.
g: Head of Design at Stripe; previously led design at Lyft and experience design at Airbnb

eps.t: NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang
eps.s: Jensen Huang looks back on 30 years of NVIDIA: how Riva 128 survived a near-death moment by simulating everything first, why AlexNet convinced him to bet on deep learning, the "mission is the boss" organization, and entering "$0 billion markets." He also covers AI safety and jobs. The most striking moment: building a company was so painful that he wouldn't do it again.
g: NVIDIA co-founder, CEO since founding it in 1993

eps.t: Car History 01: The world's first gasoline car, a woman driver and Empress Dowager Cixi
eps.ot: 【汽车史话01】世界上第一辆燃油车、女车手和慈禧太后
eps.s: The first episode of the Car History series. Auto investor Junyi Zhang starts in 1886, when the first car with an internal combustion engine was patented, and tells stories of Karl and Bertha Benz, Gottlieb Daimler and Empress Dowager Cixi, drawing lessons about the industry. One rule stands out: every powertrain shift wipes out a batch of companies.
g: Partner at Oliver Wyman; former founding partner of NIO Capital

eps.t: Behind the Chinese edition of Elon Musk's biography, and how new heroes are born (a crossover episode)
eps.ot: 48: 与《马斯克传》总策划人聊新书：幕后故事和新英雄的诞生 ×【串台知本论】
