eps.s: A crossover with CITIC Academy's podcast: Manqi Cheng and host Bingjie Sun talk with Mu Li, who led the Chinese edition of Walter Isaacson's Elon Musk, about the story behind the book, its lessons, how it differs from earlier Musk books, and twenty years of Chinese business bestsellers. Notes come from the episode page, which has no timestamps, so most views aren't tied to a speaker.
g: Deputy editor-in-chief at CITIC Press; led the Chinese edition of Isaacson's Musk biography

eps.t: Scaling Duolingo, embracing failure, and insight into Latin America's tech scene | Gina Gotthilf
eps.s: Gina Gotthilf, former head of growth at Duolingo and co-founder of Latitud, tells her career as an "A side and B side" record. She revisits optimizing landing pages for the Bloomberg presidential campaign, and how Duolingo, a rare consumer subscription success, grew from 3 million to 200 million users with almost no paid ads. She also covers a failed badge experiment, brand voice and mission, one global playbook, and Latin America's tech opportunity.
g: Co-founder and COO of Latitud; previously led growth and marketing at Duolingo

eps.t: Car History 02: Henry Ford the autocrat, and the decline of the Model T, the world's second-best-selling car
eps.ot: 【汽车史话02】集权者福特与全球第二畅销T型车的衰落
eps.s: In the second Car History episode, Junyi Zhang tells the story of Henry Ford, the first billionaire in car history: how the Model T made cars affordable for ordinary people, and why it declined under its founder's autocratic, conservative rule. His take on family businesses stands out: families bring long-term thinking, professional managers bring innovation, and the two need balance.
g: Partner at Oliver Wyman; former founding partner of NIO Capital

eps.t: A step-by-step guide to crafting a sales pitch that wins | April Dunford (author of Sales Pitch)
eps.s: Positioning expert April Dunford returns to walk through the B2B sales pitch structure from her new book "Sales Pitch": start with your view of the market, the pros and cons of the alternatives, and what a perfect solution looks like, then show your differentiated value, proof, and answers to objections. She also explains why so many deals end in no decision, how to arm your internal champion, and why category creation isn't the only path to greatness.
g: Positioning consultant, author of "Obviously Awesome" and "Sales Pitch," former marketing VP at several tech companies

eps.t: What Google Cloud Can Teach Enterprises Developing & Rolling Out AI Tools, With Kawal Gandhi
eps.s: Kawal Gandhi, who leads generative AI in Google Cloud's Office of the CTO, explains how enterprises move generative AI from prototype to production: the order of adoption, which teams go first, and why strategic positioning matters more than technology choices. He also covers TPUs versus GPUs, inference costs and data security.
g: Head of generative AI in Google Cloud's Office of the CTO

eps.t: Car History 03: GM, a breeding ground for management gurus, and a century of American carmakers' highs and lows
eps.ot: 【汽车史话03】从“盛产管理大师”的通用汽车，看美式车企百年荣辱
eps.s: In the third Car History episode, Junyi Zhang uses General Motors as a case study: founder William Durant's buying spree, how Alfred Sloan's divisional structure beat Ford, and the pressures facing GM under Mary Barra. He then turns to China's carmakers, which develop a new car in 24 months versus Germany's 36, but shouldn't bet on piling up brands.
g: Partner at Oliver Wyman; former founding managing partner of NIO Capital

eps.t: What AI means for your product strategy | Paul Adams (CPO of Intercom)
eps.s: Paul Adams, Chief Product Officer at Intercom, starts with two failures of his own: Google's social products and a Cannes talk. The heart of the episode is how Intercom tore up its strategy after ChatGPT launched and bet the company on Fin, its AI customer-service bot, and how to tell whether your own product is in AI's path. He closes with frameworks he uses: differentiation versus table stakes, the pendulum, and product-market-story fit.
g: Chief Product Officer at Intercom; formerly led global brand design at Facebook and did user research at Google

eps.t: AI Threats & Opportunities in Cyber Security With Material Security Co-Founder Ryan Noon
eps.s: Material Security co-founder Ryan Noon explains defense in depth for email and how large language models help triage security signals. He also discusses how AI supercharges attackers, the intelligence arms race between nations, and why the security industry keeps ending with giants buying startups.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Material Security, an email security company

eps.t: Is "3nm" a lie? Can a lithography plant make chips? Bo Wang on common myths about chips
eps.ot: 49: 3nm 是谎言？光刻工厂真能造芯片？与汪波聊芯片行业那些流传的误解
eps.s: Chips became a public topic for reasons outside the industry, and myths spread with them. Bo Wang, author of a popular history of chips and a lecturer at Peking University's Shenzhen graduate school, talks with Manqi Cheng and Jiahao Zhang about what "3nm" really means, whether Moore's Law is a law, the rise of CPUs and GPUs, and the role the US and Japanese governments played early on.
g: Lecturer at Peking University's Shenzhen graduate school of information engineering; author of a history of chips

eps.t: The economics Nobel, and the women over 40 who vanish from the golden career ladder
eps.ot: 谈诺贝尔经济奖与40+消失在黄金阶梯上的女人
eps.s: Starting from the work of Claudia Goldin, the 2023 Nobel laureate in economics, Peking University professor Yaohui Zhao explains why women lead early in their careers but vanish from the promotion ladder around 40. The key idea is the "motherhood penalty": after a child arrives, the pay gap between husband and wife widens. She also discusses how policy can help women balance work and family.
g: Professor at Peking University's National School of Development; studies labor and aging economics

eps.t: Reflections on a movement | Eric Ries (creator of the Lean Startup methodology)
eps.s: Eric Ries, who created the Lean Startup method, looks back on more than a decade of the movement, clears up common misreadings of MVP and pivot, and offers practical advice on when to pivot and when to let go. In the second half he discusses AI as a management technology, deciding under deep uncertainty, and why a company's mission has to be written into its governance so long-term thinking becomes a competitive advantage.
g: Author of The Lean Startup; founder and executive chairman of the Long-Term Stock Exchange (LTSE)

eps.t: #2054 - Elon Musk
eps.s: Musk joins Joe Rogan weeks before the first Cybertruck deliveries. He insists mass production is 100 to 1,000 times harder than design, runs the numbers on solar and EV batteries, explains why he bought Twitter and how X should handle speech, and warns that extreme environmentalism built into AI could be dangerous. He ends on warming Mars and why rockets launch from South Texas.
g: CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, owner of X, weeks before the first Cybertruck deliveries

eps.t: Unpacking Amazon's unique ways of working | Bill Carr (author of Working Backwards)
eps.s: Bill Carr spent 15 years at Amazon and led its digital music and video businesses. He takes apart Amazon's management mechanisms one by one: single-threaded leaders, disagree and commit, working backwards with the PR/FAQ, input metrics instead of revenue targets, Bar Raiser hiring, and the pay and org design that let people take risks. All of these, he stresses, were experiments that emerged as the company grew complex, and adopting them takes CEO backing and sustained effort.
g: Co-author of Working Backwards; former Amazon VP of digital media who led Amazon Music and Prime Video; later COO of OfferUp

eps.t: What is Digital Life? with OpenAI Co-Founder & Chief Scientist Ilya Sutskever
eps.s: OpenAI chief scientist Ilya Sutskever traces his path from an early bet on neural networks to OpenAI's capped-profit structure and the scaling road to GPT-3. He argues reliability is the biggest bottleneck today and that Transformers are enough to reach AGI. He closes with digital life and superalignment.
g: OpenAI co-founder and chief scientist

eps.t: What is it like to have a million followers on Xiaohongshu? Traffic, money and the human tests behind them
eps.ot: 50: 在小红书当百万博主有什么体会和经验？流量与商业化背后的人性考验！
eps.s: Host Hanyang interviewed Kelly Hong, a creator with a million followers on Xiaohongshu (RedNote), for a long article, then recorded this episode for what didn't fit. Taped in April 2023 and released in November, it covers how she went full-time, how Xiaohongshu changed from 2017 to 2023, how it differs from Bilibili, and how sponsorships work. Notes come only from the episode page's questions and headings.
g: Xiaohongshu creator with a million followers; former contestant on the TV show Super Brain

eps.t: EP 85: Alexandr Wang (CEO, ScaleAI): The 26-Year-Old Powering the AI Industry
eps.s: Scale AI founder Alexandr Wang talks with Logan Bartlett just before the UK AI Safety Summit. He covers data as the new code, training on human feedback, companies' private data, exploding model scale and cost, the atomic-bomb analogy, Taiwan's chip risk, regulation and hiring. The standout claim: the next two to three years will shape decades of national power.
g: Founder and CEO of Scale AI, which supplies training data to leading AI labs

eps.t: Mastering product strategy and growing as a PM | Maggie Crowley (Toast, Drift, TripAdvisor)
eps.s: Maggie Crowley, VP of Product at Toast, describes the three things the best product managers have in common, how to make complicated things simple, how to write a product strategy document that runs from mission to priorities, and what a one-page spec must say. She also argues that calling yourself "data-driven" is a red flag and that product frameworks get misused, and shares how she got into the job, grew, and why she writes in public.
g: VP of Product at Toast; previously product roles at TripAdvisor, Drift and Charlie Health; former Olympic speed skater

eps.t: Inside P&G: the rules and secrets of a 186-year-old consumer goods empire
eps.ot: 漫谈宝洁：隐藏在186年消费品王国里的规则和秘密
eps.s: Huainan Wang ran brands at P&G in the US and was coached by former CEO A.G. Lafley. He breaks down how P&G hires and promotes people, manages its brands and decides which businesses to keep, comparing it to a disciplined German army. He also asks why China hasn't yet produced a P&G of its own.
g: Former P&G brand head in the US, later a founder in China, MiraclePlus mentor

eps.t: Marketplace lessons from Uber, Airbnb, Bumble, and more | Ramesh Johari (Stanford professor)
eps.s: Stanford professor Ramesh Johari starts from transaction costs to explain what marketplaces like Uber and Airbnb actually sell, why founders should not think of themselves as marketplace founders too early, and how data science helps find, make and learn from matches. He also covers prediction versus decision-making, building a healthy experimentation culture, why rating systems are still broken, and why AI makes people more important in data science, not less.
g: Stanford professor studying online marketplace design and data science; former head of data science at oDesk (now Upwork)

eps.t: Mistral 7B and the Open Source Revolution With Arthur Mensch, CEO Mistral AI
eps.s: Mistral AI CEO Arthur Mensch goes from the Chinchilla research to Mistral 7B, explaining why models can still shrink and why inference has to be cheap. He defends open research, rebuts regulatory arguments about bioweapons and compute thresholds one by one, argues for composable guardrails to handle safety, and talks about Europe's AI talent.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Mistral AI, a French open-model company

eps.t: #400 – Elon Musk: War, AI, Aliens, Politics, Physics, Video Games, and Humanity
eps.s: Over two-plus hours, Musk and Lex Fridman range from the Israel-Hamas war, Ukraine and US-China tensions to his new chatbot Grok, aliens, X's feed and Community Notes. The standout parts are his concrete AI calls: a good AI must be tested against physics and reality, open models can trail by about six months, and after chips the next shortages are power transformers, then electricity.
g: CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, owner of X, founder of xAI, maker of the Grok chatbot

eps.t: “My God, This Is a Transformative Power” (People I (Mostly) Admire, Ep. 118)
eps.s: Fei-Fei Li tells the story of ImageNet: her 2007 bet that data mattered more than algorithms, which almost nobody believed in, until a neural network trained on it halved the error rate in 2012. She also recalls immigrating at 15, running a dry-cleaning shop through college to support her family, being tempted by money but choosing science, and how AI misuse should be handled.
g: Stanford computer science professor, co-director of its Human-Centered AI Institute, creator of ImageNet

eps.t: The first Singles' Day without Daniel Zhang: tricks, a free-for-all and open schemes
eps.ot: 失去逍遥子的第一个双十一：诡计、大混战与小阳谋
eps.s: The 15th Singles' Day, China's biggest shopping festival, and the first since Daniel Zhang left Alibaba. Former Taobao Live operations head Yuanyuan Zhao reviews the platforms' all-out brawl, who actually does the buying, the rise and fall of superstar livestreamers, and how Chinese e-commerce has changed over 15 years. A standout claim: online shopping was designed around women.
g: Former head of operations at Taobao Live, who helped launch top livestreamers Viya and Austin Li

eps.t: Brian Chesky's new playbook
eps.s: Airbnb co-founder and CEO Brian Chesky explains how he reorganized the company: merging product managers with product marketing, moving from business divisions back to a startup-style functional structure, and insisting that leaders stay in the details. He also talks about marketing as education, the "add a zero" exercise, the new Guest Favorites feature, and how he schedules his time to avoid burning out.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Airbnb

eps.t: The Worlds She Sees with Godmother of AI, Fei-Fei Li
eps.s: Fei-Fei Li tells Vijay Pande how she went from Chengdu to New Jersey, ran a dry cleaner while studying physics, and bet on data to build ImageNet with global crowdsourcing. She then turns to risk and policy: misuse worries her more than extinction, universities need public investment, and she hopes AI can bring a "dignity economy."
g: Stanford professor, co-director of Stanford's Human-Centered AI Institute, creator of ImageNet

eps.t: Scale AI's Alexandr Wang on the most powerful technological advancement of our time (Spotlight On: AI, S1E5)
eps.s: Accel's Dan Levine talks with Scale AI founder Alexandr Wang about building in AI. Wang explains why data, not algorithms, is AI's bottleneck, how far scaling laws may go, and what founders should do: avoid crowded niches, don't build too far ahead, and hold slightly irrational conviction. Highlights: Midjourney and Edison's phonograph as proof that big opportunities rarely look obvious at first.
g: Founder and CEO of Scale AI, data infrastructure for the AI industry

eps.t: The ultimate guide to product operations | Melissa Perri and Denise Tilles
eps.s: Melissa Perri and Denise Tilles, authors of Product Operations, lay out this emerging role: its three pillars, how it differs from product managers and program managers, where companies at different stages should start, how big the team should be, and whom to hire. Melissa also uses Athenahealth as a case study for building product ops in an organization with hundreds of product managers.
g: Founder of Produx Labs, teaches product management at Harvard, co-author of Product Operations
Product leader, coach, and consultant; teaches product ops at Produx Labs; co-author of Product Operations

eps.t: AI Agents That Reason and Code with Imbue Co-Founders Kanjun Qiu and Josh Albrecht
eps.s: Imbue's two co-founders explain why they build agents that act on people's behalf. They see reliability as the core bottleneck and reasoning as a set of error-correction techniques, and discuss how to evaluate coding agents and why they started with code. They envision everyone programming in natural language, with small teams using compute to write more and better software.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Imbue, which builds AI agents that reason and code
Co-founder and CTO of Imbue

eps.t: The small details of taking over a 10-billion-yuan fund: Bob Xu and his disciples
eps.ot: 接班百亿基金的琐碎小事：徐小平和他的门徒
eps.s: ZhenFund partner Yuan Liu gives an insider's account of how Bob Xu handed the fund to a younger generation: how Liu joined as the "fourth disciple," how power changed hands, how the partnership works, and how the firm studies founders. A highlight is the "hairy crab" theory of why big-company executives can disappoint as founders. Recorded in 2022.
g: Partner at ZhenFund, an angel investment firm; joined in 2014

eps.t: Redefining success, money, and belonging | Paul Millerd (The Pathless Path)
eps.s: Paul Millerd, author of The Pathless Path, talks about noticing the "default script" you may be living by, and how to find work you'd happily keep doing without betting everything: sabbaticals, small side experiments, and a new relationship with money. He also shares his real income curve in the years after quitting, how he lives with fear, and why he thinks work itself is becoming more gig-like.
g: Author of The Pathless Path, former management consultant, founder of StrategyU, independent writer and podcaster

eps.t: OpenAI's power struggle: the cast, Silicon Valley's elite politics and the irony of it all
eps.ot: OpenAI的权力游戏：脸谱、硅谷精英政治与讽刺意味
eps.s: Four days after OpenAI's board fired Sam Altman, PingWest founder Yihang Luo walks through the "coup": how it unfolded, who sat on the board, and why the company's unusual governance design failed. He also discusses Silicon Valley's elite politics and where Chinese professionals stand in it. One contrast stands out: Silicon Valley sided with Altman, while Chinese opinion favored the scientist Ilya Sutskever.
g: Founder of tech media outlet PingWest, who travels back and forth between China and Silicon Valley

eps.t: 'Hard Fork': An Interview With Sam Altman
eps.ol: Hard Fork (New York Times), rebroadcast on The Daily
eps.s: Recorded in mid-November 2023, two days before OpenAI's board fired him, Altman looks back on ChatGPT's breakout year and covers reliability, guardrails, regulation, copyright and ads. He defines real AGI as AI that does original science, and warns that AI may become superhumanly persuasive well before that.
g: CEO of OpenAI, one year after ChatGPT's launch

eps.t: Billion dollar failures, and billion dollar success | Tom Conrad (Quibi, Pandora, Pets.com, Zero)
eps.s: Tom Conrad went from writing the Finder at Apple to CTO of Pandora, VP of Product at Snap, Chief Product Officer of Quibi and now CEO of Zero. He walks through two famous failures, Pets.com and Quibi, and successes like Pandora and Snap. His core lesson: a company is an equation that turns investment into returns. He also covers choosing jobs, how deep a product CEO should go, avoiding burnout, and why he thinks there are too many founders.
g: CEO of Zero Longevity Science; former CPO of Quibi, VP of Product at Snap, CTO of Pandora; Sonos board member

eps.t: NIO, XPeng and Li Auto looking back: the bosses, their moves and their brushes with death (car history bonus episode)
eps.ot: 闲话蔚小理往事：大佬、出牌、生死时局【汽车史话番外】
eps.s: Pan Wang, one of the first writers to cover China's EV startups, retells eight years of NIO, XPeng and Li Auto: getting in around 2014, hunting for people and money, painful early deliveries, a near-death moment in 2019, an unexpected rise, and new troubles for all three CEOs in 2023. A surprise: Li Auto started out as the least likely to succeed.
g: One of the first writers to follow China's electric-car startups

eps.t: Open AI leadership shuffle, new diffusion models, and starting the cult of Q*
eps.s: Sarah and Elad look back at the lessons of the OpenAI board crisis and why companies are starting to use models from several vendors. They explain why diffusion models and video generation are taking off, and how AI could turn labor-heavy services revenue into more profitable software revenue.
g: The two No Priors co-hosts, both investors in AI companies

eps.t: The future of AI in software development | Inbal Shani (CPO of GitHub)
eps.s: GitHub's Chief Product Officer Inbal Shani on how AI is changing software development: Copilot is a copilot, not a pilot, developers need to shift toward systems and architecture thinking, and AI-generated testing is badly underrated. She also covers the common mistakes companies make when adopting AI, how Copilot was designed and measured, how GitHub Next drives innovation, and the lessons she learned the hard way leading change.
g: Chief Product Officer at GitHub; former general manager at AWS and Microsoft, engineer at Amazon Robotics

eps.t: Crafting a compelling product vision | Ebi Atawodi (YouTube, Netflix, Uber)
eps.s: YouTube product director Ebi Atawodi lays out how to craft and spread a product vision: the four ingredients of a good one, several storytelling techniques, her empathize-create-evangelize sequence, and the "ten things you should know" list. She boils the product manager's craft down to clarity and conviction, compares how the cultures at Uber, Netflix and Google shaped their products, and shares the values she leads her teams by.
g: Director of Product at YouTube for creator experience; previously product director at Netflix and led Uber's wallet and payments

eps.t: The full-stack PM | Anuj Rathi (Swiggy, Jupiter Money, Flipkart)
eps.s: Anuj Rathi, Chief Product and Marketing Officer at Jupiter Money and former growth lead at Swiggy, explains what makes product management in India different and lays out his "full-stack" toolkit: design onboarding for users who are lazy, vain and selfish, align the whole company with a one-page press release and show-don't-tell journeys, and split resources with his 4B framework. He also covers the peculiar problems of three-sided marketplaces and his three-way diagnosis of team failures.
g: Chief Product and Marketing Officer at Jupiter Money; former SVP at Swiggy, Flipkart's first product manager

eps.t: AI is the new enterprise UI with Clara Shih, CEO Salesforce AI
eps.s: Clara Shih, CEO of Salesforce AI, explains Salesforce's open approach to models and its Copilot platform. She thinks enterprise adoption is still early, and uses Gucci's customer service to show what retrieval-augmented AI can do. She also covers where AI as the new interface stops and why pricing has to come down to clear ROI.
g: CEO of Salesforce AI, running the enterprise software company's AI business

eps.t: How are China's Gen Z founders doing? Their nerve, their high "Musk score" and reality
eps.ot: 95后、00后创业者怎么样了？他们的生猛、高马斯克值与现实
eps.s: Born in 1997, Yachen Song was an early co-founder of MiniMax and later started VAST, a 3D generation company. He describes what drives founders born after 1995 and 2000, why their idol has shifted from Steve Jobs to Elon Musk, and how their brashness copes with a harsh fundraising climate. A memorable idea: the "Musk score," the nerve to set enormous goals.
g: Founder of 3D generation startup VAST and an early co-founder of AI company MiniMax

eps.t: Radical Candor: From theory to practice with author Kim Scott
eps.s: Radical Candor author Kim Scott takes the idea from theory to practice: place yourself on the two-by-two of caring personally and challenging directly, and avoid the most common failure, ruinous empathy. Feedback should be humble, immediate and in person, and you should learn to ask for criticism and reward it before you give it. She also criticizes Bridgewater-style "candor" and tells the story that led to her next book, Radical Respect.
g: Author of Radical Candor; former CEO coach at Dropbox and Twitter, Apple University faculty, and Google AdSense lead

eps.t: Geopolitics and the car industry: has China become the top car exporter? Don't waste a good crisis
eps.ot: 地缘政治与大国汽车：中国跃居第一出口国？别浪费大危机
eps.s: Junyi Zhang explains how China's car exports took off during the pandemic and overtook Japan's as the world's largest. Drawing on how Japanese carmakers used the 1970s oil crisis to break into America, Zhang weighs the opportunities and risks for Chinese carmakers going global. The key difference: Japan was a bystander then, while China sits at the center of today's great-power rivalry.
g: Partner at consultancy Oliver Wyman, formerly founding managing partner of NIO Capital

eps.t: How AI can help small businesses
eps.s: Former Square CEO Alyssa Henry talks about how AI can give small merchants the marketing and back-office help they lack, and how physical stores go digital. Drawing on her years at AWS, she weighs how cloud providers and model companies will shake out, why open source is hard to monetize, and why every chip wave has a clear number one and two.
g: Former CEO of Square, previously an executive at AWS

eps.t: What's it like helping rich people get richer? A wealth manager on what the job really involves
eps.ot: 52: “帮有钱人变得更有钱”是什么体验？与从业者聊聊财富管理在管什么
eps.s: After collapsing peer-to-peer lenders, frozen rural bank deposits, the Zhongzhi group's troubles, a falling property market and the stock market's struggle to hold 3,000 points, many Chinese saw their savings shrink. Manqi Cheng talks with a wealth manager using the pseudonym Zhaocai about how the money climate has changed, advice for people with different amounts to invest, and what helping the rich get richer feels like.
g: Wealth manager who looks after clients' money (pseudonym)

eps.t: How to tell better stories | Matthew Dicks (Storyworthy)
eps.s: Matthew Dicks, author of Storyworthy and a many-time Moth StorySlam champion, explains how to tell a good story. Every story turns on a five-second moment of change, so start from the ending and work back. He covers how to build stakes, how to use stories at work, learnable formulas for humor, his nightly habit of recording one moment from the day, how to handle nerves, and why to say yes first.
g: Author of Storyworthy, elementary school teacher, 59-time Moth StorySlam champion, corporate storytelling coach

eps.t: Human nature at work: envy, our most taboo emotion, and how it simmers in the workplace
eps.ot: 【职场人性】论嫉妒：人类最禁忌的情感，在职场里暗涌
eps.s: Yajun Wang, founder of Jingmen Management and former chief strategy officer of Longfor Group, talks openly about the workplace emotion nobody mentions: envy. Where it comes from, how it runs through every level of a company, how office layouts and company rules amplify it, and how individuals and managers can cope. His sharpest point: remove one source of envy and people invent another.
g: Founder of Jingmen Management; former chief strategy officer of property developer Longfor Group

eps.t: Jason Fried challenges your thinking on fundraising, goals, growth, and more
eps.s: Jason Fried, co-founder and CEO of 37signals, pushes back on startup orthodoxy: no fundraising, no growth targets, no long-term plans, and a team of about 75 that has kept Basecamp and HEY profitable for over twenty years. He explains the six-week "appetite" rule in Shape Up, why he trusts gut decisions, how to bootstrap, and ONCE, a new line of pay-once software.
g: Co-founder and CEO of 37signals, maker of Basecamp and HEY

eps.t: The essence of product management | Christian Idiodi (SVPG)
eps.s: SVPG partner Christian Idiodi explains why product managers are so often disliked, why a PM's first job is value risk, and his favorite discovery method: working with a handful of reference customers until they will publicly vouch for the product. He also covers borrowing trust to establish yourself fast, why managers must coach daily, why not to promote people before they've done the job, and his work spreading product thinking in Africa.
g: Partner at Silicon Valley Product Group (SVPG), founder of Innovate Africa Foundation

eps.t: The case for AI optimism
eps.s: Reid Hoffman makes the case for AI optimism: AI is a steam engine of the mind, and a doctor and tutor in every phone is the biggest access opportunity around. He pushes back on doomers and the extinction-risk statement, urges white-collar workers to start using AI now, introduces Inflection's Pi, and argues for governing while building rather than regulating first.
g: Co-founder of LinkedIn and Inflection AI, partner at the venture firm Greylock

eps.t: A nursing home shouldn't be an island: a young founder's six years building elder care
eps.ot: 53: 养老院不是一座孤岛，一名 90 后的 6 年养老创业故事 | 「2023 年终讲」合作系列
eps.s: The first episode in a year-end series with Dragon TV and Yicai. Jialin Dai, born in the 1990s, once researched 3D-printed organ repair in Australia, then returned to China in 2016 to work in elder care. She has run a nursing home in Ya'an, Sichuan, for over four years and is building a second. She talks about running it, efforts to mix old and young, and how new technology could change elder care.
g: Founder of the elder care company Shouyang, running a nursing home in Ya'an, Sichuan

eps.t: From Saudi Arabia's grand visions to portraits of Chinese fortune-seekers in the Middle East
eps.ot: 从萨特曼的宏大叙事，聊到赴中东掘金的中国人肖像
eps.s: Jiacheng Capital founding partner Li Li led a 16-day trip to four cities in three Middle Eastern countries and interviewed more than 100 people. She traces the waves of Chinese heading to the region, sketches five types of Chinese living there, and covers market differences, business culture and startup opportunities. A key insight: in Saudi Arabia and its neighbors, government ambitions drive the market.
g: Founding partner of investment firm Jiacheng Capital and author of the book Light Company

eps.t: Four stories: the 2023 year-end episode
eps.ot: 54: 四个故事 【2023 年终节目】
eps.s: LatePost's 2023 year-end special. Host Hanyang tells four stories, tagged wandering around, an office chair, hot-pot mutton and making art, and wishes listeners a happy new year. The episode page doesn't describe the stories. It only adds further reading: his piece on food in Changchun, Yang Li's piece on Hong Kong, an earlier episode on hydropower, and a few books.
g: Host of LatePost's podcast and a LatePost writer

eps.t: The hierarchy of engagement | Sarah Tavel (Benchmark, Greylock, Pinterest)
eps.s: Benchmark partner and Pinterest's first product manager Sarah Tavel breaks down her two frameworks: the hierarchy of engagement for consumer products (core action, retention, self-perpetuation) and the hierarchy of marketplaces (focus, tip, dominate). Using Pinterest, YouTube, REKKI, Hipcamp and DoorDash, she explains why to track real engagement rather than vanity metrics like MAU and GMV, and why she likes markets that look small but have a current pushing them forward.
g: General partner at Benchmark; previously an investor at Greylock and Pinterest's first product manager

eps.t: From zero to 4.7 million: Li Cheng on the boom in Chinese car exports
eps.ot: 55: 从 0 到 470 万，与车云程里聊中国汽车出海大爆发
eps.s: China was expected to export about 4.7 million cars in 2023, and a photo of Toyota chief Akio Toyoda passing BYD's booth made the rounds. Li Cheng, founder of auto media site Cheyun, visited the Munich and Tokyo motor shows that year. With Manqi Cheng he traces three phases of Chinese car exports, what's new this time, and his view: the cars are strong, but brand and culture need time.
g: Founder of auto media sites Cheyun and Diandongbang; former editor-in-chief of Tencent Auto

eps.t: Strategies for becoming less distractible and improving focus | Nir Eyal
eps.s: Nir Eyal, author of Hooked and Indistractable, explains how to become harder to distract. Distraction, he argues, is mostly an escape from internal discomfort, not a product of phone notifications. He offers a four-step framework and concrete tools: the ten-minute rule, a timeboxed calendar, and several kinds of pacts. He then describes what an indistractable workplace needs, and why he objects to calling ordinary phone use addiction.
g: Writer on behavioral design; author of the bestsellers Hooked and Indistractable

eps.t: Guangmi Li on a year of global AI models: humanity's $100 billion science bet and an uneven US-China landscape
eps.ot: 口述全球大模型这一年：人类千亿科学豪赌与参差的中美景观
eps.s: Shixiang founder Guangmi Li looks back on 2023's global AI race. Real capability sits with three labs, OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, and matching GPT-4 is the ticket to the finals. He calls it a $100 billion bet pushed by a few scientists, paid for by tech giants. He runs the cost numbers, maps the alliances, weighs open versus closed models, and predicts a new Moore's law era: ever smarter, ever cheaper.
g: Founder of Shixiang, who spent most of 2023 in Silicon Valley investing in AI model companies

eps.t: The UX Research reckoning is here | Judd Antin (Airbnb, Meta)
eps.s: Judd Antin, who ran research and design at Airbnb, explains why he says user research is facing a reckoning: too much interesting-but-unusable work, researchers treated as a service desk called in at the end, and plenty of "user-centered performance." His fix: researchers need many methods and business fluency, and companies must embed research from start to finish. He also rebuts common PM complaints and argues NPS should give way to a plain satisfaction question.
g: Former head of research and design studio at Airbnb, early Facebook research team builder, now independent advisor

eps.t: Four questions for a (partial) look back at 2023 in business: a crossover with Yicai's business podcast
eps.ot: 56: 四个问题（不完全）回顾 2023 商业事件 | 串台（挖坑）《商业就是这样》
eps.s: The first episode of 2024, a year-end crossover with Yicai's podcast "Business Is Like That." Each side poses four questions; this episode airs answers from its hosts Wenjie Xiao and Yue Xiaoya. Topics include choosing what to cover in its history series and the Tencent–Qihoo 360 feud, Alibaba's shake-up, and car exports from early optimism to late-year risks. Only points the page attributes to a speaker are included.
g: Co-host of Yicai's podcast "Business Is Like That"
Co-host of Yicai's podcast "Business Is Like That"

eps.t: A live event with Xiao Lin: living better as one small person in cycles no one controls
eps.ot: 与小Lin的线下活动｜不可控周期中，提高微小个体的生命质量
eps.s: After publishing her book Shishi, Bilibili finance creator Xiao Lin spoke at a live event about her path from a New York investment bank to a startup to making videos, and how she creates hit content. She also discusses how ordinary people can live better through economic cycles they can't control, and why everyone should understand a bit of finance.
g: Bilibili finance video creator, former JPMorgan investment banker, author of Shishi (Tides of the Times)

eps.t: The engineering mindset | Will Larson (Carta, Stripe, Uber, Calm, Digg)
eps.s: Carta CTO Will Larson starts with how engineering management changed after the zero-interest-rate era, then covers how to use systems thinking without falling into its traps, why good engineering strategy is usually boring, and how he wrote about a thousand essays alongside demanding jobs. He also shares how to get engineering and product managers on the same side, how to report engineering efficiency to a board, what makes values real, and the Digg V4 rewrite disaster he lived through.
g: CTO of Carta, former engineering leader at Stripe, Uber and Calm, author of An Elegant Puzzle and Staff Engineer

eps.t: How to be more innovative | Sam Schillace (Microsoft deputy CTO, creator of Google Docs)
eps.s: Sam Schillace, Microsoft's deputy CTO and co-founder of Writely (which became Google Docs), talks about how disruptive innovation actually happens: spotting good ideas that look dumb, why optimism is a deliberate choice, running cheap experiments at the edges, and his rule that users are lazy. Later he covers career choices, why younger people fear failure more, and how he expects AI to reshape software.
g: Microsoft corporate VP and deputy CTO, co-founder of Writely (later Google Docs), former Box engineering SVP

eps.t: A No Priors clip show: the best of 2023
eps.s: A best-of-2023 compilation, not a new interview. Clips come from Ilya Sutskever, Alyssa Henry, Mustafa Suleyman, Daphne Koller, Reid Hoffman, Noam Shazeer, Arthur Mensch and Jensen Huang, covering OpenAI's capped-profit structure, AI for small businesses, guardrails on open-source models, and how Nvidia balances getting products out the door with long-term exploration.

eps.t: Unconfuse Me with Bill Gates, Episode 6: Sam Altman
eps.s: Just after the board crisis, Bill Gates and Altman cover what AI must master in the next two years, a plan to oversee only the world's biggest compute clusters, the collapsing cost of intelligence, and AI's effect on jobs. The surprise: everyone expected AI to replace manual work first and creative work last, and the opposite happened.
g: CEO of OpenAI, speaking just after the November 2023 board crisis

eps.t: Taking control of your career | Ethan Evans (Amazon)
eps.s: Former Amazon VP Ethan Evans explains how to take charge of your career: his "magic loop" for getting promoted, why senior managers get stuck, how to invent systematically, and how to stand out in interviews. He also revisits the botched Appstore launch that enraged Jeff Bezos and how he won back trust, the Amazon ownership principle he helped write, and his contrarian bet on remote work.
g: Former Amazon VP who helped launch Prime Video, Appstore and Prime Gaming, now executive coach and instructor

eps.t: What is African farming really missing? Yi Li on her 165 acres in Kenya
eps.ot: 57: 非洲农业不发达，到底都是缺点啥？和李奕聊聊她在肯尼亚的一千亩地
eps.s: This episode took half a year to arrange. Yi Li, a former McKinsey consultant, now farms about 1,000 mu (roughly 165 acres) in Kenya. She talks with host Hanyang about what farming in Africa actually involves, whether the land is rich or poor, getting along with locals and selling produce, and moving from consulting to the fields. Notes come only from the episode page, which lists questions, not answers.
g: Runs a farm of about 165 acres in Kenya; former McKinsey consultant and podcast host

eps.t: Do PDD and Miniso's rise mean shoppers are trading down? Miniso's road to going global
eps.ot: 拼多多、名创优品崛起，是消费降级胜利吗？漫谈名创全球化之路
eps.s: Business writer Shuaibo Shen, who is writing a book on Miniso, starts with how he researches China's county towns, then traces how Miniso perfected a single store before opening worldwide. He asks whether consumers are really trading down, what mindset Chinese brands need abroad, and which two paths consumer brands can take. A twist: Western luxury is royal goods made available to commoners.
g: Business writer, author of The Trillion-Yuan Business Hidden in County Towns

eps.t: The art and wisdom of changing teams | Heidi Helfand (Author of Dynamic Reteaming)
eps.s: Heidi Helfand, author of Dynamic Reteaming, argues that team change is unavoidable, so rather than chasing permanent stability, learn to do change well. She walks through five patterns of reteaming, how to run a transparent reorg and make decision rights clear, how isolated teams incubate new products, how pairing and rotation spread knowledge, and the common anti-patterns. She closes with the three levels of listening from coach training.
g: Author of Dynamic Reteaming and reteaming consultant; early employee at Expertcity and AppFolio, later at Procore

eps.t: Coding in Collaboration with AI with Sourcegraph CTO Beyang Liu
eps.s: Sourcegraph CTO Beyang Liu explains why retrieving the right context is the key to the AI coding assistant Cody, and how to design the retrieval pipeline. He goes from removing developer toil to a future "AI engineer" and the reliability problem of chained tasks, argues for simple baselines and small models, and closes on coordination and the skills that will matter more.
g: Co-founder and CTO of Sourcegraph, a code search company

eps.t: Good Strategy, Bad Strategy | Richard Rumelt
eps.s: Strategy scholar Richard Rumelt breaks down the kernel of good strategy and the usual diseases of bad strategy, and suggests dropping the word altogether in favor of an "action agenda": pick the one challenge that is both important and solvable, then attack it with focus and an edge others lack. He also covers how office politics kills strategy, why founders should treat strategy as a bet, and why reading history beats theory for building judgment.
g: Strategy scholar, professor emeritus at UCLA Anderson, author of Good Strategy Bad Strategy and The Crux

eps.t: Geoffrey Moore on finding your beachhead, crossing the chasm, and dominating a market
eps.s: Crossing the Chasm author Geoffrey Moore revisits the technology adoption life cycle: why visionary customers can't save you, how to pick a beachhead that is big enough to matter but small enough to win, and the different playbooks for the early market, bowling alley, tornado and main street. He argues sales must center on the customer's compelling reason to buy, that positive cash flow marks the crossing, and that the model fits B2B best.
g: Management consultant, author of Crossing the Chasm and Inside the Tornado

eps.t: Building the factories of the future with Covariant CEO Peter Chen
eps.s: Covariant co-founder and CEO Peter Chen talks about foundation models for robots: why data, not architecture, is the real advantage, why warehouse picking is the starting point, why simulation isn't enough, what a ChatGPT moment for robotics would take, and how people and robots will split the work in future factories.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Covariant, a robotics AI company

eps.t: A Light Year co-founder starts over: Jinhui Yuan on what AI infrastructure actually does
eps.ot: 58: 光年之外联创再出发，与袁进辉聊 AI Infra 到底做什么？| AI 大爆炸
eps.s: The first episode of the "AI Big Bang" series. Jinhui Yuan founded OneFlow and co-founded Light Year. After Meituan bought Light Year, he started again with SiliconFlow, which builds software for running large models. He talks with Manqi Cheng and Qianming He about failing and trying again, what an AI framework is, why he moved from training to running models, selling pure software in China, and what makes AI infrastructure hard to copy.
g: Founder of SiliconFlow; earlier founded OneFlow and co-founded Light Year

eps.t: Managing nerves, anxiety, and burnout | Jonny Miller (Nervous Systems Mastery)
eps.s: Nervous-system coach Jonny Miller explains how to handle nerves, anxiety and burnout: change your body's state before arguing with your thoughts, use breath as a switch to calm down or wake up, and train your sense of what's happening inside your body. He introduces "emotional debt" and a feather-brick-dump-truck warning model for burnout, argues emotions are information for good decisions, and says burnout costs far more than people think.
g: Founder of the Nervous System Mastery course, coaching tech workers on regulating body and mind

eps.t: The real 1990s Shanghai behind Blossoms Shanghai: dangerous Huanghe Road and the early stock market
eps.ot: 《繁花》真实版上海90年代：充满危险气息的黄河路和股市
eps.s: Riding the hit TV series Blossoms Shanghai, Shanghai-born economist Jie Liang mixes personal memories with expertise to recreate the 1990s: the gangland air of Huanghe Road, the chaos of the newly reopened Shanghai Stock Exchange, and China's first stock market takeover battle. The show's big takeover fight turns out to be based on that real event.
g: Associate professor at Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, economist and Shanghai native

eps.t: The Copilot for Ecommerce with Shopify VP of Core Product Glen Coates
eps.s: Shopify's VP of Core Product Glen Coates describes the reorganization after the 2020 checkout "code red," how to avoid duplicate systems, and how Shopify builds AI as a merchant partner that suggests but never submits, using structured product data and semantic search to lift sales. He also maps the search race among ChatGPT, Google and Perplexity.
g: Shopify's VP of Core Product and founder of the B2B e-commerce platform Handshake

eps.t: Will AI-made 3D get its TikTok moment? VAST on a future where anyone can create in 3D
eps.ot: 59: AI 3D 生成会有“抖音时刻”吗？与 VAST 聊人人玩 3D 的未来 | AI 大爆炸
eps.s: The second "AI Big Bang" episode, on AI that generates 3D. VAST, founded in early 2023, sends CEO Yachen Song and CTO Ding Liang to discuss its first product, Tripo, how 3D differs from text and images, when 3D gets a Midjourney-style tool breakthrough and a TikTok-style platform, competition, and pairing young founders with veterans. Both guests' views are grouped under Yachen Song.
g: Founder and CEO of AI 3D startup VAST (notes merged with CTO Ding Liang)

eps.t: Wu Xiaobo on a short history of Chinese entrepreneurs: if big business dries up, young people should live the life they like
eps.ot: 和吴晓波聊中国企业家小史：如果未来没有大生意，年轻人不如过自己喜欢的人生
eps.s: Business writer Wu Xiaobo traces the generations of Chinese entrepreneurs since the country opened up its economy. He argues society is entering a conservative era and that today's "sixth wave" of founders is in an unusual spot. He also suggests that if AI leaves fewer big opportunities, young people should stop chasing fantasies and live the life they like.
g: Business writer whose new book, a biography of the liquor maker Moutai, had just come out

eps.t: Lessons from Atlassian | Megan Cook (Head of Product, Jira)
eps.s: Megan Cook, head of product for Jira, shares how Atlassian works: fighting fear on teams with play and psychological safety, how remote teams plan in-person gatherings and protect deep-work time, and how winning executive support is a journey, including for unglamorous work like raising user satisfaction. She also explains the stage gates Atlassian used to incubate 15 product lines, how Jira stays ahead, and her own missed chance to build an automation platform.
g: Head of product for Jira at Atlassian

eps.t: Even Northeasterners should get to know the Northeast again: Fengze and Zhongqing on China's northeast, recorded there
eps.ot: 60: 东北人也应该再次了解东北：和丰泽、重轻一起在东北聊聊东北
eps.s: Host Hanyang returns to a favorite subject: China's northeast. He and fellow Northeasterners Fengze and Zhongqing have toured the region for four years making episodes. Recorded there, this one answers listener questions about Harbin's tourism boom, comparing the Nordic countries with the Northeast, wedding gifts, what the Northeast is, whether you can go home again, and where to go and eat. By its own account, it is "very subjective."
g: Northeasterner and hydropower engineer working in Africa (notes merge all three speakers)

eps.t: Inside OpenAI | Logan Kilpatrick (head of developer relations)
eps.s: Logan Kilpatrick, who runs developer relations at OpenAI, explains how the company actually works: why the team was back at work days after the board crisis, where its speed comes from, and why the research team is kept deliberately small. He also talks about which products startups should avoid building, why good prompting is mostly about giving context, where GPTs and agents are heading, and why GPT-5 won't change everything.
g: Head of developer relations at OpenAI, formerly a machine learning engineer at Apple

eps.t: Build AI products at on-AI companies with Emily Glassberg Sands from Stripe
eps.s: Emily Glassberg Sands, Stripe's head of information, explains how a company that isn't an AI company got employees using LLMs at scale, spun up apps with time-boxed accelerator teams, and built natural-language assistants into Radar and Sigma. She looks ahead to financial foundation models and an "economic operating system," and notes that AI startups are monetizing earlier than ever.
g: Head of Information at Stripe, covering data science, growth and ML infrastructure

eps.t: Making time for what matters | Jake Knapp and John Zeratsky (Authors of Make Time, Character VC)
eps.s: Jake Knapp and John Zeratsky, authors of Sprint and Make Time, explain how to make room for what matters: not by handling busywork faster, but by changing the defaults your company and your phone hand you. Build each day around one highlight, then run the highlight-laser-energize-reflect loop as an experiment. They share concrete tactics like deleting apps, staying logged out, cutting the internet and slowing email, and explain where the five-day design sprint came from.
g: Author of Sprint and Make Time, co-founder of VC firm Character, Gmail designer and Google Meet co-founder
Author of Sprint and Make Time, co-founder of Character, former GV partner and Google product designer

eps.t: Meta's AI Chief Yann LeCun on AGI, Open-Source, and AI Risk
eps.s: Ahead of the TIME100 Impact Awards in Dubai, TIME's Billy Perrigo asks Yann LeCun about the limits of language models, Meta's AI goals, open source and AI risk. Highlights: his math showing a four-year-old has seen 50 times more data than a model's entire training text, and why he finds the idea of AI wanting to dominate us preposterous.
g: Meta's chief AI scientist, honored at the TIME100 Impact Awards for decades of AI work

eps.t: RAG is the key for smarter productivity tools with Notion CEO Ivan Zhao
eps.s: Notion co-founder and CEO Ivan Zhao talks about software as Lego blocks, why GPT-4 made him bet the company, and how retrieval features like Notion Q&A mean people no longer need to organize their information. He also uses software history's cycles of bundling and unbundling to explain why the AI era is bundling again.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Notion, the notes and collaboration software

eps.t: Building a world-class sales org | Jason Lemkin (SaaStr)
eps.s: SaaStr founder Jason Lemkin walks through building a B2B sales team from scratch: founders close the first ten customers themselves, hire two reps you would buy from, and only bring in a VP of Sales once both hit quota. He also covers how to split the roadmap between product and sales, why customer success and product teams shouldn't be turned into revenue tools, the myths around trials and annual contracts, and why big conferences lose money.
g: Founder of SaaStr and investor; co-founder and CEO of EchoSign, later acquired by Adobe

eps.t: How Netflix builds a culture of excellence | Elizabeth Stone (CTO)
eps.s: Elizabeth Stone, Netflix's CTO and an economist by training, talks about what economic thinking offers a tech company, how she rose quickly at several companies, and how she holds teams to a high bar. She explains Netflix's culture in detail: talent density comes before candor and "freedom and responsibility," the keeper test replaces performance reviews, and hiring means finding people who raise the whole team. She also explains why Netflix's centralized, full-stack data team can stay objective.
g: Netflix CTO, formerly its VP of Data and Insights and Lyft's VP of Science; PhD in economics

eps.t: Improving search with RAG architecture with Pinecone CEO Edo Liberty
eps.s: Pinecone builds a vector database, which finds information by meaning rather than keywords. Founder and CEO Edo Liberty explains its role in retrieval-augmented generation (looking up documents before a model answers), compares it with keyword search and database plug-ins, defends staying closed-source and rebuilding as serverless, and pours cold water on "infinite context" and fine-tuning on private data.
g: Founder and CEO of Pinecone, a vector database company

eps.t: How to avoid burning out: a conversation with psychologist Yan Xu
eps.ot: 61: 和心理学家许燕一起聊聊怎么避免心理枯竭
eps.s: A special episode tied to LatePost's year-end reporting. 2023, the first year after the pandemic, saw young Chinese flock to temples and lotteries, joke about "going crazy" and chase civil-service jobs. Psychologist Yan Xu of Beijing Normal University, former head of China's social psychology association, and LatePost writer Menglong Zeng look back at the year's mood: the pandemic's lasting effects, economic and job stress, earlier burnout, and how to live as a full human being.
g: Psychology professor at Beijing Normal University; former dean there and former head of China's social psychology association

eps.t: How to discover your superpowers, own your story, and unlock personal growth | Donna Lichaw
eps.s: Executive coach Donna Lichaw uses superhero metaphors to explain her story-driven leadership: leaders first need to see the stories they tell themselves, their superpowers and their kryptonite, before they can lead others. She brings product methods like user research and lean experiments to personal growth, and talks about handling impostor feelings, managing energy, and working backward from the ending you want to find your purpose.
g: Executive coach and author of The Leader's Journey; a former product manager and designer

eps.t: Demis Hassabis — Scaling, superhuman AIs, AlphaZero atop LLMs, AlphaFold
eps.s: Dwarkesh Patel and Demis Hassabis spend an hour on the technical details: what the brain teaches AI, why AlphaZero-style search should sit on top of language models, whether scaling will hit a wall, what training Gemini taught him, and open weights and security. The standout: AGI-like systems within a decade wouldn't surprise him, but a model caught lying should make labs pause.
g: CEO of Google DeepMind, the lab behind AlphaGo, AlphaFold and Gemini

eps.t: Competition makes for better chip design with AMD CTO Mark Papermaster
eps.s: AMD CTO Mark Papermaster recounts how the company first rebuilt its CPU business before turning to AI. He introduces the MI300 accelerator and AMD's open software approach, and explains why he opposes locking customers into closed systems. He also covers how chips keep getting faster as Moore's Law slows, AI moving from data centers to PCs and devices, and the supply constraints from advanced packaging, electricity, and geopolitics.
g: Chief technology officer of chipmaker AMD; previously led chips and hardware at IBM and Apple

eps.t: Zhilin Yang on a year of building an AI model startup: adding to humanity's ideals, contrarian bets with real odds, and Sora
eps.ot: 和杨植麟聊大模型创业这一年：人类理想的增量、有概率的非共识和Sora
eps.s: Zhilin Yang, founder of Moonshot AI, looks back on his first year building an AI model company: why AGI needs a new kind of organization, why he bet on long context and consumer products, and how to weigh near-term product-market fit against changing the world. In a segment recorded later, he calls Sora video generation's "GPT-3.5 moment" and answers Yann LeCun's criticism.
g: Founder and CEO of Moonshot AI, the company behind the Kimi assistant

eps.t: Making Meta | Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth (CTO)
eps.s: Meta CTO Boz looks back on his years as an early Facebook engineer: how News Feed succeeded despite a user revolt, why communication is the job, how to get leverage from your boss, how open information should be, and how deep a founder should go into details. He also covers his rotation-heavy career path, what Meta learned from its stock price collapse and recovery, Vision Pro versus Quest 3, and his own shift from identity threat to curiosity.
g: Meta CTO and head of Reality Labs; early Facebook engineer who helped build News Feed and mobile ads

eps.t: Inside TikTok: Culture, strategy, monetization, and more | Ray Cao
eps.s: Ray Cao, who leads global monetization product strategy and operations at TikTok, explains how the company works from the inside: a culture of context over control, product, engineering and sales working side by side, how it goes global and local at once, and the hiring mistakes made during hypergrowth. The second half turns to making content and running ads on TikTok: how its content graph differs from Google and Meta, and how a new advertiser should start testing.
g: Head of global monetization product strategy and operations at TikTok; spent six years at Google expanding Google Shopping worldwide

eps.t: Big tech earnings and the current AI debates, with Sarah Guo and Elad Gil
eps.s: The two hosts talk with each other this time. Using big tech's earnings reports, they tally how much is going into AI and what is coming back. They cover Gemini 1.5 and Google's comeback, long context versus retrieval, inference-time compute and domain-specific models, narrow agents and the opening for applications, the many challengers to Nvidia, and the geopolitics of chip manufacturing.
g: The two hosts of No Priors, both technology investors

eps.t: Jensen Huang on How to Use First-Principles Thinking to Drive Decisions (View From The Top)
eps.ol: Stanford GSB View From The Top
eps.s: At Stanford GSB, Jensen Huang explains how NVIDIA had to invent both technology and markets, how a few OpenGL manuals saved it, and how core beliefs carried him through 10 to 15 years with no market. He also covers a management style where information isn't power, computing's shift from retrieval to generation, and AI regulation. The most useful idea: after a setback, ask whether your assumptions changed.
g: NVIDIA co-founder and CEO, 31 years in, leading about 30,000 people

eps.t: #416 – Yann Lecun: Meta AI, Open Source, Limits of LLMs, AGI & the Future of AI
eps.s: In his third Lex Fridman conversation, Yann LeCun spends nearly three hours on why LLMs fall short, JEPA world models, open source, AI doomers and humanoid robots. Highlights: a 4-year-old has seen more data than any LLM has read, anyone chasing human-level AI should abandon generative models, and open source is the only guard against a few companies controlling AI.
g: Meta's chief AI scientist, NYU professor and one of the pioneers of deep learning

eps.t: Product management theater | Marty Cagan (Silicon Valley Product Group)
eps.s: Marty Cagan, author of the new book TRANSFORMED, talks about product management theater: pandemic over-hiring, expensive money and generative AI have combined into a reckoning for product managers who only do project management. He contrasts feature teams with empowered product teams, spells out what a PM is actually responsible for, value and viability, outlines the principles of the product operating model, and urges people stuck in feature teams to level themselves up.
g: Founder of Silicon Valley Product Group (SVPG) and author of INSPIRED, EMPOWERED and TRANSFORMED

eps.t: With Yusen Dai and Peak Ji: piecing together the Sora puzzle, and the AI model knockout round
eps.ot: 与戴雨森和季逸超聊，一幅Sora的信息拼图和大模型淘汰赛
eps.s: After Sora's release, Yusen Dai and Peak Ji of ZhenFund piece together many interviews into one picture: the people and methods behind Sora, how hard it is to catch up, how far we are from a world simulator, plus bubbles, the pace of AI apps, and the knockout round among model makers. The episode page doesn't say who said what, so unclear points are credited to Dai.
g: Managing partner at ZhenFund and an early angel investor in Moonshot AI
Guest from the ZhenFund side and developer of the Mammoth browser

eps.t: Designing the Future: Dylan Field on AI, Collaboration, and Independence
eps.s: Figma co-founder and CEO Dylan Field looks back on life after the collapsed Adobe deal and explains how FigJam and Dev Mode grew out of what users were already doing. He talks about what design means in the AI era, why new ways of interacting won't kill the interface, and Figma's ambition to cover everything from idea to code.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Figma, the collaborative design software company

eps.t: Can philosophy help young people find meaning? A conversation with philosophy professor Yuhui Jiang
eps.ot: 62: 对谈哲学教授姜宇辉：哲学能解决年轻人的意义危机吗？
eps.s: Listeners care about business, but also about happiness, pain, meaning and death. Yuhui Jiang, a philosophy professor at East China Normal University who translates Gilles Deleuze, talks with LatePost writer Likun Zhu about what philosophy is and isn't, how ordinary people can get into it, three life strategies it offers, and whether it can help young people facing the emptiness of scrolling and shopping. The episode page only lists headings.
g: East China Normal University professor of French philosophy and media theory; translated A Thousand Plateaus

eps.t: The happiness and pain of product management | Noam Lovinsky (Grammarly, FB, Thumbtack, YT)
eps.s: Noam Lovinsky, chief product officer at Grammarly, walks through his time at YouTube, Thumbtack, Facebook's new product experimentation team, and Grammarly. He explains why he argued to cut his own project, how fast growth hides problems, how a services marketplace switched to instant quotes, and how big companies should reward internal incubation teams. He closes with career advice: go where you will grow, and do work that gives you energy.
g: Chief product officer at Grammarly; former Thumbtack CPO, Facebook NPE founding member, early YouTube PM

eps.t: Sam Altman: OpenAI, GPT-5, Sora, Board Saga, Elon Musk, Ilya, Power & AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #419
eps.s: Altman's fullest account of the November 2023 board crisis, which he calls the most painful experience of his career and which convinced him no single person should control AGI. He also covers Elon Musk's lawsuit, Sora, why GPT-4 "kind of sucks," letting AI think longer on hard problems, and why compute will be the currency of the future.
g: CEO of OpenAI, back in the job after the board ousted him

eps.t: Wang Xiaochuan on his first year back as a founder: answering Xiaohu Zhu and a third path for China's AGI
eps.ot: 和王小川聊再创业这一年：回应朱啸虎与中国AGI第三种可能
eps.s: Baichuan founder Wang Xiaochuan offers a third view on China's AI race, between Zhilin Yang's tech-first camp and Xiaohu Zhu's market-first camp: a step slower on ideals, three steps faster on real use. He answers Zhu point by point, lays out his vision of AI advisors, three model worlds and medicine, revisits Sogou's history, and explains why he stopped chasing GPT and killed a Sora copy.
g: Founder and CEO of Baichuan AI; earlier founded the search company Sogou

eps.t: The ultimate guide to PR | Emilie Gerber (founder of Six Eastern)
eps.s: Emilie Gerber, founder of the PR firm Six Eastern, lays out a practical PR playbook for tech companies. She explains why press coverage is often worth more as third-party validation than as a signup driver, how to pitch funding news, which outlets want which stories, how to write pitches and follow up with reporters, and how to explain yourself by naming a famous rival. She also covers podcasts, executives' social accounts, why press releases are mostly dead, and how to budget for an agency.
g: Founder and CEO of PR firm Six Eastern; formerly PR at Uber and product communications at Box

eps.t: Speed will win the AI computing battle with Tuhin Srivastava from Baseten
eps.s: Baseten co-founder and CEO Tuhin Srivastava talks about the infrastructure that runs AI models: why engineers want code rather than no-code, how inference differs from training, and how output speeds rose from about 90 tokens per second to several hundred. He explains why speed is an AI company's biggest edge, and why enterprise adoption is overhyped in the short run but underestimated in the long run.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Baseten, which runs AI models in production for companies

eps.t: Everyone here has doubts about having a job: Tiaohai founder Liang Ergou and investor Mable on bars, craft beer and young people
eps.ot: 63: 来这的人都对上班这件事有所怀疑：和跳海创始人二狗与投资人 Mable 聊聊酒吧、精酿和年轻人
eps.s: After writing about the craft beer bar Tiaohai, host Hanyang invites its founder Liang Ergou and angel investor Mable to talk about the bar's philosophy and business model, how to open one in another city, what young people in China's biggest cities are like, whether social media is a burden, what's wrong with the traditional craft beer scene, and what makes Beijing special. Views are grouped under Liang Ergou.
g: Founder of craft beer bar Tiaohai (notes merged with angel investor Mable)

eps.t: Kunal Shah on winning in India, second-order thinking, the philosophy of startups, and more
eps.s: Kunal Shah, founder of Indian fintech company CRED, looks at products and startups through philosophy and evolution. He explains his Delta 4 scoring test for whether a product will take off, why Indian-born CEOs tend to preserve a founder's principles, and what makes India different: low income and a loose sense of time cap revenue per user, low trust breeds super apps, and society doesn't yet reward risk takers. He also covers how founders must evolve as companies grow, curiosity, and second-order thinking.
g: Founder and CEO of Indian fintech CRED; previously founded and sold Freecharge; studied philosophy

eps.t: Open sourcing AI app development with Harrison Chase from LangChain
eps.s: LangChain co-founder and CEO Harrison Chase explains how an open-source framework stays stable while models change fast, and why agent designs are moving from free-running loops to controlled state machines. He covers two kinds of AI memory, why long context windows won't replace RAG, and why a few-shot data flywheel is more practical than fine-tuning.
g: Co-founder and CEO of LangChain, an open-source toolkit for building AI apps

eps.t: Making a tuxedo cat do the bath dance: Alibaba Tongyi's Liefeng Bo on the open questions in multimodal AI
eps.ot: 64: 让奶牛猫跳洗澡舞，与阿里通义薄列峰聊多模态共识中的变量是什么？| AI 大爆炸
eps.s: In early 2024 a dancing tuxedo cat went viral, powered by Animate Anyone from Alibaba's Tongyi XR Lab. Lab head Liefeng Bo talks about the shock of Sora, EMO, which makes a portrait talk from a voice clip, what a dancing feature taught his team, and his career across the deep-learning shift. The big open question, he says, is world models.
g: Alibaba Tongyi Lab scientist heading its XR Lab; ex-principal applied scientist at Amazon Go

eps.t: How to speak more confidently and persuasively | Matt Abrahams (professor, speaker, author)
eps.s: Matt Abrahams, a Stanford business school lecturer and host of the podcast Think Fast, Talk Smart, covers two things. First, how to calm speaking anxiety: relabel nerves as excitement, rehearse in your head, control your breathing, and dare to be dull. Second, how to get better at speaking off the cuff: prepare for the unexpected, and reach for ready-made structures when making small talk, giving feedback, toasting, answering questions, or apologizing.
g: Stanford business school lecturer in communication; host of Think Fast, Talk Smart; author of Think Faster, Talk Smarter

eps.t: You asked for Xiaohu Zhu, so here he is: why he won't back AI model makers
eps.ot: 你们要的朱啸虎，来了
eps.s: GSR Ventures' Xiaohu Zhu gives his "realist" view of generative AI: skip model makers, back only apps that earn money now; sell to businesses first and wait for an "iPhone 3 moment" before betting on consumers. He expects progress to slow after GPT-5, letting the US experiment while China follows cheaply. He also sizes up Huiwen Wang, Wang Xiaochuan and Zhang Yiming, and warns startups not to burn cash.
g: Managing partner at GSR Ventures, a Chinese venture capital firm

eps.t: The power of a faith recharge: LimX Dynamics' Hua Chen on Nvidia GTC and new progress in humanoid robots
eps.ot: 65: 信仰充值的威力：与逐际动力谌骅聊聊 GTC 和人形机器人新进展 | AI 大爆炸
eps.s: LimX Dynamics co-founder Hua Chen starts from recent news: Figure AI's funding, Nvidia unveiling its robot model GR00T at the GTC conference, and a new demo of Tesla's Optimus humanoid. He explains why legged movement is so hard to control, what reinforcement learning and data-driven control have changed, and how humanoid-robot startups differ in China and the US.
g: Co-founder of robotics company LimX Dynamics; PhD in electrical and computer engineering, Ohio State

eps.t: Zigging vs. zagging: How HubSpot built a $30B company | Dharmesh Shah (co-founder/CTO)
eps.s: HubSpot co-founder and CTO Dharmesh Shah explains how he built the company his own way: zero direct reports, measuring laughs per minute to improve his talks, a long bet on small businesses, full transparency after going public, and a constant fight against complexity. He also shares his flash tags for signaling how strongly he holds an opinion, the four P's for judging ideas, culture as a product, and why AI will let people describe what they want instead of clicking through software.
g: Co-founder and CTO of HubSpot

eps.t: The argument for humanoid AI robots with Brett Adcock from Figure
eps.s: Figure founder and CEO Brett Adcock lays out the business case for humanoid robots: human labor is about half of GDP, the world is built for human bodies, and the technology has finally caught up. He also covers the factory-first, home-later rollout, how Figure splits the work with OpenAI, how the team moves fast, and his views on AGI.
g: Founder and CEO of humanoid robot maker Figure; earlier founded electric aircraft company Archer

eps.t: Bending the universe in your favor | Claire Vo (LaunchDarkly, Color, Optimizely, ChatPRD)
eps.s: Claire Vo, chief product officer at LaunchDarkly, talks about bending your career and your organization toward what you want: designing your own promotions, staying in your zone of genius, making every team deadline one notch faster while keeping the bar high. She also covers what it is really like to be a woman in tech leadership, the combined product-and-engineering CPTO role, building ChatPRD on the side, and which parts of a PM's job AI will take over. She closes by defending sales-led companies.
g: Chief product and technology officer at LaunchDarkly; former CPO at Color and Optimizely; creator of ChatPRD

eps.t: An oral business history: China's great overseas buying spree, peaking with the $43 billion Syngenta deal
eps.ot: 商业口述史：中资到海外买买买的大时代，以430亿美元并购先正达为最高潮
eps.s: Wei Wang, who once ran deals at Sinochem, recounts China's overseas buying spree after 2009: from Lenovo and Geely swallowing bigger companies to the $43 billion Syngenta deal that marked its peak, and the end that followed. He also explains how cross-border deals work: know why you're buying, how to live together afterward, and why price matters more than the deal itself.
g: VP and board secretary at a Fortune Global 500 firm; formerly ran acquisitions at Sinochem

eps.t: Elon Musk: AI, Space, X, Mars, speed and hardcore
eps.ol: In Good Company (Norges Bank Investment Management)
eps.s: Norway's sovereign-fund chief Nicolai Tangen talks with Musk for 46 minutes about how fast AI is moving and what holds it back, electric cars and Chinese rivals, how many tons Mars will take, and what X is for. Highlights: his timeline of AI bottlenecks, from chips to transformers to electricity to data, and his hardcore playbook of speed plus tolerance for failure.
g: CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, owner of X, founder of xAI

eps.t: A framework for finding product-market fit | Todd Jackson (First Round Capital)
eps.s: Todd Jackson, partner at First Round Capital, lays out the framework his firm distilled from hundreds of early-stage companies for finding product-market fit in B2B. PMF, he says, is made of demand, satisfaction, and efficiency, and companies climb through four levels, each with its own focus and its own warning signs when stuck. He uses Vanta, Lattice, Plaid, Looker, and Ironclad to show how to adjust the four P's when stuck, and explains customer interviews built around willingness to pay.
g: Partner at First Round Capital; former VP of product and design at Dropbox and product lead for Gmail

eps.t: Hyperscaler strategy in AI, the application landscape heats up, and what we know now about agents with Sarah and Elad
eps.s: The two hosts discuss how frontier models spread faster than expected, why cloud providers and big tech became model companies' main funders, and what Microsoft hiring the Inflection team means. They also cover open spaces for apps like AI video and time-series data, Devin-style agent interfaces, and why prosumers will adopt AI before enterprises.
g: Co-hosts of No Priors, both AI investors

eps.t: Choosing a haircut, why perms are pricey, how to blow-dry: salon owner Bao Ge on the hair business
eps.ot: 66: 怎么选发型、为啥烫发贵、咋吹头发：和理发店老板宝哥聊聊美发这个生意和到底该怎么整整头发？
eps.s: While getting a dye job, host Hanyang talks with Bao Ge, owner of the salon Daxiang Styling: how stylists build careers, how to find a style that suits you and explain it to your stylist, why perms and dye jobs cost so much, and how salons are run. The show notes list only the questions, not his answers.
g: Owner of the hair salon Daxiang Styling

eps.t: The GitLab way: Kindness, transparency, and short toes | David DeSanto (CPO)
eps.s: GitLab is a fully remote public company. Chief Product Officer David DeSanto explains how it runs: recorded meetings and a public handbook make it radically transparent, backed by values like assuming good intent and having "short toes." He also covers why remote work needs 150% over-communication, how product strategy shifted from breadth to depth, and how AI features span the whole software lifecycle using different models for different tasks.
g: Chief Product Officer at GitLab, the software development platform

eps.t: Guangmi Li on the AGI build-out era: power plus chips equals intelligence
eps.ot: 和广密聊AGI大基建时代：电+芯片=产出智能
eps.s: In this AI model quarterly, Shixiang CEO Guangmi Li reviews early 2024. AGI, he argues, has entered a build-out era: power plus chips equals intelligence, data centers and energy are the bottleneck, and the race is now a marathon. He casts models and products as a mountain's south and north faces, estimates GPT-4 and GPT-5's power and costs, and weighs OpenAI's strategy, big-tech alliances, and Jensen Huang versus Sam Altman.
g: Founder and CEO of Shixiang, an investor who tracks global AI model companies

eps.t: Lessons from 1,000+ YC startups: Resilience, tar pit ideas, pivoting, more | Dalton Caldwell (YC)
eps.s: Dalton Caldwell, managing director at Y Combinator, draws on more than 20 YC batches to explain the simplest rules of startups: don't die, a good pivot feels like going home, and beware tar pit ideas that look wonderful but have trapped founders for decades. He also covers why investors say no, why market size matters little at the earliest stage, why founders shouldn't delegate too soon, and why growth hacking and A/B testing are a waste of time for very early companies.
g: Managing director and partner at Y Combinator; founder of imeem and App.net

eps.t: The Future of AI Artistry with Suhail Doshi from Playground AI
eps.s: Playground AI founder Suhail Doshi explains why he bet on image generation in 2022, the pitfalls and tricks of training an image model from scratch, and why industry benchmarks can't be trusted. He also describes the company's shift from text-to-image toward image editing, and the long-term goal of one large vision model that can generate, edit and understand images.
g: Founder and CEO of Playground AI, an image generation tool; previously founded Mighty

eps.t: Vision, conviction, and hype: How to build 0 to 1 inside a company | Mihika Kapoor (Product, Figma)
eps.s: Figma product manager Mihika Kapoor was the most-nominated name when Lenny asked Twitter who the best PM to work with was. She breaks down how she builds new products from scratch inside a big company: rallying the team around a visual vision, forming opinions early and labeling how sure she is, generating hype for bottom-up projects, asking non-users why they don't use the product, and shaping culture from below. She ends on how to tend a new idea like a flame until it spreads company-wide.
g: Product manager at Figma and early PM on FigJam, building new products from scratch; founder of Design Nation

eps.t: Fei-Fei Li: The “Godmother of AI”, Keeping Humanity at the Heart of the AI Revolution (YAP E285)
eps.s: An AI primer for a general audience. Fei-Fei Li explains what machine learning is, why AI is a "gray box," what it still can't do, and how vision went from the first eyes to computer vision. She then lays out human-centered AI, talks about jobs and dignity and the danger of concentrated power, and sketches two possible worlds in 2034.
g: Stanford professor, co-director of Stanford HAI, author of the memoir The Worlds I See

eps.t: Has venture capital's key stopped working? Mengqiu Wang on lying low, a smaller game, and rodents
eps.ot: 风险投资的钥匙失灵了吗？和梦秋聊：蛰伏、更少人的游戏和啮齿动物
eps.s: Qingliu Capital founding partner Mengqiu Wang describes how China's venture rules changed in two years. The dollar-fund relay, where each round paid more until an IPO, has broken. Investors now lie low and make money on consensus bets, and the industry has shrunk sharply. She likens herself to a rodent in the age of dinosaurs: first, stay alive.
g: Founding partner of Qingliu Capital; former VP of technology at Baidu

eps.t: Sam Altman (OpenAI) - The Possibilities of AI [Entire Talk]
eps.s: At Stanford's entrepreneurship lecture series, Altman takes student questions on why now is the time to build, why he doesn't mind spending tens of billions, and why OpenAI ships imperfect products early. Highlights: PhD-level AI might not move GDP for years, GPT-5 will be smarter across the board, and society itself is a kind of AGI.
g: Co-founder and CEO of OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT

eps.t: A conversation with NVIDIA's Jensen Huang
eps.s: At Stripe Sessions, Stripe CEO Patrick Collison talks with Jensen Huang about management and AI. Huang explains why 60 executives report to him with no one-on-ones, how CUDA dragged NVIDIA's value to about $1 billion before paying off a decade later, and why AI factories turn electricity into intelligence. The surprise: he wishes the audience plenty of pain and suffering.
g: Co-founder and CEO of NVIDIA, the company that makes GPUs and AI computing platforms

eps.t: How to build deeper, more robust relationships | Carole Robin (Stanford professor, "Touchy Feely")
eps.s: Carole Robin taught Stanford's famous "Touchy Feely" interpersonal dynamics course for over 20 years. She explains how to move a relationship from functional to robust or even exceptional: open up a little more each time, show vulnerability the right way, and spot the old beliefs that quietly run you. She also lays out practical formulas for giving feedback, asking instead of advising, and repairing things after you mess up.
g: Longtime lead teacher of Stanford's "Touchy Feely" course, co-founder of Leaders in Tech, co-author of Connect

eps.t: OpenAI's Sora team thinks we've only seen the "GPT-1 of video models"
eps.s: The three leads of OpenAI's Sora explain their video generation model: why they built it from scratch with a diffusion transformer and spacetime patches, how video models scale, what artists said after trying it, safety concerns and current limits. They see today's Sora as the "GPT-1" of video, and video as one path toward world simulators and embodied AI.
g: Co-lead of OpenAI's Sora video generation team
Co-lead of OpenAI's Sora video generation team
Co-lead of OpenAI's Sora video generation team

eps.t: How ordinary people can protect their wealth: Guaranteed Bubble author Ning Zhu on why diversifying is better
eps.ot: 67: 与《刚性泡沫》作者朱宁聊普通人保住财富：为什么多元化投资更好？
eps.s: LatePost feature writer Menglong Zeng and Fangyi Gong, editor-in-chief of LatePost Finance, sit down with economist Ning Zhu in Beijing to talk about how ordinary people should invest in uncertain times and how to read China's economy. He also shares his own portfolio and admits his mistakes, including joining Lehman Brothers in 2008.
g: Economist, deputy dean of the Shanghai Advanced Institute of Finance, author of Guaranteed Bubble

eps.t: Twitter's ex-Head of Product on Elon, consumer products, culture, more | Kayvon Beykpour
eps.s: Kayvon Beykpour ran product at Twitter.
