He recounts his first meeting with Elon Musk and being fired while on paternity leave, then explains how he turned a cautious, stagnant product organization into one that shipped: treating the "sacred cows" as a roadmap, acquiring founders to lead the riskiest bets, and staffing projects with true believers. He also reflects on the limits of frameworks and metrics, why Periscope failed, and how to sharpen consumer product taste.
g: Former head of product and consumer GM at Twitter, co-founder and CEO of Periscope

eps.t: How to run an art museum: Modern Art Museum Shanghai director Guangzhao Yu on art and staging shows
eps.ot: 68: 怎么运营一家美术馆？和艺仓美术馆馆长余光照聊聊艺术、艺术馆和怎么办展
eps.s: In a gallery at Modern Art Museum Shanghai, host Hanyang talks with its director, Guangzhao Yu: where museums come from, where the money comes from, who the visitors are, and how an exhibition gets made. Plus: with digital art everywhere, why visit a museum at all? The show notes list only the questions, not his answers.
g: Director of Modern Art Museum Shanghai

eps.t: This will make you a better decision maker | Annie Duke (Thinking In Bets, former pro poker player)
eps.s: Annie Duke, former pro poker player and author of Thinking in Bets, remembers her friend Daniel Kahneman's humility and lays out concrete ways to decide better: make your intuition explicit, use meetings only for discussion, shorten supposedly long feedback loops with intermediate signals, and tie premortems to kill criteria. She also describes how she helped First Round Capital rework its investment decisions and why people almost always quit too late.
g: Former pro poker player, author of Thinking in Bets and Quit, special partner at First Round Capital

eps.t: Cognition's Scott Wu on how Devin, the AI software engineer, will work for you
eps.s: Cognition founder Scott Wu starts from his competitive programming days, then explains how Devin, an AI software engineer, works, why its interface looks the way it does, and what it is and isn't good at. He rejects the idea that AI will wipe out programmers, arguing there will be more engineers, who will act more like architects and product managers.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Cognition, maker of the AI software engineer Devin

eps.t: Business strategy with Hamilton Helmer (author of 7 Powers)
eps.s: Hamilton Helmer, author of 7 Powers, explains how strategy relates to what he calls power: a structure that lets a company earn above-average returns for a long time. He covers when startups should start thinking about strategy, which powers are actually available early on, which moats are overrated, and why operational excellence isn't power. He then turns to how generative AI changes competition and why the US debt path worries him.
g: Strategy scholar, author of 7 Powers, investor at Strategy Capital

eps.t: Context windows, computer constraints, and energy consumption with Sarah and Elad
eps.s: The two hosts start with AI music generators like Suno and Udio and Apple's small on-device models, then ask whether platforms will swallow the apps built on them, whether AI compute spending is rational, how long context windows will get, and why energy and data centers are becoming the next bottleneck.
g: Co-hosts of No Priors, both AI investors

eps.t: In conversation with Sam Altman
eps.ho: Chamath Palihapitiya, Jason Calacanis, David Sacks, David Friedberg
eps.s: The four All-In investor hosts grill Altman on how the next model will ship, open source and staying ahead, a possible AI device, regulation, copyright, the board drama and his lack of equity. Highlights: his idea of “universal basic compute” instead of cash, and an ideal assistant that acts like a senior employee who pushes back, not an alter ego.
g: Co-founder and CEO of OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT

eps.t: A framework for PM skill development | Vikrama Dhiman (Gojek)
eps.s: Vikrama Dhiman, head of product at Gojek, shares his framework for product manager growth, the three Ws: what you produce, what you bring, and how you work with others. He also covers the three mindset traps that stall mid-level and senior PMs, how to choose which skill to build next, paths for switching into product, and how to define the PM role when nobody else can.
g: Head of product at Gojek, overseeing product, design, program management and user research

eps.t: Be fundamentally different, not incrementally better | Jag Duggal (Nubank, Facebook, Google)
eps.s: Jag Duggal, chief product officer at Nubank, explains how the Latin American digital bank grew mostly by word of mouth: using the Sean Ellis score as a gate before scaling, mining it for the bullseye customer, and doing user research properly. He makes the case for being fundamentally different rather than incrementally better, then covers Nubank's expansion, its vision of an AI-native private banker for everyone, and his early failure with radio ads at Google.
g: Chief product officer at Nubank; former Facebook product director and head of Google display ads product and strategy

eps.t: Music consumers are becoming the creators with Suno CEO Mikey Shulman
eps.s: Suno co-founder and CEO Mikey Shulman explains why the team moved from audio AI to music generation, why they bet on transformers and audio tokenization, and why music quality can only be judged by ear. He also discusses a business model aimed at everyday people, and predicts the line between making and listening will disappear as people spend more time on music.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Suno, an AI music generation company

eps.t: Everyone feels uncomfortable being alive
eps.ot: 69: 每个人活着都不舒服
eps.s: University lecturer Xiaowei Wang, author of The Depths of Everyday Life, talks with host Hanyang about why everyone seems uncomfortable with life: everyday consumer living, modernization arriving too fast, whether the internet kept its promises, and sayings like "as long as you're happy" and "emotional value." The show notes list only the questions, not his answers.
g: University lecturer and author of The Depths of Everyday Life

eps.t: Why not asking for what you want is holding you back | Kenneth Berger (exec coach, first PM @Slack)
eps.s: Kenneth Berger, Slack's first product manager and now an executive coach, makes the case for asking for what you want: why it's really about being honest with yourself, how to find the real desire hiding inside a complaint, how to ask clearly yet humbly, and how to take a no at face value. He uses his own story of being fired three times in one year at Slack as a cautionary tale, and talks about working with founders and replacing fear with vision as fuel.
g: Executive coach for startup leaders, Slack's first product manager

eps.t: Geoffrey Hinton | On working with Ilya, choosing problems, and the power of intuition
eps.s: A research-focused talk with Joel Hellermark. Hinton recalls working with Ilya Sutskever and admits Ilya was right that scale matters most. He explains why predicting the next word requires understanding, how networks can beat their training data, why digital minds share knowledge far better than brains, his early bet on Nvidia GPUs, and how he picks research problems.
g: A founding figure of deep learning; University of Toronto professor and former Google researcher.

eps.t: The Data Foundry for AI with Alexandr Wang from Scale
eps.s: Scale AI founder Alexandr Wang traces the company's path from self-driving car data and government projects to data for large language models. He explains frontier data and hybrid human-AI synthetic data, why model benchmarks are distorted, and his view of the road to AGI: steady progress through data flywheels, one domain at a time, rather than a single breakthrough.
g: Founder and CEO of Scale AI, which supplies training data for AI

eps.t: How YC fosters AI Innovation with Garry Tan
eps.s: YC president Garry Tan talks about how YC grew from a niche subculture into a large institution, how much of each batch is now AI and how fast their early revenue is growing, and why "GPT wrapper" is the wrong label. He also covers how YC picks founders, why startups can beat incumbents, the harm of raising too much, younger founders, and San Francisco's governance and math education.
g: President and CEO of Y Combinator, the startup accelerator

eps.t: Zhifei Li on Mobvoi's IPO, GPT-4o, and the hidden pain of building a frontier tech startup
eps.ot: 和李志飞聊IPO、GPT-4o和你不知道的前沿科技创业的痛
eps.s: After Mobvoi listed in Hong Kong as the first generative AI stock, founder Zhifei Li looks back on 12 years of frontier tech: the arrogance, the low points and the return to practicality. He weighs GPT-4o's push to unify text, sound and images in one model and the price war among large models, and admits he is pessimistic about frontier tech startups.
g: Founder and CEO of Mobvoi, a Chinese AI company

eps.t: Unorthodox frameworks for growing your product, career, and impact | Bangaly Kaba (YT, IG, FB)
eps.s: Bangaly Kaba, former head of growth at Instagram and now a product director at YouTube, shares a set of unorthodox frameworks: impact equals environment times skills for choosing where to work, doing "understand work" before executing, using the managing-complex-change model and Bloom's taxonomy to lead teams, and his own adjacent user theory. He also revisits Instagram's compounding growth loops, the connection pivot and account recovery, plus his rough stretch at Instacart.
g: Product management director at YouTube; former head of growth at Instagram and VP of product at Instacart

eps.t: The surprising truth about what closes deals: Insights from 2.5m sales conversations | Matt Dixon
eps.s: Matt Dixon, author of The Challenger Sale, studied 2.5 million sales calls and found that most lost deals aren't lost to a competitor but to customer indecision. Buyers aren't afraid of missing out; they're afraid of messing up. He walks through his JOLT method for handling that fear, then uses a dental equipment company to revisit the core of Challenger selling: give the customer a business insight they hadn't considered, then lead them to what only you can offer.
g: Sales researcher, author of The Challenger Sale and The JOLT Effect, formerly led sales research at CEB

eps.t: Into her third thousand and one nights: MICO World's Emily on six years taking Chinese apps to the Middle East
eps.ot: 70: 开始第三个一千零一夜，与米可世界 Emily 聊中东出海 6 年
eps.s: Emily, who runs MICO World's Middle East business, tells Manqi Cheng about six years and more than 2,000 days in Egypt: running the voice-chat social app YoHo, how users differ across Middle Eastern countries, a policy crisis in 2020, and her advice to Chinese companies going abroad on hiring, location and fundraising.
g: Head of Middle East business at MICO World, part of Newborn Town; runs apps like YoHo

eps.t: Inside the organization Jensen Huang built: a distributed operating system that works like a GPU
eps.ot: 谈谈黄仁勋搭建的组织系统：分布式操作系统，“就像一台GPU”
eps.s: Yajun Wang, former chief strategy officer at Longfor Group, unpacks Jensen Huang's counterintuitive management methods. He argues Nvidia's organization works like its product: a GPU that spreads decisions out and processes them in parallel. Copying Nvidia, he says, means giving people context, not tightening control, and without love there is no innovation.
g: Former chief strategy officer at property developer Longfor; studies strategy and organizations

eps.t: Inside Canva: Coaches not managers, giving away your Legos, and embracing AI | Cameron Adams
eps.s: Canva co-founder and chief product officer Cameron Adams explains how a design company that has been profitable for years builds product. A lead investor tried to halve their valuation two days before signing, which pushed them to stay profitable. Canva has almost no traditional managers, just coaches. He also covers the year-long first version, search-driven growth, early international expansion, the move to subscriptions, and Canva's three-part AI plan.
g: Canva co-founder and chief product officer; earlier a designer on Google Wave

eps.t: The evolution and promise of RAG architecture with Tengyu Ma from Voyage AI
eps.s: Voyage AI founder and Stanford professor Tengyu Ma explains RAG, where an AI looks things up before answering. He argues answer quality hinges mostly on retrieval, and that RAG will always be far cheaper than stuffing everything into a long context. He also covers how much domain-specific embedding models help, why RAG systems will get simpler, lessons from starting a company, and what academia should work on.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Voyage AI, which builds embedding models for search; Stanford professor

eps.t: Lessons from a 2-time unicorn builder, 50-time startup advisor and 20-time board member | Uri Levine
eps.s: Waze co-founder Uri Levine draws on ten startups and twenty boards to lay out the advice from his book: fall in love with the problem, not the solution; treat a startup as a long journey of failures; measure product-market fit by retention; and focus on one thing per stage. He also tells how Waze failed abroad again and again, how to pitch investors, his 30-day firing test, and how to watch users unlike yourself.
g: Waze co-founder, serial entrepreneur, author of Fall in Love with the Problem, Not the Solution

eps.t: How the ARC Prize is democratizing the race to AGI with Mike Knoop from Zapier
eps.s: Zapier co-founder Mike Knoop explains why he and François Chollet launched the $1 million ARC Prize. He argues the popular definition of AGI measures the wrong thing, and that LLMs are essentially memorization systems that won't reach general intelligence through scale alone. He also covers how Zapier uses AI, how agents will spread, and why he opposes regulating AGI based on theory.
g: Co-founder of the automation tool Zapier and co-founder of the ARC Prize

eps.t: MiniMax's angel investor on the startup's backstory and the poker game of AI model funding
eps.ot: 和MiniMax天使投资人聊，MiniMax幕后故事和大模型资本扑克牌
eps.s: Yu Chen, a partner at Yunqi Partners and MiniMax's first investor, tells the story behind his MiniMax bet, looks back on a decade's three waves of AI, and compares the large-model funding race to poker: the giants hold the most chips, and for startups further back, the top job is raising money.
g: Partner at Yunqi Partners; angel investor in Chinese AI company MiniMax

eps.t: If you think scaling laws alone will reach AGI, change careers: Yi Ma of HKU on intelligence
eps.ot: 71: “如果相信只靠 Scaling Laws 就能实现 AGI，你该改行了”，与香港大学马毅聊智能
eps.s: This is the audio version of LatePost's written interview with Yi Ma of the University of Hong Kong. He tells Manqi Cheng why scaling alone won't reach AGI, why deep networks are really doing compression, how to turn large models from black boxes into explainable white boxes, and why intelligence needs closed feedback loops. He also weighs in on AI doom talk and regulation.
g: HKU computer science department head and director of its Institute of Data Science

eps.t: The paths to power: How to grow your influence and advance your career | Jeffrey Pfeffer (Stanford)
eps.s: Stanford business school professor Jeffrey Pfeffer walks through his book, 7 Rules of Power, and explains why political skill directly affects pay and promotion. He covers getting out of your own way, breaking rules, building a personal brand, networking, acting powerful, and why power feeds on itself. He closes on how practice and coaching close the knowing-doing gap, and why power costs you autonomy and privacy.
g: Professor of organizational behavior at Stanford business school; author of 7 Rules of Power

eps.t: Hard-won lessons building 0 to 1 inside Atlassian | Tanguy Crusson (Head of Jira Product Discovery)
eps.s: Atlassian's Tanguy Crusson looks back on building new products inside a big company: how HipChat and Stride lost to Slack, the painful integration after buying Statuspage, an IT operations proposal that sat in limbo for months, and how Jira Product Discovery made it through the internal incubator Point A. His lessons: test old assumptions, stop watching competitors, create scarcity on purpose, start with ten lighthouse customers, and leave if the environment won't allow it.
g: Head of Jira Product Discovery at Atlassian; worked on HipChat, Stride and the Statuspage integration

eps.t: After hearing 100 designers complain, I found how AI could help: Motiff on niche generative-AI openings
eps.ot: 72: “听完一百位设计师的抱怨后，我找到了用AI帮他们提效的办法” ，与 Motiff 聊 AIGC 细分机会
eps.s: Haoran Zhang, VP of operations at Motiff, talks with LatePost writer Jing Chen about AI design tools. Generative AI makes ever more realistic content, yet the interfaces that hold it are still built layer by layer by hand. After interviewing over 100 designers, the team built a productivity tool. They also discuss competing with Figma, going global from day one, and why real-world AI adoption lags expectations.
g: VP of operations at Motiff, an AI-powered interface design tool

eps.t: Can AI replace the camera? with Joshua Xu from HeyGen
eps.s: HeyGen co-founder Joshua Xu explains why AI could become the new camera, why HeyGen started with AI avatars, and why it assembles videos from separate parts instead of generating them end to end. He also covers personalized and real-time video, how HeyGen guards against deepfakes, and why only customers can judge whether the results are good.
g: Co-founder and CEO of the AI video company HeyGen

eps.t: Making an impact through authenticity and curiosity | Ami Vora (CPO at Faire, ex-WhatsApp, FB, IG)
eps.s: Faire chief product officer Ami Vora, formerly of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, talks about making an impact through authenticity and curiosity: how to choose a job, defusing disagreement with the word "fascinating," running product reviews, uniting a team around a metaphor, why execution beats strategy, and how she handles feedback about her style as a woman leader. She also covers splitting team goals, why senior leaders only get bad options, and building trust with Faire's founder CEO.
g: Chief product officer at Faire; formerly led product and design at WhatsApp and ads products at Facebook

eps.t: Guangmi Li on the past six months in AI: Perplexity's sudden rise and the app boom that hasn't come
eps.ot: 口述全球大模型这半年：Perplexity突然火爆和尚未爆发的AI应用生态
eps.s: In the third AI model quarterly, Guangmi Li reviews the first half of 2024 from the app side. He explains why Perplexity suddenly took off, argues that AI-native apps haven't broken out at scale yet, and discusses GPT-5's progress, what protects model makers from rivals, and how startups relate to the giants.
g: Founder and CEO of Shixiang, an investor who tracks global AI model companies

eps.t: The social radar: Y Combinator’s secret weapon | Jessica Livingston (co-founder of YC, author)
eps.s: YC co-founder Jessica Livingston explains the people-reading skill colleagues call her social radar: what she watched for in early interviews, such as how co-founders treat each other, whether they're truly all in, whether they get defensive, and whether they're sincere and relentless. She uses Airbnb and GOAT to show why founders matter more than ideas, how anyone can practice this instinct, and how YC's batch model came from inexperience.
g: Y Combinator co-founder, author of Founders at Work, host of The Social Radars podcast

eps.t: State Space Models and Real-time Intelligence with Karan Goel and Albert Gu from Cartesia
eps.s: Cartesia co-founders Albert Gu and Karan Goel explain the trade-off between state space models (SSMs) and Transformers: SSMs compress history into a running state so compute grows only linearly, and the best designs are hybrids built mostly from SSM layers. They also cover Sonic, their low-latency voice model, why speech synthesis is far from solved, and plans to run efficient models on devices and build one unified multimodal model.
g: Cartesia co-founder, Carnegie Mellon professor and co-creator of the Mamba model
Co-founder and CEO of Cartesia, which builds real-time voice models

eps.t: Dylan Field live at Figma's Config: Intuition, simplicity, and the future of design
eps.s: Recorded live at Figma's Config conference, co-founder and CEO Dylan Field talks about what design is, the debate over AI-generated designs, treating intuition as a hypothesis generator, what it takes to change his mind, what good product managers add, and why keeping things simple is so hard. He also looks back on the lesson of taking three and a half years to ship Figma, and on buying top designers coffee for feedback.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Figma

eps.t: Are niche e-commerce sites a dead end? I built Thailand's biggest beauty e-commerce platform
eps.ot: 73: 垂类电商是伪命题？我做了个泰国最大的美妆电商平台
eps.s: Qinggui Huang, founder of Konvy, Thailand's biggest beauty e-commerce platform, tells LatePost writer Jing Chen why he went to Thailand to sell online in 2012, why his first funding round came only in year ten, and how he guarantees authentic products. He also explains selling offline in a market where little shopping happens online, and boosting efficiency where staff won't grind.
g: Founder of Konvy, a Thai online beauty retailer

eps.t: Pattern Breakers: How to find a breakthrough startup idea | Mike Maples, Jr. (Partner at Floodgate)
eps.s: Mike Maples Jr., founding partner at seed fund Floodgate, went through twenty years of his investment records and found about 80% of exit profits came from companies that pivoted. He lays out the framework of his book Pattern Breakers: breakthrough ideas come from inflections, insights, and founder-future fit, and they win through movements, storytelling and a willingness to be disagreeable. He also covers earning secrets from surprises, how to pitch, and how big companies can incubate pattern-breaking projects.
g: Founding partner at seed fund Floodgate, author of Pattern Breakers, early investor in Twitter, Lyft and Okta

eps.t: Visiting the Rust Belt: counterintuitive truths about the US election and the people no one sees (with Silicon Valley 101)
eps.ot: 74: 走访锈带：美国大选的反直觉认知与不被看见的人 | 串台硅谷 101
eps.s: After touring America's Rust Belt, the declining old industrial heartland, with Keda, Hanyang sits down in the Bay Area with Hongjun of Silicon Valley 101. They test a popular story: deindustrialization cost workers their jobs, angry workers elected Trump, and a trade war followed. He shares scenes from steel mills, coal mines, train stations and ruins, and the people left unseen after industry left.
g: Host of LatePost Chat; toured the US Rust Belt with Keda

eps.t: Building product at Stripe: craft, metrics, and customer obsession | Jeff Weinstein (Product lead)
eps.s: In the longest episode in the show's history, Stripe product lead Jeff Weinstein breaks down how he works: pairing go-go-go urgency with long-term compounding, finding a customer's burning problem before worrying about craft, listening to customers directly and using real payment to test demand, designing metrics from the customer's point of view, and Stripe's internal Study Group ritual. He also tells how Stripe Atlas automated company incorporation and how to push a new business inside a big company.
g: Product lead at Stripe; ran payments infrastructure products, then led Stripe Atlas, which incorporates startups

eps.t: The Best of 2024 (so far) with Sarah Guo and Elad Gil
eps.s: A best-of compilation from the first half of 2024, with clips from Stripe's Emily Glassberg Sands on AI and fintech, Figma's Dylan Field on AI and creative design, Figure's Brett Adcock on iterating on humanoid robots, OpenAI's Sora team, Cognition's Scott Wu, Scale AI's Alexandr Wang and others.

eps.t: Building a world-class data org | Jessica Lachs (VP of Analytics and Data Science at DoorDash)
eps.s: Jessica Lachs, who runs analytics and data science at DoorDash, explains how she built a top data team. Analytics, she argues, should help decide what to do next, not just answer tickets. She covers why she centralizes reporting but embeds people with business teams, how to protect time for exploration, what she looks for in hires, and how to pick simple metrics and convert every lever into one common currency. She also tells her own self-taught story and DoorDash's early all-hands-on-deck culture.
g: VP of Analytics and Data Science at DoorDash, and its first city general manager

eps.t: He Xiaopeng on Tesla's FSD, swimming in a sea of blood, and heroes and losers in chaotic times
eps.ot: 和何小鹏聊，FSD、“在血海游泳”、乱世中的英雄与狗熊
eps.s: In the first episode of From Steam Engines to Self-Driving, XPeng chairman He Xiaopeng talks about his company's roots in smart driving, how large models are reshaping autonomous driving, the cost of copying Tesla's Full Self-Driving, and the knockout round in carmaking's "sea of blood," including his own overhaul of XPeng.
g: Chairman and CEO of Chinese electric carmaker XPeng

eps.t: How AI is opening up new markets and impacting the startup status quo with Sarah Guo and Elad Gil
eps.s: The hosts start from a Goldman Sachs report skeptical of AI and push back on the claim that AI is overhyped. They then discuss the new openings AI creates, from replacing service labor to AI-driven acquisitions and incubation, and how public markets and startup team sizes may be affected.
g: The two No Priors hosts, both investors

eps.t: A big-tech employee jailed in the US? A shared risk for Chinese going global: deportation on arrival
eps.ot: 75: 大厂员工被关美国监狱？聊聊出海人的共同风险：入境被遣返怎么办
eps.s: Former ByteDance employee Lody ("Liu Xiaoyan" on Xiaohongshu) tells Manqi Cheng about his five-day ordeal in March 2023: flying to the US for a meeting, he was detained at Houston's airport, had his visa canceled, spent two days in a private prison and was deported. He describes how it changed his career and offers entry advice for Chinese working abroad.
g: Former ByteDance employee who worked on TikTok's overseas business

eps.t: What most people miss about marketing | Rory Sutherland (Vice Chairman of Ogilvy UK, author)
eps.s: Ogilvy UK vice chairman Rory Sutherland draws on history and everyday life to argue that marketing is badly underrated. Good products don't win on their own; timing and psychology matter just as much. The odd quirks in a product are worth keeping. People's seemingly irrational choices under uncertainty are often rational. Over-reliance on metrics kills judgment. And fame pays off disproportionately, so marketing belongs alongside product development, not after it.
g: Vice chairman of Ogilvy UK; writer on behavioral science and marketing; author of Alchemy

eps.t: Unveiling DeepSeek: A More Extreme Story of Chinese Tech Idealism
eps.ot: 揭秘DeepSeek：一个更极致的中国技术理想主义故事
eps.s: After DeepSeek-V2 set off a price war among Chinese AI models, Liang Wenfeng explains why DeepSeek prices at cost and focuses on new model designs instead of apps. His recurring theme: the real China-US gap is originality versus imitation, and Chinese firms should become contributors, not free riders. He also describes a young, homegrown team where ideas rise from below and anyone can use the GPUs without approval.
g: Founder of DeepSeek and of the quant hedge fund High-Flyer

eps.t: 5 essential questions to craft a winning strategy | Roger Martin (author, advisor, speaker)
eps.s: Strategy advisor Roger Martin walks through his five-question strategy framework, using Figma's whiteboard product FigJam as a worked example. There are only two ways to win, he argues: be different or be cheaper. And an advantage lasts only when rivals can't or won't copy the capabilities behind it. He also explains why business schools teach strategy wrong, how incumbents should face a shifting customer tide, and why fixing the most painful gap beats chasing a perfect plan.
g: Former dean of the Rotman School at the University of Toronto, author of Playing to Win, strategy advisor

eps.t: Low-Code in the Age of AI and Going Enterprise, with Howie Liu from Airtable
eps.s: Airtable co-founder and CEO Howie Liu explains how the product wrapped an app-building platform in the familiar look of a spreadsheet, then grew into the enterprise. He also discusses the jobs of a product manager and where AI fits in Airtable: embedding models in structured data and workflows to cover companies' long tail of needs, and why code generation won't replace no-code.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Airtable, the spreadsheet-style app-building platform

eps.t: The ultimate guide to paid growth | Timothy Davis (Shopify)
eps.s: Timothy Davis, who leads performance marketing at Shopify, lays out how to buy growth with ads: who should do it, how to run small "signs of life" tests, how to choose between platforms, and when to start. The second half digs into separating signal from the noise platforms hand you, using incrementality experiments to correct attribution, and how to move from an agency to an in-house team.
g: Head of performance marketing at Shopify; ex-IBM; advised Pinterest, LinkedIn, Redfin, Eventbrite on paid growth

eps.t: Google DeepMind's Vision for AI, Search and Gemini with Oriol Vinyals from Google DeepMind
eps.s: Gemini co-lead Oriol Vinyals talks about building Gemini after Google Brain and DeepMind merged, how chat and search relate, and why very long context matters. He also discusses how to split compute among pre-training, reinforcement learning and reasoning, the hard problem of reward functions, and the timeline for AGI.
g: VP of Research at Google DeepMind and co-lead of Gemini

eps.t: #438 – Elon Musk: Neuralink and the Future of Humanity
eps.s: Musk's hour and a half at the start of Lex Fridman's eight-hour Neuralink episode. He covers how fast brain implants will get, why human bandwidth matters next to AI, xAI and Optimus, his five-step engineering algorithm, and how falling birth rates and piled-up laws sink civilizations. A striking claim: over a day, a person outputs less than one bit per second.
g: CEO of Tesla and SpaceX; founder of Neuralink and xAI

eps.t: Lessons from scaling Uber and Opendoor | Brian Tolkin (Head of Product at Opendoor, ex-Uber)
eps.s: Brian Tolkin, head of product at Opendoor and Uber's 100th employee, talks about how operations-heavy tech companies work: how product and ops teams share the load, and when technology should take over from people. He also explains how he runs product reviews, how he gets teams to think from the customer's side, and how to experiment with small samples. Later he covers Zillow turning from rival to partner, staying calm under pressure, and early uberPOOL mistakes.
g: Head of product and design at Opendoor; Uber's 100th employee, moved from ops to product, launched uberPOOL globally

eps.t: Plasma revives hope when you despair: Tsinghua's Yi Tan on 20 years researching fusion and 2 building a startup
eps.ot: 76: “等离子体总在你绝望时又给你希望”，与清华谭熠聊核聚变20年研究和2年创业
eps.s: Yi Tan, founder of Startorus Fusion and associate professor at Tsinghua University, talks fusion with LatePost tech writer Qianming He. He argues the field's slow past is no guide to its future, and that fusion has its own scaling laws. He explains why he chose the spherical tokamak design and how he has raised money since founding the company in 2021, aiming for fusion power within a decade.
g: Founder and chief scientist of Startorus Fusion; associate professor at Tsinghua University

eps.t: How embracing your emotions will accelerate your career | Joe Hudson (Art of Accomplishment)
eps.s: Executive coach Joe Hudson argues that two things hold most people back: the wrong relationship with the critical voice in their head, and a tense relationship with their own emotions. He suggests replacing "should" with experiments, letting emotions flow instead of managing them, and treating enjoyment as an efficiency tool. He also shares concrete practices: personal life principles, "five-star meetings," and a daily seven-minute gratitude exchange.
g: Executive coach, founder of Art of Accomplishment, former VC; has coached leaders at OpenAI, SpaceX, and Apple

eps.t: Innovating Spend Management through AI with Pedro Franceschi from Brex
eps.s: Brex co-founder and CEO Pedro Franceschi talks about simplifying the company after moving from co-CEOs to a single CEO, and how Brex puts AI to work in its expense assistant, accounting suggestions, marketing and compliance. He also explains the choice to drop about 20,000 small customers and focus on startups and large enterprises.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Brex, the corporate card and spend management company

eps.t: Improve strategy, influence, and decision-making by understanding your brain | Evan LaPointe
eps.s: Evan LaPointe, founder of CORE Sciences, uses a simplified model of the brain, three systems for safety, reward, and meaning, topped by focus and capability, to explain how people behave at work. He covers why personality differences derail vision debates, how to run meetings, influence people, build relationships, and shape a team's "habitat." His most striking claim: most teams are stuck in busy mode and should spend about a quarter of their time in open or deep thinking.
g: Founder of CORE Sciences; four-time founder whose analytics product Satellite was acquired by Adobe, then led product strategy there

eps.t: Not just a war among carmakers: Momenta founder Xudong Cao on how self-driving suppliers survive
eps.ot: 77: 不仅是车企的战争，与 Momenta 创始人曹旭东聊智驾供应商生存法
eps.s: Momenta founder Xudong Cao tells Manqi Cheng how driver-assistance has changed since 2023: why it now helps carmakers sell cars, his "Moore's law for self-driving," why the market will concentrate, why Momenta supplies carmakers directly, how to build end-to-end systems, and his management rule of doing things with leverage.
g: Founder and CEO of self-driving technology company Momenta

eps.t: Elon Musk in conversation with Donald Trump (X Spaces live interview)
eps.s: In an August 2024 X Spaces livestream delayed by a cyberattack, Musk interviews Donald Trump. Trump does most of the talking; Musk explains why he endorsed him and weighs in on vetting immigrants, underrated nuclear-war risk, nuclear power, a slow energy transition, and a government efficiency commission. His sharpest point: rules only pile up, so eventually everything becomes illegal.
g: CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, owner of X, newly endorsing Trump

eps.t: How AI can help build smarter systems for every team with Eric Glyman and Karim Atiyeh of Ramp
eps.s: Ramp co-founders Eric Glyman (CEO) and Karim Atiyeh (CTO) trace Ramp's path from a consumer price-tracking app to a vision of "self-driving money." They explain how they use AI across product, sales and marketing to boost productivity, how they pick vendors and models, and what lies ahead for finance jobs.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Ramp, the corporate card and finance automation company
Co-founder and CTO of Ramp

eps.t: Tiancheng Lou on robotaxis and ACRush: the better driver assistance gets, the further it is from driverless
eps.ot: 和楼天城聊聊Robotaxi和ACRush：“L2做得越厉害，离L4越远”
eps.s: Pony.ai co-founder and CTO Tiancheng Lou takes stock of self-driving. Robotaxis catch on only when no one sits at the wheel. Progress climbs in steps of hours without a human takeover, and many teams stall between 100 and 1,000 hours for lack of good measurement. Driver assistance and driverless are different roads, and past human level more data hurts. He also covers lidar, smart roads and twenty years of coding contests.
g: Co-founder and CTO of Pony.ai; a competitive programmer known as ACRush

eps.t: Unorthodox PM tips: Automating user insights, unselling candidates, decision logs, more | Kevin Yien
eps.s: Kevin Yien, who leads merchant experience product at Stripe, shares an unorthodox PM playbook: work in engineering, design, or sales before becoming a PM, treat writing as clarity at scale, draw clear boundaries around a problem while sweating the final details. He also walks through concrete tactics like decision logs, an "unsell" letter sent with every offer, and automating user interview outreach, plus how he rebuilt his confidence after a layoff and what his daughter's AI drawings taught him.
g: Leads merchant experience product at Stripe; built Square's restaurant and ecosystem teams; former head of product and design at Mutiny

eps.t: Succeeding as an introvert, building zero-to-one, and PM’ing your career like a product | Deb Liu
eps.s: Deb Liu, CEO of Ancestry and former VP of product at Facebook, shares career advice: keep learning, turn setbacks into stepping stones, plan your career the way you'd plan a product, and, as an introvert, make your work visible. She also covers building a zero-to-one business inside Facebook, why growth is won inch by inch through many small experiments, and how to structure your first 90 days in a new role.
g: CEO of Ancestry; former Facebook VP of product who built Facebook Marketplace; ex-PayPal and eBay director; Intuit board member

eps.t: The marketplace for AI compute with Jared Quincy Davis from Foundry
eps.s: Foundry founder Jared Quincy Davis argues that today's AI clouds are still basically co-location: inflexible and badly underused. He describes Foundry's products for sharing and bidding on GPU capacity and for keeping clusters running through failures, and explains how compound AI systems that sample many answers and pick the best with a verifier will change the shape of compute demand.
g: Founder and CEO of the AI compute platform Foundry, formerly a DeepMind researcher

eps.t: How to consistently go viral: Nikita Bier’s playbook for winning at consumer apps
eps.s: Nikita Bier, who has repeatedly taken apps to number one on the App Store, retraces how tbh and Gas were born, went viral, and got sold. His playbook: target teenagers, look for latent demand where people get value in awkward ways, build a repeatable testing process, validate one stage at a time, and compress the aha moment into seconds. He also criticizes big-company PMs for staying far from the pixels, and explains ethical growth, fighting rumors, and why he values growth over longevity.
g: Serial founder and consumer app growth advisor; founded tbh (sold to Facebook) and Gas (sold to Discord); ex-Facebook PM

eps.t: TikTok is fast, Temu is ruthless, Shopee is resilient: Jianggan Li on Southeast Asia's e-commerce war
eps.ot: 78: TikTok 快、Temu 狠、Shopee 韧，与墨腾创投李江玕聊东南亚电商大战
eps.s: Jianggan Li, CEO of Momentum Works, talks with LatePost reporter Jing Chen about e-commerce and investing in Southeast Asia: why it isn't one market, why Lazada fell behind Shopee, whether Temu's low prices can work there, what Shopee is up against, how TikTok is absorbing Tokopedia, and who still invests in the region. Based on the episode description and timestamps.
g: CEO of Momentum Works; formerly ran Easy Taxi and Foodpanda in Southeast Asia

eps.t: Cloud Strategy in the AI Era with Matt Garman, CEO of AWS
eps.s: AWS CEO Matt Garman recalls how AWS started with building blocks developers already knew, then won over the hardest customers, from banks to intelligence agencies. He covers AWS's three bets on generative AI, its approach to open models and in-house chips, tight compute supply, and why inference will become a new basic unit of computing.
g: CEO of Amazon Web Services (AWS)

eps.t: Building toward a bright post-AGI future with Eric Steinberger from Magic.dev
eps.s: Eric Steinberger, co-founder and CEO of Magic.dev, explains why he is approaching AGI through coding, and why he bets on models that read huge amounts of context at once instead of retrieving pieces. He also covers how to split compute between training and answering, using AI to keep solving AI safety, and what society might look like after AGI.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Magic.dev, which approaches AGI through coding

eps.t: Embracing chaos, inquiry over advocacy, poking the bear, and “impact, impact, impact” | Vlad Loktev
eps.s: Vlad Loktev, former VP of Product at Airbnb and now a partner at Index Ventures, looks back on how he worked through Airbnb's hypergrowth years: put impact above everything, ask before you argue, challenge senior people once you've done the homework, build teams from people with sharp strengths, let the minor fires burn, use manufactured chaos to force creativity, and don't copy other companies' playbooks. He closes with his near-burnout in 2018.
g: Partner at Index Ventures; former VP of Product and general manager at Airbnb

eps.t: From the steam engine to driverless cars, part 3: Xing Meng on how Tesla's FSD evolved
eps.ot: 从蒸汽机到无人驾驶3｜和孟醒聊特斯拉FSD进化史
eps.s: Xing Meng of 5Y Capital has test-driven many versions of Tesla's FSD. Drawing on that, he traces Tesla's shift from hand-written rules to a single model that drives end to end, explains why driver assistance and driverless cars follow entirely different product logic, and asks whether end-to-end is self-driving's ultimate weapon.
g: Partner at 5Y Capital, chairman of KargoBot, former COO of Didi's self-driving unit

eps.t: The original growth hacker reveals his secrets | Sean Ellis (author of “Hacking Growth”)
eps.s: Sean Ellis coined the term "growth hacking." Here he walks through his famous test question, how disappointed would you be without this product: why 40% is the bar, who to ask, what to do when the score is low, and how to mine must-have users for positioning and growth ideas. Then he lays out the order of growth after product-market fit: activation first, then engagement, referral and revenue, acquisition last. Also north-star metrics, ICE scoring, and AI.
g: Growth advisor who coined "growth hacking," author of Hacking Growth, former growth lead at Dropbox and Eventbrite

eps.t: The Road to Autonomous Intelligence with Andrej Karpathy
eps.s: Andrej Karpathy looks back on the decade it took self-driving to go from demo to product, compares Tesla's and Waymo's approaches, and explains why humanoid robots make sense. He also covers Transformers, synthetic data, a small "cognitive core" model, AI as an external brain for people, and Eureka Labs, his AI education company.
g: Founder of Eureka Labs; former OpenAI researcher and Tesla's director of AI

eps.t: AGI changes course: Guangmi Li predicts Strawberry, OpenAI o1, and self-play RL | Global AI Model Quarterly 4
eps.ot: AGI范式大转移：和广密预言草莓、OpenAI o1和self-play RL｜全球大模型季报4
eps.s: In the fourth Global AI Model Quarterly, recorded before OpenAI released o1, Guangmi Li argues that the gains from scaling up language pretraining are slowing. Self-play reinforcement learning, where models learn by practicing against themselves, will drive the second half of the race to AGI. He also surveys Silicon Valley's startup hot spots in coding, video, and robots, and OpenAI's position.
g: Founder and CEO of Shixiang, an investor who tracks AI model companies worldwide

eps.t: How LinkedIn became interesting: The inside story | Tomer Cohen (CPO at LinkedIn)
eps.s: LinkedIn's chief product officer Tomer Cohen tells how he turned a feed full of self-promotion into a place where professionals exchange knowledge: redefining the product's purpose, pulling the AI teams together into a matching engine, and carving out two million members to test the new experience. He also explains his team principle, be wrong but never unclear, what it really means for a product leader to be AI-first, and how he planned his career around conviction and impact.
g: Chief product officer at LinkedIn; previously led LinkedIn's mobile and feed overhaul

eps.t: Elon Musk | All-In Summit 2024
eps.ho: Chamath Palihapitiya, Jason Calacanis, David Sacks, David Friedberg
eps.s: Musk live on stage at the All-In Summit. The first half is about government: rules that only pile up, approvals slower than building rockets, debt interest now above defense spending, and his case for trimming government a few percent a year. The second half covers Starship, Boeing, AI-driven abundance, Tesla's chips and the Optimus robot. Boldest forecast: humanoid robots will outnumber people at least two to one.
g: CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, owner of the social platform X

eps.t: Land your dream job in today’s market: negotiation tactics, job search councils, more | Phyl Terry
eps.s: Phyl Terry, author of Never Search Alone, treats a job search like building a product: form a council of six to eight job seekers, write down what you want and don't want, then go on a listening tour to find a narrow, clear fit between you and the market. He also covers drafting your own job mission with OKRs, negotiating for the resources you need before talking money, exercises for managing emotions, and why asking for help is a habit of senior people.
g: Author of Never Search Alone, founder of Job Search Councils, former CEO of Creative Good

eps.t: Future of LLM Markets, Consolidation, and Small Models with Sarah and Elad
eps.s: Sarah and Elad debate whether the LLM market is consolidating or getting more competitive, and how collapsing API prices push model companies to specialize. They cover progress in small and multimodal models, what AI companies can learn from Google and Uber about data scraping and content limits, and the new wave of AI chips, including AMD's purchase of ZT Systems.
g: Co-hosts of the No Priors podcast, both investors

eps.t: Building SaaS on large AI models: a decade of lessons from China's first AI SaaS product manager
eps.ot: 79: 大模型+SaaS 怎么做？与中国最早的 AI SaaS 产品经理聊聊十年经验
eps.s: Wei Wang, an iFlytek vice president who runs its Tingjian unit, talks with Manqi Cheng about AI software-as-a-service in the age of large models: how they shook up iFlytek Tingjian, why iFlytek insists on charging, ten years of selling software, hardware and service together, compliance when going overseas, and his early days in speech research. Based on the episode description and timestamps.
g: iFlytek vice president and head of Tingjian; led development of iFlytek Tingjian in 2015

eps.t: From Steam Engines to Driverless Cars, Part 4: Waymo and Its Rivals, After Four Months of Quiet Scouting
eps.ot: 从蒸汽机到无人驾驶4｜Waymo和它的对手们：我暗中考察了四个月
eps.s: Xing Meng spent four months riding Waymo's driverless cars in Phoenix and traces how the company grew out of DARPA's robot-car races and Google X. He also looks at the rivals: Cruise's rise and fall, Uber's exit, and where Zoox and Aurora stand. His most striking view: self-driving will have no ChatGPT-style breakout moment. The real turning point is when the business pays for itself.
g: 5Y Capital partner, KargoBot chairman, former COO of Didi's self-driving unit

eps.t: The things engineers are desperate for PMs to understand | Camille Fournier (“The Manager’s Path”)
eps.s: Camille Fournier, author of The Manager's Path and former CTO of Rent the Runway, talks about the PM habits that most annoy engineers, why rewrites from scratch are usually a trap, how long engineers should code before moving into management, and why to hold fewer one-on-ones and stop using long hours to paper over unclear priorities. The second half turns to her new book: how platform teams should be built, measured, and work with business teams.
g: Author of The Manager's Path and Platform Engineering; former CTO of Rent the Runway; ex Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan, Two Sigma

eps.t: OpenAI's o1 is here: SiliconFlow's Jinhui Yuan on its new approach and what it means for developers
eps.ot: 80: OpenAI o1 来了！与硅流袁进辉聊 o1 新范式和开发者生态
eps.s: The day after OpenAI released o1, SiliconFlow founder Jinhui Yuan talks with Manqi Cheng and Qianming He about its new approach: how reinforcement learning, chain-of-thought and extra thinking at answer time improve reasoning, what that means for GPU demand, and what he sees among AI app developers on SiliconFlow's cloud. Based on the episode description and timestamps.
g: Founder of SiliconFlow, a cloud platform for running AI models

eps.t: Former OpenAI researcher Yi Wu on o1: the starting gun for digging a second gold mine
eps.ot: 和OpenAI前研究员吴翼解读o1：吹响了开挖第二座金矿的号角
eps.s: After OpenAI released o1, former OpenAI researcher and Tsinghua professor Yi Wu breaks down the model and the reinforcement learning behind it. He explains why post-training is a second gold mine, why its three key ingredients are hard, and whether one all-purpose model still makes sense. He also recalls 2019 at OpenAI, when the team kept digging without knowing where the gold was.
g: Tsinghua assistant professor, founder of Biansai Technology, former OpenAI researcher

eps.t: Rethinking SEO in the age of AI | Eli Schwartz (SEO advisor, author)
eps.s: Eli Schwartz, author of Product-Led SEO, looks at how search changes as Google rolls out AI Overviews: informational queries at the top of the funnel get swallowed by AI answers, and SEO's value shifts to the middle of the funnel, where people intend to buy. He argues SEO is a product problem that PMs should own, and covers which companies shouldn't do SEO at all, what to measure, programmatic versus editorial content, myths about AI content and backlinks, and what the Google antitrust ruling reveals.
g: SEO and growth advisor, author of Product-Led SEO, former head of SEO at SurveyMonkey

eps.t: Transforming Customer Service through Company Agents, with Sierra's Bret Taylor
eps.s: Sierra co-founder and CEO Bret Taylor sorts AI agents into personal, role-based and company agents, and argues that branded customer service agents will become a company's digital front door, like websites in 1995. He also covers software moving from rules to goals and guardrails, outcome-based pricing, how the AI market rhymes with cloud computing, and where interfaces are heading.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Sierra; chair of OpenAI's board

eps.t: How did games become part of everyday life? A history of gaming communities
eps.ot: 81: 游戏怎么变成了生活？游戏社区发展史
eps.s: Hanyang and Zhongqing, host of the podcast Bu Zai Chang, start from Xiaohongshu and trace how video games went from one-off "publications" to part of daily life: from one-time purchases to ongoing services, more ways to enjoy games, and tools that let anyone make content. They end by asking what a community really is. Recorded before Black Myth: Wukong. Both hosts' views are credited to Zhongqing.
g: Host of the podcast Bu Zai Chang; his views here merge with Hanyang's

eps.t: The Frontier of Spatial Intelligence with Fei-Fei Li
eps.s: Fei-Fei Li and World Labs co-founder Justin Johnson tell a16z's Martin Casado why now is the time to bet on spatial intelligence. She traces her path from betting on data with ImageNet to seeing image storytelling solved far sooner than expected, and explains why understanding the 3D world is a fundamentally different problem from language, with big implications for AR and robots.
g: Co-founder of World Labs, Stanford professor, creator of ImageNet

eps.t: Becoming a super IC: Lessons from 12 years as a PM individual contributor | Tal Raviv (Riverside)
eps.s: Tal Raviv has spent 12 years as a product manager without managing people. He explains how to be a "super IC": why he stayed, how senior ICs should be paid and promoted, how AI lets one person do a team's documentation work, his no-Slack-before-noon system, building a team that doesn't depend on the PM, spotting which two departments really win, and why customer feelings matter as much as logic.
g: Product lead at Riverside; a career individual-contributor product manager

eps.t: Why Human Data is Key to AI: Alexandr Wang from Scale AI (Frontier Data Foundries)
eps.s: Scale AI founder Alexandr Wang tells a16z's David George that AI rests on compute, algorithms and data, and that public data has largely run dry, so the world needs data foundries. He explains why agents still don't work, why big tech's huge AI spending is rational, why renting out models is a weak business, why enterprises are slow, and why Scale kept its headcount flat.
g: Founder and CEO of Scale AI, which supplies training data to AI labs

eps.t: Using AI to evaluate employee performance with Rippling's COO Matt MacInnis
eps.s: Rippling COO Matt MacInnis explains the company's "compound startup" approach and Talent Signal, an AI product that reads employees' actual work and flags how new hires are doing. He covers why it's designed the way it is, how it guards against bias, which decisions it must never make, and the concerns critics have raised.
g: COO of Rippling, which makes HR, IT and finance software

eps.t: Wang Xiaochuan returns to talk o1 and reinforcement learning: a path from fast thinking to slow thinking
eps.ot: 王小川返场谈o1与强化学习：摸到了一条从快思考走向慢思考的路
eps.s: After o1's release, Baichuan founder Wang Xiaochuan returns to explain how large language models relate to reinforcement learning, borrowing Confucius on learning versus thinking and the idea of fast and slow thinking. He also covers using reinforcement learning in medicine and how startups can stay out of the big companies' firing range.
g: Founder and CEO of Baichuan, a Chinese AI model company

eps.t: Lessons in product leadership and AI strategy from Glean, Google, Amazon, and Slack | Tamar Yehoshua
eps.s: Tamar Yehoshua, president of product and technology at Glean and former CPO of Slack, shares career lessons: do your current job well, read people's motivations, and follow the best people instead of making five-year plans. She argues a company doesn't need to run well to win, describes what she learned from Bezos and Butterfield, and how she pairs with engineering. The second half covers how AI will change product work and what to watch for when building non-deterministic LLM products.
g: President of product and technology at Glean, former Slack CPO, ex Google Search and Amazon A9 VP

eps.t: What's the point of being alive?
eps.ot: 82: 人活着有啥意思
eps.s: Hanyang and his old friend Fengze ask what the point of living is, a companion to the earlier episode with Xiaowei Wang on why living feels so hard. They argue that a sense of meaning is a basic need, that much modern work has been emptied of meaning, and that a person's worth shouldn't be measured by work alone. Both hosts' views are credited to Fengze.
g: Hydropower engineer working in Africa, an old friend of the show; views merged with Hanyang's

eps.t: How marketplaces win: Liquidity, growth levers, quality, more | Benjamin Lauzier (Lyft, Thumbtack)
eps.s: Benjamin Lauzier, former VP of product and growth at Thumbtack and an early Lyft employee, lays out how marketplaces work: which side to focus on before product-market fit, how to measure and predict liquidity, which businesses suit a marketplace model, why marketplaces fail, and whether to control or empower the supply side. He also tells how Lyft used a mentor-driver program to fight an Uber 30 times its size, and compares French and American product cultures.
g: Former VP of product and growth at Thumbtack, Lyft's 30th employee who led driver product, now founder of Nurra Health

eps.t: Thinking like a gardener, slime mold, the adjacent possible: Product advice from Alex Komoroske
eps.s: Alex Komoroske, who led Chrome's open web platform at Google and corporate strategy at Stripe, talks product and organizations through a string of metaphors: LLMs as magical duct tape that changes the industry's base assumptions, curiosity and taste as the skills that matter most in the AI era, kayfabe in big companies, slime-mold coordination costs, working like a gardener rather than a builder, voluntary "nerd clubs," and plotting a path with the adjacent possible plus a distant north star.
g: Founder of an AI-era web startup, former Stripe strategy head, 13 years at Google leading Chrome's open web platform

eps.t: The Sheriff of Silicon Valley: Lina Khan's FTC agenda for M&A, AI Acquisitions, and Non-Competes
eps.s: FTC Chair Lina Khan lays out her approach to antitrust: how merger review weighs the risk of big companies buying early competitors, and what that means for startup exits. She also explains why she supports open-weight models and a ban on non-competes, and why she thinks simpler rules are better.
g: Chair of the U.S. Federal Trade Commission (FTC), the antitrust enforcer

eps.t: Will mergers and acquisitions take off? Fubin Lu on five years of quietly buying companies worldwide
eps.ot: 并购重组会兴起吗？和陆复斌聊他隐蔽做全球并购这5年
eps.s: Fubin Lu talks about five years of quietly buying internet companies around the world: how buying a company differs from venture investing, how he picks targets, and how he remakes them after the deal. He also weighs whether China's policy push will revive mergers. His key point: an acquisition isn't a financial game. You have to run the business yourself.
g: Investor who buys controlling stakes in internet companies worldwide

eps.t: Conscious leadership: Unlocking vision, strategy and purpose | JM Nickels (Uber, Waymo, DoorDash)
eps.s: JM Nickels, who has led product at Uber, DoorDash and Waymo, explains what he calls conscious leadership: how to handle fear in high-pressure meetings, and why his work got better once he stopped obsessing over how he came across. He also covers how to come up with a good vision and strategy, how to balance vision with execution, and what makes each of the three companies different. He closes on what emotions are for at work and getting clear on your life's objective function.
g: Product lead for Uber's mobility business, former product leader at Waymo and DoorDash, built the first Uber Pool

eps.t: Launching AI products with Braintrust's CEO Ankur Goyal
eps.s: Braintrust founder Ankur Goyal explains why evals are core infrastructure for AI products, why companies moved from fine-tuning to prompting, and why many retreated from free-form agents to deterministic workflows. He also shares his views on data warehouses, TypeScript and how to build an AI team.
g: Founder and CEO of Braintrust, an AI evals company; previously founded Impira

eps.t: From Steam Engines to Driverless Cars, Part 5: Eight years on the self-driving startup roller coaster
eps.ot: 从蒸汽机到无人驾驶5｜谈谈自动驾驶创投过山车这8年
eps.s: As he leaves Didi for 5Y Capital, Xing Meng looks back on eight years of booms and busts in self-driving startups. He explains why he returned to venture capital just as many were leaving, what a startup incubator should really do, and the trap of sky-high early valuations. Most interesting: he holds up the cycle as a mirror for today's AI model industry.
g: 5Y Capital partner, former COO of Didi's self-driving unit

eps.t: Behind the product: NotebookLM | Raiza Martin (Senior Product Manager, AI @ Google Labs)
eps.s: Raiza Martin, who leads NotebookLM, tells how it grew from a tiny Google Labs experiment into a hit. She explains how a very small team works with almost no process, how Audio Overviews emerged from poking at what new models could do, and why she treats fun as a real goal. She also covers building in public on Discord, handling a viral scare, and the long-term idea of turning any input into any output.
g: Senior AI product manager at Google Labs; leads the NotebookLM product

eps.t: Harari's Nexus: even without AI, everyone has to find meaning (a crossover with CITIC Academy's podcast)
eps.ot: 83: 《智人之上》：没有AI，寻找意义也是每个人的必解题 | 串台《知本论》
eps.s: In a crossover with CITIC Academy's podcast, anthropologist Changgeng Yuan, host Bingjie Sun and Manqi Cheng discuss Yuval Noah Harari's new book Nexus: how human information networks work, what AI changes as a new force, and why modern people struggle to find meaning even without AI. Speakers aren't marked in the notes, so views are credited to Yuan.
g: Anthropologist, PhD from the Chinese University of Hong Kong; taught at SUSTech and Yunnan University

eps.t: Why most public speaking advice is wrong—and how to finally overcome anxiety | Tristan de Montebello
eps.s: Speaking coach Tristan de Montebello argues that most public speaking advice treats symptoms, not causes. He explains why getting better at speaking changes your whole life, why your best talks happen when you stop thinking about speaking, and plays a few practice games live with Lenny. He closes with two ways to prepare a talk: squeeze it like an accordion, and decide the one line the audience should remember.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Ultraspeaking; fastest ever to reach the World Championship of Public Speaking final in 2017

eps.t: Why did Tesla's stock fall while Uber's rose? Talking through Tesla's robotaxi event
eps.ot: 特斯拉股价跌了，Uber却涨了？漫谈特斯拉Robotaxi大会
eps.s: A look back at Tesla's robotaxi event: why it felt more like a fan party, what business problems face the two-seat Cybercab and the plan to let private owners add their cars to a robotaxi fleet, and whether the Optimus robots were remotely operated. The most telling detail: after the event, Tesla's stock fell while Uber's rose.
g: A guest in this discussion, not named in the public show notes

eps.t: Xiaodi Hou on Tesla's We, Robot event: smoke versus reality
eps.ot: 84: 与侯晓迪聊特斯拉 We,Robot：烟雾与现实
eps.s: After Tesla's We, Robot event, Bot Auto founder Xiaodi Hou talks with Manqi Cheng about the smoke and reality of robotaxis: why L4 self-driving should be judged by all-in operating cost per mile, what he makes of end-to-end models and world models, what stands between L4 and profit, and why he started again in Houston after leaving TuSimple. Based on the episode description and timestamps.
g: Founder and CEO of Bot Auto; TuSimple co-founder and former CTO, CEO and chairman

eps.t: Becoming more strategic, navigating difficult colleagues, founder mode, more | Anneka Gupta
eps.s: Anneka Gupta, chief product officer at Rubrik, talks about finding fun in hard situations, scheduling by energy instead of time, and how a product leader works with a hands-on founder. The most useful part is her definition of being strategic: explain a simple, compelling why and push for big changes, starting with how well you summarize in meetings. She also covers deciding at 70 percent certainty, giving and taking hard feedback, and breaking into product management.
g: Chief product officer at Rubrik, product management lecturer at Stanford GSB, former president of LiveRamp

eps.t: Gaming, Nobel Prizes and At-Risk Businesses in the AI Era
eps.s: Sarah and Elad go from NotebookLM and Stanford students' consumer AI prototypes to game NPCs and player mods, the social isolation AI companions may bring, o1's test-time compute, and AI's first Nobel Prizes. They close by asking which software and jobs AI will hit first, and which companies are "AI-durable."
g: Co-hosts of the No Priors podcast, both investors

eps.t: How to see like a designer: The hidden power of typography and logos | Jessica Hische
eps.s: Lettering designer Jessica Hische, who just redesigned Lenny's logo, uses that project to explain when an early company should spend on brand, how a logo redesign narrows round by round, and how non-designers can train their eye for type. The best part is optical correction: letters that are mathematically perfect look wrong, so good fonts break the rules on purpose. She also covers brand systems, pricing, avoiding burnout, and AI.
g: Lettering artist, type designer and children's book author; designed logos for Mailchimp, Eventbrite and Philz Coffee

eps.t: Waymo's Journey to Full Autonomy: AI Breakthroughs, Safety, and Scaling
eps.s: Waymo co-CEO Dmitri Dolgov traces the path from the DARPA challenges to about 100,000 paid rides a week. He explains why full autonomy is hard because of the long tail of rare events, why Waymo sticks with multiple sensors and simulation-based evaluation, and why trust, not capital, limits expansion.
g: Co-CEO of Waymo, the driverless ride-hailing company

eps.t: How many steps does it take to build a country from scratch? | The Road to Industrialization, Part 1
eps.ot: 85: 国家从无到有，拢共分几步？｜工业化之路 01
eps.s: The first episode of a new series, The Road to Industrialization. Hanyang and Fengze, who spent three years on engineering projects in Africa, invent a country called "Zeyangpolis" with about 50 million people, limited resources and a very high birth rate, then work out how it could rise from nothing. The page doesn't record the details, and both hosts' views are credited to Fengze.
g: Hydropower engineer with a PhD who spent three years on projects in Africa

eps.t: Meta's head of product on working with Mark Zuckerberg, early growth tactics, and more | Naomi Gleit
eps.s: Naomi Gleit, Meta's head of product and Facebook employee number 29, tells how she got in the door and became a PM, how Mark Zuckerberg has changed, and how his inner circle works. She then walks through the early growth team's methods: growth accounting, the 7 friends in 10 days target, and removing barriers. The second half is her working principles: the PM as conductor, extreme clarity, canonical docs, simplifying, and having a point of view.
g: Head of product at Meta, Facebook employee number 29, longest-tenured executive after Zuckerberg

eps.t: We, Robot, part 2: Huazhe Xu of Tsinghua and Galaxea on what Optimus really shows
eps.ot: 86: We, Robot-2，清华叉院/星海图许华哲看“Optimus”的门道
eps.s: Following up on Tesla's We, Robot event, Galaxea co-founder and Tsinghua assistant professor Huazhe Xu talks with Manqi Cheng, starting from the remote control behind Tesla's Optimus robots. He covers reinforcement learning, imitation learning, multimodal models and world models, then touch, robot body design and the data bottleneck, ending with universal basic income and the risk of AI going against human goals.
g: Galaxea co-founder; assistant professor at Tsinghua's IIIS, where he leads the embodied AI lab

eps.t: #2223 - Elon Musk
eps.s: A week before the 2024 U.S. election, Musk sits down with Joe Rogan. He ranges from Diablo leaderboards to why he bought Twitter, the Justice Department's hiring suit against SpaceX, Community Notes, speech and gun rights, drug makers, drug policy, immigration and the vote, and Tesla. A standout: his one-question test for any drug, whether it makes people better.
g: CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, owner of X, touring swing states before the election

eps.t: 4 questions Shreyas wishes he'd asked himself sooner | Former PM leader at Stripe, Twitter, Google
eps.s: Speaking to about a thousand people at Lenny's summit, Shreyas Doshi shares four questions he wishes he had asked himself sooner: why am I so busy, do I really have taste, why does work frustrate me, and am I really listening. Highlights: a real product strategy that everyone has agreed on cuts annual planning from weeks to three days, and sloppy "two-way door" decisions quietly pile up into feature debt. He also covers catchy metaphors, authority, and planning a career around your superpowers.
g: Former product leader at Stripe, Twitter, Google and Yahoo; now writes and advises on product management

eps.t: Product Management Is Dead, So What Are We Doing Instead? | Lenny & Friends Summit 2024
eps.s: Claire Vo's talk at the 2024 Lenny & Friends Summit. The title makes a blunt claim: product management is dead, so what are we doing instead? Only the title and running time were available for this episode, with no summary, chapters or transcript, so we can note the theme but not any specific arguments.

eps.t: Rituals of Great Decision-Making | Lenny & Friends Summit 2024
eps.s: Shishir Mehrotra's talk at the 2024 Lenny & Friends Summit, about the recurring rituals behind great decision-making. Only the title and running time were available for this episode, with no summary, chapters or transcript, so we can note the theme but not any specific arguments.

eps.t: Forecasting the Future with Kalshi: America's First Regulated Prediction Market
eps.s: Kalshi CEO Tarek Mansour explains how his CFTC-regulated exchange for event contracts spent nearly three years getting licensed, then sued its regulator to win the right to list election contracts. He defends prediction markets as tools for hedging and pooling information, not gambling: the price is the probability.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Kalshi, a regulated prediction market exchange

eps.t: Another strange new gadget at home: Narwal on how new consumer electronics are born
eps.ot: 87: 家里又多了个“怪东西”！与云鲸聊新消费电子品的诞生
eps.s: Bin Zhuang, who runs Narwal's floor washer line, talks with LatePost writer Jiahao Zhang about how new kinds of consumer electronics are born: what makes a new category succeed, how to tell real needs from fake ones before green-lighting a product, and why floor washers appeared and how they relate to vacuums and robot vacuums. Sponsored by Narwal. Based on the episode description and timestamps.
g: Runs Narwal's floor washer line; formerly led R&D on robot vacuums, drones, gimbals and lidar

eps.t: Zhihu's Zhou Yuan on a newsroom run by everyone, the paradox of loneliness, AI and fate
eps.ot: 和知乎周源聊，社会化编辑部、孤独的悖论、AI与宿命
eps.s: Zhihu founder Zhou Yuan talks about how AI models are shaking up online communities, and compares Zhihu's own AI search tool, Zhihu Zhida, with Perplexity. He revisits why he started Zhihu, as a newsroom the whole of society could join, along with the fight against ByteDance, strategic wobbles after going public, and a founder's loneliness and sense of fate.
g: Founder, chairman and CEO of Zhihu, a major Chinese Q&A community

eps.t: Just evil enough: Subversive marketing strategies for startups | Alistair Croll
eps.s: Alistair Croll, author of Lean Analytics, walks through his new book Just Evil Enough. His case: getting a product in front of people matters as much as building it. Startups should hunt for "zero-day" marketing tricks nobody has used, scouting product, medium and market for openings. He lays out 11 kinds of plays, many examples, and hard ethical lines, and argues that as AI makes building cheap, distribution becomes the scarce part.
g: Author of Lean Analytics and Just Evil Enough; serial entrepreneur and startup advisor

eps.t: A conversation with OpenAI's CPO Kevin Weil, Anthropic's CPO Mike Krieger, and Sarah Guo
eps.s: Investor Sarah Guo hosts OpenAI CPO Kevin Weil and Anthropic CPO Mike Krieger on building AI products: planning when models improve this fast, using evals to measure progress, the new skills PMs need, teaching enterprise users, and where proactive, asynchronous AI is heading. Only a page summary and chapter titles were available, with no attribution by speaker, so the views are recorded jointly.
g: Chief product officers of OpenAI and Anthropic, in a joint conversation hosted by Sarah Guo

eps.t: Breaking the rules of growth: Why Shopify bans KPIs, optimizes for churn, and prioritizes intuition
eps.s: Archie Abrams, VP of product and head of growth at Shopify, explains several ways Shopify breaks the usual growth rules: it lowers the barrier to starting a business instead of fighting churn, keeps long-term holdouts on every experiment and checks GMV a year later, sets teams absolute-number goals rather than conversion rates, and runs the core product on a hundred-year vision and taste with no KPIs. He also covers attribution once self-serve and sales merge, and discount psychology from Udemy.
g: VP of product and head of growth at Shopify, leading a 600-person growth organization; formerly at Udemy

eps.t: NVIDIA's Jensen Huang on AI Chip Design, Scaling Data Centers, and his 10-Year Bets
eps.s: Jensen Huang explains how NVIDIA, with Moore's law running out, gets rapid system-level gains by designing software and hardware together and treating the whole data center as the unit of computing, and how xAI's 100,000-GPU cluster came online in weeks. He also lays out his ten-year bets on AI factories, digital employees, robotics and AI-designed chips.
g: Founder and CEO of NVIDIA

eps.t: SpaceX Starship's fifth flight: a success more perfect than anyone expected
eps.ot: 88: SpaceX 星舰第五飞：“即便成功，也没想到是如此完美的成功”
eps.s: After Starship's fifth test flight, Liang Chen, a former chief designer in Chinese commercial spaceflight, reviews the launch with Manqi Cheng: why catching the Super Heavy booster with the launch tower's arms was a major breakthrough, how low cost plus frequent launches drives fast iteration, how Falcon, Dragon, Starship and Starlink fit together, the timeline for crewed Mars landings, and where China's commercial space industry stands.
g: Ex-chief designer at a Chinese space startup, deputy chief designer of a reusable rocket, Beihang PhD

eps.t: Everything you've ever wanted to know about SAFe and the product owner role | Melissa Perri
eps.s: Melissa Perri, founder of Product Institute, explains how the product owner role grew out of Scrum, why she flatly does not recommend SAFe, and what large companies must add beyond a development process when they go digital: product strategy, organization design, product operations, incentives and career paths. She also advises product owners who want to become real product managers, from how to write a resume to whether certifications are worth it.
g: Founder and CEO of Product Institute, author of Escaping the Build Trap and Product Operations

eps.t: Simplify To Win | Lenny & Friends Summit 2024
eps.s: Ami Vora's talk at the 2024 Lenny & Friends Summit, on winning by simplifying. Only the title and running time were available for this episode, with no summary, chapters or transcript, so we can note the theme but not any specific arguments.

eps.t: Kai-Fu Lee: what should we do if America achieves AGI dominance?
eps.ot: 和李开复聊聊：如果美国形成AGI霸权，我们应该怎么办？
eps.s: After the US election, Kai-Fu Lee warns about AGI dominance: whoever first builds AGI that crushes its rivals becomes a monopolist. China, he argues, shouldn't match the spending. It should cut the cost of running AI by building models, infrastructure and apps together, and race to build AI-first apps. He also sizes up OpenAI, Google and Nvidia and predicts a consumer app boom in 2025.
g: Founder and CEO of 01.AI, chairman of the venture firm Sinovation Ventures

eps.t: How To Craft An Elite Career | Lenny & Friends Summit 2024
eps.s: This is Nikhyl Singhal's talk at the 2024 Lenny & Friends Summit on how to build a top-tier career. Only the title and running time are available for this session, with no transcript or chapter notes, so we can record the topic but not the specific points he made.

eps.t: Becoming an AI PM | Aman Khan (Arize AI, ex-Spotify, Apple, Cruise)
eps.s: Aman Khan of Arize AI breaks AI product managers into three types, explains how someone without a technical degree can switch into AI PM work with a portfolio of working prototypes, and argues PMs matter more, not less, in the AI era. He then covers how top AI PMs avoid bandwagons, why cake mix and the IKEA effect hold product lessons, and how individual-contributor PMs keep their energy and explore when the path is unclear.
g: Head of product at Arize AI; previously a product manager at Spotify, Apple and Cruise

eps.t: AI and the Future of Math, with DeepMind's AlphaProof Team
eps.s: Three members of Google DeepMind's AlphaProof team explain the system that reached silver-medal level at the International Math Olympiad: AlphaZero-style reinforcement learning applied to formal proofs in Lean, plus inventing its own problem variants to learn from mid-solve. They discuss why it can't yet build theories, what it means for verifying code, and why humans must get better at asking questions. Speaker attributions are inferred.
g: Google DeepMind researcher who leads the team behind AlphaProof
Google DeepMind researcher and one of AlphaProof's technical leads
Google DeepMind researcher who worked on AlphaGo, AlphaZero and MuZero

eps.t: When technology meets art: NVIDIA and Xinpianchang on how AI is reshaping creative work
eps.ot: 89: 当技术遇上艺术:与 NVIDIA 和新片场聊 AI 如何重塑创作
eps.s: Chengqiu Shi, a senior technical marketing manager at NVIDIA China, and Xingliang Yin, chairman and CEO of Xinpianchang, talk with Manqi Cheng about how computing and AI are reshaping film and entertainment: how high-tech filmmaking already was before AI, how generative AI lowers the bar from idea to finished work, and where people fit in creative work now. Speakers aren't marked, so views are assigned by topic.
g: Chairman and CEO of Xinpianchang, a film and video creation platform
Senior technical marketing manager at NVIDIA China

eps.t: Building Wiz: the fastest-growing startup in history | Raaz Herzberg (CMO and VP Product Strategy)
eps.s: Raaz Herzberg, an early Wiz employee who went from engineer to product to CMO, walks through the company's early pivot from network security to cloud security: how to tell polite interest from real pull, and why the founders sold the first few million dollars themselves. She then explains how she took over marketing with no experience, made noise with bold booths and branding, why the CMO job is hard, what product people can learn from marketing about clarity, and how she lives with impostor syndrome.
g: CMO and VP of product strategy at Wiz, its first product manager, formerly a security product leader at Microsoft

eps.t: How To Do The Product Review Right (By Doing It Wrong) | Lenny & Friends Summit 2024
eps.s: Figma's Yuhki Yamashita and Mihika Kapoor share the stage at the 2024 Lenny & Friends Summit. The premise is playful: show how a product review goes wrong in order to teach how to do it right. Only the title and running time are available, with no transcript or chapter notes, so we can record the topic but not their specific points.

eps.t: Behind the product: Replit | Amjad Masad (co-founder and CEO)
eps.s: Replit co-founder and CEO Amjad Masad demos a single prompt turning into a deployable feature-voting app with a database in minutes, then explains the AI-specific runtime and multi-model setup behind it. The second half is about what this means for PMs, designers, engineers and founders: cheaper software creates far more demand, generating ideas becomes the new bottleneck, learning to code needs an AI-native approach, and companies should drop fixed roadmaps and blur role boundaries.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Replit, the online coding platform

eps.t: Model Plateaus and Enterprise AI Adoption with Cohere's Aidan Gomez
eps.s: Cohere CEO Aidan Gomez explains why he isn't building a ChatGPT rival and instead focuses on getting AI deployed inside enterprises, and why customization should start cheap. He also covers flattening model progress, test-time compute as a new lever, AGI, and why he doesn't think models are becoming commodities.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Cohere, and a co-author of the Transformer paper

eps.t: When every country wants its own AI model: Yu Chen of Yunqi Partners on sovereign AI
eps.ot: 90: 当每个国家都想要自己的大模型？与云启陈昱聊主权 AI
eps.s: With Jensen Huang meeting Masayoshi Son in Tokyo and many countries pouring money into AI infrastructure, Yunqi Partners partner Yu Chen talks with Manqi Cheng about "sovereign AI," AI a country controls itself: where the demand comes from, opportunities in chips, computing centers and AI infrastructure, China's AI data-center boom and its risks, and what it means for ordinary people.
g: Partner at Yunqi Partners; first-round investor in MiniMax, DeepRoute.ai and Zilliz

eps.t: The ultimate guide to founder-led sales | Jen Abel (co-founder of JJELLYFISH)
eps.s: Jen Abel helps early-stage founders make their first sales. She walks through founder-led sales step by step: why the founder must sell, how to write a cold email, why to hand-pick 30 people before using tools, how admitting weakness on a first call gets honest answers, why nearly half of B2B companies must sell a service first, and how to get through procurement. Her core point: early sales is about learning, and the problem is almost always at the top of the funnel.
g: Co-founder of JJELLYFISH; formerly led enterprise sales at The Muse and General Assembly
