eps.t: Ethereum's Vitalik Buterin on the power of large language models, his philosophy of technology, and cats
eps.ot: 和以太坊Vitalik Buterin聊：LLM的权力、技术哲学观与猫
eps.s: Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin contrasts the philosophies behind AI and crypto: AI concentrates power, while crypto aims to spread it out. The heart of the talk is how the two can meet and keep each other in check. He also covers how crypto applications are evolving, brain-computer interfaces and his personal life.
g: Co-founder of Ethereum, the blockchain platform

eps.t: Qing Cheng: Buddhism is not a painkiller for the mind
eps.ot: 91: 成庆：佛学不是精神的止痛药
eps.s: Qing Cheng, a history professor at Shanghai University, talks with Hanyang about Buddhism today: how far it has become emotional healing and wellness consumption, what young people buy when they "consume Buddhism," what studying it should mean, whether it makes you a better self or frees you from clinging to self, and whether people still believe they can reach the Buddha's insight.
g: Shanghai University historian of Ming-Qing Chan thought and modern Chinese Buddhism; teaches Vistopia's Buddhism course

eps.t: Identify your bullseye customer in one day | Michael Margolis (UX Research Partner at GV)
eps.s: Michael Margolis, UX research partner at GV, walks through the one-day research sprint he has run with more than 300 portfolio companies. Narrow your target to a "bullseye customer," then combine five customers, three prototypes and one day of interviews so the whole team watches live and agrees on the spot. He also covers recruiting and screening, interview structure, telling real demand from polite encouragement, and common research mistakes.
g: UX research partner at GV (Google Ventures), author of Learn More Faster, former Gmail user researcher

eps.t: How a great founder becomes a great CEO | Jonathan Lowenhar (co-founder of Enjoy The Work)
eps.s: Jonathan Lowenhar coaches founders on becoming CEOs. He argues that "founder mode" has become an excuse to skip learning the CEO craft. He lists nine common ways CEOs fail; the most common is "fire, then aim," and the fix is planning backward from where the company needs to end up. He also explains the Magic Box method for selling a company, how to hire executives, a four-part go-to-market framework, and why to trust the quiet voice in life-or-death moments.
g: Co-founder of Enjoy The Work, a coaching firm for startup CEOs; former division head and serial founder

eps.t: Bolt's Eric Simons on Enabling Everyone to Generate Websites with AI
eps.s: StackBlitz CEO Eric Simons explains how Bolt.new builds on years of work running a full development environment in the browser, so anyone can describe a website and get it built and deployed. He also covers open-sourcing the prompts, community as a way to keep users, the moment AI coding models got reliable enough, and a future of "software composers."
g: Co-founder and CEO of StackBlitz, the company behind Bolt.new

eps.t: How did Jensen Huang build a $3 trillion Nvidia?
eps.ot: 黄仁勋和3万亿美元英伟达是如何炼成的？
eps.s: Marking the Chinese edition of The Nvidia Way, translator Yajun Wang and others trace Jensen Huang's life, Nvidia's ups and downs and its key strategic bets. They also unpack his management tools: whiteboard meetings, regular top-five reports and a "captain" for every project. Together, these explain how Nvidia grew into a $3 trillion company.
g: Translator of The Nvidia Way into Chinese, former chief strategy officer at Longfor Group

eps.t: Chuang Peng of Yunshi Capital meets 1,000 startups a year: the limits and doubts of Chinese companies going global
eps.ot: 92: 每年聊 1000 个项目，我看到出海者们的局限和犹豫 | 对话云时资本彭创
eps.s: Chuang Peng, founder of Yunshi Capital, which mainly backs Chinese companies expanding abroad, talks with LatePost reporter Jing Chen about his path from investing in Youzan and 51 Credit Card to Africa and then overseas expansion, founders' limits and doubts, the "go global or go bust" anxiety, what his fund backs, raising a dual-currency fund, and advice for young investors.
g: Founder and partner of Yunshi Capital; formerly managing partner at Hongtai Fund and VP at Hillhouse

eps.t: Geoffrey Hinton, Nobel Prize in Physics 2024: Official interview
eps.s: An official Nobel Week interview. Hinton separates AI's near-term risks, from lost jobs and fake videos to phishing, bioweapons and released model weights, from the long-term risk of AI that outsmarts us, which he now gives even odds within 4 to 19 years. He also explains how continental drift taught him to stick with unpopular ideas, and what he regrets.
g: Co-winner of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics and a pioneer of deep learning.

eps.t: Seth Godin's best tactics for building remarkable products, strategies, brands and more
eps.s: Marketing author Seth Godin starts with his early days as a product manager at Spinnaker and talks about taste and standards, why a brand is a promise rather than a logo, and how AI companies can build one. He walks through the four key choices in his new book "This is Strategy," the idea of tension, and seeing systems. He closes on being remarkable, Google's restrained homepage, and why Jaguar's rebrand and the Cybertruck created buzz, not customers.
g: Marketing author and entrepreneur; wrote "Purple Cow" and "This is Strategy," founded altMBA, early Spinnaker PM

eps.t: ByteDance vs. the "six little dragons": the fight for survival among China's AI model startups (crossover with Crossing)
eps.ot: 93: 字节VS六小龙，大模型创业生存战 | 串台「十字路口Crossing」
eps.s: LatePost teams up with the podcast Crossing for a year-end look at China's AI model startups in 2024, built on LatePost's story about giants closing in. They cover how fast the technology might improve, where the six best-known startups stand, how ByteDance went from laggard to leader, what Alibaba, Tencent and Baidu are doing, and how apps are growing. Speakers weren't marked, so views are credited to Manqi Cheng.
g: Head of tech coverage at LatePost; wrote its AI startup survival story; views merged with co-hosts

eps.t: What is an AI founder who raised nearly 400 million yuan up to? Fanchao Qi's first interview
eps.ot: 融了近4亿的AI创业者在干嘛？岂凡超的第一次访谈
eps.s: In his first interview, DeepLang AI founder Fanchao Qi explains how the company, after raising nearly 400 million yuan, shifted from training models to building products. He argues that a model is not a product, and he wants to rebuild how people get content around individual pieces of information rather than whole articles. He also introduces the new product, Yujing.
g: Founder and CEO of the AI company DeepLang AI

eps.t: Making and Leading Products People Love (Scott Belsky) | Lenny & Friends Summit 2024
eps.s: This is Scott Belsky's talk at the 2024 Lenny & Friends Summit on how to make products people genuinely love, and how to lead the teams that build them. Only the title and running time are available, with no transcript or chapter notes, so we can record the topic but not the specific points he made.

eps.t: Fei-Fei Li on a Human-Centered Approach to AI
eps.s: Fei-Fei Li tells Dax Shepard about her immigrant teenage years in New Jersey, the math teacher who became a second father, and her family's dry cleaner. She then explains how physics led her to AI, why she built ImageNet, and why she argues for human-centered AI: machine values are human values, and AI is more like electricity than nuclear weapons.
g: Stanford computer science professor, co-director of Stanford HAI, creator of ImageNet

eps.t: How To Win Friends & Influence Decisions (Julie Zhuo) | Lenny & Friends Summit 2024
eps.s: This is Julie Zhuo's talk at the 2024 Lenny & Friends Summit. The title riffs on Dale Carnegie's "How to Win Friends and Influence People," and the subject is how to sway decisions inside a company. Only the title and running time are available, with no transcript or chapter notes, so we can record the topic but not her specific points.

eps.t: How Diamond Cooling Could Power the Future of AI, with Akash Systems
eps.s: Akash Systems' two co-founders explain how they bond lab-grown diamond to semiconductors to cool GPU servers. They argue heat is the root bottleneck for AI compute, and that lowering temperatures buys reliability, performance and energy headroom. They also discuss a sovereign cloud customer in India, the CHIPS Act and U.S. manufacturing. (The transcript lacks speaker labels, so attributions are inferred.)
g: Co-founder and CEO of Akash Systems, trained in materials science and electrical engineering
Akash Systems co-founder with a background in silicon carbide devices

eps.t: Behind the product: Duolingo streaks | Jackson Shuttleworth (Group PM, Retention Team)
eps.s: Jackson Shuttleworth, who leads Duolingo's retention team, spends a whole episode on one feature: the streak. He explains why it's the biggest growth lever after the courses themselves, the key experiments like switching from an XP goal to one lesson a day, the trade-offs between the first seven days, flexibility and keeping the streak meaningful, and the roles of clarity, notification timing and celebration. He also shares how 600-plus experiments in four years got done.
g: Group Product Manager on Duolingo's retention team; former management consultant

eps.t: A former presidential campaign member on how candidates find product-market fit with America's story
eps.ot: 与总统竞选成员聊，总统候选人与美国叙事如何PMF？
eps.s: A guest who worked on Barack Obama's presidential campaign breaks down US elections through the lens of startups and products: how campaigns scale up at breakneck speed, how a candidate fits the national story voters believe in, and how relations between Silicon Valley and Washington are shifting after the 2024 election.
g: A guest who worked on Barack Obama's presidential campaign

eps.t: Live in Silicon Valley: a meetup with Zhongqing, host of Bu Zai Chang, and old friend Fengze
eps.ot: 硅谷线下活动：与《不在场》主播重轻和老朋友丰泽一起聊聊
eps.s: A 37-second announcement: LatePost Chat is holding an in-person event in Silicon Valley, joined by Zhongqing, host of the podcast Bu Zai Chang, and old friend Fengze. Like recording a short episode live, the three will talk about this trip to the US and how they make their shows, take audience questions, and look ahead to next year.

eps.t: How Shopify builds a high-intensity culture | Farhan Thawar (VP and Head of Eng)
eps.s: Shopify's head of engineering Farhan Thawar covers three themes: choosing the harder path, creating intensity inside an organization, and hiring. He explains why pair programming is the most underrated management tool, describes Shopify's weekly updates and six-week reviews, its periodic deletion of all recurring meetings, its preference for building infrastructure and deleting code, and its use of work trials and a thousand interns instead of interviews. He also admits that hedging a technology choice in his first week wasted 100 engineers' time for 18 months.
g: VP and Head of Engineering at Shopify; early leader at Xtreme Labs and founder of Helpful

eps.t: Revolutionizing Customer Success with Agency's Elias Torres
eps.s: Drift co-founder Elias Torres talks about his new company, Agency. Helping OpenAI serve enterprise customers and doing consulting showed him that large models can take care of customers at scale, so he wants AI to keep service one-on-one even as companies grow. He also criticizes heavy Salesforce-style software and the advice to "do things that don't scale," and discusses hiring and change management.
g: Founder and CEO of Agency, and co-founder of Drift

eps.t: What do industrial designers actually do?
eps.ot: 95: 工业设计师到底在干啥？
eps.s: Host Hanyang talks with industrial designer Zhibin about what the job really is: what students learn, how it relates to other design fields and product managers, where it sits in making a product, and what high- and low-paid designers solve. They review the iPhone and the Li Auto MEGA, the details people take for granted, and traps non-expert bosses fall into. The show page lists only the questions.
g: Industrial designer and host of the podcast WildloG

eps.t: Meta's Chief AI Scientist Yann LeCun Makes the Case for Open Source
eps.s: Kara Swisher talks with Yann LeCun about open-source AI, regulation, Elon Musk and AI doom. Highlights: the months-long internal debate behind Meta's decision to release Llama 2 openly, his view that scaling LLMs alone won't reach human-level AI, and his blunt verdict that extreme voices pushing to regulate AI research are delusional.
g: Meta's chief AI scientist, NYU professor and Turing Award winner

eps.t: Behind the founder: Marc Benioff
eps.s: Salesforce co-founder and CEO Marc Benioff talks about hoarding domain names early on, how a line from Steve Jobs led to AppExchange, the "end of software" stunt of 2000, and his method for launching Agentforce: try every tactic, then scale the winner. He also discusses beginner's mind, what agents and a "digital workforce" are, AI's uneven impact on jobs, why a CEO must conduct the whole orchestra, and the painful 10% layoff two years ago.
g: Co-founder, chairman and CEO of Salesforce; former Oracle executive

eps.t: AI model quarterly, year-end special: Guangmi Li predicts how AI products will overtake Google
eps.ot: 大模型季报年终特辑：和广密预言LLM产品超越Google之路
eps.s: The year-end special of the Global AI Model Quarterly for Q4 2024. Guangmi Li predicts every AI model product will end up fighting to become the next Google. He sizes up OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI and the AI coding tools Cursor and Devin, and lays out his key calls for 2025 and 2026.
g: Founder and CEO of Shixiang, an investor who tracks global AI model companies

eps.t: The Best of 2024 with Sarah Guo and Elad Gil
eps.s: A 2024 highlights compilation with no new interviews. It features clips from Jensen Huang, Andrej Karpathy, Bret Taylor, OpenAI's Sora team, Dmitri Dolgov, Dylan Field and Alexandr Wang, covering computing at data center scale, brand AI agents replacing websites, video models as models of the world, the long tail of self-driving, and the data flywheel toward AGI.

eps.t: Tiancheng Lou on robotaxis: trying to learn from the best human drivers left me in despair
eps.ot: 96: 和楼天城聊 Robotaxi：学习人类优秀司机，让我绝望
eps.s: Just after Pony.ai went public, co-founder and CTO Tiancheng Lou looks back with Manqi Cheng on five years when outsiders saw little progress. He explains why Pony.ai stopped copying human drivers and had its system practice inside a simulated world, why driver assistance and full self-driving are different problems, when robotaxis will scale and make money, and how the team rode out the industry's ups and downs.
g: Co-founder and CTO of self-driving company Pony.ai

eps.t: Why great AI products are all about the data | Shaun Clowes (CPO at Confluent)
eps.s: Confluent CPO Shaun Clowes starts with why most product managers aren't good enough: they should focus outside the building and use LLMs to hunt for evidence they're wrong. He argues AI products live or die on data management, not the model, and that AI-built SaaS clones won't dislodge the incumbents. He also covers B2B growth teams and product-led growth, treating data as a compass, "bingo card" career moves, and a failed product he kept alive two years too long.
g: Chief Product Officer at Confluent; former CPO at MuleSoft and Metromile, product leader at Atlassian

eps.t: Inside Gong: How teams work with design partners, their pod structure, autonomy, trust, and more
eps.s: Gong co-founder and chief product officer Eilon Reshef explains how Gong's product organization works: small pods organized around user tasks, a group of design-partner customers for every feature, and a culture of real autonomy and fast calls on 50-50 decisions. He then covers how to measure AI feature quality, his "spiral" method for learning a new field, Gong's extremely narrow early target customer, and the lesson from his previous company's premature sales expansion.
g: Co-founder and chief product officer of Gong, which analyzes sales conversations

eps.t: A three-hour interview with Li Xiang (podcast edition): homebody, AI, family, games and the ranked ladder
eps.ot: 对李想的3小时访谈（播客版）：宅男、AI、家庭、游戏和天梯
eps.s: A long interview with Li Xiang after the setback of Li Auto's MEGA minivan. He explains why Li Auto sees itself as an AI company, why it builds its own foundation model and assistant, Lixiang Tongxue, and his three stages of AI. He then covers the road to fully driverless L4, reviews MEGA and the company's organizational problems, and talks about gaming ladders, family and personal choices.
g: Founder, chairman and CEO of Li Auto, the Chinese electric-car maker

eps.t: How can a Chinese product build an overseas brand from scratch? A conversation with global brand builder Eric
eps.ot: 97: 中国产品如何从 0 到 1 搭海外品牌？| 对话国际品牌操盘手 Eric
eps.s: Eric runs social commerce for a multinational consumer goods group and draws on selling via TikTok in Southeast Asia, Japan and North America to explain why going global is hard for Chinese brands. He covers why hot categories pay only briefly while brands last, how TikTok and marketplaces split the work, and how to pick partners and manage local teams. His key warning: putting down local roots needs the CEO.
g: Global TikTok e-commerce head at a consumer goods multinational; ran China and Asia-Pacific e-commerce ~10 years

eps.t: Scripts for navigating difficult conversations | Alisa Cohn (executive coach)
eps.s: Executive coach Alisa Cohn shares word-for-word scripts for hard conversations: giving performance feedback, turning down a promotion request, handling defensiveness, the pre-firing ultimatum, and the firing itself. She also argues a leader's job isn't to make people happy, suggests three questions to end every meeting, recommends a "founder prenup" before starting a company together, and talks about two of her own low points.
g: Executive coach to leaders at startups like Etsy and Venmo and big companies like Microsoft and Google

eps.t: Sam Altman on the future of AI and humanity
eps.ol: ReThinking with Adam Grant (TED Audio Collective)
eps.s: Organizational psychologist Adam Grant presses Altman on what he learned from his firing, what humans stay good at, and how AI changes work and learning. Highlights: the newest model is smarter than him in almost every way yet his life barely changed, and chess history shows people keep overriding AI's correct answers.
g: Co-founder and CEO of OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT

eps.t: Behind the founder: Drew Houston (Dropbox)
eps.s: Dropbox founder Drew Houston looks back on 18 years in three acts: viral early growth; the squeeze from Apple, Google and Microsoft, then the low point and soul-searching after Google Photos in 2015; and the post-pandemic reset around a new mission of more enlightened work, the launch of Dash and a rebuilt team. He also talks about managing a founder's psychology, using the Enneagram to see blind spots, what founder mode means, and growing faster than the company.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Dropbox

eps.t: Erik Bernhardsson on Creating Tools That Make AI Feel Effortless
eps.s: Modal founder Erik Bernhardsson explains why he built his own file system, scheduler and container runtime to turn GPUs into a shared pool billed by actual run time. He also covers the different economics of training and inference, when it's worth training your own model, multi-tenant clouds versus enterprise data gravity, and why AI coding won't mean fewer engineers.
g: Founder and CEO of Modal, a cloud platform for on-demand GPUs

eps.t: A conversation with Yann LeCun, the godfather of AI (CES 2025 fireside chat)
eps.s: At CES 2025, Rajeev Chand of Wing Venture Capital put claims by Sam Altman, Jensen Huang and others to Yann LeCun; only the moderator's recap survives. Highlights: he calls "AGI" a terrible term, says autoregressive LLMs have no way to reach human-level intelligence, bets on his JEPA work, and expects robotics' "ChatGPT moment" in three to five years.
g: Meta's Chief AI Scientist and Turing Award winner, leading new-architecture work at FAIR

eps.t: How to build your product team from scratch, attract top product talent, go multi-product, and more
eps.s: Rohini Pandhi, head of product at Mercury and formerly at Square, on building a product team from scratch: when to hire the first PM, how three kinds of PMs map to product stages, and how to design interviews and attract senior talent. She then explains how Mercury organized itself to launch several new products in 2024, why quality is a durable advantage, how to choose expansion areas and when to charge, and the nonprofit she co-founded, Transparent Collective.
g: Head of product for expansion at Mercury; former Square PM; co-founder of Transparent Collective

eps.t: Kai-Fu Lee on moving part of 01.AI's team into Alibaba: only big tech can chase giant models
eps.ot: 98: 李开复聊零一部分团队并入阿里：只有大厂能追逐超大模型
eps.s: After 01.AI moved its giant-model team into a joint lab with Alibaba Cloud, Kai-Fu Lee explains why the company stopped pre-training giant models and switched to the small, fast, cheap Yi-Lightning. He also covers why piling on more computing power now brings shrinking returns, why AI startups face money questions much earlier, and where apps built around AI from the ground up can win.
g: Founder and CEO of 01.AI; chairman of venture firm Sinovation Ventures

eps.t: Fei-Fei Li on Spatial Intelligence and Human-Centered AI
eps.s: Fei-Fei Li walks Reid Hoffman from ImageNet to spatial intelligence: language is only half of intelligence, and the other half is understanding and acting in a 3D world. She also explains why people, not AI, should be the subject of the sentence, why rules should target applications rather than science fiction, and how contact-free cameras can help nurses.
g: Stanford professor, co-director of Stanford HAI, co-founder of World Labs

eps.t: How to break out of autopilot and create the life you want | Graham Weaver (Stanford GSB professor)
eps.s: Stanford GSB professor and Alpine Investors founder Graham Weaver explains why most of us live on autopilot and how to get off it. He offers concrete exercises: ask what you would do if you could not fail, list nine lives you would be excited to live, and write your fears down so they become to-do items. He also admits that financial success changed nothing inside, and shares why Alpine bets on management teams.
g: Stanford GSB lecturer and founder and CEO of private equity firm Alpine Investors

eps.t: How AI Agents Are Transforming Customer Support, with Decagon's Jesse Zhang
eps.s: Decagon's Jesse Zhang explains why customer support is the ideal first job for AI agents, why the company's edge lies in the orchestration and observability software above the model, and how to trade off latency in voice. He also admits he's fairly pessimistic about near-term commercial adoption for most agent categories.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Decagon, which builds AI agents for customer support

eps.t: Crafting A Compelling Product Vision (Ebi Atawodi) | Lenny & Friends Summit 2024
eps.s: This is Ebi Atawodi's talk at the 2024 Lenny & Friends Summit on how to craft a product vision that actually persuades people and gets a team to follow it. Only the title and running time are available, with no transcript or chapter notes, so we can record the topic but not her specific points.

eps.t: Why the Godfather of AI Now Fears His Creation (ft. Geoffrey Hinton)
eps.s: A long, philosophical conversation. Hinton explains why in 2023 he decided digital intelligence beats brains: copies can pool what they learn. He argues AI agents will seek control, and uses a prism thought experiment to claim chatbots already have subjective experience, so humans are neither special nor safe. He also covers China, open model weights, jobs and basic income, and how language understanding works.
g: Nobel physics co-laureate and deep learning pioneer who left Google to speak about AI risk.

eps.t: 10 growth tactics that never work | Elena Verna (Amplitude, Miro, Dropbox, SurveyMonkey)
eps.s: Growth advisor Elena Verna returns for a third time with a list of growth tactics she has seen fail again and again: hiring a growth lead too early or as a rescue, redesigns, copying competitors, assuming your problem is unique, relying on channels you do not own, clinging to one growth model, and testing everything. She closes with a contrarian view: a full-time job is not the only way to monetize your skills, and your career goal should be optionality, not a title.
g: Growth advisor who led growth at Miro, Amplitude, Dropbox, and SurveyMonkey

eps.t: MiniMax founder Junjie Yan: don't build AI models with a mobile internet mindset
eps.ot: 99: MiniMax 创始人闫俊杰：做大模型，千万别套用移动互联网的逻辑
eps.s: As MiniMax open-sources its MiniMax-01 model, Junjie Yan explains why the company insists on letting technology lead: why it open-sources, why more users don't make a smarter model, what went right and wrong with Hailuo's text and video products, and its bet on linear attention and agents. Most candid is his account of missing 2024 goals set with a mobile internet mindset.
g: Founder and CEO of AI model company MiniMax

eps.t: Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis: The Path To AGI, Deceptive AIs, Building a Virtual Cell
eps.s: Alex Kantrowitz asks Demis Hassabis what stands between today's AI and AGI. He says three to five years, with reasoning, planning, memory and consistency still missing, and a 50% chance that one or two new breakthroughs are needed. He names deception as the trait to guard against most, and covers agents reshaping the web, the Astra assistant and glasses, and plans for a virtual cell and new materials.
g: CEO of Google DeepMind, leading work on Gemini, AlphaFold and the Astra assistant

eps.t: What Can We Do About Wildfires? With Convective Capital's Bill Clerico
eps.s: Bill Clerico, an investor focused on wildfire technology, takes stock after the Los Angeles fires. He argues that worsening wildfires owe more to a century of fire suppression, the power grid and housing pushing into wildland than to climate change alone. He also covers why prescribed burns stall, layered home defense, utility-caused fires, California's broken insurance market and the promise of firefighting drones.
g: Founder of Convective Capital, a fund investing in wildfire technology

eps.t: Yi Wu explains OpenAI's Operator: where AI reasoning starts moving from abstract problems toward the physical world
eps.ot: 和吴翼技术解读OpenAI Operator：推理从抽象世界走向物理世界的开端
eps.s: Recorded right after OpenAI launched Operator, an AI that uses a web browser for you. Yi Wu calls it an o1 that can see and act in a loop, and names three hard parts: base model, data and training system. He revisits OpenAI's failed 2016 web agent project, the five levels of AI, what agents are worth, why data doesn't improve itself, and openings for startups and academics.
g: Assistant professor at Tsinghua's Institute for Interdisciplinary Information Sciences, former OpenAI researcher

eps.t: An operator’s guide to product strategy | Chandra Janakiraman (CPO at VRChat, ex-Meta, Headspace)
eps.s: VRChat CPO Chandra Janakiraman turns the theory in books like Good Strategy Bad Strategy and Playing to Win into a repeatable playbook. His two-year "small-s strategy" runs five phases over 8 to 12 weeks, built around clustering problems and scoring them to pick three pillars. His 5-to-10-year "big-S strategy" works backward from an imagined future. Stories from Zynga and Meta show that only execution proves a strategy, and he closes on how AI will change the craft.
g: CPO and EVP at VRChat; formerly product lead at Meta, CPO at Headspace, and GM at Zynga

eps.t: NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang's Vision for the Future
eps.s: Cleo Abram of Huge Conversations asks Jensen Huang to explain, in plain terms, where AI is going. He starts with NVIDIA's founding bet that computers need both step-by-step and parallel processing, then covers the 2012 decision to rebuild computing, robots learning in virtual worlds, and AI safety. His most vivid image: a GPU is a time machine that lets you see the future sooner.
g: Co-founder and CEO of NVIDIA, the company that makes GPUs and AI computing platforms

eps.t: How does Silicon Valley see DeepSeek? Fusion Fund's Lu Zhang on open source, agents and bets beyond AI
eps.ot: 100: 硅谷怎么看 DeepSeek ？与 Fusion Fund 张璐聊开源、Agent和“除了AI”
eps.s: As DeepSeek R1 dominates the conversation, Silicon Valley investor Lu Zhang explains what it means from an investor's seat: how open and closed models stack up, whether cheaper models raise or lower demand for computing power, and how capable agents really are. She also lays out her bets: small industry-specific models, healthcare, insurance and space tech.
g: Founding partner of Silicon Valley venture firm Fusion Fund

eps.t: Linear’s secret to building beloved B2B products | Nan Yu (Head of Product)
eps.s: Linear's head of product Nan Yu explains why this B2B tool is genuinely loved: speed and quality are not a trade-off, requests that help managers' reports but hurt frontline workflows get a flat no, every request traces back to a real person and a moment that felt bad, and ideas come from pushing one trait to the extreme before finding the middle. He also covers PMs bridging engineering and sales, treating a few deadlines as sacred, and job hunting as if you already work there.
g: Head of Product at Linear; previously at BI company Mode and clothing brand Everlane

eps.t: Rick Caruso on LA's Wildfires, Policy Failures, and the Path Forward
eps.s: Developer and former Los Angeles mayoral candidate Rick Caruso argues the damage from the Palisades fire could have been greatly reduced, blaming an empty reservoir, fire department budget cuts and failed leadership. He uses the survival of his own Palisades Village to explain layered defense, proposes rebuilding zone by zone so residents can start within a year, and discusses public safety, homelessness and California's finances.
g: Founder of Caruso, real estate developer, and 2022 Los Angeles mayoral candidate

eps.t: Tobi Lütke's leadership playbook: First principles, infinite games, and maximizing human potential
eps.s: Shopify founder and CEO Tobi Lütke lays out how he leads, built on two ideas: reasoning from first principles and unlocking human potential. He kills and restarts projects on the spot when they feel wrong, runs without KPIs while relying heavily on data, rebuilds products from today's building blocks, and used that logic to go fully remote in the pandemic. He also talks about playing positive-sum games with customers over a hundred-year horizon and why product quality comes down to how much the team cares.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Shopify

eps.t: Jiayi Pan walks through the DeepSeek-R1, Kimi k1.5 and OpenAI o1 reports: the cleanest algorithm is the most beautiful
eps.ot: 逐句讲解DeepSeek-R1、Kimi K1.5、OpenAI o1技术报告——“最优美的算法最干净”
eps.s: Berkeley PhD student Jiayi Pan reads OpenAI's o1 blog post and the DeepSeek-R1 and Kimi k1.5 reports section by section. He explains why reinforcement learning keeps improving reasoning, why R1 chose the simplest algorithm and plain rule-based rewards, how R1-Zero taught itself to think longer, R1's training recipe, distillation and costs, and what k1.5 adds on reward models, response length and training systems.
g: PhD student at Berkeley's AI lab; author of TinyZero, a small open replication of R1-Zero

eps.t: DeepSeek, Deep Research, and 2025 Predictions with Sarah and Elad
eps.s: Sarah and Elad unpack the DeepSeek shock: what R1 really means, how to read the $5.5 million training cost, and why models keep getting cheaper and more alike. They discuss how Deep Research raises the bar for knowledge work and the risk of treating it as a default authority, then make 2025 predictions on vertical AI apps, self-driving, a consumer AI comeback and robotics.
g: No Priors co-host, serial entrepreneur and investor
No Priors co-host and founder of the venture firm Conviction

eps.t: Xiaohu Zhu returns: a one-year sequel to China's realist generative-AI story
eps.ot: 朱啸虎又来了：中国现实主义AIGC故事的1周年连载
eps.s: After DeepSeek's breakout, Xiaohu Zhu returns and revises last year's views. He now concedes AGI is at least possible, argues that open source has put closed-model leaders under a curse, and says the bottleneck to scaling has shifted to high-quality data. He also covers how Chinese model companies should pivot, why the data flywheel failed, how to measure agents, and the openings in apps and overseas markets.
g: Managing partner at GSR Ventures, a venture capital firm

eps.t: OpenAI researcher on why soft skills are the future of work | Karina Nguyen
eps.s: Karina Nguyen has done post-training and product research at both Anthropic and OpenAI. She explains the trade-offs in training a model, why there is no data wall for post-training, and how Canvas and Tasks were built quickly with synthetic data and evals. She argues that hard skills like coding will be matched by models, while creativity, taste, listening, and management become more valuable, and compares the cultures of the two labs.
g: OpenAI researcher leading Frontier Product Research; formerly at Anthropic on Claude 3 post-training and evals

eps.t: Wang Xiaochuan on AI and medicine: toward the mathematical principles of life science
eps.ot: 101: 与王小川聊AI✖️医疗：通向“生命科学的数学原理”
eps.s: As Baichuan releases a medical-enhanced model, Wang Xiaochuan explains why "building a doctor" is the central goal of his AI work: what AlphaGo and the Wei Zexi case taught him, whether general models will simply absorb medicine, why AI doctors start with pediatrics and care outside hospitals, and who pays. His long-range vision: turning life into mathematics.
g: Founder and CEO of Baichuan; earlier founded search engine company Sogou

eps.t: Junxian He walks through DeepSeek's nine key papers and what's new in each: a game for the brave
eps.ot: 逐篇讲解DeepSeek关键9篇论文及创新点——“勇敢者的游戏”
eps.s: HKUST assistant professor Junxian He walks through DeepSeek's key papers in order, from its first LLM, mixture-of-experts work, V2 and V3 to Coder, Math, Prover and R1. He traces two threads: making base models cheaper, and using reinforcement learning to build reasoning. Drawing on his own team's R1-like experiments, he sorts out which ideas are original algorithms and which are engineering or clever combinations.
g: Assistant professor of computer science at HKUST; his team released the Chinese benchmark C-Eval

eps.t: How Harvey AI is Changing the Legal Industry with Winston Weinberg
eps.s: Harvey CEO Winston Weinberg recalls starting with GPT-3 answering landlord-tenant questions, and explains the platform strategy of expanding into many workflows, then collapsing them into a simple interface. He covers reliability bars by product type, going after top law firms first, why AI displaces tasks rather than jobs, changing law-firm billing, expansion into tax and audit, and his management lessons.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Harvey, which builds AI for lawyers, and a former lawyer

eps.t: A founder’s guide to crisis management | Uri Levine (Waze co-founder, serial entrepreneur)
eps.s: Waze co-founder Uri Levine returns to talk about startup crises. He splits them into two kinds: cash crises, where you must compute your runway immediately and decide the same day, and losing product-market fit, which usually means going back to square one. Drawing on Order.chat, Fibo, WeSki, Pontera, and Waze facing Google's free navigation, he covers transparency with the team, cutting costs, when to pivot or quit, and why extra cash is the only preparation that works.
g: Waze co-founder, serial entrepreneur (Moovit, Pontera), author of Fall in Love with the Problem, Not the Solution

eps.t: Talking with academician Ya-Qin Zhang about consciousness, lifespan, robots, biological intelligence and the extension of our species
eps.ot: 和张亚勤院士聊，意识、寿命、机器人、生物智能和物种的延伸
eps.s: Ya-Qin Zhang, dean of Tsinghua's Institute for AI Industry Research, lays out a three-step timeline for AI: information, physical and biological intelligence. He discusses how universities and companies should divide work on large models, why robotaxis are past the proving stage, how large models ease robotics' old problems, and how longer lives, human-machine fusion, education and work may change.
g: Dean of Tsinghua's Institute for AI Industry Research (AIR); former president of Baidu

eps.t: AI CEO Alexandr Wang | This Past Weekend w/ Theo Von #563
eps.ol: This Past Weekend w/ Theo Von
eps.s: On Theo Von's show, Scale AI founder Alexandr Wang explains AI for a mass audience: chips, algorithms and data, and Scale as an Uber for AI that pays people to correct models. He argues AI will create jobs and make everyone a manager of AI agents, scores the US-China race weeks after DeepSeek, and discusses censorship, cyberwar and the Taiwan chip risk.
g: Founder and CEO of Scale AI, which supplies training data to OpenAI, Google and Meta

eps.t: Building Hard Tech in Hard Markets: Kyle Vogt on Cruise, Twitch, and The Bot Company
eps.s: Cruise and Twitch co-founder Kyle Vogt recounts how Cruise went from retrofit kits to robotaxis, credits Tesla's business model, and runs the numbers on remote operation. He also explains why his new venture, The Bot Company, is building home robots, avoiding humanoids, staying tiny, and will never sell.
g: Founder of The Bot Company and co-founder of Cruise and Twitch

eps.t: Qianchuan Zhang, after leaving ByteDance and MiniMax, warns of the threat AGI poses to humanity
eps.ot: 离开字节、MiniMax的张前川，发出AGI对人类威胁的预警
eps.s: Qianchuan Zhang looks back on his years at Baidu, 360, Zhihu and ByteDance, tracing how search and recommendation evolved, and talks about user-generated communities, where people's time goes, and Xiaohongshu going global. The second half turns to AGI risk: where people fit in the AI business loop, three possible futures, the ways humanity could go extinct, and a proposal to give every person a share of compute.
g: Worked at Baidu, 360, Zhihu, ByteDance and MiniMax, mostly on search and recommendation

eps.t: How to find work you love | Bob Moesta (Jobs-to-be-Done co-creator, author of "Job Moves”)
eps.s: Jobs-to-be-Done co-creator Bob Moesta applies his method to job hunting. Drawing on over a thousand interviews with people who switched jobs, he breaks a move into pushes and pulls, identifies four job-search "jobs," and argues you should design your career like a product: find what gives you energy and what drains it, then prototype roles through informational interviews. He also covers the jobcation, pay versus experience, weaknesses as superpowers, and why employers should fit the job to the person.
g: Co-creator of Jobs-to-be-Done, co-founder and CEO of The Rewired Group, co-author of Job Moves

eps.t: Walking through the new attention papers from DeepSeek, Kimi, and MiniMax: "brute-force elegance on hardware"
eps.ot: 逐篇讲解DeepSeek、Kimi、MiniMax注意力机制新论文——“硬件上的暴力美学”
eps.s: MIT PhD student Songlin Yang walks through three papers on reading long text cheaply: DeepSeek's NSA, Kimi's MoBA, and MiniMax-01. The first two let the model read only the important parts, while the third mixes compressed-memory linear attention with standard attention. Starting from how attention and GPU memory work, she weighs each team's trade-offs, ranks the papers, and discusses open source and talent flows.
g: PhD student at MIT's Computer Science and AI Lab who studies efficient attention

eps.t: Virtual Cell Models, Tahoe-100 and Data for AI-in-Bio with Vevo Therapeutics and the Arc Institute
eps.s: Five guests from Vevo Therapeutics and the Arc Institute introduce Tahoe-100, an open single-cell perturbation dataset of about 100 million cells. They discuss why virtual cell models are limited by data, how perturbation data adds causal information, roughly which GPT stage the field has reached, and platform biotech companies and competition from China.
g: Co-founder and chief scientific officer of Vevo Therapeutics
Co-founder and CEO of Vevo Therapeutics
Co-founder of the Arc Institute, a biomedical research nonprofit
Chief technology officer of the Arc Institute
Core investigator at the Arc Institute and co-founder of Vevo

eps.t: DeepSeek kicks off open-source week: what does open-sourcing a large model actually mean?
eps.ot: 102: DeepSeek 启动开源周，大模型开源到底在开什么？
eps.s: As DeepSeek opens its open-source week with FlashMLA, PhD student and former DeepSeek intern Zihan Wang unpacks what "open source" really includes: DeepSeek's steady focus on efficiency, how low-level computing code gets optimized, how to read a GitHub project, and the five levels of openness. He also covers why some labs release their best models, and the risk of misuse.
g: PhD student at Northwestern University's MLL Lab; interned at DeepSeek in 2024

eps.t: Tracing AI model optimization through attention: DeepSeek's and Kimi's latest attention upgrades explained
eps.ot: 103: 用Attention串起大模型优化史，详解DeepSeek、Kimi最新注意力机制改进
eps.s: With DeepSeek's NSA and Kimi's MoBA released back to back, two Tsinghua PhD students who study efficient attention start from how attention works: how a model decides what to look at while reading. They map the two main paths, sparse and linear, explain why GPU-friendly sparsity works in blocks and why sparsity during training matters, and discuss new problems from long reasoning, video and audio, and memory limits.
g: Tsinghua computer science PhD student studying efficient model architectures; first author of InfLLM
Tsinghua electronic engineering PhD student working on neural network efficiency; co-first author of MoA

eps.t: An inside look at X’s Community Notes | Keith Coleman & Jay Baxter
eps.s: Community Notes lets ordinary X users add context to misleading posts. Product lead Keith Coleman and founding ML engineer Jay Baxter explain how it works: notes show only when people who usually disagree both find them helpful, the company has no button to change a note, and all code and data are public. They also cover how a tiny team proved itself under four CEOs, the measured drop in misleading posts' spread, the upside of anonymity, and LLM-drafted notes.
g: Product lead for X's Community Notes; previously ran Twitter's consumer product management team
Founding machine learning engineer and researcher on Community Notes; designed its ranking algorithm

eps.t: Building the Platform for Scientific Breakthrough, with Noubar Afeyan of Moderna and Flagship Pioneering
eps.s: Moderna co-founder Noubar Afeyan argues that starting companies can be a parallel, repeatable profession, and that breakthroughs can't be planned, only grown through variation, selection and iteration. He separates risk from uncertainty, revisits the lessons of Joule, and covers generative AI for protein design, clinical trials as the real bottleneck, the value of platform companies, and a "polyintelligence" of humans, machines and nature.
g: Founder and CEO of biotech company builder Flagship Pioneering, and Moderna co-founder

eps.t: #2281 - Elon Musk
eps.s: Recorded at the height of DOGE's cost-cutting push. Musk first walks through what he says he found in the federal books: payments with no stated purpose, about 20 million dead people listed as alive, debt interest above the defense budget. Then he turns to Starship's heat-shield tiles, Mars launch windows, falling birth rates and why AI must tell the truth. The online transcript lacks the final stretch.
g: CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, founder of xAI, then leading the DOGE cost-cutting effort

eps.t: Matt Mullenweg on the future of open source and why he’s taking a stand
eps.s: WordPress co-founder and Automattic CEO Matt Mullenweg explains why he sees open source as the most important idea of his generation, why Meta's Llama doesn't qualify, and why a well-maintained open-source core matters more in the AI era. He answers critics at length on the WP Engine trademark fight, lays out who owns the WordPress trademark and his "one leader, always forkable" model of governance, and shares how he turned Tumblr around and how Automattic thinks about acquisitions.
g: Co-founder of WordPress; founder and CEO of Automattic, which runs WordPress.com and Tumblr

eps.t: Three hours with Manus founder Xiao Hong: the world isn't a straight line, so be a variable that shifts the game
eps.ot: 对Manus创始人肖弘的3小时访谈：世界不是线性外推，做博弈中的重要变量
eps.s: A long, relay-style interview with Xiao Hong, founder of Monica and Manus. The first half revisits his first startup, from a WeChat article editor to a customer-management tool on WeCom to selling the company, with lessons on timing, making money, and fundraising. The second half covers taking Monica overseas, how he sorts AI apps, the contest between models and apps, and the vision of AI agents behind Manus.
g: Founder of the AI assistant Monica and the AI agent Manus

eps.t: Finding a backer for linear attention: ByteDance said no, MiniMax said yes
eps.ot: 104: 我给线性注意力找“金主”，字节 say No，MiniMax say Yes
eps.s: Yiran Zhong, the main force behind MiniMax's linear attention, recounts how his team dropped sparse attention in 2021, spent three years making linear attention, a cheaper way for models to read long text, both accurate and fast, then hunted for a company willing to bet on it, landing in MiniMax-01. He also discusses hybrid designs, long-text data and plans for the next model.
g: Senior research director at MiniMax, chief champion of its Lightning Attention approach

eps.t: National Security Strategy and AI Evals on the Eve of Superintelligence with Dan Hendrycks
eps.s: Dan Hendrycks, director of the Center for AI Safety, argues that AI safety is mostly a matter of national governance, not just lab alignment. He lays out his "Mutual Assured AI Malfunction" (MAIM) deterrence framework, chip export controls and enforcement, explains why Humanity's Last Exam marks the end of closed-ended academic benchmarks, and notes that agent capabilities are still near the floor.
g: Director of the Center for AI Safety

eps.t: Notion's lost years, near collapse during COVID, staying small to move fast, building horizontal
eps.s: Notion co-founder and CEO Ivan Zhao looks back on the company's "lost years": building a developer tool nobody wanted, then hiding the vision of "everyone can make software" inside everyday notes and docs, and laying off the team after betting on the wrong technology. He talks about balancing commerce with personal values, staying small by building systems instead of hiring, the database that nearly collapsed during COVID, how a horizontal product sells to enterprises, and why AI favors bundled tools.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Notion, the all-in-one workspace for notes, docs and projects

eps.t: Amid controversy, Luchen's Yang You on what DeepSeek really costs third-party clouds, and why he quit selling model access
eps.ot: 105: 潞晨尤洋争议中谈三方云平台 DeepSeek 成本：为何我不做 MaaS 了？
eps.s: After Luchen Technology paused its DeepSeek API service and Yang You's claim that third-party platforms lose money stirred controversy, he explains why offline speed tests don't hold up in production, how a billing mismatch makes model-as-a-service lose money on idle machines, who can actually make it work, and why Luchen is pivoting to post-training platforms and video models.
g: Founder of Luchen Technology and creator of the open-source training framework Colossal-AI

eps.t: Building Lovable: $10M ARR in 60 days with 15 people | Anton Osika (CEO and co-founder)
eps.s: Lovable lets people who can't code build software from a sentence. Co-founder and CEO Anton Osika builds an Airbnb clone live from one prompt and explains how the product grew out of the open-source project GPT Engineer, then exploded by word of mouth within three months of launch. He covers his "scaling law" for keeping AI from getting stuck, packaging the product for non-programmers, how a team of fifteen hires and prioritizes, and why future product teams need generalists, taste and user intuition.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Lovable; creator of the open-source project GPT Engineer

eps.t: Agents #1: ZhenFund's Yusen Dai says every industry will get its "Lee Sedol moment" and attention is not all you need
eps.ot: 106: 与真格戴雨森长聊 Agent：各行业都会遭遇“李世石时刻”，Attention is not all you need|Agent#1
eps.s: The first episode of an agent series. ZhenFund's Yusen Dai explains why AI agents, AI that carries out tasks for you, became usable in 2025 after o1 and R1, and why they break the internet's old formula of users × time × monetization. He also covers why DeepSeek succeeded, the cost math of replacing human labor, each industry's coming "Lee Sedol moment," when to start making money, and who gains.
g: Managing partner at ZhenFund, an early-stage venture investor in China

eps.t: Zero to ~$40M ARR: How Bolt's pivot changed AI product development forever | Eric Simons (CEO)
eps.s: StackBlitz co-founder and CEO Eric Simons tells how his near-dead company launched Bolt, an AI tool that builds web apps from a prompt, and went from zero to $20 million in annual revenue in two months. The in-browser operating system they spent seven years building met Claude 3.5 Sonnet just as it crossed the coding threshold. He covers surviving on a low burn rate, pricing after the explosion, running a small long-tenured team, and why PMs suit the AI coding era.
g: Co-founder and CEO of StackBlitz, the company behind the AI app builder Bolt

eps.t: Copilot, Agent Mode, and the New World of Dev Tools with GitHub's CEO Thomas Dohmke
eps.s: GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke walks through Copilot's agent mode and Project Padawan, the four conditions agents need for broad adoption, the bigger value beyond writing code, and why programming languages won't disappear. He also explains Copilot's economics, priced by compute rather than by the labor it replaces, and GitHub's multi-model, open approach.
g: CEO of GitHub, the code hosting and collaboration platform

eps.t: Haivivi's Yong Li on an AI Jellycat earning ¥10 million a month, where niche AI hardware meets mass consumer goods
eps.ot: 107: 与Haivivi李勇聊月入千万的AI Jellycat：小众AI硬件×大众消费品的交叉口创业
eps.s: Haivivi founder Yong Li tells how BubblePal, an AI plush charm, came about. At Tmall Genie he found kids were AI hardware's real users; later he left price-war-ridden learning gadgets to sell emotional comfort, making design trade-offs on tight cash. He explains why AI toys won't be winner-take-all, how to handle values in kids' products, and what it takes to reach adults and go overseas.
g: Founder and CEO of Haivivi, an AI plush toy maker; formerly on Alibaba's Tmall Genie team

eps.t: The hidden power of introverts: How to thrive without changing who you are | Susan Cain
eps.s: Susan Cain, author of Quiet, on how introverts can thrive at work without changing who they are: how to tell introversion from shyness, how to get past the fear of public speaking, how to make your contributions visible, how to speak up in meetings, and how to say no. She also covers how managers can support introverted employees, how to raise introverted kids, and how to design a career around your own temperament.
g: Author of the bestsellers Quiet and Bittersweet

eps.t: Verdict with Ted Cruz: Elon Musk (Part 1)
eps.s: A two-part conversation on Senator Ted Cruz's podcast. Part 1 covers DOGE, from more software licenses than staff to "magic money computers" that can send out cash and a $1 trillion savings goal, plus AI, robots and Taiwan's chips. Part 2 turns to what a self-sustaining Mars city needs and his path from Zip2 and PayPal to SpaceX, including Russian missile prices that jumped from $4 million to $19 million.
g: CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, founder of xAI, then leading DOGE's federal cost-cutting push

eps.t: Talking with Xianpeng Lang: ten years of self-driving, the key technical details, and Tesla
eps.ot: 和郎咸朋聊，自动驾驶10年演进史、关键技术细节和特斯拉
eps.s: Xianpeng Lang, who leads self-driving at Li Auto, traces a decade of three shifts: HD maps plus hand-written rules, a bird's-eye camera view, and end-to-end models that drive directly. He explains why Tesla kept jumping up a level first, how Li Auto was forced to build its own system in 2021 and bet on end-to-end in 2024, and his plans for L3, world-model exams and reinforcement learning.
g: Vice president of autonomous driving R&D at Li Auto

eps.t: Yi Ma on the history of intelligence: "DNA was the first large model," and intelligence is about reducing entropy
eps.ot: 108: 与马毅聊智能史:“DNA是最早的大模型”，智能的本质是减熵
eps.s: Yi Ma, dean of computing and data science at the University of Hong Kong, traces intelligence from evolution to machines. He defines it as a feedback loop that finds predictable structure in a world drifting toward disorder, and calls DNA the first "large model." With that lens he weighs today's models, o1/R1-style reasoning, DeepSeek and open source, academia's role, and what comes next: transparent, self-correcting systems and embodied AI.
g: Dean of computing and data science at the University of Hong Kong; computer vision scholar

eps.t: Why Can't AI Make Its Own Discoveries? — With Yann LeCun
eps.s: Alex Kantrowitz asks Yann LeCun why AI that has read everything can't make its own discoveries. LeCun says LLMs are retrieval machines, scaling data won't reach human-level AI, and a "country of geniuses in a data center" is nonsense. The standout: his math showing a four-year-old has taken in about as much data through vision as the largest text models. He also covers JEPA, open source and DeepSeek.
g: Meta's Chief AI Scientist, Turing Award winner and a founder of deep learning

eps.t: The Robotics Revolution, with Physical Intelligence's Cofounder Chelsea Finn
eps.s: Physical Intelligence co-founder Chelsea Finn explains why the company is building a general model that can control any robot, why diverse data matters more than sheer volume, and why human videos can't replace a robot's own experience. She walks through Hi Robot's two-level design and shares her views on humanoids, open source and the timeline to commercialization.
g: Co-founder of robotics AI company Physical Intelligence and Stanford professor

eps.t: An Interview with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman About Building a Consumer Tech Company
eps.s: Tech analyst Ben Thompson talks with Altman about how OpenAI accidentally became a consumer tech company: why ChatGPT launched on GPT-3.5, whether to run ads, and what DeepSeek taught them. The standout: in five years he'd rather own a billion-user product than the best model, because AI will spread like the transistor.
g: Co-founder and CEO of OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT

eps.t: Superhuman's secret to success | Rahul Vohra (CEO and founder)
eps.s: Superhuman founder Rahul Vohra looks back on ten years of building the email app: why growth comes from word of mouth rather than viral mechanics, why the product seemed to slow down and how he restructured his leadership team to fix it, and why he staked the brand on a single attribute, speed. He also explains mandatory one-on-one onboarding in the early days, his engine for finding product-market fit, applying game design to business software, and how the $30-a-month price came about.
g: Founder and CEO of the email app Superhuman; previously founded Rapportive, acquired by LinkedIn

eps.t: How to win in the AI era: Ship weekly, embrace technical debt, ruthlessly cut scope, and more
eps.s: Captions co-founder and CEO Gaurav Misra breaks down how an AI-native consumer app runs: every engineer ships a marketable feature every week, technical debt is treated as leverage, and a secret roadmap sits alongside the public one. He also looks back at Snap's designer-led culture and how prototypes built internal consensus, discusses where AI video is safe and where it isn't, the rise of AI-generated ads, and the lesson of leaving Captions on the shelf for 18 months after it already had product-market fit.
g: Co-founder and CEO of the AI video app Captions; early Snap employee who led its design engineering team

eps.t: Conversations Are the Source of Truth in Healthcare with Abridge CEO Shiv Rao
eps.s: Abridge founder Shiv Rao, a practicing cardiologist, explains how ambient AI that listens to doctor-patient conversations and drafts clinical notes became a way into the whole healthcare workflow. He covers why Abridge went after large health systems first, why medical speech is far from solved, how doctors' edits keep improving the model, and how it extends into orders, clinical trial matching and decision support.
g: Founder and CEO of AI medical documentation company Abridge, and practicing cardiologist

eps.t: Elon Musk and DOGE team interview with Bret Baier (Special Report)
eps.s: Fox's Bret Baier interviews Elon Musk alongside several DOGE staffers. Musk lays out the goal of cutting $1 trillion from the deficit at $4 billion a day, uses a survey billed at almost $1 billion and loans to people over 120 to show how common waste and fraud are, and blames disconnected government databases. He also answers critics and talks about attacks on Tesla stores.
g: CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, leading DOGE as a special government employee

eps.t: A better way to plan, build, and ship products | Ryan Singer (creator of “Shape Up")
eps.s: Ryan Singer, author of "Shape Up," walks through the product method born at Basecamp: set an appetite for how much time a problem deserves instead of estimating, have product, design and a senior engineer shape the solution before work starts, then hand the whole thing to the team to break down themselves. He admits Basecamp was unusual and shares where other teams stumble: what to do when time runs out, how much detail to give, when to adopt it, and how PMs should move upstream.
g: Author of "Shape Up"; early employee at 37signals (Basecamp), where he worked on product for over a decade

eps.t: How Digital Life Kha'Zix uses AI: hand anything you've done three times over to AI
eps.ot: 109: 数字生命卡兹克如何用 AI：把任何重复3遍的事AI化
eps.s: AI blogger Digital Life Kha'Zix explains how he went from fintech product manager to full-time AI creator, why he shut down Chat Fund, a fund Q&A product, and how AI runs his content pipeline, research and online groups. He weighs in on general-purpose agents, thin wrapper apps, DeepSeek's mass appeal and the Manus controversy, and on how ordinary people can bring AI into their own fields.
g: Runs the AI media account Digital Life Kha'Zix; formerly a product manager at fund-data platform Jiuquaner

eps.t: Q1 2025 AI model quarterly: Guangmi Li on today's biggest contrarian view, and AGI's main road and summit
eps.ot: 25年Q1大模型季报：和广密聊当下最大非共识、AGI的主线与主峰
eps.s: The Q1 2025 edition of the AI model quarterly. Guangmi Li reverses his view from six months ago and bets on pre-training again, calls coding the key training ground for AGI, and pulls his AGI timeline to late 2026 or early 2027. He also explains why OpenAI and Anthropic diverged, where agents and long context get stuck, who captures the profits, and what China needs to catch up.
g: Founder and CEO of Shixiang, an investor who tracks global AI model companies

eps.t: Yann LeCun, a legend in AI, thinks LLMs are nearly obsolete
eps.s: A long Newsweek AI Impact interview, available only as an article with extensive quotes. LeCun says LLMs will soon be largely obsolete and tells young researchers to skip them. He uses a four-year-old's visual data and 20-hour driving lessons to show AI lacks physical understanding, explains JEPA, and rejects AI doom: the smartest people, he notes, are rarely the ones in charge.
g: Meta's Chief AI Scientist, NYU professor and Turing Award winner

eps.t: Public Markets, Image Gen, and Specialized Models, with Sarah and Elad
eps.s: The two hosts start with the Ghibli-style image craze and where image generation goes next, then discuss the public market slide and how tariffs affect startup fundraising. The second half covers converging foundation models, where specialized models can still win, a maturing AI stack, and how MCP is speeding up agent development.
g: No Priors co-host, serial entrepreneur and investor
No Priors co-host and founder of the venture firm Conviction

eps.t: Become a better communicator: Specific frameworks to improve your clarity, influence, and impact
eps.s: Communication coach Wes Kao returns with a toolkit for talking and writing at work: sell the idea before the details, remember that concise is not the same as short, say how sure you really are, and think of the most obvious objection before you speak. She also covers managing up, giving feedback that actually changes behavior, delegating with her CEDAF checklist, using Claude as a writing aid, and what she learned going solo.
g: Executive communication coach, co-founder of Maven, and co-creator of altMBA with Seth Godin

eps.t: Robot foundation models and VLA, paper by paper: why humans are the smartest VLA
eps.ot: 逐篇讲解机器人基座模型和VLA经典论文——“人就是最智能的VLA”
eps.s: Jianyu Chen, a Tsinghua assistant professor and founder of Robotera, walks through 20-plus papers on robot foundation models and vision-language-action (VLA) models: from SayCan and VoxPoser, which stitch together existing models, to the RT series, cross-robot data, fast-slow dual systems, future prediction and reinforcement learning. He also explains his move from self-driving cars to robots, and why his company sells to researchers before businesses.
g: Assistant professor at Tsinghua's IIIS and founder of robotics company Robotera

eps.t: Demis Hassabis on AI, game theory, multimodality, and the nature of creativity
eps.s: Reid Hoffman and Aria Finger take Demis Hassabis from childhood chess to AlphaFold: why Deep Blue disappointed him, what AlphaGo's Move 37 showed, and his three levels of creativity. He also covers a video model learning physics from YouTube, coding in plain language, why DeepMind stayed in London, and how AlphaFold did a billion years of PhD work in a year.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Google DeepMind, the lab behind AlphaGo and AlphaFold

eps.t: Yann LeCun: Human Intelligence is not General Intelligence
eps.s: AI Inside hosts Jason Howell and Jeff Jarvis ask Yann LeCun where AI stands and what comes next. He says LLMs are useful but unreliable, human intelligence is highly specialized so "general intelligence" is a misnomer, and the missing piece is world models that understand physics and plan. The standout: his defense of open source, saying Llama spoils things for exactly three companies while enabling thousands.
g: Meta's Chief AI Scientist, NYU professor and Turing Award winner

eps.t: OpenAI’s CPO on how AI changes must-have skills, moats, coding, startup playbooks, more | Kevin Weil
eps.s: OpenAI's chief product officer Kevin Weil describes building products in the eye of the storm: the underlying models change every few months, you design for what they are about to be able to do, and writing evals has become a core skill. He also covers how OpenAI organizes teams and what it wants in PMs, reasoning about models as if they were people, fine-tuning and model ensembles, where startups fit, AI tutoring and creativity, and lessons from Facebook's Libra.
g: OpenAI's chief product officer, former product lead at Instagram and Twitter, co-creator of Facebook's Libra

eps.t: From Job Displacement to AI Trainers, Brendan Foody on Work in the AI Age
eps.s: Mercor founder Brendan Foody talks about using LLMs to predict job performance and recruiting experts to train models for AI labs. He argues that evals are upstream of model capabilities, discusses which skills lose value first and why reinforcement fine-tuning teaches company-specific skills so efficiently, and describes a single global labor market shared by people and AI agents.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Mercor, an AI-powered hiring platform

eps.t: OpenAI's Sam Altman talks ChatGPT, AI agents and superintelligence - live at TED2025
eps.s: On the TED stage, Chris Anderson pressed Sam Altman on whether AI rips off artists, why OpenAI is going open source, how to keep AI agents safe, and who gave him the power to shape our future. Highlights: his view that smart models will become interchangeable so the product decides who wins, and how becoming a father changed how he sees the future.
g: Co-founder and CEO of OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT

eps.t: Everyone’s an engineer now: Inside v0’s mission to create 100 million builders | Guillermo Rauch
eps.s: Vercel founder and CEO Guillermo Rauch explains what v0 is for: growing the number of people who can ship a product from tens of millions of developers to 100 million. He argues that translation-style coding jobs will disappear, that understanding how things work and using precise words matters more, and that working prototypes will replace documents as how teams communicate. He demos v0 live and shares tips on using it, feedback loops, advice for his kids, and how to develop taste.
g: Founder and CEO of Vercel, maker of v0, and creator of Next.js and Socket.IO

eps.t: Agents #2: Mingshi Capital's Ling Xia says the battle for the all-purpose AI gateway is coming, so startups should specialize
eps.ot: 110: 与明势夏令聊Agent竞争：通用入口之战就要来，创业要做垂、做专|Agent#2
eps.s: Part two of an agent series. Mingshi Capital partner Ling Xia argues that model makers are moving beyond base models into memory, tools and general agents, so a fight over the all-purpose phone assistant is coming. Startups should avoid that battlefield, rebuild workflows in small, fragmented industries and charge for results. He also covers GPT-4o image generation, agents' effect on advertising, and robotics' missing "GPT-3 moment."
g: Partner at Mingshi Capital, a Chinese venture firm, leading its tech investments

eps.t: Predicting the Earth with Josh Goldman: How KoBold Uses AI to Find Critical Minerals
eps.s: KoBold Metals co-founder Josh Goldman explains how data and AI help find critical minerals like copper and lithium. He argues the scarce thing is information about where deposits are, describes an active learning system built on fragmented geological data, and uses Zambia's Mingomba copper deposit to show how ore grade drives profit. He also covers rare earth refining geopolitics and how KoBold fights confirmation bias.
g: Co-founder of KoBold Metals, which uses AI to find critical minerals

eps.t: Building a magical AI code editor used by over 1m developers in 4 months: Inside Windsurf
eps.s: Varun Mohan, co-founder and CEO of Windsurf (formerly Codeium), tells how the company pivoted twice from GPU virtualization to an AI coding editor, why he believes the value sits in the application layer, and why he built enterprise sales early. He explains why AI writing 90 percent of code doesn't mean 10x productivity, describes his "dehydrated" hiring philosophy and how engineers' roles change, demos Windsurf, and argues you should make your own product obsolete every 6 to 12 months.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Windsurf (formerly Codeium), previously worked on self-driving cars

eps.t: Artificial intelligence could end disease, lead to "radical abundance," Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis says
eps.s: On 60 Minutes, Scott Pelley visits DeepMind and asks Demis Hassabis how fast AI is moving. He describes an ever-steeper exponential curve, expects AGI within five to ten years, and thinks AI could help cure disease within a decade. He also discusses whether machines could become conscious, why AI still lacks curiosity, and his worries about bad actors and a race that cuts safety corners.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Google DeepMind; Nobel laureate for protein-structure AI

eps.t: Agents #3: How Pokee.ai's Bill Zhu builds agents, with reinforcement learning on the back end and a language model up front
eps.ot: 111: Pokee.ai 朱哲清的 Agent 造法：强化学习作后端，语言模型作前端|Agent#3
eps.s: Part three of an agent series. Bill Zhu, founder of Pokee AI and former head of applied reinforcement learning at Meta, explains his design: a language model only understands requests, while a reinforcement-learning back end plans and picks tools. His product acts directly in users' real accounts. He also covers RL's hunger for data, approval design, moving from individuals to enterprises, the horizontal-agent race and his research method.
g: Founder of Pokee AI; former head of Meta's applied reinforcement learning team

eps.t: Inside Deep Research with Isa Fulford: Building the Future of AI Agents
eps.s: OpenAI researcher Isa Fulford explains how Deep Research was built: why it started with read-only research and synthesis, how reinforcement learning, expert data and graders turned a prototype into a product, and when reinforcement fine-tuning is worth it. She also discusses trust and safety and a general agent that works like a remote coworker.
g: OpenAI researcher and one of the main builders of Deep Research

eps.t: Full interview: 'Godfather of AI' on hopes, fears and predictions for future of AI
eps.s: CBS's Brook Silva-Braga sits down with Hinton again. He says AI has moved faster than he expected and agents make it scarier. He puts the chance of AI taking over at 10 to 20%, likening us to owners of a cute tiger cub. He also covers big gains in health and education, job losses, released model weights, the US–China race, and companies putting profit before safety.
g: Nobel physics co-laureate and deep learning pioneer, now a leading voice on AI risk.

eps.t: Inside monday.com’s transformation: Radical transparency, impact over output, & the path to $1B ARR
eps.s: Daniel Lereya, monday.com's chief product and technology officer, retraces the company's path from about $4 million to $1 billion in annual recurring revenue. A wake-up call, when a competitor shipped 30 new column types at once, pushed the team toward ambitious goals and judging work by impact. He also covers radical transparency, launching five products at once, turning a performance crisis into MondayDB, using time traps to ship early, and letting go of old superpowers.
g: Chief product and technology officer at monday.com, who joined when the company had 30 or 40 people

eps.t: Three hours with Energy Singularity founder Zhao Yang: how far are we from taming nuclear fusion?
eps.ot: 对能量奇点创始人杨钊3小时访谈：人类驯服可控核聚变还有多少路程？
eps.s: Zhao Yang, founder of Energy Singularity, starts from E=mc² and the fusion "triple product" to explain his bet on high-temperature superconducting tokamaks: stronger magnets mean smaller, cheaper machines. He reviews building HH70, an all-high-temperature-superconducting tokamak, lays out a three-step plan through HH170 to a demo power plant, and discusses Helion, AI's link to energy, and managing a hardware team.
g: Founder of fusion company Energy Singularity, with a Stanford PhD in physics

eps.t: Spirit AI's Yang Gao on embodied AI: how a robot-like person builds human-like robots
eps.ot: 112: 与千寻高阳聊具身：一个像机器人的人，怎么做像人的机器人
eps.s: Yang Gao, co-founder of Spirit AI and a Tsinghua assistant professor, maps out embodied AI, AI with a body working in the physical world. He says the field has moved from research to engineering, proposes L0–L5 levels, and favors wheeled two-armed robots now and end-to-end models eventually. He explains what internet video, teleoperation and reinforcement learning each add, how much data is needed, and why brain and body go together.
g: Co-founder and chief scientist of Spirit AI; assistant professor at Tsinghua University

eps.t: The rise of Cursor: The $300M ARR AI tool that engineers can’t stop using | Michael Truell
eps.s: Cursor co-founder and CEO Michael Truell describes the "after code" future he imagines, where people express intent in high-level logic close to English but stay in control. He recounts the detour into mechanical engineering before returning to programming, explains why every magic moment in Cursor involves a custom model, and shares how he thinks about moats in a market with a very high ceiling, why Copilot fell behind, how to use AI coding well, and early hiring lessons.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Anysphere, the company behind the AI code editor Cursor

eps.t: O3 and the Next Leap in Reasoning with OpenAI's Eric Mitchell and Brandon McKinzie
eps.s: Two OpenAI researchers who worked on o3 explain how reasoning models differ from traditional pretrained models and why tools make long reasoning truly useful. They also discuss folding the model picker into the model itself, two dimensions of task difficulty, biases in model vision, the training data most needed next, and how to make use of output variance.
g: OpenAI researcher who worked on o3
OpenAI researcher who worked on o3

eps.t: Scale AI's Alexandr Wang on Securing U.S. AI Leadership
eps.s: At CSIS, Alexandr Wang tells Gregory Allen why Scale chose to work with the military despite staff pushback, describes Thunderforge, which uses AI agents for military planning, and argues the US-China AI race could be winner-take-all. He says America needs data dominance, abundant energy and rigorous testing, because chip export controls alone won't settle it.
g: Founder and CEO of Scale AI, a data and AI testing firm working with the Pentagon

eps.t: Inside Devin: The AI engineer that's set to write 50% of its company’s code this year | Scott Wu
eps.s: Scott Wu, co-founder and CEO of Cognition, introduces Devin, an autonomous AI engineer. He explains how a 15-person engineering team runs about five Devins per person, why engineers go from bricklayers to architects, why you should still learn to code, and how to hand tasks to an agent. He also shares his views on stickiness in AI apps, how fast this technology spreads, and startup basics, with a live demo of Devin editing the website and building a codebase wiki.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Cognition, the company behind Devin, an autonomous AI software engineer

eps.t: Metaso's Kerui Min, part 1: back to the beginning, and the predictions that came true
eps.ot: 113: 秘塔闵可锐1：回到故事开始，那些「神预言」
eps.s: Part one of two with Metaso's Kerui Min, recorded in March 2023. He traces his path from Boson and Cheetah Mobile to founding Metaso, and explains why pretraining was the real shift, why hand-written rules can't scale, the BERT-versus-GPT debate, and generative AI's unit economics. He also covers the business reality of Xiezuocat and legal translation, dodging giants, and early takes on open source, compute and Chinese VCs.
g: Founder and CEO of Metaso, maker of the Xiezuocat writing tool and legal translation

eps.t: Metaso founder Kerui Min, part 2: "I'm not an actor"
eps.ot: 114: 秘塔闵可锐2：“我不是演员”
eps.s: Part two with Metaso founder Kerui Min, recorded after his app Learn Something Today launched. He covers what the product still lacks, his habit of deciding in ten minutes, and why general AI agents aren't reliable yet. Most striking is his survival-first stance: with giants spending billions, Metaso skips big funding and chases revenue. He also explains which products model companies will build, and why DeepSeek wins.
g: Founder and CEO of Metaso, a Chinese maker of AI search and learning apps

eps.t: How have I been complicit in creating the conditions I say I don’t want? | Jerry Colonna
eps.s: Executive coach and former venture capitalist Jerry Colonna uses pointed questions to show how to see your own part in the situations you say you don't want. He shares his equation for growing as a leader, why attachment to outcomes deepens suffering, why even a growth mindset should be held loosely, and why dysfunctional teams trace back to members' unexamined patterns, especially the leader's. He also reflects on humans in the AI era and the legacy he hopes to leave.
g: Executive coach, co-founder and CEO of leadership firm Reboot, co-founder of VC firm Flatiron Partners

eps.t: Gaming as the Future of Education with Duolingo CEO Luis von Ahn
eps.s: Duolingo founder Luis von Ahn explains why the hardest part of learning is getting people to stick with it, and the logic behind short lessons, streaks and an 83% target success rate. He also covers how LLMs removed the content bottleneck, how Duolingo picks new subjects, its seemingly risky brand marketing, and how AI will slowly change schools.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Duolingo, and inventor of reCAPTCHA

eps.t: How Palantir built the ultimate founder factory | Nabeel S. Qureshi (founder, writer, ex-Palantir)
eps.s: Nabeel Qureshi spent nearly eight years at Palantir as a forward deployed engineer, living on client sites and building software there. He explains why the company turns out so many founders and product leaders: how it hires, why it has no titles, how on-site engineers iterate several times a week, how one-off solutions became the Foundry platform, and why cleaning up data is the underrated secret. He also covers defense ethics, lessons from his own startup, and working with AI like a chess player.
g: Spent nearly eight years as a Palantir forward deployed engineer; early GoCardless employee; now a founder and writer

eps.t: How Huawei's supernode shakes up AI computing: Lingjie Xu of Magic Compute on what's changing in chips
eps.ot: 115: 华为发布超节点，如何搅动AI算力市场？与魔形智能徐凌杰聊芯片层新变化
eps.s: After Huawei unveiled its CloudMatrix 384 supernode, which links hundreds of chips into one big machine, Lingjie Xu, a Magic Compute co-founder who worked at Nvidia, AMD and Alibaba Cloud, explains the chip layer: scaling up versus scaling out, why memory is the first wall, and how training and inference economics differ. Highlights: how his team made DeepSeek inference profitable, and who loses from the supernode and the H20 ban.
g: Magic Compute co-founder running chips and servers; ex-Nvidia, AMD, Samsung and Alibaba Cloud

eps.t: How Revolut trains world-class PMs: The “Local CEO” model, raw intellect & building wow products
eps.s: Dmitry Zlokazov, global head of product at the financial super-app Revolut, explains why the company produces such strong PMs. Each product owner runs their area like a local CEO. Three kinds of product owners share the same core skills. Teams go deep on one case before turning it into a repeatable process. New products cut features but never quality. Hiring favors raw intellect and hunger over seniority. He also explains how he picks what to dig into among nearly a hundred projects.
g: Global head of product at Revolut, also running its retail business

eps.t: AI is Making Enterprise Search Relevant, with Arvind Jain of Glean
eps.s: Glean founder Arvind Jain explains why search inside companies only became workable with large language models, and why giant context windows still don't replace retrieval. He also covers how permissions turned Glean into a security product, why employees need to be taught to use AI, and how far the move from search to assistants to agents still is from his vision.
g: Founder and CEO of Glean, which builds workplace search and AI assistants; Rubrik co-founder

eps.t: Nobel Prize Conversations: Geoffrey Hinton
eps.s: Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton recalls zigzagging through Cambridge, his habit of explaining everyday puzzles, what universities and companies each do well, and why he left Google. On AI, he argues language models truly understand, that "hallucination" is really confabulation, just like human memory, that AI will probably surpass us within 20 years, and that companies should be made to spend a third of compute on safety.
g: 2024 Nobel physics laureate and neural-network pioneer who left Google to speak about AI risk

eps.t: When an AI researcher writes sci-fi: Meta's Yuandong Tian on a future where what you think is what you get
eps.ot: 116: 当AI研究者写科幻，与Meta田渊栋聊他的智能想象：我们终会“所思即所得”
