eps.s: Meta researcher Yuandong Tian, also a sci-fi novelist, starts from his book's world: why the speed of links between computing units decides how smart a system gets, why technology ends at "what you think is what you get," and how endless abundance can kill ambition. He also covers AI's real effects on jobs, research, teams and writing, including why AI research still only impresses outsiders.
g: Meta AI research scientist, long at FAIR, and author of the sci-fi novel Poxiao Zhizhong

eps.t: Microsoft CPO: If you aren’t prototyping with AI you’re doing it wrong | Aparna Chennapragada
eps.s: Microsoft CPO Aparna Chennapragada on building enterprise AI products when the technology changes weekly but workplace habits change slowly. She lays out the three ingredients of a good agent, why "NLX is the new UX" and conversation needs design too, how prototype-first development changes the PM's job, why you must keep refreshing your mental model of what AI can do, and the zero-to-one lessons she took from Google Lens and Google Now.
g: Microsoft CPO leading AI product strategy for productivity tools and agents; formerly Robinhood CPO and Google VP

eps.t: An Interview with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang About Chip Controls, AI Factories, and Enterprise Pragmatism
eps.s: During Computex, Stratechery's Ben Thompson interviews Jensen Huang. Huang explains why he considers the US AI diffusion rule and limits on chip sales to China a mistake, tallies what the H20 ban cost NVIDIA, and walks through how AI factories compete on output per watt. His sharpest line: with a weak architecture, even free chips aren't cheap enough.
g: Co-founder and CEO of NVIDIA, the company that makes GPUs and AI computing platforms

eps.t: Elon Musk at the Qatar Economic Forum 2025
eps.s: At the Qatar Economic Forum, Bloomberg's Mishal Husain presses Musk on Tesla sales, politics and what comes next. He says Tesla sales have turned around and he'll stay CEO, estimates SpaceX will carry about 90% of mass to orbit this year, is in no rush to take Starlink public, likens OpenAI's for-profit turn to a rainforest charity becoming a lumber company, and plans to spend far less on politics.
g: CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, scaling DOGE work back to a day or two a week

eps.t: Yin Qi on 14 years of building AI companies: success that can't pay for itself never lasts
eps.ot: 117: 印奇的AI创业14年：所有不能闭环的辉煌都是暂时的
eps.s: Megvii co-founder and Qianli Technology chairman Yin Qi looks back on 14 years of building AI companies. He explains why joining Qianli is his second startup, why he's putting AI in cars before robots, how self-driving should be judged, why the VLA hype is overblown and how the supplier field will shrink. His key lesson: an AI company must earn enough to support itself before its tech ideals can last.
g: Chairman of Qianli Technology, which builds AI for cars, and co-founder of Megvii

eps.t: Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis + Google Co-Founder Sergey Brin: Scaling AI, AGI Timeline, Simulation Theory
eps.ol: Big Technology Podcast (live at Google I/O 2025)
eps.s: Live at Google I/O, Alex Kantrowitz interviews Demis Hassabis alongside Google co-founder Sergey Brin. Hassabis covers pairing scale with new breakthroughs, how "thinking" added 600+ Elo to AlphaGo, two ways to define AGI, synthetic data, an agent-first web and a computational universe. Asked whether AGI arrives before or after 2030, he says just after.
g: CEO of Google DeepMind, the team building Gemini

eps.t: Unconventional product lessons from Binance, N26, Google, more | Mayur Kamat (CPO at N26)
eps.s: Mayur Kamat, CPO of the European mobile bank N26, describes how Binance worked: extremely flat, nightly leadership meetings, and no decision stuck for more than a day. He explains how to pick high-leverage problems and dig into the details yourself, offers PMs advice on choosing jobs and career paths, argues that product strategy is overrated and experiments should drive decisions, explains why fintech produces good PMs, and shares lessons from Google Hangouts and where AI actually helps today.
g: CPO of N26; former global head of product at Binance, VP of product at Agoda; previously at Google and Microsoft

eps.t: Google DeepMind C.E.O. Demis Hassabis on Living in an A.I. Future
eps.s: Right after Google I/O 2025, Hassabis talks about AGI timelines, safety, education and jobs. He puts AGI five to ten years away and sets a high bar: matching everything a human brain can do. Most striking is his outlook: serious risks from AI agents within two or three years, and further out, scientific breakthroughs bringing abundance and a hard question of how to share it.
g: CEO of Google DeepMind and Nobel laureate, running Google's AI research

eps.t: Mercedes-Benz CEO Ola Källenius: a CEO in transition, and a 139-year-old Mercedes in transition
eps.ot: 对话奔驰全球CEO康林松：转型期CEO和转型之中的139岁奔驰
eps.s: Interviewed during a China visit, Mercedes-Benz CEO Ola Källenius takes tough questions: why Mercedes is losing share in China, why going electric is slower than expected, and what luxury means once technology is everywhere. He explains why he won't cut prices, why China R&D now serves the world, how Mercedes owns its software architecture while using partners, and how he makes decisions as a CEO in transition.
g: Global CEO of the Mercedes-Benz Group

eps.t: Growth tactics from OpenAI and Stripe’s first marketer | Krithika Shankarraman
eps.s: Krithika Shankarraman was OpenAI's first marketing lead and Stripe's first marketing hire. Her view of marketing is anti-playbook: diagnose before you act. She walks through her four-step DATE framework, why being different beats being cheaper, how Stripe's marketing job changed by stage, the review process that makes teams faster, why brand is really about expectations, where marketing sits in a company, and the new questions of taste and pricing in the AI era.
g: Executive in residence at Thrive Capital; OpenAI's first marketer and VP of marketing; Stripe's first marketing hire

eps.t: AI Consolidation, Biotech Opportunities, and World Models with Sarah and Elad
eps.s: The two hosts discuss how leaders are emerging across AI categories, how coding tools are splitting into real-time and background camps, and whether the top two startups in a market should merge. Elad lists overlooked biology markets like fertility and anti-aging, and the flaws in how biotech is funded. They close on world models, reinforcement learning environments and the surprises that unconstrained search can turn up.
g: No Priors co-host, serial entrepreneur and investor
No Priors co-host and founder of the venture firm Conviction

eps.t: Born to grind: Renjie Guo, the robot-vacuum boss born in 1997, now builds home robots
eps.ot: 118: 天生卷王郭人杰：从97年的扫地机总裁到创业做家庭通用机器人
eps.s: Born in 1997, Renjie Guo went from a gifted-youth college program and P&G to running Dreame's robot-vacuum division. He recounts the Douyin sales boom and stockouts, the move to Tmall and JD.com, going premium amid price wars, a profit overhaul and two demotions. Then he explains why his new startup, Lexiang, starts with robots for developers before moving into the home.
g: Founder of Lexiang, a consumer and home robot startup; former head of Dreame's robot-vacuum unit

eps.t: Three hours with YouWare founder Chaoping Ming: today's agents are like a gorilla that just picked up a fire stick
eps.ot: 对YouWare创始人明超平3小时访谈：今天Agent像大猩猩刚拿起一根烧火棍
eps.s: YouWare founder Chaoping Ming traces his product instincts to debate, OnePlus and CapCut, then recounts building Noisee at Moonshot AI and choosing to shut it down, plus his startup's early detour into over-polishing. Later he discusses value per token, why the "shell" around a model and its community matter, coding as a new way to create, super agents versus specialized ones, and why agents are still primitive.
g: Founder and CEO of YouWare, formerly a product manager at Moonshot AI

eps.t: Why Uber’s CPO delivers food on weekends | Sachin Kansal
eps.s: Uber's chief product officer Sachin Kansal explains why he drives and delivers food on weekends, how he turns what he finds on the road into team OKRs, and the decision-making behind shipping fast. He also shares career advice for new PMs, how Uber mixes robotaxis with human drivers in one network, the efficiency logic behind Uber's turn to profitability, several product calls he made against the data, and lessons from his years at Palm.
g: Chief product officer at Uber; previously at Palm and the taxi app Flywheel

eps.t: Xiangyu Zhang on the struggles of multimodal AI research and two "GPT-4 moments" in the next two years
eps.ot: 和张祥雨聊，多模态研究的挣扎史和未来两年的2个“GPT-4时刻”
eps.s: StepFun chief scientist Xiangyu Zhang, with co-host Guangmi Li, traces his research from ResNet to the Step models: why still images couldn't repeat GPT's success, why bigger models got worse at math, and what o1-style reasoning really learns. Later he covers visual chains of thought, long context and memory, and the bottleneck of environments and feedback, and predicts two GPT-4 moments: multimodal reasoning and autonomous learning.
g: Chief scientist at StepFun, a Chinese AI model company

eps.t: Fei-Fei Li: World Models and the Multiverse
eps.s: In this short conversation, Fei-Fei Li explains why she founded World Labs: language is a lossy compression of the world, while physics and interaction happen in 3D. She shares why trees have no eyes, how losing stereo vision forced her to drive at a crawl, and her vision of AI generating endless virtual worlds, a kind of multiverse.
g: Co-founder and CEO of World Labs, Stanford computer science professor

eps.t: Anthropic's CPO on what comes next | Mike Krieger (co-founder of Instagram)
eps.s: Mike Krieger, Instagram co-founder and now Anthropic's chief product officer, reflects on his first year: how his views on AI capabilities and timelines have shifted, where the new bottlenecks in product development are now that AI writes most of the code, and how product and research teams work together. He also discusses Anthropic's position as a challenger, where AI startups can defend themselves, why MCP matters, and what he learned from shutting down his news app, Artifact.
g: Chief product officer at Anthropic, co-founder of Instagram, and co-founder of the news app Artifact

eps.t: Teaching AI to Understand the Physical World, with Dr. Fei-Fei Li of World Labs
eps.s: Fei-Fei Li explains why she started World Labs, why AI without spatial intelligence is incomplete, and why creative tools and XR will be the first markets for 3D world models. She covers robot shapes and training data and the scarcity of 3D data, looks back at ImageNet, a data bet few believed in, and insists AI should help people, not replace them.
g: Co-founder and CEO of World Labs; co-director of Stanford's Human-Centered AI Institute

eps.t: Mercado Libre: 18k engineers, 30k deploys a day, & their own fleet of planes | Sebastian Barrios
eps.s: Sebastian Barrios, who long ran product and engineering at Mercado Libre, explains how Latin America's most valuable company works: product and engineering as one, very few PMs, leaders who dig into the user experience, no cascading OKRs, and the platform guardrails and internal AI platform behind roughly 30,000 deploys a day. He also covers a "high-performance team" culture, the weekly status email he writes to himself, and getting a call from Steve Jobs as a teenager.
g: Former head of product and engineering at Mercado Libre; now SVP of engineering at Roblox

eps.t: How does an AI video app go viral? Answers from PixVerse and its 60 million users
eps.ot: 119: AI视频产品怎么Go Viral？6000万用户的PixVerse的答案
eps.s: Xuzhang Xie, co-founder of PixVerse maker AIsphere, explains why he left investing for AI video, how templates let ordinary people make their first shareable video, and what made hits like the Venom transformation go viral. He also covers a lean, low-GPU approach, the economics of consumer subscriptions, the demands he thinks are fake, and how the global video-generation race is shaping up.
g: PixVerse co-founder handling fundraising, partnerships and strategy; former investor at Lighthouse Capital

eps.t: Lovart founder Mian Chen looks back on two years of building AI apps: "This moment feels so good!"
eps.ot: Lovart创始人陈冕复盘应用创业这两年：这一刻就是好爽啊！！
eps.s: Lovart founder Mian Chen explains how a decade at Mobike, Missfresh, and ByteDance shaped his business judgment. He recounts how his first product went through a subsidy war, a takedown, near-empty bank accounts, and failed fundraising in 2023, and how he built the design agent Lovart once AI agents matured. He also covers timing user growth, how general and specialized agents will shake out, and teams in the AI era.
g: Founder of the AI design agent Lovart, former business lead at ByteDance

eps.t: 35 years of product design wisdom from Apple, Disney, Pinterest and beyond | Bob Baxley
eps.s: Bob Baxley, who led design for Apple's online store and the App Store, shares lessons from more than thirty years in design: why moving from one strong culture to another can bounce you out, the strategic value of design as a way of thinking, where design should sit in an organization, why tenets beat empty principles, why you should draw pictures as late as possible, the moral responsibility that comes with software being an emotional medium, and what Apollo teaches champions of good ideas.
g: Veteran design executive who has led design teams at Apple, Pinterest, Yahoo, and ThoughtSpot

eps.t: Will we have Superintelligence by 2028? With Anthropic's Ben Mann
eps.s: Right after the Claude 4 launch, Anthropic co-founder Ben Mann discusses its better behavior, its long-running agent skills and how to think about agent costs. He covers timelines for superhuman AI and an economic Turing test, what to do as expert feedback grows scarce, why safety policy centers on biology, why computer use isn't open to consumers yet, and where MCP came from.
g: Anthropic co-founder who leads Labs, home of MCP and Claude Code

eps.t: #208 Alexandr Wang - CEO, Scale AI
eps.s: A three-hour talk (the transcript covers the first two) that opens with brain implants and uploading minds, then covers his Los Alamos childhood and the founding of Scale AI. The meatiest part is AI warfare: AI agents drafting military plans for human commanders, AI-versus-AI fights decided by how many copies each side runs, and the risk that open models like DeepSeek carry poisoned training data.
g: Scale AI founder and CEO; the company supplies AI training data and builds defense AI.

eps.t: Insta360's JK Liu after the STAR Market IPO: isn't this an extreme sport too?
eps.ot: 120: 科创板后再访Insta360刘靖康：这何尝不是一种极限运动！
eps.s: After Insta360 listed on Shanghai's STAR Market, founder JK Liu returns. He talks about three levels of innovation and needs users can't put into words, why the camera market has room for several companies, and how to defend against DJI for the first time. He also covers which advantages rivals can catch up to, building on existing strengths, lessons from a quality crisis, and managing by context, not control.
g: Founder and chairman of Insta360, maker of 360-degree and action cameras

eps.t: How to build a team that can “take a punch” | Hilary Gridley (Head of Core Product, Whoop)
eps.s: Hilary Gridley, head of core product at the fitness wearable company Whoop, explains how to build a team that can take a punch: using ideas from cognitive behavioral therapy to help people climb out of the spiral after criticism, communicating transparently so the team understands how leaders think, a "magic question" for learning how others judge, changing team behavior through habits and reward loops, modeling self-care, and how AI shortens the feedback loop for learning.
g: Head of core product at Whoop; formerly senior product director at Big Health and product marketing manager at Dropbox

eps.t: Sam Altman: The Future of OpenAI, ChatGPT's Origins, and Building AI Hardware
eps.s: At YC's AI Startup School, Garry Tan asks Sam Altman how OpenAI grew from eight people and a coin-flip decision, and what comes next: an always-on assistant, new devices, robots and the energy to power them. His message to young founders: models are far ahead of products, so this is the best time to build, just don't clone ChatGPT.
g: OpenAI co-founder and CEO; in YC's first summer founders batch in 2005

eps.t: Godfather of AI: I Tried to Warn Them, But We've Already Lost Control! Geoffrey Hinton
eps.s: Geoffrey Hinton splits AI risk into misuse by people (cyberattacks, homemade viruses, outrage-driven feeds, killer robots) and superintelligence deciding it doesn't need us, which his gut puts at 10–20%. He warns mass job loss comes first and suggests training as a plumber, explains what he saw at Google that turned him toward warning, and argues chatbots already have subjective experience.
g: Nobel-winning "godfather of AI" who left Google after a decade to warn about AI risk

eps.t: Fei-Fei Li: Spatial Intelligence is the Next Frontier in AI
eps.s: At Y Combinator's AI Startup School, Fei-Fei Li tells young founders how she has chased near-delusional problems: betting on data to build ImageNet, watching the 2012 breakthrough, and now building spatial intelligence at World Labs. She uses 540 million years of vision to explain why 3D is harder and more important than language, and shares her dry-cleaning business at 19 and why she hires for fearlessness.
g: Co-founder and CEO of World Labs, Stanford professor, creator of ImageNet

eps.t: Rokid's Misa Zhu on Eddie Wu, Alibaba, and year 11 in the "dark forest" of hardware startups
eps.ot: 和Rokid祝铭明聊，吴妈、阿里、硬件创业黑森林的第11年
eps.s: Rokid founder Misa Zhu tells how Alibaba rescued and bought his first startup, how he built M Lab there, and how Eddie Wu backed him to leave and make AI glasses. He revisits the 2019 pivot from speakers to AR glasses, the layoffs, and a launch days before COVID. Then: why glasses need a display, how phones lose ground, what protects a hardware company, and how he leads.
g: Founder and CEO of Rokid, which makes AI and AR glasses; former Alibaba executive

eps.t: The Operating System for Self Driving Cars (and Tanks, and Trucks...) With Qasar Younis and Peter Ludwig of Applied Intuition
eps.s: Applied Intuition CEO Qasar Younis and CTO Peter Ludwig explain how the company went from engineering tools to a vehicle operating system, why centralized computing matters, and why cars need an Android-style compatibility layer. They discuss China's auto industry and industrial policy, the convergence of self-driving approaches, safety and adoption timelines, and the risk that autonomy becomes a commodity before anyone profits from it.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Applied Intuition, which builds self-driving software for vehicles
Co-founder and CTO of Applied Intuition

eps.t: Sam Altman on AGI, GPT-5, and what's next - the OpenAI Podcast Ep. 1
eps.s: In the first OpenAI Podcast episode, Andrew Mayne talks with Sam Altman about why AGI's definition keeps moving, when GPT-5 arrives, the Stargate compute build-out, whether ads would hurt user trust, and using ChatGPT as a new dad. Two lines stand out: superintelligence means discovering new science, and selling answers would destroy trust.
g: OpenAI co-founder and CEO, and a new father

eps.t: Alexandr Wang: Building Scale AI, Transforming Work with Agents & Competing With China
eps.ho: Garry Tan, Jared Friedman et al.
eps.s: Scale AI founder Alexandr Wang returns to YC to trace Scale from a doctor-chatbot idea to a data business that kept arriving before each AI wave. He argues people will end up managing swarms of agents, that a company's real asset will be its own tuned model, and he lays out where China leads on data, energy and robot costs.
g: Founder and CEO of Scale AI, supplying data and AI apps to labs and governments

eps.t: AI prompt engineering in 2025: What works and what doesn’t | Sander Schulhoff
eps.s: Sander Schulhoff wrote one of the first prompt-engineering guides and runs HackAPrompt, a contest for tricking AI into misbehaving. He walks through which prompting tricks still work in 2025 (examples, context, breaking problems down, self-checks, voting) and why telling a model "you are a math professor" no longer improves accuracy. The second half covers prompt injection: why it can't be fully fixed, which defenses fail, and what goes wrong once AI can act on its own.
g: Founder of Learn Prompting and HackAPrompt, lead author of The Prompt Report, AI red-teaming researcher

eps.t: Elon Musk: Digital Superintelligence, Multiplanetary Life, How to Be Useful
eps.s: At Y Combinator's AI Startup School, Garry Tan talks with Musk in front of young founders. Musk revisits Zip2, PayPal and SpaceX, explains first principles and keeping ego in check, and walks through the rush to build xAI's Memphis supercomputer. He expects digital superintelligence this year or next and humanoid robots to far outnumber people, and argues AI safety rests on rigorous truth-seeking.
g: CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, founder of xAI

eps.t: Mercedes-Benz's Xin Wang on German carmakers, who gets a say, and tech battles in an industry upheaval
eps.ot: 和奔驰王忻聊，产业大转折下的德国汽车、话语权和技术battle
eps.s: Xin Wang runs autonomous driving and connected-car R&D at Mercedes-Benz China, after nearly 18 years at Delphi. He traces twenty years of tech cycles in China's car industry, the shifting role of suppliers, and how his team pushed local R&D during COVID and won headquarters' trust. He also covers the camera-only CLA, AI in cars, luxury, safety, and Mercedes' once-in-a-century turning point.
g: Head of autonomous driving and connected-car R&D at Mercedes-Benz China

eps.t: From ChatGPT to Instagram to Uber: The quiet architect behind the world’s most popular products
eps.s: Peter Deng, former VP of product at OpenAI and Instagram's first head of product, gives his first podcast interview. He explains why even AGI still needs builders to turn it into useful products, how AI will change education, and the Uber lesson that sometimes the interface doesn't matter. He also covers how AI startups can beat incumbents, scaling from 1 to 100, five types of product managers, and how he hires, manages and picks jobs.
g: General partner at Felicis; previously VP of product at OpenAI (ChatGPT), Instagram's first product lead, and Uber rider product lead

eps.t: He Wang on embodied AI's years on the academic fringe, and the man-made chaos after the funding blitz
eps.ot: 和王鹤聊，具身智能的学术边缘史和资本轰炸后的人为乱象
eps.s: Peking University professor and Galbot founder He Wang explains how embodied AI, meaning robots that learn by acting in the world, went from a fringe idea in computer vision to an investor craze. He covers how it differs from internet AI, whether language is intelligence, and his long bet on synthetic data. He also sets a test for the industry: no teleoperation, and 10,000 units within five years.
g: Founder and CTO of robotics startup Galbot; assistant professor at Peking University

eps.t: The source code of Ed Huang's inner world: PingCAP's CTO on Black Mirror, beautiful code and creative freedom
eps.ot: 121: PingCAP黄东旭的“内在世界源代码”：《黑镜》、程序之美和创作自由
eps.s: PingCAP co-founder and CTO Ed Huang starts from a programmer's sense of beauty: beating complexity with a few simple rules, TiDB and TiKV's detours to the cloud and abroad, what databases do once AI models become their main users, how AI amplifies programmers, and whether models are a new species. Most striking: he sold his house to live in an RV, removing single points of failure from his life.
g: PingCAP co-founder and CTO, a lead designer of the distributed databases TiDB and TiKV

eps.t: Meet AlphaEvolve: The Autonomous Agent That Discovers Algorithms Better Than Humans With Google DeepMind's Pushmeet Kohli and Matej Balog
eps.s: DeepMind's Pushmeet Kohli and Matej Balog introduce AlphaEvolve, an agent that discovers algorithms: Gemini proposes code changes, an evaluation function filters them, and an evolutionary loop keeps iterating. They trace its lineage from AlphaGo to FunSearch, explain why the evaluator is central, discuss extending it to biology and chemistry, and ask whether speeding up Gemini's training counts as self-improvement.
g: Vice president of science research at Google DeepMind
Google DeepMind research scientist and a core member of the AlphaEvolve team

eps.t: Naming expert shares process for creating billion-dollar brands: Vercel, Azure, Windsurf, Sonos
eps.s: David Placek founded Lexicon Branding, the firm behind names like Pentium, BlackBerry, Sonos and Azure. He explains why the right name usually feels uncomfortable at first, the lasting advantages a distinctive name brings, and his process of identify, invent and land, including small teams working under disguised assignments and linguists screening for risk. He ends with a do-it-yourself method for founders with no budget, with stories behind Vercel, Windsurf and others along the way.
g: Founder of Lexicon Branding, the naming firm behind Pentium, BlackBerry, Sonos, Azure, Vercel and Windsurf

eps.t: Allen Zhu invested in 10 minutes, and Pop Mart and miHoYo are trying too: Fuzozo's Zhaozhi Sun on AI toys
eps.ot: 122: 10分钟朱啸虎投资，泡泡玛特、米哈游都在试；Fuzozo孙兆治聊AI潮玩
eps.s: Zhaozhi Sun, founder of the AI companion toy Fuzozo, explains why he pitched it as an AI buddy that offers only emotional value, and how he stripped a desktop robot down to a pocket-sized furball. He also covers pet-raising mechanics, layered memory and voice synthesis tradeoffs, plus pricing, production capacity, big companies moving in, and what on-device models could change.
g: Founder of AI companion toy Fuzozo; previously designed cars and robots at XPeng, Didi and Pengxing

eps.t: Catching up with Mengqiu Wang: venture capital is pretty dull, so let's also talk travel, books and feminism
eps.ot: 和梦秋的catch-up：创投挺无聊，也聊聊旅行读书和女性主义
eps.s: Crystal Stream Capital founding partner Mengqiu Wang returns for her annual catch-up. She says the funding winter isn't over, and DeepSeek put good AI in everyone's hands without sparking an app boom. She weighs in on Manus, Yuanbao, general-purpose agents, AI glasses and robots. Then come travel, books, the film Her Story, feminism, her unhurried outlook and her choice not to have children.
g: Founding partner of Crystal Stream Capital; former VP of technology at Baidu

eps.t: I’ve run 75+ businesses. Here’s why you’re probably chasing the wrong idea. | Andrew Wilkinson
eps.s: Andrew Wilkinson, co-founder of the holding company Tiny, draws on roughly 75 ventures, successes and failures alike. He explains how to pick a business idea (fish in unglamorous ponds with little competition and take an easy first win), when to bootstrap versus raise venture money, what he looks for in acquisitions, and hard lessons on hiring. He also shows how he automates his work with AI agents, and why money never fixed his anxiety but treatment did.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Tiny, which buys and holds companies; founder of design agency Metalab

eps.t: Chai-2: The AI Model Accelerating Drug Discovery with Chai Discovery Co-Founders Jack Dent and Joshua Meier
eps.s: Chai Discovery co-founders Joshua Meier and Jack Dent introduce Chai-2, a generative model that designs antibodies from scratch for a chosen target, with about 20% of designs binding as intended. They discuss how they built the benchmark, why they opened access to partners, how far this is from real drugs, and the engineering culture of a team of about ten.
g: Co-founder of Chai Discovery, which uses AI to design drug molecules
Co-founder of Chai Discovery, which uses AI to design drug molecules

eps.t: Solo founder, $80M exit, 6 months: The Base44 bootstrapped startup success story | Maor Shlomo
eps.s: Base44 founder Maor Shlomo explains how he built an AI app-building tool alone, with no outside money, to profitability in about six months, then sold it to Wix for $80 million up front. He covers starting with three friends, growing through public updates on LinkedIn and a hackathon, building the tech around large language models, a step he cut, the acquisition talks, and life as a solo founder.
g: Founder of Base44, an AI app builder he built solo and sold to Wix in 2025; former Explorium CEO

eps.t: Living on AI alone: 5Y Capital's Xing Meng and two challengers recount a 72-hour survival test
eps.ot: 123: 当只有AI，人会活成怎样？与五源孟醒和两位挑战者还原72小时AI生存
eps.s: 5Y Capital partner Xing Meng ran a 72-hour AI survival challenge: each person got 100 yuan, a bottle of water and plenty of AI tools. He explains the design and why AI agents keep hitting walls in a world built for humans. Two challengers, a director who can't code and a humanities grad turned developer, recount surviving on AI and making a short film and a livestream demo.
g: 5Y Capital partner, host of the Tech Isn't Boring podcast, creator of the 72-hour challenge
Humanities grad turned AI app developer (travel app Adventure Snap); challenge participant
Young film director, challenge participant, and maker of the AI short film 7.41

eps.t: Kai Yu on 30 years in tech: less a battlefield than a story of people crossing paths
eps.ot: 余凯口述30年史：世界不止刀光剑影，是一部人来人往的江湖故事
eps.s: Horizon Robotics founder Kai Yu recounts 30 years across academia, Baidu, startups, investors and the car industry: bidding for Geoffrey Hinton's team, recruiting Andrew Ng, Horizon's scattered first five years and its 2019 focus on cars. He then covers planning around ways to die, dealing with carmakers, when driver assistance becomes standard, the new chip design robots need, and why AI should do people's heavy work.
g: Founder and CEO of Horizon Robotics, which makes chips and software for assisted driving

eps.t: Why Platforms Win and Point Solutions Fail with Rippling CEO Parker Conrad
eps.s: Rippling founder Parker Conrad talks about starting over after Zenefits failed, and why integrated platforms will beat point solutions. He covers how to pick business leaders who can carry real responsibility, how AI affects software jobs, must-be-exact work like payroll, and permission systems. He also explains why Rippling isn't going public yet: private secondary markets already provide liquidity, and public markets lack high-growth comparables.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Rippling, which makes connected HR, IT and finance software

eps.t: Choosing the hard way: ex-Li Auto president Yanan Shen spends 500 million yuan building homes for China's middle class
eps.ot: 124: 理想前总裁的没苦硬吃，沈亚楠怎么花5亿给中国中产造家
eps.s: Former Li Auto president Yanan Shen spent three years building Qixidi, which designs and delivers whole homes as products. After the first launch drew ten times fewer visitors than hoped, he revisits how the brand was pitched, how to explain a new category and how to run construction. He also covers a Home Depot-style model, money discipline, and how 500 million yuan of his own reshaped his goals.
g: Founder and CEO of Qixidi, which builds complete smart homes; former president of Li Auto

eps.t: Rapidly test and validate any startup idea with the 2-day Foundation Sprint
eps.s: Jake Knapp and John Zeratsky, creators of the Design Sprint, introduce the Foundation Sprint: a core team spends two days, about 10 hours, deciding the customer and problem, how they differ from alternatives, and the approach, then writes a one-sentence founding hypothesis they can test. Weekly design sprints, prototypes and a scorecard follow. They also explain why, when AI can build prototypes in minutes, slowing down to think first matters more than ever.
g: Co-founder of Character Capital, inventor of the Design Sprint, formerly at Google and Google Ventures
Co-founder of Character Capital, co-creator of the Design Sprint, formerly at Google Ventures

eps.t: Cloning "me" with AI: Mindverse's Fangbo Tao on identity models
eps.ot: 125: 用AI复刻一个「我」，与心识宇宙陶芳波聊身份模型
eps.s: Mindverse founder Fangbo Tao traces his path from early data mining to recommendation systems at Facebook and research at Alibaba, and explains why he builds "identity models" bound to real people instead of digital doubles or assistants. He covers training on first-person memories, why he rejects retrieval-based personalization, and how Me.bot, Talks and the open-source Second Me test expression, social connection and a neutral identity layer.
g: Founder and CEO of Mindverse; former AI researcher at Facebook and Alibaba

eps.t: Decoding AgiBot's near-backdoor listing: six days at the daily price cap, and why copying it is hard
eps.ot: 126: 解读智元机器人“类借壳”：6个涨停板！可想学不简单
eps.s: After buyers linked to AgiBot took control of Swancor Advanced Materials, its stock repeatedly hit the daily limit. Investor Chao Wang walks through the filing: what the deal bought, why it stopped at 29.99%, why it isn't a backdoor listing, what stands between AgiBot's robots and the listed company, whether other shareholders can cash out, whether rivals can copy it, and how realistic IPO and Hong Kong exits are.
g: Partner at Lanqiao Capital, an investment firm

eps.t: Are robots running out of data? Steve Xie on simulation, synthetic data, Meta's mega-deal and Alexandr Wang
eps.ot: 机器人遭遇数据荒？与谢晨聊：仿真与合成数据、Meta天价收购和Alexandr Wang
eps.s: Lightwheel founder Steve Xie draws on simulation work at Cruise, Nvidia and NIO to explain how synthetic data can ease robotics' data shortage, and why simulating robots is far harder than simulating cars. He maps the industry's layers, argues the real-data and simulation camps are converging, and reads Meta's Scale AI deal as a bet on data as raw material. He also flags bubble risks.
g: Founder and CEO of Lightwheel; formerly led simulation at Nvidia and Cruise

eps.t: The AI-native startup: 5 products, 7-figure revenue, 100% AI-written code. | Dan Shipper (Every)
eps.s: Dan Shipper, co-founder of Every, explains how a 15-person company runs a daily newsletter, several AI apps and a consulting arm, with engineers who no longer write code by hand. He floats hot takes (AI may bring jobs back to the US, non-programmers underrate Claude Code, define AGI by how long a leash you can give an agent), then covers compounding engineering, the allocation economy, the top predictor of enterprise AI success, and putting writing back at the center of his work.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Every, an AI newsletter, app incubator and consulting company

eps.t: Asimov: Building An Omniscient RL Oracle with ReflectionAI's Misha Laskin
eps.s: Misha Laskin of Reflection AI introduces Asimov, a code-research agent built on the idea that an AI should first absorb an organization's entire codebase and unwritten knowledge before writing code. He explains why reinforcement learning is limited by reward signals rather than compute, what "jagged superintelligence" means, and how frontier labs moving into products threatens startups. He expects deployment to take decades, with coding among the first categories to be cracked.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Reflection AI

eps.t: Anthropic co-founder: AGI predictions, leaving OpenAI, what keeps him up at night | Ben Mann
eps.s: Anthropic co-founder Ben Mann explains why Meta's huge pay packages struggle to lure people from Anthropic, why scaling laws are accelerating rather than stalling, and how an "economic Turing test" could measure truly transformative AI. He discusses the hit to jobs and how individuals should adapt, recounts leaving OpenAI because safety wasn't the top priority, walks through constitutional AI, and shares his own estimate of how badly things could go.
g: Anthropic co-founder and product engineering tech lead; one of the authors of OpenAI's GPT-3 paper

eps.t: ZhenFund's Yusen Dai on AI's 2025 halftime: OpenAI's IMO gold, Kimi K2's comeback, agents and the talent war
eps.ot: 127: 与真格戴雨森 25 AI 中场复盘：OpenAI的IMO金牌、Kimi K2翻盘、Agent普及和抢人大战
eps.s: ZhenFund's Yusen Dai reviews AI in the first half of 2025. Starting from OpenAI's general model reaching gold-medal level at the International Math Olympiad, he discusses how much room post-training and longer thinking still have. He also covers Silicon Valley's talent war, ChatGPT Agent and Chinese agent products, Kimi K2 and open source, the three big labs, the compute demand agents create, and what to check by year-end.
g: Managing partner at ZhenFund, an early-stage Chinese venture firm

eps.t: Fireside chat with Fed Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman (Integrated Review of the Capital Framework for Large Banks Conference)
eps.s: At a Federal Reserve conference on bank capital rules, Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman asks Sam Altman what regulators should know about AI. He covers intelligence getting over ten times cheaper each year, how jobs will change and why banks adopted early. The starkest warning: AI has broken voice authentication, and a fraud crisis is coming.
g: Co-founder and CEO of OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT

eps.t: #475 – Demis Hassabis: Future of AI, Simulating Reality, Physics and Video Games
eps.s: In his longest recent conversation, Hassabis ranges from why nature is learnable and how Veo 3 picked up physics from video, to games, a virtual cell, how to test for AGI, and energy abundance. The big idea: anything shaped by natural selection has structure that classical learning algorithms can capture, and where that limit lies is itself a physics question.
g: CEO of Google DeepMind; Nobel laureate for AlphaFold's protein structure prediction

eps.t: The Power of Quality Human Data with SurgeAI Founder and CEO Edwin Chen
eps.s: Edwin Chen, founder of Surge AI, talks about running a human-data company that has never raised money yet brings in over $1 billion a year. He explains why data quality has no ceiling, how to measure annotators, why RL environments are so hard to build and why human feedback won't go out of date, and he takes aim at LMArena and academic benchmarks.
g: Founder and CEO of Surge AI, which supplies human-made training data for AI

eps.t: Pricing your AI product: Lessons from 400+ companies and 50 unicorns | Madhavan Ramanujam
eps.s: Pricing expert Madhavan Ramanujam, drawing on his new book Scaling Innovation, explains how to win market share and wallet share at the same time. He covers keeping early pricing simple enough for customers to repeat, B2B negotiation and value selling, why AI companies must get monetization right from day one, a 2x2 of attribution and autonomy for choosing a pricing model, how to run a proof of concept, and a few hard rules on willingness to pay, price increases and churn.
g: Pricing expert, former Simon-Kucher managing partner, author of Monetizing Innovation and Scaling Innovation, co-founder of AI investor 49 Palms

eps.t: Reading the Kimi K2 report section by section, alongside ChatGPT Agent and Qwen3-Coder: the power of systems engineering
eps.ot: 逐段讲解Kimi K2报告并对照ChatGPT Agent、Qwen3-Coder等：“系统工程的力量”
eps.s: Ohio State PhD student Boyuan Zheng defines AI agents and sorts them into types, then walks through Moonshot AI's Kimi K2 technical report: data rewriting, its tool-synthesis pipeline, reward design for reinforcement learning, and training infrastructure. He compares it with ChatGPT Agent, Qwen3-Coder, and Manus's post on context engineering, and ends with agents that improve themselves and a future where everyone has an army of agents.
g: PhD student at Ohio State who researches language agents

eps.t: He saved OpenAI, invented the “Like” button, and built Google Maps: Bret Taylor (Sierra)
eps.s: Bret Taylor traces the path from the failure of Google Local to the birth of Google Maps, recalls how one piece of blunt feedback from Sheryl Sandberg made him ask daily what the most impactful thing is, and explains how founders fool themselves. He argues programming will become operating code-generating machines, lays out the three layers of the AI market, explains why agents will push software toward outcome-based pricing, and covers getting AI productivity now and choosing a go-to-market model.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Sierra, OpenAI board chair; former Salesforce co-CEO and Facebook CTO, co-creator of Google Maps

eps.t: America's Plan to Dominate the Full AI Stack with Sriram Krishnan
eps.s: Sriram Krishnan, the White House's senior AI policy advisor, walks through America's AI Action Plan. He calls DeepSeek the race's starting gun and keeps score by the share of the world's AI usage running on American tech. The plan has three pillars: build compute and energy, clear barriers to innovation, and export the American stack to allies. He also defends open-source models, federal rules and a robotics push.
g: Senior White House policy advisor on artificial intelligence

eps.t: How a niche AI app reached billion-yuan revenue: Cece founder Yongliang Ren's first account of his 14-year journey
eps.ot: 128: 小众AI场景拿到10亿级收入：测测任永亮首次讲述14年创业史
eps.s: Cece founder Yongliang Ren tells how he moved from preventive medicine to computing and built a broad psychology platform on astrology and personality tests. The product grew from test tools and a community to human counseling, AI chat, and now a home companion robot in development. He also covers what protects specialized AI, how AI and humans split the work, reward systems as a design lens, and AI's social impact.
g: Founder and CEO of Cece, a platform for astrology, personality tests and counseling

eps.t: Brian Chesky's secret mentor who scaled Airbnb (after dying 9 times & building a hotel empire)
eps.s: Chip Conley joined Airbnb at 52 as both Brian Chesky's mentor and his direct report. He explains why mixing young and old on a team works, how to survive a founder who runs everything, and how older people can hold their own in tech. He also talks about building a hotel group, nearly dying nine times, managing with Maslow's pyramid, why midlife is a chrysalis rather than a crisis, and turning anxiety into an equation.
g: Founder of the Modern Elder Academy and the Joie de Vivre hotel group; former Airbnb hospitality and strategy head

eps.t: The Shifting Value of Content in the AI Age with Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince
eps.s: Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince explains how AI is breaking search's old deal of content for traffic. AI companies send back less and less traffic, so he wants AI crawlers blocked by default to create scarcity and a paid market for content. He also covers inference moving to devices and the edge, energy limits, and the identity and payment roles the network must play for AI agents.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Cloudflare, the web infrastructure and security company

eps.t: Sam Altman Shows Me GPT 5... And What's Next
eps.s: Recorded as GPT-5 launched, Cleo Abram asks Sam Altman what the model can do and what comes next. He covers when AI might make a real scientific discovery, why compute and power are the bottlenecks, who gains and who struggles as jobs change, and a candid admission: a too-flattering model hurt some fragile users.
g: OpenAI co-founder and CEO, interviewed the week GPT-5 launched

eps.t: David Li on 11 years of building lidar: an industry's big chance is really the nation's chance
eps.ot: 李一帆口述激光雷达11年创业史：你仔细想行业的机会来自哪？是国家、民族的机会
eps.s: Hesai CEO David Li tells the 11-year story of his lidar company: from a robotics PhD at UIUC and gas sensing in Silicon Valley to lidar in Shanghai, cutting prices 99.5% with in-house chips, winning Li Auto and foreign carmakers, and going public. He also explains why lidar is a safety part like an airbag, how to work with carmakers, and why an industry's chance is a nation's chance.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Hesai, which makes lidar sensors for cars and robots

eps.t: Inside ChatGPT: The fastest growing product in history | Nick Turley (OpenAI)
eps.s: ChatGPT head Nick Turley gives his first long podcast interview just before GPT-5 ships. He explains how ChatGPT went from a hackathon project, launched in ten days and meant to be shut down after the holidays, to roughly 700 million weekly users. He covers shipping before polishing, where retention comes from, why chat isn't the end state, the rushed decisions behind free access and the $20 plan, handling sycophancy, team building, and AI search's relationship with content creators.
g: Head of ChatGPT at OpenAI; previously a product leader at Dropbox and Instacart

eps.t: The one question that saves product careers | Matt LeMay
eps.s: Matt LeMay, author of Impact-First Product Teams, explains how product teams can prove they're worth funding in an age of layoffs. Start by asking: if you were the CEO, would you fund your own team? Then watch out for the low-impact death spiral and the best-practices trap. His three steps: keep team goals one step from company goals, protect impact at every stage, and estimate impact in the goal's own units. He also covers pushing back on executives without saying yes or no.
g: Product management consultant and author of Product Management in Practice and Impact-First Product Teams; former Pitchfork music critic

eps.t: Chips, Neoclouds, and the Quest for AI Dominance with SemiAnalysis Founder and CEO Dylan Patel
eps.s: SemiAnalysis's Dylan Patel tours AI infrastructure: open-source models and inference optimization, the fate of roughly 200 neoclouds, Nvidia's lasting edge and the lessons of specialized chips, data center bottlenecks that keep shifting, and how AI capital spending is lifting the US economy. He closes on export-control trade-offs and why China subsidizes its chips.
g: Founder and CEO of SemiAnalysis, a semiconductor and AI infrastructure research firm

eps.t: How a Chinese AI founder built a startup directly in the US: FinalRound's Michael on $10M+ in subscription revenue
eps.ot: 129: 中国AI founder如何直接在美国创业？一个千万美元订阅收入案例 | 对话FinalRound创始人Michael
eps.s: Michael, the 27-year-old founder of FinalRound AI, tells how he built an AI job-search product in the US. He started with a real-time interview assistant, faced accusations of cheating, and passed $10 million in annual revenue through 100-plus weekly experiments and agent-run SEO, news-driven marketing and ad testing. He also discusses Silicon Valley's funding shifts, long hours and equity, and plans to assess how candidates work.
g: Founder of FinalRound AI, an AI job-search platform

eps.t: How to Win When AI Changes Everything
eps.s: Just after GPT-5's launch, Sam Altman tells Nikhil Kamath how young people can get ahead in the AI era: the skill to build first, which AI startups survive as models improve, whether wealth will pile up in one company, deflation, robots, new devices, and India. His most candid point: nobody really has a plan, him included.
g: OpenAI CEO, just after the GPT-5 launch, on careers and business in the AI era

eps.t: Why ChatGPT will be the next big growth channel (and how to capitalize on it) | Brian Balfour
eps.s: Reforge founder Brian Balfour predicts that the AI technology shift will soon bring a matching distribution shift, and ChatGPT is the likeliest next big platform. Using Facebook, Google, iOS and LinkedIn, he walks through the four-step cycle where platforms open up and then tighten, why no one can sit it out, why startups must concentrate their bets, and how to pick a platform and plan an exit. He closes with hard constraints for AI transformation and finding the slowest part of the system.
g: Founder and CEO of Reforge; formerly head of growth at HubSpot

eps.t: AI model quarterly with Guangmi Li: the labs split up, ChatGPT pulls ahead, and the window for AI apps shrinks
eps.ot: 和广密聊大模型季报：分化与收敛、全家桶与垂直整合、L4体验与挖矿窗口
eps.s: Episode 7 of the Global AI Model Quarterly. Guangmi Li sees the top labs splitting up: perhaps only OpenAI and Google will keep building do-everything models, Anthropic is focusing on coding and agents, and consumers are converging on ChatGPT. He talks products at length for the first time, from labs moving into apps to office work as the next frontier, and shares his concentrated-bet investing and bubble watch.
g: Founder and CEO of Shixiang, an investor who tracks global AI model companies

eps.t: How Intercom rose from the ashes by betting everything on AI | Eoghan McCabe (founder and CEO)
eps.s: Eoghan McCabe returned as Intercom's CEO just as net new ARR was heading to zero, then bet everything on Fin, an AI customer service agent, right after ChatGPT launched. He explains focusing on one strategy, rebuilding culture with values and hard performance rules, and pricing by outcomes. He also discusses how agents will reshape organizations and jobs, how incumbents can compete with young AI companies, and what years of therapy did to his leadership.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Intercom, the customer service software company

eps.t: How Agentic AI is Transforming The Startup Landscape with Andrew Ng
eps.s: Andrew Ng on how agentic AI is changing startups. He argues scaling isn't the only path forward, that agents are held back by evals and talent, and that coding took off first. Once code is fast to write, deciding what to build becomes the bottleneck. Founders need both technical understanding and customer empathy, and AI fluency is reshaping teams and hiring.
g: Managing general partner at AI Fund; co-founder of Google Brain and Coursera

eps.t: Agents #4: Phone agents arrive. From the new AutoGLM 2.0 to how AI models will remake phones
eps.ot: 130: 手机Agent大幕拉开！从刚上线的AutoGLM 2.0聊起，大模型如何改造手机|Agent#4
eps.s: Part four of an agent series. Zhipu's Xiao Liu, who leads AutoGLM, starts from the just-launched AutoGLM 2.0: why phone and computer agents are moving to the cloud, which tasks are worth handing off, how to design payments and safety, screen tapping versus APIs, and relations with big apps. He also traces his team's research path, costs, market education and his minimum bar for AGI.
g: Zhipu AI researcher who leads algorithms, engineering and product for the AutoGLM team

eps.t: Inside the expert network training every frontier AI model | Garrett Lord
eps.s: Handshake CEO Garrett Lord first explains why frontier labs need human experts to produce data in post-training and what those experts actually do. Then he describes how Handshake used a decade-old network of students and PhDs to incubate Handshake AI inside the existing company, passing $50 million in revenue within months. He also covers what AI means for young people's jobs and how training data will evolve.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Handshake, the career platform for college students

eps.t: How does Microsoft use AI? Microsoft's commercial and advertising leaders on AI-driven growth
eps.ot: 131: 微软怎么用AI？与微软商用市场、广告业务管理层聊AI驱动的增长
eps.s: Weizhi Duan, who leads Microsoft's commercial and emerging-markets business in Greater China, and Xiulan Huang, who runs its China advertising business, explain how Microsoft and its clients use AI. They cover Copilot's measurable results in sales, live translation in Teams, AI across the whole ad process, why data governance decides enterprise success, and getting non-technical staff to use AI. They also share expectations ahead of GPT-5 and career lessons.
g: Microsoft Greater China vice president, head of commercial enterprise and emerging markets
Vice president of Microsoft Advertising in China

eps.t: Zhilin Yang one year on: Kimi K2, AI that acts, the brain in a vat, and the beginning of infinity
eps.ot: 和杨植麟时隔1年的对话：K2、Agentic LLM、缸中之脑和“站在无限的开端”
eps.s: After Kimi K2's release, Moonshot AI founder Zhilin Yang returns a year later. He explains how models are moving from a brain in a vat that only thinks to agents that search, write code and act in the digital world, and how K2 learns more from the same data. He also covers why Kimi went open source, why the model is the product, and managing a team like reinforcement learning.
g: Founder and CEO of Moonshot AI, the company behind the Kimi models and assistant

eps.t: How 80,000 companies build with AI: Products as organisms and the death of org charts | Asha Sharma
eps.s: Microsoft's AI platform lead Asha Sharma draws on thousands of enterprise customers to describe products and organizations in the AI era. Products are shifting from finished goods to organisms that keep learning, with post-training and reinforcement learning as the key tools. Interfaces move from GUIs toward composable parts, and org charts give way to work charts. She also shares her planning-by-seasons method and the invisible foundations that decide whether a platform wins.
g: Corporate VP of product for Microsoft's AI platform; formerly Instacart COO and Meta product VP

eps.t: Reshaping America's Economy for the Superintelligence Century with Jacob Helberg
eps.s: Jacob Helberg, awaiting confirmation as Under Secretary of State when this was recorded, on America's economy in the superintelligence century. He covers ending reliance on China for refining critical minerals, why the US is shifting from consumption to production, and why AI will expand output rather than cut jobs. He also discusses the global order, the US-China tech stack race and nuclear power.
g: US Under Secretary of State for Economic Affairs (a nominee at recording)

eps.t: Talking EDA after a $35 billion merger: two chip engineers explain its barriers, AI speedups and China's chances
eps.ot: 132: 350亿美元大并购后聊 EDA｜两位芯片工程师的全面科普：壁垒、AI 加速、国产机会
eps.s: With Synopsys buying Ansys for about $35 billion, chip design engineer Ge Wen and chip architect Wairui Laoge explain EDA, the software used to design chips. They cover where it fits in chip design, why it only earns money at the design stage, what keeps rivals out, how giants grew through acquisitions, how AI is changing EDA and engineers, where Chinese EDA can break in, and what advanced packaging changes.
g: Engineer at a major global chip design company and author of a book on chips
Senior chip architect and author of a book on how computing demand reshapes chip design

eps.t: How we restructured Airtable's entire org for AI | Howie Liu (co-founder and CEO)
eps.s: Airtable CEO Howie Liu explains how he is "refounding" a decade-old SaaS company for the AI era: the CEO returning to hands-on work with AI, splitting R&D into fast-thinking and slow-thinking groups, and making an agent the default way to use the product. He also covers how PM, design, engineering and even sales and marketing roles are blending, why to explore by feel before building evals, and how to take advice.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Airtable, the no-code app-building platform

eps.t: A New Operating System for Physicians with OpenEvidence Founder Daniel Nadler
eps.s: OpenEvidence founder Daniel Nadler on how his clinical search tool, open only to doctors, became part of American physicians' daily routine in about 18 months. He explains why clinical decisions differ from paperwork, how citations and pointing to sources earn trust, and why treating doctors as consumers drove growth. He also covers the explosion of medical knowledge, AI's relationship to doctors, and preventive medicine.
g: Founder of OpenEvidence, a clinical search tool for doctors only

eps.t: Yi Yin and Di Ou on Salomon's surprise boom in China: niche trail running and the young women who made it cool
eps.ot: 与殷一、欧迪聊聊萨洛蒙：中国意外的增长阀门、小众越野跑与少女故事
eps.s: Salomon China GM Yi Yin and Xiaohongshu fashion lead Di Ou explain why a French ski and trail-running brand founded in 1947 unexpectedly took off in China after 2021: serious trail running as the base, fashion and new outdoor fans bringing in newcomers, and women who then brought men back. They also discuss how Xiaohongshu spots audiences, how post-purchase sharing fuels growth, and the Shanghai Anfu Road store.
g: General manager of Salomon China, the French outdoor and trail-running brand
Head of fashion and apparel brand business at Xiaohongshu (RedNote)

eps.t: How AI is reshaping the product role | Oji and Ezinne Udezue
eps.s: Oji and Ezinne Udezue, a married couple who have both been chief product officers several times over, discuss how AI is changing product management. The core value of the job is the same, but the PM-to-engineer ratio, the PRD, and team structure are all shifting. They cover "shipyard" teams, what to hire for now, AI at the core versus the edges, and lessons from fifty combined years: pick the right problem, keep it simple, have opinions, and go watch users.
g: Former CPO of Calendly and Typeform; led product at Twitter, Atlassian and Microsoft; co-author of Building Rocketships
Former CPO of WP Engine and VP of Product at Procore; co-author of Building Rocketships

eps.t: Sam Altman on God, Elon Musk and the Mysterious Death of His Former Employee
eps.s: In one of his most combative interviews, Tucker Carlson presses Sam Altman on who sets ChatGPT's morals, whether he believes in God, how it handles suicidal users, military use, government access to chats, Elon Musk and a former employee's death. The revealing part: what keeps him up isn't the big moral calls but small tweaks that reach hundreds of millions.
g: OpenAI CEO, questioned on ChatGPT's morals, privacy and safety

eps.t: Elon Musk on DOGE, Optimus, Starlink Smartphones, Evolving with AI, Why the West is Imploding
eps.ho: Chamath Palihapitiya, Jason Calacanis, David Sacks, David Friedberg
eps.s: At the All-In Summit, the four hosts ask Musk for his DOGE verdict: government is basically unfixable. Then the talk turns to technology: why Optimus's hand is so hard, the AI5 chip, Starlink direct to phones, a fully reusable Starship and its heat shield, and having Grok rewrite Wikipedia. He closes on birth rates, his worries about the West, and Mars.
g: CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, founder of xAI, after his stint at DOGE

eps.t: $46B of hard truths: Why founders fail and why you need to run toward fear | Ben Horowitz (a16z)
eps.s: Ben Horowitz has been a CEO and spent years as an investor. He explains why hesitation is the deadliest flaw in a leader, how founders usually fail by losing confidence, how a CEO should hire to free up their own time, and what the real reason to start a company is. He also revisits his essay "Good Product Manager, Bad Product Manager," asks whether AI is a bubble, where the opportunities sit, and why the US must stay ahead in AI.
g: Co-founder of the venture firm a16z; earlier co-founded and ran the cloud company LoudCloud

eps.t: OpenAI's Shunyu Yao on six years of AI agents, what models will swallow, and a centralized yet diverse future
eps.ot: 对OpenAI姚顺雨3小时访谈：6年Agent研究、人与系统、吞噬的边界、既单极又多元的世界
eps.s: Recorded in May 2025. OpenAI researcher Shunyu Yao looks back on six years of research on language agents, from picking problems to ReAct and coding environments, and explains why AI's second half is about designing tasks and rewards. He also covers how startups can ride ever-improving models with new interfaces, why memory and context are the next bottleneck, and a future that grows both more centralized and more diverse.
g: OpenAI researcher and author of ReAct and SWE-agent, key work on AI agents

eps.t: The ultimate guide to AEO: How to get ChatGPT to recommend your product | Ethan Smith (Graphite)
eps.s: Graphite CEO Ethan Smith lays out answer engine optimization (AEO): how to get ChatGPT and other AI assistants to recommend your product. He compares AEO with SEO, then walks through the full playbook, from choosing questions and tracking results to building pages and earning mentions elsewhere on the web. He insists on controlled experiments over popular advice, and uses research data to show why purely AI-generated content doesn't work.
g: CEO of growth agency Graphite; 18 years in SEO, now focused on getting AI assistants to recommend products

eps.t: Jared Kushner: BrainCo, Affinity Partners, and the Geopolitics of AI
eps.s: Jared Kushner on Affinity Partners' investing philosophy and BrainCo, the enterprise AI company he co-founded with Elad Gil. Topics include why countries get mispriced, using AI to approve building permits, and energy and AI policy, plus his approach to Middle East diplomacy, his read on Gaza, and the return on investing in Israel's Phoenix.
g: Founder of the investment firm Affinity Partners; former senior White House advisor

eps.t: Interns earning 4,000 yuan a day and programmers turned gig workers: Maimai CEO Fan Lin on 2025's AI talent market
eps.ot: 133: 4000日薪的实习生和零工化的程序员，与脉脉CEO林凡盘点25年AI人才市场 |串台「职」无不言
eps.s: A crossover episode. Maimai founder Fan Lin draws on his Silicon Valley trip this year and Maimai's hiring data to review 2025's AI talent market: the math behind Meta's huge pay offers, how big tech is reworking performance reviews and stock grants to win talent, and which schools and roles benefit. He also covers junior programmers being replaced, white-collar work moving to online gig platforms, and how individuals should respond.
g: Founder and CEO of Chinese professional network Maimai; Tsinghua CS graduate and early Sogou team member

eps.t: Why experts writing AI evals is creating the fastest-growing companies in history | Brendan Foody
eps.s: Mercor CEO Brendan Foody explains why the "age of evals" has arrived: the biggest bottleneck at AI labs is now measuring whether a model did a good job, so having top experts write tests and grading rubrics has become a fast-growing business. He describes how Mercor spotted the opportunity and went from $1M to $400M in annualized revenue in 16 months, which careers and skills look promising, and why he thinks superintelligence isn't coming soon.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Mercor, which recruits experts to write evals and training data for AI labs

eps.t: AI Agents Talking to AI Agents: Reinventing Commerce with Decagon CEO Jesse Zhang
eps.s: Decagon CEO Jesse Zhang on how AI customer service agents moved from digital-native companies into banks, airlines and telecoms, and how a growing company shifts from grabbing deals to long-term building. He explains per-conversation pricing and what protects Decagon from the model labs, and looks ahead to one conversational front door per brand and agents dealing directly with agents.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Decagon, which builds AI customer service agents

eps.t: From managing people to managing AI: The leadership skills everyone needs now | Julie Zhuo
eps.s: With a new edition of "The Making of a Manager" out, Julie Zhuo explains how management skills carry straight over to working with AI: defining success, combining resources and designing process. She shares why her startup hires no product managers and how she diagnoses with data and treats with design. She also covers "willow tree" leadership in times of rapid change, strengths and weaknesses, feedback, executing plans you disagree with, and what she most wants her kids to learn.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Sundial, former VP of Design at Facebook, author of "The Making of a Manager"

eps.t: Why can't $100 million offers keep Meta's AI talent? Pokee AI's Bill Zhu on how AI teams are organized
eps.ot: 134: Meta AI人才动荡，上亿美元为何留不住人？| 与Pokee AI朱哲清盘点 AI 组织
eps.s: Bill Zhu, former head of applied reinforcement learning at Meta and founder of Pokee AI, starts from the talent exodus at Meta's new AI lab. He explains how layers of approval, fights over credit and internal team races slow down frontier research, compares how OpenAI, Anthropic and Google organize and make money, and shares the AI-native ways of working he's testing with his eight-person team.
g: Founder and CEO of Pokee AI; former head of Meta's applied reinforcement learning team

eps.t: Why AI evals are the hottest new skill for product builders | Hamel Husain & Shreya Shankar
eps.s: Using real logs from a property-management AI assistant, Hamel Husain and Shreya Shankar demonstrate how to build an evaluation system for an AI product: first a human reads traces and writes error notes, then an LLM categorizes and counts them, and finally you write binary LLM judges for the few stubborn failure modes, calibrated against human labels. They also address the online debate over whether evals are worth doing, and how evals relate to A/B tests and PRDs.
g: AI evaluation consultant who teaches an evals course on Maven with Shreya Shankar
Researcher at UC Berkeley who teaches an evals course on Maven with Hamel Husain

eps.t: Reinventing K-12 Education Using AI with Alpha School Principal Joe Liemandt
eps.s: Joe Liemandt, founder of the software company Trilogy and principal of Alpha School, explains its model: two hours of AI-driven academics a day, then hands-on afternoon workshops. Teaching follows knowledge level rather than age, adults shift from lecturing to motivating, and rewards of time and money drive students. He also covers the education market, his critique of ChatGPT in classrooms and ideas for changing public schools.
g: Principal of Alpha School and founder of the software company Trilogy

eps.t: A 4-step framework for building delightful products | Nesrine Changuel (Spotify, Google, Skype)
eps.s: Nesrine Changuel worked on product at Skype, Spotify and Google, where she was formally in charge of delight. She explains how to build products people feel attached to: the difference between decorative "confetti" and real delight, three ways to create it, a four-step model, a grid for sorting ideas, and a 50-40-10 roadmap split. Examples from Chrome, Google Meet and Spotify show how to test ideas, win leadership support, and avoid delight backfiring.
g: Product advisor; former PM at Skype, Spotify and Google (Chrome, Meet); author of Product Delight

eps.t: Yitang Zhang at 70: a mathematician chasing a second lightning strike
eps.ot: 135: 专访张益唐：70岁数学家，追逐第二次闪电
eps.s: Mathematician Yitang Zhang, now 70, looks back on his 2013 breakthrough: proving there are infinitely many pairs of primes less than 70 million apart. He discusses progress and difficulties on the Landau–Siegel zeros problem, how he picks problems, intuition and working alone, what AI can and can't do in math research, his plans after returning to China and his views on mathematical talent.
g: Mathematician and professor at Sun Yat-sen University's Hong Kong institute; proved bounded gaps between primes

eps.t: The Impact of AI, from Business Models to Cybersecurity, with Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora
eps.s: Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora starts with search monetization and how agents threaten the app layer, then explains why enterprises can't yet let AI act alone and what makes a business hard to copy. His main case is that cybersecurity must become a platform and cut response times under an hour. He also covers AI's gains in sales, support and back-office work, and his acquisition strategy.
g: Chairman and CEO of cybersecurity firm Palo Alto Networks; former Google chief business officer

eps.t: Finding hidden growth opportunities in your product | Albert Cheng (Duolingo, Grammarly, Chess.com)
eps.s: Albert Cheng has led growth and monetization at Duolingo, Grammarly and Chess.com. He explains how he uses explore-versus-exploit to find growth opportunities, and the biggest win at each company: praising good moves in chess game reviews, letting Grammarly's free users taste premium suggestions, and amplifying Duolingo's screenshot-worthy moments. He also covers retention and resurrection in subscription products, how brand and experiments amplify each other, taking Chess.com from almost no experiments to a thousand a year, and hiring for agency over experience.
g: Head of growth and monetization at Chess.com; previously led the same at Duolingo and Grammarly

eps.t: Sam Altman on Sora, Energy, and Building an AI Empire
eps.s: Shortly after Sora's launch, Sam Altman explains on the a16z Podcast why OpenAI is betting at once on a personal AI assistant, a giant infrastructure build-out and research, and why it made a video app. He also covers AI doing science as his Turing test, regulation, energy and ads. The surprise: he once opposed vertical integration and now thinks he was wrong.
g: OpenAI CEO, amid a huge compute build-out and the Sora app launch

eps.t: An Interview with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman About DevDay and the AI Buildout
eps.s: Ben Thompson talks with Sam Altman during OpenAI's DevDay about the logic behind its huge compute deals, apps inside ChatGPT, ads and shopping, the Sora video app, and copyright. Highlights: Altman compares AI to the transistor, which seeped into everything, and calls the infrastructure spending a company-wide bet on timing that only time will judge.
g: OpenAI co-founder and CEO, turning ChatGPT into a platform and building massive compute

eps.t: Scale AI CEO on Meta's $14B deal, scaling Uber Eats to $80B, & what frontier labs are building next
eps.s: In his first interview as Scale AI's new CEO, Jason Droege clears up Scale's independence after Meta's investment, traces how training data moved from crowdsourced rankings to expert tasks and RL environments, and explains why enterprise AI is "easy to learn, hard to master" and usually takes 6 to 12 months to deploy. He then looks back on building Uber Eats from zero: reading customer incentives, filtering new businesses by model and margin, not losing first, and his hiring bar.
g: CEO of Scale AI; founded and led Uber Eats, and earlier co-founded Scour with Travis Kalanick

eps.t: Humans&: Bridging IQ and EQ in Machine Learning with Eric Zelikman
eps.s: Humans& founder Eric Zelikman looks back on STaR and Quiet-STaR, his methods for training models to reason, and assesses today's uneven frontier models and the industry's habit of measuring progress by how long agents run on their own. He lays out his new company's goal: models that understand and remember people and strengthen human agency rather than simply replacing people.
g: Founder of Humans&, former xAI researcher, and author of the STaR method

eps.t: AI: What Could Go Wrong? with Geoffrey Hinton
eps.ol: The Weekly Show with Jon Stewart
eps.s: Hinton gives Jon Stewart a plain-language tour of neural networks: brain cells that vote, layers that spot a bird, why backpropagation waited decades, and how chatbots predict the next word. Then the risks: digital minds share knowledge instantly and never die, countries might cooperate against AI takeover, a smarter AI could talk us out of unplugging it, and chatbots may already have subjective experience.
g: Nobel physics laureate and neural-network pioneer, now warning about AI risks

eps.t: Minghui Wu's 19-year story: painful pivots, enterprise agent models, the real world as a numbers game, and an IPO
eps.ot: 吴明辉口述19年史：漫长的沉浮、痛苦急转、企业级Agentic Model、现实世界的数值游戏、IPO
eps.s: Before Mininglamp's Hong Kong IPO, founder Minghui Wu tells his 19-year story: starting out with partner Feng Li, building Miaozhen on ad verification, missing mobile, and spinning off Mininglamp Data to emulate Palantir. After a 2019 merger, the sprawling EIP plan failed, and by 2022 one month of cash was left. He then explains DeepMiner and how private data, small specialized models and agents will reshape enterprise software.
g: Founder, CEO and CTO of Mininglamp Technology, a marketing-data and enterprise AI company

eps.t: Inside Google's AI turnaround: AI Mode, AI Overviews, and vision for AI-powered search | Robby Stein
eps.s: Google's VP of Search Robby Stein explains why AI is expanding search rather than killing it, how AI Overviews, Lens and AI Mode divide the work, and what the query fan-out behind AI answers means for content creators. He also looks back at building Stories and Close Friends at Instagram, and lays out his product principles: relentless improvement, metrics as a dashboard, clarity over cleverness, and not worshipping lean teams.
g: VP of Product for Google Search; former Instagram product lead behind Stories, Reels and Close Friends

eps.t: Sora's new world and Lovart's four-month review: Mian Chen on building industry-specific AI agents | Agent #5
eps.ot: 136: Sora新世界 & Lovart 4个月复盘 | 与陈冕聊怎么做垂类Agent|Agent#5
eps.s: Lovart founder Mian Chen first breaks down the newly launched Sora app, arguing it's really AI social and that the giants will follow. He then reviews Lovart's users and revenue since launch, the interface and context design of an AI design agent, and its North American strategy, plus his views on the design profession, the next wave of consumer opportunities and the pace of AI startups.
g: Founder and CEO of Lovart, a startup building an AI design agent

eps.t: Machines Like Us: Geoffrey Hinton on AI's future
eps.ol: Machines Like Us (The Globe and Mail)
eps.s: A policy-minded conversation. Hinton explains why he split his savings across three banks, why digital AI shares knowledge far better than brains, and his central proposal: "maternal AI" that cares about people the way a mother cares for her baby. He also covers whether rival countries can jointly prevent an AI takeover, whether AI already has subjective experience, and his talks with Trudeau and other politicians.
g: Deep learning pioneer and Nobel laureate who now warns the public about AI risks

eps.t: Unlocking the Road to Energy Abundance with Base Power CEO and Co-Founder Zach Dell
eps.s: Base Power CEO Zach Dell explains how his company builds, installs and runs home batteries in Texas and sells power directly to households. He argues America isn't short of electricity but leaves most grid capacity idle, and that solar plus storage will dominate the coming decades. He also covers rising delivery costs, utility incentives, nuclear's prospects, and team, culture and fundraising.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Base Power, a Texas home-battery and electricity company

eps.t: Figma's CEO: Why AI makes design, craft, and quality the new moat for startups | Dylan Field
eps.s: Figma co-founder and CEO Dylan Field talks about steadying the team after the Adobe deal collapsed, keeping a 13-year-old company moving like a startup, and why Figma keeps adding products like FigJam and Make along the user's workflow. His central point: AI makes code cheap, so design and craft now decide who wins. He also covers getting users to value fast, how to build taste, and Figma's slow launch.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Figma, the collaborative design tool used by product teams

eps.t: Agents are an opportunity, and so are the tools for building them: starting from OpenAI's DevDay | Agent #6
eps.ot: 137: Agent 是机会，造 Agent 的工具也是|从OpenAI开发者日聊起｜Agent#6
eps.s: AGI House co-founder Henry Yin and investment lead Naomi Xia start from OpenAI's DevDay launches: AgentKit, Agent Builder and apps inside ChatGPT. They map how the tools for building agents divide up the work and which capability leaps created each layer, discuss the state of reliability, evaluation and voice infrastructure, and estimate how big the tooling market could get and where the investment opportunities are.
g: AGI House co-founder and CTO; Tsinghua Yao Class alum and Berkeley PhD dropout
Early-stage investment lead at AGI House; backed Composio, LiveKit and others

eps.t: How to measure AI developer productivity in 2025 | Nicole Forsgren
eps.s: Nicole Forsgren, creator of the DORA and SPACE frameworks, explains how to measure and improve engineering productivity in the age of AI. Old metrics like lines of code lie even more now, AI both breaks and reshapes developer flow, and speed only matters if it serves the right strategy. She also walks through the seven steps from her new book Frictionless, how to set a baseline with surveys, and how to prove developer experience investments in language leaders care about.
g: Senior director at Google, creator of the DORA and SPACE frameworks, author of Accelerate

eps.t: AI Engineering 101 with Chip Huyen (Nvidia, Stanford, Netflix) | Chip Huyen
eps.s: Chip Huyen, author of AI Engineering, explains in plain terms how pre-training, post-training, reinforcement learning, evals, and RAG actually work. Her core message: good AI products come from talking to users, preparing data, and writing better prompts, not from chasing news or swapping frameworks. She also covers why AI productivity gains are hard to measure in companies, which engineers benefit most, and what changes in the next few years.
g: Author of AI Engineering; former NVIDIA NeMo core developer and Netflix AI researcher; taught ML at Stanford

eps.t: Reinventing the Developer Terminal with Warp Co-Founder and CEO Zach Lloyd
eps.s: Warp CEO Zach Lloyd talks about AI as intelligence without consciousness, and how Warp pivoted from a terminal collaboration tool into an agentic development environment built around the terminal. He maps coding moving from hand-written code to prompting to automation, and discusses the value of senior engineering judgment, competing with the big labs, slowing model progress, and why automation beats productivity tools.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Warp, former engineering lead on Google Sheets

eps.t: From using your phone to a phone that knows you: OPPO's Yulong Wan on on-device AI | Agent #7
eps.ot: 138: 从你用手机到它更懂你，OPPO的手机AI实践 |与小布负责人万玉龙聊端侧AI｜Agent#7
eps.s: Yulong Wan, head of OPPO's Breeno assistant, explains how a phone maker does AI: splitting work between phone and cloud, personalization built on memory and context, why OPPO stopped pretraining its own models, and why Breeno's monthly users fell short. The second half covers how services reach users in the agent era, mobile protocols, a butler-plus-advisors endgame and the generational shift in voice interaction.
g: General manager of OPPO ColorOS's intelligent assistant division and head of the Breeno assistant

eps.t: How Block is becoming the most AI-native enterprise in the world | Dhanji R. Prasanna
eps.s: Block CTO Dhanji Prasanna explains how he moved the company from business-unit silos to a functional structure, rebuilt its identity as a technology company, and rolled out Goose, Block's open-source AI agent, so every employee can automate work. He shares real productivity numbers, who benefits most, a vision of agents working overnight, and career lessons: code quality doesn't decide product success, start small, and question basic assumptions.
g: CTO of Block; former head of engineering at Cash App; early work on Google Wave and Google+

eps.t: An open-sourced journey through AI papers: the full history of model approaches, infrastructure and data, language, and multimodality
eps.ot: 开源一段论文探索之旅：模型范式、Infra和数据、语言、多模态的完整变迁史
eps.s: Meituan product lead Qingchi Xie distills 200-plus papers read over a year into a guided tour: programmable GPUs, AlexNet, and Transformers, then ZeRO, scaling laws, 10,000-GPU training, GPT and InstructGPT, then GANs, diffusion, CLIP, and DiT. His running themes: architectures take off by fitting hardware, compute eventually beats hand design, post-training has huge leverage, and once product people see the limits, waiting can be a strategy.
g: Product lead at Guangnian Zhiwai, Meituan's AI unit

eps.t: A second 3-hour talk with Li Xiang: the CEO as an AI model, MoE, Liang Wenfeng, VLA, energy, memory, human nature, intimacy and wisdom
eps.ot: 对李想的第二次3小时访谈：CEO大模型、MoE、梁文锋、VLA、能量、记忆、对抗人性、亲密关系、人类的智慧
eps.s: The host quizzes Li Auto founder Li Xiang like a "CEO language model." He ranks AI tools by whether people will pay for them, walks through how Li Auto trains its self-driving model, and explains how a simulated "world model" cut testing costs to about 4,000 yuan per 10,000 km. Later he covers strategy, his 2030 goal of building AI devices, team "energy," memory, intimacy and human wisdom.
g: Founder, chairman and CEO of the carmaker Li Auto

eps.t: The Best of 2025 (So Far) with Sarah Guo and Elad Gil
eps.s: A best-of compilation of No Priors episodes from 2025 through October, so no separate arguments are listed.
