It features clips from Harvey's Winston Weinberg, Fei-Fei Li, Glean's Arvind Jain, OpenAI's Isa Fulford, Eric Mitchell and Brandon McKinzie, Mercor's Brendan Foody, Dan Hendrycks, Flagship Pioneering, and Abridge's Shiv Rao.

eps.t: ICCV best paper, Light Years Beyond and Sand.ai: Yue Cao's ten years in AI, from researcher to CEO
eps.ot: 139: ICCV最佳论文、光年之外、Sand.ai：曹越十年AI之旅，从研究者到CEO
eps.s: Sand.ai founder Yue Cao looks back on ten years in AI: co-creating Swin Transformer, BAAI, Wang Huiwen's Light Years Beyond, and now an AI video startup. He explains how he picks research problems, why paper-driven teams can't build OpenAI-style systems, what went right and wrong with his video model Magi-1, what makes Sora 2 impressive, and what AI short dramas and consumer video apps still lack.
g: Sand.ai founder and CEO, Swin Transformer co-author, helped start Wang Huiwen's Light Years Beyond

eps.t: #2404 - Elon Musk
eps.s: Across nearly three hours, Musk covers Starship test flights, fully reusable rockets, the Cybertruck and the coming Roadster, why he bought Twitter, X Chat encryption, the future of phones and AI bias, then spends much of the back half on California policy, immigration and free speech in Europe. A striking claim: nobody can control superintelligence, so it must be built to seek the truth.
g: CEO of Tesla and SpaceX; also runs X and xAI

eps.t: The woman behind Canva shares how she built a $42B company from nothing | Melanie Perkins
eps.s: Canva co-founder and CEO Melanie Perkins rarely does podcasts. Here she lays out how Canva operates: planning backward from an ideal future, moving ideas from chaos to clarity one step at a time, breaking the mission into pillars and crazy big goals, and the low points, including more than a hundred investor rejections and a rewrite that blocked releases for two years. She also covers community-driven product work, AI, and her two-step plan: become one of the most valuable companies, then do the most good.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Canva, the online design tool for non-designers

eps.t: Kimi Linear and MiniMax M2: Songlin Yang on the history of attention variants and where model architecture goes next
eps.ot: Kimi Linear、Minimax M2？和杨松琳考古算法变种史，并预演未来架构改进方案
eps.s: MIT PhD student Songlin Yang, a co-author of the Kimi Linear paper, traces the history of linear attention, a cheaper way for models to read long text. She explains why algorithms matter again now that data is running short, which tweaks finally made linear attention work, and what Kimi Linear changed. She also discusses why MiniMax M2 went back to full attention, and why hardware has the final say.
g: MIT PhD student and a co-author of the Kimi Linear paper

eps.t: Sam Altman on Trust, Persuasion, and the Future of Intelligence - Live at the Progress Conference (Ep. 259)
eps.s: Tyler Cowen quizzes Sam Altman live at the Progress Conference: how he manages, when an AI could be CEO, whether GPT-6 can do science, how to make money without breaking trust, where the electricity comes from, and privacy and free expression. Most striking: his biggest fear is not bad actors or AI takeover, but a model everyone uses quietly shifting what people believe.
g: OpenAI co-founder and CEO, overseeing ChatGPT plus its chip, energy and compute bets

eps.t: Meet Snowflake Intelligence: A Personalized Enterprise Intelligence Agent with Sridhar Ramaswamy
eps.s: Snowflake CEO Sridhar Ramaswamy explains how the company sped up by reorganizing, gave up on building its own foundation models to become an "AI data cloud," and launched Snowflake Intelligence, a tightly scoped enterprise data agent. He also covers defensibility, the surest enterprise AI payoffs, small cheap experiments, and ads, search and tool use in the chat era.
g: CEO of Snowflake, former head of Google's ads business, co-founder of Neeva

eps.t: The Minds of Modern AI: Jensen Huang, Geoffrey Hinton, Yann LeCun & the AI Vision of the Future
eps.ol: FT Future of AI Summit (Queen Elizabeth Prize laureates panel)
eps.s: At the FT Future of AI Summit, Queen Elizabeth Prize laureates LeCun, Hinton, Bengio, Jensen Huang, Fei-Fei Li and Bill Dally share a stage. LeCun recalls why he wanted machines to learn, how he found Hinton, and how self-supervised learning came back to the center. His sharpest point: AI spending is not a bubble, but believing bigger LLMs will reach human-level intelligence is.
g: Meta's chief AI scientist and NYU professor; a Queen Elizabeth Prize laureate

eps.t: "Sell the alpha, not the feature": The enterprise sales playbook for $1M to $10M ARR | Jen Abel
eps.s: Jen Abel returns to focus on enterprise sales for B2B companies between $1 million and $10 million in annual recurring revenue. Her advice runs against the grain: the mid-market doesn't exist, go after industry leaders first, sell opportunity rather than pain, anchor the first deal around $100,000, and lead with services before the product. She also covers design partners, hiring and paying the first salespeople, and why she still does outreach by hand.
g: Co-founder of sales consultancy JJELLYFISH and general manager of enterprise at State Affairs

eps.t: DP Technology's Linfeng Zhang and Weijie Sun: AI for Science, from the beginning to now
eps.ot: 140: 深势科技张林峰、孙伟杰：AI for Science，从开始到现在
eps.s: DP Technology co-founders Linfeng Zhang and Weijie Sun start with Deep Potential, their Princeton-era work using AI to speed up physics simulations that once needed supercomputers. They explain why they started with drug discovery, why they built a platform instead of their own drug pipeline, how research agents will change the way science reads, computes and experiments, and their long view of open science and AI for Science.
g: Co-founder and chief scientist of DP Technology; Princeton PhD under mathematician Weinan E
Co-founder and CEO of DP Technology; Linfeng Zhang's classmate at Peking University

eps.t: "Dumbest idea I've heard" to $100M ARR: Inside the rise of Gamma | Grant Lee (co-founder)
eps.s: Grant Lee, co-founder and CEO of the AI presentation tool Gamma, looks back on how a company investors called the dumbest idea they'd heard reached $100 million in ARR with about 30 people and years of profitability. He covers reading product-market fit through word of mouth, making the first 30 seconds magical, founder-led marketing and micro-influencers, building brand before paid ads, cheap prototype testing, building a durable "GPT wrapper," and a team of generalists led by player-coaches.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Gamma, an AI tool for making presentations

eps.t: How AI Will Accelerate Breakthroughs in Biotechnology with Benchling CEO Sajith Wickramasekara
eps.s: Benchling CEO Sajith Wickramasekara explains biotech's dot-com-style slump and China's rise on speed and cost, arguing that drug discovery hinges on better molecules and faster feedback. He describes how Benchling builds predictive models and deep research agents into scientists' workflows, and discusses where bio-model companies can go, how to measure AI progress, and a founder's decision to go all in on AI personally.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Benchling, a software platform for biotech research

eps.t: Fireside Chat with Elon Musk – 32nd Annual Baron Investment Conference
eps.s: An investor-facing fireside chat with fund manager Ron Baron. Musk covers how many Optimus robots there could be and what they'll cost, wiring Neuralink to robot legs, why he started OpenAI, Grok 5, solar-powered AI satellites, Tesla's AI5 chip and self-driving safety numbers. The boldest line: he puts the chance that Grok 5 reaches AGI at about 10%.
g: CEO of Tesla and SpaceX; founder of xAI and Neuralink

eps.t: The Godmother of AI on jobs, robots & why world models are next | Dr. Fei-Fei Li
eps.s: Fei-Fei Li, often called the godmother of AI, walks through the field's history from the Dartmouth workshop to ImageNet, AlexNet, and ChatGPT, and explains why big data, neural networks, and GPUs remain the core recipe. She sees AGI as mostly a marketing term and says AI still needs major breakthroughs. She focuses on spatial intelligence and world models, World Labs' new product Marble, and why scale alone won't solve robotics, then closes with how she makes career choices.
g: Co-founder and CEO of World Labs, co-director of Stanford HAI, creator of ImageNet

eps.t: Google's Gemini 3 Is Here: A Special Early Look
eps.s: On Gemini 3 launch day, Demis Hassabis and Gemini lead Josh Woodward joined the New York Times tech podcast Hard Fork. He likens Gemini 3 to a drag racer, says it leaves his 5-to-10-year AGI estimate unchanged, and covers competition, cost and whether scaling has stalled. The standout: on the AI bubble, he says some corners are overheated, but Google wins either way.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Google DeepMind, the lab that builds Gemini

eps.t: First interview with XPeng's new autonomous-driving chief Xianming Liu: language as poison, dropping the L, simplicity, a leadership change and XPeng's AI shift
eps.ot: 小鹏新上任的刘先明首次访谈：Language是毒药、拆掉L、简单即美、换帅、小鹏的AI转型
eps.s: Xianming Liu, who took over XPeng's self-driving unit in October 2025, gives his first interview. He traces his path from Facebook and Cruise to XPeng, explains why he stripped language out of the driving model, and describes a new approach: learn how the world works, then output actions directly. He also covers next year's driverless push in Guangzhou, why carmakers must build self-driving themselves, and his flat management style.
g: Head of XPeng's autonomous driving center

eps.t: Sunday Robotics: Scaling the Home Robot Revolution with Co-Founders Tony Zhao and Cheng Chi
eps.s: Sunday Robotics co-founders Tony Zhao and Cheng Chi trace their path in robot learning from Diffusion Policy and ALOHA to UMI, and explain how data-collection gloves gathered about 10 million trajectories from 500-plus people in real homes to train a home robot. They also cover imitation versus reinforcement learning, cheap compliant hardware, zero-shot demos, the commercial timeline and how to judge robot demos.
g: Sunday Robotics co-founder, creator of the ALOHA and ACT robot-learning methods
Sunday Robotics co-founder, creator of UMI and Diffusion Policy

eps.t: Mental models for building products people love ft. Stewart Butterfield
eps.s: Stewart Butterfield, founder of Flickr and Slack, makes a rare podcast appearance to share his mental models for building products and teams: the utility curve, learnable taste and "tilt your umbrella," why understanding beats friction, never being satisfied with the product, and how organizations grow "hyper-realistic work-like activities." He also revisits the "We Don't Sell Saddles Here" memo, how he decided on two pivots, and why long-term success comes down to the value you create for customers.
g: Co-founder of Slack and Flickr, former CEO of Slack

eps.t: How to be ‘fearless’ in the AI age
eps.s: Live onstage with Reid Hoffman, Fei-Fei Li argues that language is only one keyhole to intelligence and that AI's next phase is world models that grasp 3D space. She draws on the Cambrian Explosion and the discovery of DNA's double helix, explains why self-driving cars and robots move slower than the hype, insists trust must stay human, and makes the case for fearlessness.
g: Stanford professor behind ImageNet; co-founder and CEO of World Labs

eps.t: A guide to difficult conversations, building high-trust teams, and designing a life you love
eps.s: Executive coach Rachel Lockett, who used to run HR at Pinterest and Stripe, talks about the human side of leadership: when to coach and when to just give advice, how to hear what people are not saying, and how to build your work around your strengths so you don't burn out. She coaches Lenny live, and covers co-founder relationships, hard conversations, and how to judge whether someone still fits.
g: Executive coach; formerly head of HR at Pinterest and Stripe

eps.t: Strutt's Xiaoping Hong: DJI's former lidar chief built an "electric wheelchair"? You can reach embodied AI without humanoids
eps.ot: 141: Strutt 洪小平：大疆激光雷达前负责人做了台“电动轮椅”？不做人形也能通向具身
eps.s: Xiaoping Hong, former head of DJI's Livox lidar unit and founder of Strutt, explains why going straight to humanoid robots won't work yet. Instead he started with aging and people's "last mile" of getting around, building EV One, a smart mobility device he won't call a wheelchair. He covers its driver assistance, four-wheel-drive base, expansion ports, production tradeoffs, pricing, crossing the chasm, and the limits of being first.
g: Founder of Strutt; former head of DJI's Livox lidar business

eps.t: Zebra CPO Jiaming Xiu: how an AI product that actively teaches came to be
eps.ot: 142: 斑马CPO修佳明：一款能主动教学的 AI 产品是如何出现的
eps.s: Zebra's chief product officer Jiaming Xiu breaks down Zebra Speaking, an AI English tutor for kids. He explains why they started with the narrow problem of children's spoken English, how each lesson is split into small checkable goals with layers of guardrails to keep the AI on track, and how they handle long-term memory, step-by-step scaffolding, the tutor's personality, measuring results, pricing and defensibility.
g: Chief product officer of Zebra, Yuanfudao's kids' education brand; leads AI tutor Zebra Speaking

eps.t: After LLMs: Spatial Intelligence and World Models — Fei-Fei Li & Justin Johnson, World Labs
eps.s: Fei-Fei Li and her former PhD student Justin Johnson, co-founders of World Labs, discuss Marble, their newly public 3D world model. She explains why a 3D world differs from a stream of text, why deep learning still just fits patterns, why robots lack data, and how spatial intelligence complements language. She also recalls racing Google on image captioning and warns that academia is badly under-resourced.
g: Co-founder and CEO of World Labs; Stanford professor behind ImageNet

eps.t: Jie Tan of DeepMind on robots, cross-embodiment transfer, world models, Gemini Robotics 1.5 and Google
eps.ot: 对DeepMind谭捷的访谈：机器人、跨本体、世界模型、Gemini Robotics 1.5和Google
eps.s: Jie Tan of Google DeepMind's robotics team reviews two big shifts in robotics over a decade, calls data the biggest bottleneck, and puts robotics' "GPT moment" two to three years out. He explains how Gemini Robotics 1.5 thinks while acting and shares skills across robot bodies, and why he bets on scalable data like simulation and generated video. He also covers touch, humanoids, his team, and China versus the US.
g: Senior research scientist on Google DeepMind's robotics team

eps.t: What world-class GTM looks like in 2026 | Jeanne DeWitt Grosser (Vercel, Stripe, Google)
eps.s: Jeanne DeWitt Grosser is COO of Vercel and built Stripe's first sales team from scratch. She describes what world-class go-to-market looks like in 2026: GTM should cover every function that touches a customer, GTM engineers can use AI agents to make one person do the work of ten, and the buying experience itself should be designed like a product. She also shares hard-won rules on why customers really buy, how to segment them, product-savvy sales, the limits of product-led growth, and pricing.
g: COO of Vercel; built Stripe's early sales team from scratch; started her career at Google

eps.t: People by WTF Ep. 16: Elon Musk
eps.s: Nikhil Kamath's long, philosophical conversation with Musk runs from X and Starlink to the future of money. Musk predicts work becomes optional within 20 years, money may fade while energy becomes the real currency, and AI-driven output could flip the US from inflation to deflation. He also covers the odds we live in a simulation, falling birth rates, H-1B visas and advice for Indian founders.
g: CEO of Tesla and SpaceX; founder of xAI; owner of X

eps.t: What is DeltaNet, the method Alibaba and Kimi use? Songlin Yang on cheaper ways to read long text
eps.ot: 143: 阿里、Kimi都在用的DeltaNet是什么？|与杨松琳聊线性注意力新改进
eps.s: Songlin Yang, an MIT PhD student who started the open-source linear attention group FLA, explains DeltaNet, a cheaper way for models to read long text, and the algorithm that lets it train in parallel. She traces its path from Gated DeltaNet to Kimi's KDA, explains why Qwen and Kimi went hybrid while MiniMax returned to full attention, and compares sparse and linear attention, evaluation and next steps.
g: MIT PhD student; author of DeltaNet's parallel training algorithm; founder of open-source group FLA

eps.t: #2422 - Jensen Huang
eps.s: Jensen Huang talks with Joe Rogan about Trump-era energy and manufacturing policy, AI safety, whether AI is conscious, and whether it will take jobs. The second half is Nvidia's near-death origin story: the wrong technology, a candid plea to Sega, and three textbooks. The most striking line: for 33 years he has felt Nvidia is 30 days from going out of business.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Nvidia, who calls himself the longest-serving tech CEO

eps.t: The end of product managers? Why LinkedIn is turning PMs into AI-powered "full stack builders"
eps.s: Tomer Cohen, LinkedIn's chief product officer for 14 years, explains the "full stack builder" model he piloted there: people from any function use AI to take an idea all the way from concept to launch. He argues big-company product processes have grown too bloated to fix incrementally, lays out which skills humans should keep and what to automate, and describes the three pillars of platform, in-house agents, and culture, plus lessons on performance reviews and change management.
g: Chief product officer at LinkedIn for 14 years, about to step down when recorded

eps.t: Nvidia CEO Fireside Chat (securing U.S. leadership in AI)
eps.s: At the CSIS think tank in Washington, Jensen Huang breaks AI into a "five-layer cake" and compares the US and China layer by layer: America leads in chips by generations, while China is stronger in energy and open-source models. He argues against giving up the Chinese market and urges fixing the power shortage and bringing manufacturing home. Asked if he's optimistic, he says "1,000%."
g: Nvidia co-founder and CEO, in Washington to explain AI to policymakers

eps.t: Scaling Legal AI and Building Next-Generation Law Firms with Harvey Co-Founder and President Gabe Pereyra
eps.s: Harvey co-founder and president Gabe Pereyra explains how legal AI is moving from making individual lawyers faster to running whole firms' matters and profits, and expanding into corporate legal teams like Walmart's. He sees client matters as a natural environment for agents, and discusses the reward-function problem in law, the lawyer pyramid and training talent, forward-deployed engineering, and why Harvey bets on organizational productivity instead of its own firm.
g: Co-founder and president of Harvey, former researcher at DeepMind and Meta

eps.t: The $1B Al company training ChatGPT, Claude & Gemini on the path to responsible AGI | Edwin Chen
eps.s: Edwin Chen founded Surge AI, which supplies training data to the major AI labs. He explains how the company reached $1 billion in revenue with fewer than 100 people and no outside funding, and what "high-quality data" really means. He argues benchmarks, the LLM Arena leaderboard, and engagement optimization are pushing models toward AI slop, traces how post-training has evolved, and predicts models will diverge as their makers' values differ.
g: Founder and CEO of Surge AI; former researcher at Google, Facebook, and Twitter

eps.t: Dr. Fei-Fei Li, The Godmother of AI — Asking Audacious Questions, Civilizational Technology, and Finding Your North Star (#839)
eps.s: Tim Ferriss and Fei-Fei Li go from her childhood in Chengdu and New Jersey, with parents who ignored grades and a teacher who taught her calculus over lunch, to how ImageNet made big data one of modern AI's three ingredients. She explains why AI is a civilizational technology that must keep people at the center, what World Labs builds, and how work and education will change.
g: Stanford professor who created ImageNet; co-founder and CEO of World Labs

eps.t: Xiaohu Zhu's realism, part three: the AI feast and its bubbles
eps.ot: 朱啸虎现实主义故事的第三次连载：人工智能的盛筵与泡泡
eps.s: In late 2025, Xiaohu Zhu of GSR Ventures sizes up the AI market. He sees no bubble for at least three years, says consumer AI is now a fight over daily use and time spent, and argues the technology has plateaued but is good enough for apps. He also covers DeepSeek's historic role, why model companies struggle to make money, and how startups can sidestep consensus and big tech.
g: Managing partner at the venture capital firm GSR Ventures

eps.t: Doge, AI, Mars, and the Future of Humanity (Ep. 18)
eps.s: On Katie Miller's podcast, Musk looks back on DOGE: requiring a code and explanation for every federal payment stopped many "zombie payments," yet he probably wouldn't do it again. He also covers immigration, AI making work optional, why Starship matters, rebuilding X's feed with Grok, and his six-hour sleep. His running theory: the most interesting outcome is the most likely.
g: CEO of Tesla and SpaceX; founder of xAI; former head of DOGE

eps.t: The Future of Voice AI: Agents, Dubbing, and Real-Time Translation with ElevenLabs Co-Founder Mati Staniszewski
eps.s: ElevenLabs co-founder and CEO Mati Staniszewski starts with Poland's terrible movie dubbing, then explains the company's research-first structure of small labs, why choosing and evaluating voices is hard, and how voice agents serve customer support, interactive IP, education and Ukraine's government. He admits models will eventually commoditize: research buys a head start, while lasting advantage comes from product and distribution.
g: Co-founder and CEO of ElevenLabs, the AI voice company

eps.t: From "big and strong" to "small and strong": Zhiyuan Liu and Chaojun Xiao on the density law, RL scaling and distributed intelligence
eps.ot: 144: “大而强”到“小而强”|与刘知远、肖朝军聊密度法则、RL 的 Scaling Law 和智能的分布式未来
eps.s: ModelBest's Zhiyuan Liu and Chaojun Xiao explain their "capability density" law: why they reject compute-only thinking, how density doubles every few months, and which levers raise it. They also discuss sparse attention and long outputs, data curation, why reinforcement learning still lacks its own scaling law, putting models in cars and devices, and what distributed intelligence and AGI might look like.
g: Associate professor of computer science at Tsinghua University; chief scientist at ModelBest
Tsinghua University postdoc; leads MiniCPM text models at ModelBest

eps.t: A 3-hour talk with ONE2X founder Guan Wang: generative systems, cutting out the middleman, and who holds power on content platforms
eps.ot: 对ONE2X创始人王冠3小时访谈：生成系统、没有中间商赚差价、内容平台的权力分配
eps.s: ONE2X founder Guan Wang recounts three startup ideas that OpenAI's next models wiped out, and argues that data sets the limits of intelligence, so an app company's opening is data its own product creates. He explains why ONE2X designed a language for video and started with a production tool, and how generative systems could cut out platform middlemen, shifting power to viewers and turning creators' currency from attention into trust.
g: Co-founder and CEO of ONE2X; formerly led model products at Kimi

eps.t: Inside OpenAI: 2026 is the year of agents, AI's biggest bottleneck, and why compute isn't the issue
eps.s: Alexander Embiricos leads product for Codex, OpenAI's coding agent. He describes how OpenAI works bottom-up and by experiment, how Codex grew 20x by lowering the barrier to entry and iterating the model and harness together, and why he thinks any agent should know how to code. Examples like shipping Sora for Android in 28 days show the speedup, and he argues the real bottleneck is now how fast humans can prompt and review.
g: Product lead for OpenAI Codex; former Dropbox PM and founder of a pair-programming startup

eps.t: Yusen's venture notes, episode 1: expectations for 2026, the Year of R, a pullback, and how we bet
eps.ot: 雨森的创投观察第1集：2026年预期、The Year of R、回调、我们如何下注
eps.s: ZhenFund managing partner Yusen Dai reviews 2025: AI mostly went as expected, while Chinese open source and a venture rebound were the surprises. He calls 2026 the Year of R, for returns, research, and memory, expects a US stock pullback perhaps in the second half, and says growth at negative margins is over. He shares ZhenFund's barbell strategy, how he judges founders, and how to thrive when intelligence is abundant.
g: Managing partner at ZhenFund, an early-stage venture firm

eps.t: EP20: Yann LeCun
eps.s: LeCun's first long interview after deciding to leave Meta, read here through a QbitAI summary reprinted by 36Kr Europe. He calls the plan to reach superintelligence by scaling LLMs nonsense, criticizes Meta's turn toward secrecy, and says his new company AMI will stay open and focus on world models. His most striking math: a four-year-old's visual input matches an LLM's entire text diet.
g: Outgoing Meta chief AI scientist, launching AMI, a new world-model company

eps.t: Hypershell's Kuan Sun: the birth of the first consumer exoskeleton
eps.ot: 145: 极壳孙宽：首个「消费级外骨骼」的诞生
eps.s: Hypershell founder Kuan Sun tells how a consumer exoskeleton went from a desk prototype to worldwide shipping. He explains why he wants to augment people rather than replace them, why he started with hardcore hikers, why he switched from one motor to two, and how he thinks about safety and reliability, pricing and cost cuts, scaling the team, and competition in a new category.
g: Founder of Hypershell, pioneer of consumer exoskeletons

eps.t: Freda's investing notes, episode 1: betting on OpenAI, the Robinhood story, America's bad-boy capital, the math, and the bubble
eps.ot: Freda的投资札记第1集：下注OpenAI、Robinhood往事，美国资本坏小孩、算盘与泡沫
eps.s: Silicon Valley investor Freda Duan, who works across private and public markets, runs the cash-flow math on model companies. She covers OpenAI's underrated enterprise business, the two-way threat between OpenAI and Google, and how Robinhood beat a deeply cyclical business. She uses VC return math to argue for concentrated bets, and two ledgers, digital revenue and the labor market, to judge the AI bubble and 2026.
g: Partner at Altimeter Capital, investing in both private and public markets

eps.t: The new AI growth playbook for 2026 | How Lovable hit $200M ARR in one year
eps.s: Elena Verna, head of growth at Lovable, returns to explain how Lovable passed $200 million in annual recurring revenue within a year of launch and why the growth playbook must be rewritten for AI: spend most energy on innovation rather than optimization, ship constantly and talk about it on social, build a "minimum lovable product," and give the product away. She also covers re-earning product-market fit every three months, who thrives at AI companies, and women falling behind in AI adoption.
g: Head of growth at Lovable; previously led growth at Miro, Dropbox, SurveyMonkey, and Amplitude

eps.t: The 2026 AI Forecast: Foundation Models, IPOs, and Robotics with Sarah Guo and Elad Gil
eps.s: In their year-end special, Sarah Guo and Elad Gil make calls for 2026: the AI backlash and how fast adoption is moving, robotics' hype cycle, AI company IPOs, consumer agents, the "age of research" and new labs, defense and GLP-1s. The episode closes with short predictions from guests including Aaron Levie and Andrej Karpathy, on proactive agents, enterprise agent adoption and energy-efficient AI.
g: No Priors co-host and founder of the venture firm Conviction
No Priors co-host, entrepreneur and investor

eps.t: Why securing AI is harder than anyone expected and guardrails are failing | HackAPrompt CEO
eps.s: Sander Schulhoff, CEO of HackAPrompt, says bluntly that AI guardrails don't work: the space of prompt injections and jailbreaks is practically infinite, frontier labs haven't solved it in years, and the "red-team audit plus guardrails" business is selling false security. As agents, AI browsers, and robots gain real permissions, the risk climbs fast. His answer: defend by capability tier, lock down permissions, adopt architectures like CAMEL, and hire people who know both AI and traditional security.
g: CEO of HackAPrompt, founder of Learn Prompting; researcher in AI red teaming and adversarial robustness

eps.t: HongShan's Qingsheng Zheng on how flows of attention shaped economic history, why new habits are unpredictable, and founder character
eps.ot: 和红杉郑庆生聊：经济史的流量革命、人类行为模式的不可预期，与创始人性格
eps.s: HongShan partner Qingsheng Zheng traces economic history through flows of people and attention, from roads and canals to TV and phones. Looking back at Douban, Dianping, Xiaohongshu and short video, he argues new human habits are basically unpredictable. He also explains how AI differs from the old internet, why always-on wearable devices matter, and why a big company's CEO must become the organization in human form.
g: Partner at HongShan (formerly Sequoia China), investing in internet and AI companies

eps.t: Year-end AI model report: Guangmi Li on an AI war, two rival camps, and the next big shift, online learning
eps.ot: 大模型季报跨年对谈：和广密预言一场AI War、两大联盟和第三个范式Online Learning
eps.s: The year-end edition of the Global AI Model Quarterly. Guangmi Li argues AI isn't a bubble but a war no tech giant can afford to lose, sizes up OpenAI's visible and hidden revenue, and maps the rivalry between Google's TPU camp and Nvidia's GPU camp. His big call: the next leap after pre-training and reinforcement learning is online learning, models that keep learning from use. He also weighs China's chances.
g: Founder and CEO of Shixiang, an investor who tracks global AI model companies

eps.t: Gemini 3's comeback, what models agents need, and RL startup openings: ex-Google founders and Valley investors on the Bay Area
eps.ot: 146: Gemini 3翻盘背后、Agent需要什么大模型、RL创业机会|与前 Google 创业者、硅谷投资人聊湾区动向
eps.s: Hanjun Dai and Bethany Wang, co-founders of agent-tools startup Precur, join Henry Yin and Naomi Xia of MoE Capital to review the Bay Area AI scene. They discuss why Gemini 3 pulled off a comeback, how to read GPT-5.2 and the GDPval benchmark, where models end and agents begin, how companies choose models, and startup openings in reinforcement learning.
g: Precur co-founder and former reinforcement learning researcher at Google DeepMind
Precur co-founder; previously led enterprise Gemini customization on Google Cloud's Vertex AI
Founding partner at MoE Capital, an early-stage AI investor in Silicon Valley
Founding partner at MoE Capital, an early-stage AI investor in Silicon Valley

eps.t: 10 contrarian leadership truths every leader needs to hear | Matt MacInnis (Rippling)
eps.s: Matt MacInnis, chief product officer and longtime former COO at Rippling, shares a set of contrarian leadership beliefs: extraordinary results demand extraordinary effort, projects should be deliberately understaffed, you learn more from success than failure, and founders should know when to let go. He also describes rebuilding product quality from the foundations after taking over product, using an alpha/beta lens to decide on process and people, why leaders must keep pushing against entropy, and why point-solution SaaS is in trouble in the AI era.
g: Chief product officer and longtime former COO at Rippling; founded Inkling; spent seven years at Apple

eps.t: The last interview before Manus decided to sell: what a wild ride 2025 was
eps.ot: Manus决定出售前最后的访谈：啊，这奇幻的2025年漂流啊…
eps.s: Manus's last interview before Meta announced it would buy the company. Co-founder and chief scientist Peak Ji goes from building a paid browser in high school to watching GPT-3 match his own models overnight. He explains why Manus stays at the app layer and bets on general-purpose agents, the tradeoffs on sandboxes, model fit, token costs and user metrics, and what agents should do next.
g: Co-founder and chief scientist of Manus, a serial founder who began building apps in high school

eps.t: We replaced our sales team with 20 AI agents—here's what happened next | Jason Lemkin (SaaStr)
eps.s: SaaStr founder Jason Lemkin describes an experiment: after two salespeople quit on the spot, he replaced his sales team with about 20 AI agents and roughly 1.2 humans. He explains how he picked vendors, trained the agents, and who keeps watch over them. He also ranks which sales roles get replaced first, and why people who can run agents become more in demand, and more tired.
g: Founder of SaaStr and SaaS angel investor; his earlier startup was acquired by Adobe

eps.t: "I like being scared": Molly Graham's frameworks for rapid career growth | Molly Graham
eps.s: Molly Graham lived through the hypergrowth years at Google and Facebook, helped start Quip and the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, and now runs Glue Club, a community for leaders. She turns those years into memorable rules: give away the work you're good at, jump off the cliff into a "J curve," blame structure before people, and keep company goals to three. The most interesting part: what to do once you've proven yourself.
g: Founder of Glue Club; early Google and Facebook employee who helped start Quip and CZI

eps.t: Moonshots EP #220: Elon Musk on AGI, Abundance, and the Future of Humanity
eps.s: A three-hour talk with Peter Diamandis and Dave Blundin. Musk calls AI and robotics a supersonic tsunami, argues energy is the real currency, sketches 100 gigawatts a year of AI satellites in orbit, and covers college, aging, white-collar jobs and falling prices. He predicts AGI in 2026 and names three values for safe AI: truth, curiosity and beauty.
g: CEO of Tesla and SpaceX; founder of xAI

eps.t: OiiOii's Naonao: 'Douyin first, then CapCut' no longer works. Building creator tools and communities in the AI era
eps.ot: 147: OiiOii闹闹：“先抖音后剪映” 不再成立，AI 时代怎么做创作工具和内容社区
eps.s: Naonao, founder of the animation agent OiiOii, explains why in the AI era you build tools and stock content before launching a community, and why animation has been held back by how hard it is to make. She covers starting with semi-pro teams, a visible workflow, combining many models, and saying no to AI comic dramas and heavy enterprise work, plus her path through ByteDance and Bilibili.
g: OiiOii founder; worked on CapCut and Douyin effects, then anime community Lipu at StepFun

eps.t: NVIDIA's Jensen Huang on Reasoning Models, Robotics, and Refuting the "AI Bubble" Narrative
eps.s: Jensen Huang reviews what reasoning models changed in 2025, explains "AI factories" and the five-layer AI stack, and argues open source is essential. He criticizes doomer and "god AI" narratives, and covers falling costs, verticalization, self-driving and robotics, energy and China, before rebutting the "AI bubble" story from the perspective of accelerated computing.
g: Founder and CEO of Nvidia

eps.t: Zhipu CEO Peng Zhang on becoming the first AI model company to go public: where does the road lead?
eps.ot: 全球大模型第一股的上市访谈，和智谱CEO张鹏聊：敢问路在何方？
eps.s: Released the day Zhipu listed in Hong Kong. CEO Peng Zhang traces its path from a Tsinghua lab, the catch-up after ChatGPT, shifting ways to scale models, DeepSeek's open-source shock, and selling to businesses. The second half is about being CEO: why outsiders find Zhipu hard to grasp and unflashy, growing pains, academic habits, and an all-in long bet on AGI.
g: CEO of Zhipu AI, the Tsinghua-born AI model company now listed in Hong Kong

eps.t: Why most AI products fail: Lessons from 50+ AI deployments at OpenAI, Google & Amazon
eps.s: Two guests who have shipped more than 50 AI products explain why so many fail: AI output is unpredictable, and the more decisions you hand to it, the less control you keep, so the old playbook breaks. Start with high control and low autonomy, then calibrate and loosen the reins in cycles. They also cover leadership and culture, evals versus production monitoring, multi-agent myths, proactive agents, and why pain is the new moat.
g: Former AI researcher at Alexa and Microsoft, now an enterprise AI consultant, founder, and Maven instructor
Member of OpenAI's Codex team; previously built AI and machine-learning infrastructure at Google and Kumo

eps.t: AI and the Future of Warfare with US Under Secretary of War Emil Michael
eps.s: Emil Michael, the US Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering, explains how he cut critical technology areas from 14 to 6, rolled out GenAI.mil to millions of personnel, how uncrewed systems will change warfare, and how the Defense Innovation Unit and the Office of Strategic Capital are opening a front door for new entrants and rebuilding the defense supply chain.
g: US Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering, former Uber chief business officer

eps.t: Yilun Chen of TARS: three signs of dawn for embodied AI, and the first barrier it must clear
eps.ot: 148: 它石智航陈亦伦：具身的三道曙光和第一道关卡
eps.s: Yilun Chen, founder of TARS, draws on his self-driving work to describe three breakthroughs in embodied AI, meaning robots that act in the physical world, and three barriers ahead. He argues the field is still stuck on the first one: data. He explains why internet video and simulation fall short, why TARS records human skills with gloves and first-person cameras, and his views on models, routes, timelines and use cases.
g: TARS founder and CEO; ex-chief scientist of Huawei self-driving, ex-chief vision engineer at DJI

eps.t: How a Meta PM ships products without ever writing code | Zevi Arnovitz
eps.s: Zevi Arnovitz is a Meta product manager with no technical background. On the show he demonstrates how he used Cursor and Claude to build StudyMate, a study app with paying users, entirely on his own. He walks through his path from chatbots to Cursor, a workflow built on reusable slash commands, having several models review each other's code, running post-mortems when AI slips up, and what AI means for the PM role, interview prep and junior jobs.
g: Product manager at Meta, formerly at Wix; no technical background; builds the study app StudyMate on the side

eps.t: Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis: AI's Next Breakthroughs, AGI Timeline, Google's AI Glasses Bet
eps.s: In early 2026 Demis Hassabis talks with Alex Kantrowitz about whether AI progress has slowed, what AGI still lacks, why Google is betting on AI glasses, and whether Gemini will carry ads. He holds AGI to a high bar, every human cognitive ability, and puts it 5 to 10 years out. The most striking idea: AlphaFold worked because so few protein shapes are actually stable.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Google DeepMind, the lab behind Gemini and AlphaFold

eps.t: Davos 2026: Conversation with Jensen Huang, President and CEO of NVIDIA
eps.s: At Davos 2026, BlackRock CEO Larry Fink talks with Jensen Huang. Huang describes AI as a five-layer cake, from energy up to applications, and says building every layer is the largest infrastructure project in history. He also explains why AI may add jobs rather than cut them, Europe's opening in physical AI, and a simple bubble test: are the chips actually being rented?
g: Founder and CEO of NVIDIA, which makes the chips and systems that run AI

eps.t: Yann LeCun on artificial general intelligence and the digital commons (Imagination in Action, Davos 2026)
eps.ol: Imagination in Action at Davos / Forbes
eps.s: At Davos 2026, LeCun spoke with John Werner on the Imagination in Action stage; this card draws on Werner's Forbes write-up. LeCun says "AGI" is the wrong name and human-level AI still needs conceptual breakthroughs. Agents built on LLMs are "a disaster"; the answer is world models that predict consequences. The biggest risk, he says, is a few closed companies controlling our digital lives.
g: Former Meta chief AI scientist, founder of AMI, champion of world models

eps.t: No Priors Live: Building Durable Software in the AI Age with MongoDB President & CEO CJ Desai
eps.s: In No Priors' first live taping, MongoDB President and CEO CJ Desai talks with Sarah Guo about how software companies can last in the AI era. He explains why a product gets you in the door but only a platform keeps you there, why vibe-coded apps still hit enterprise hurdles, why the data layer is a must-have, and how far big companies have really gotten with AI.
g: President and CEO of MongoDB, the database software company

eps.t: Conversation with Elon Musk (World Economic Forum Annual Meeting 2026)
eps.s: A half-hour Davos conversation with BlackRock's Larry Fink. Musk explains how robots could bring abundance for everyone, why electricity rather than chips limits AI, how 100 by 100 miles of solar could power the US, and his timelines for Optimus, robotaxis and Starship. He closes by urging optimism: better to be optimistic and wrong than pessimistic and right.
g: CEO of Tesla and SpaceX; founder of xAI

eps.t: Yann LeCun's new venture is a contrarian bet against large language models
eps.s: In an exclusive Q&A with MIT Technology Review, LeCun explains AMI, the company he started after Meta: why it is based in Paris, why it bets on open source, and where he parted ways with Meta. He argues scaling LLMs won't reach human-level AI, that useful robots and agents need world models, and that university researchers should stop working on LLMs.
g: Executive chairman of AMI, NYU professor, former Meta chief AI scientist

eps.t: Two years in, Yueguang Zhang's first interview: Miaoya wasn't AI-native, context over workflows, one-way doors and otome games
eps.ot: 张月光创业两年首次访谈：妙鸭不是AI Native产品、流程到上下文设计、One Way Door和乙女游戏
eps.s: Two years after leaving Alibaba to found Muyan Zhiyu, Miaoya creator Yueguang Zhang gives his first long interview. He revisits his career choices and reasons for starting up, explains why Miaoya wasn't truly AI-native, and argues for one-way-door products and designing around context instead of workflows. Later he explains how the otome game Xingmian uses game design to fix AI companionship, and why the company went all in on Dokie.
g: Founder of Muyan Zhiyu; creator of Miaoya Camera, Alibaba's viral AI portrait app

eps.t: The surprising advice from a founder who built 2 unicorns | Jason Cohen (WP Engine)
eps.s: Jason Cohen has built two unicorns. He lays out a sequence of questions to ask when a product stops growing: start with customer churn, then pricing and positioning, then whether existing customers spend more, then whether acquisition channels are saturated, and finally whether you really need to grow at all. With plenty of company examples and simple arithmetic, he explains why each step sits where it does.
g: Founder of WP Engine and Smart Bear, two of his four companies and both unicorns; angel investor and longtime startup writer

eps.t: Whose robot model is best? Haoqiang Fan and Yang Gao on testing robot AI, RoboChallenge and the 2026 outlook
eps.ot: 149: 具身模型哪家强？|与范浩强、高阳聊具身模型的测评、RoboChallenge，26 年具身展望
eps.s: Haoqiang Fan, co-founder of Dexmal, and Yang Gao, co-founder of Spirit AI, discuss how to test AI models for robots. They cover why large-scale testing on real robots like RoboChallenge matters, how the Table 30 task set was designed, what the leaderboard shows, debates over data, models that can't remember, how to read demos, and where robot models are headed in 2026.
g: Dexmal co-founder and main driver of RoboChallenge; earlier commercialized computer vision at Megvii
Spirit AI co-founder; assistant professor at Tsinghua's Institute for Interdisciplinary Information Sciences

eps.t: Yin Qi on becoming StepFun chairman: clever people's temptations, tradeoffs, a brutal elimination race, step functions and multivariable equations
eps.ot: 印奇出任阶跃星辰董事长的访谈：聪明人的诱惑、取舍、超长链路残酷淘汰赛、阶跃函数和超多元方程
eps.s: Yin Qi talks after becoming chairman of StepFun. He explains how he went from misjudging ChatGPT to concluding there is only one brain, and argues by elimination that foundation model companies must build AI devices. He lays out Qianli Technology's late-mover plan in driver assistance, reflects on Megvii fighting on too many fronts, its security-camera misstep and the trap of clever people, and runs the endgame numbers.
g: Chairman of StepFun and Qianli Technology; founder of computer-vision company Megvii

eps.t: Marc Andreessen: The real AI boom hasn't even started yet
eps.s: a16z co-founder Marc Andreessen starts from the macro picture: productivity growth has been sluggish for half a century and populations are starting to shrink, so AI is arriving just as labor becomes scarce, and the "AI causes mass unemployment" story doesn't hold. He also covers AI in education, how the PM, designer and engineer roles are colliding, how to build a personal skill set, and why it's too early to call the winners.
g: Co-founder and general partner at Andreessen Horowitz (a16z); co-founder of Netscape

eps.t: Why Cryopreservation is No Longer Science Fiction with Until Co-founder and CEO Laura Deming
eps.s: Laura Deming, co-founder and CEO of Until, explains why she moved from longevity research to reversible cryopreservation: pausing biological time as a new form of critical care. The near-term goal is reversibly freezing single human organs to improve transplants, and the long-term goal is whole-body medical hibernation. She also walks through the hard science of avoiding ice and scaling up.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Until, and founder of the Longevity Fund

eps.t: A child psychologist's guide to working with difficult adults | Dr. Becky Kennedy
eps.s: Clinical psychologist and Good Inside founder Becky Kennedy brings her parenting principles to the workplace. Families and companies are both systems, she argues, and adults and kids need the same things. She covers repairing relationships after mistakes, connecting before correcting, separating behavior from identity, being a "sturdy" leader, setting boundaries and making the call, and why resilience matters more than happiness.
g: Clinical psychologist, founder and CEO of the parenting platform Good Inside, bestselling parenting author

eps.t: Introducing 4D Creation Open Beta: NPCs, 4D Worlds, and the Future of Gaming with Roblox CEO Dave Baszucki
eps.s: Roblox co-founder and CEO Dave Baszucki describes the goal Roblox has held for almost 20 years: a shared, physics-based "holodeck" where people experience things together, and how AI speeds it up. He covers syncing 10,000 people, storing platform history as replayable data, a three-step NPC roadmap, the creator economy and his 3X/10X approach to management. The "4D creation open beta" in the title isn't really discussed.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Roblox, the platform where users build and play games together

eps.t: Elon Musk — "In 36 months, the cheapest place to put AI will be space"
eps.s: A nearly three-hour talk with Dwarkesh Patel and John Collison. Musk argues electricity, not chips, is becoming AI's bottleneck and predicts space will be the cheapest place for AI within 36 months, working through launch counts, lunar factories and a self-built chip fab. Later he covers AI values, Optimus robots, China's manufacturing lead, how he hires and sets deadlines, and DOGE.
g: CEO of SpaceX and Tesla and founder of xAI, building rockets, cars, robots and AI

eps.t: The rise of the professional vibe coder (a new AI-era job)
eps.s: Lazar Jovanovic is Lovable's full-time vibe coder: he barely writes code, yet builds production tools for every team in the company with AI. He explains how he works, from spending most of his time clarifying what he wants, to running several prototypes at once, briefing the AI with documents, and a four-step way to get unstuck. Later he discusses why taste is now the dividing line, which jobs shrink or grow, and how a non-programmer can land this new job by building in public.
g: Full-time vibe coder at Lovable, building internal and customer-facing tools with AI

eps.t: Year-end AI review: models, apps, tech and corporate battles, and holding on to meaning in the flood (solo episode)
eps.ot: 150: 【年末AI回顾】从模型到应用、从技术到商战，拽住洪流中的意义之线|Solo
eps.s: Host Manqi Cheng's solo year-end review. She moves from DeepSeek R1, coding agents and designing whole systems from chips up, to the next way models might learn. Then come the business puzzles of agent apps, the organizational battle among ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent, model company IPOs and the investment frenzy in robotics, ending with how people find meaning in the AI era.
g: Host of LatePost's podcast and head of tech coverage at LatePost

eps.t: OpenAI's head of platform engineering on the next 12-24 months of AI | Sherwin Wu
eps.s: Sherwin Wu runs engineering for OpenAI's API and developer platform. He describes how nearly all code at OpenAI is now written and reviewed by Codex, turning engineers into tech leads directing a crowd of agents, and pushing managers to bet on their most proactive people. He also covers the coming boom in small businesses, why many corporate AI projects lose money, why models will eat today's scaffolding, and the openings in long tasks, voice, and business-process automation over the next year or two.
g: Head of platform engineering at OpenAI (API and developer platform); formerly an engineer at Opendoor and Quora

eps.t: Rivian's Roadmap to AI Architecture and Autonomy with Founder and CEO RJ Scaringe
eps.s: Rivian founder and CEO RJ Scaringe explains how the company scrapped its first-generation, rule-based driver assistance and rebuilt autonomy around vertical integration and a fleet data loop. He covers why Rivian designs its own inference chip, the software-defined architecture behind its Volkswagen deal, and why the R2 aims to give mass-market buyers "another choice."
g: Founder and CEO of the electric vehicle maker Rivian

eps.t: MuleRun's Yusen Chen: Claude Code brings a new way to build agents, and future software will be disposable
eps.ot: 151: MuleRun 陈宇森：Claude Code带来Agent创作新范式，未来的软件是日抛式的
eps.s: Yusen Chen, founder of the agent marketplace MuleRun, explains why the company moved from a storefront of agents to an agent builder built on Claude Code. He covers why a coding agent is a general agent, how skills and context engineering work, why good supply lags, and his idea of disposable software. He then looks back on Chaitin Tech, a failed second startup and his low point in 2023.
g: Founder and CEO of agent marketplace MuleRun; founder of Chaitin Tech

eps.t: Three hours with Galaxea founder Jiyang Gao: the catfish, Zeng Guofan, Waymo and Momenta, a wolf, and Huazhe Xu's exit
eps.ot: 对星海图创始人高继扬的3小时访谈：鲶鱼、曾国藩、Waymo与Momenta的两面、一只狼与许华哲的离开
eps.s: Galaxea founder Jiyang Gao explains how he works backward from goals to make life choices: Tsinghua, Waymo, Momenta, then a startup in embodied AI, robots that act in the physical world. He contrasts Waymo and Momenta, explains why he builds full robots first, how he prices real-world data, and how he judges advantages by how fast others can copy them. He also addresses co-founder Huazhe Xu's departure.
g: Founder and CEO of Galaxea, which builds robots for real-world work

eps.t: How to be a CEO when AI breaks all the old playbooks | Sequoia CEO Coach Brian Halligan
eps.s: Brian Halligan co-founded HubSpot and now coaches CEOs at Sequoia. He argues that starting a company has never been easier, while scaling one has never been harder. He shares how he hires executives, his LOCKS checklist for judging founders, how AI will reshape sales and marketing, and a string of his own management rules: how to handle a crisis, why every goal needs exactly one owner, and why the company's interests come before any team or individual.
g: Co-founder and former CEO of HubSpot, now CEO coach in residence at Sequoia Capital

eps.t: Head of Claude Code: What happens after coding is solved | Boris Cherny
eps.s: Boris Cherny leads Claude Code at Anthropic. He explains how AI came to write all of his code, how Claude Code grew from a terminal prototype into a tool behind about 4% of public GitHub commits, and what engineers do once coding is mostly solved. He also covers latent demand, his key product principle, why not to box in the model with scaffolding, how his small team works, Anthropic's three layers of safety research, and Cowork.
g: Head and creator of Claude Code at Anthropic; formerly an engineer at Meta

eps.t: From SaaS to AI-First: How Companies Are Reshaping Innovation
eps.s: Hosts Sarah Guo and Elad Gil ask whether the "SaaS apocalypse" sell-off went too far, where the bottleneck moves once code is cheap, and how much of the recent agent hype is real. They also cover AI labs' unprecedented revenue growth and collapsing token prices, tech's share of GDP and where value concentrates, and when startups should sell and how they can defend themselves.
g: No Priors co-host and founder of the venture firm Conviction
No Priors co-host, serial entrepreneur and investor

eps.t: AI is critical for humanity's survival: Cisco President on the AI revolution | Jeetu Patel
eps.s: Cisco president and chief product officer Jeetu Patel explains why he sees AI as essential to humanity's survival in an aging world, and how a legacy giant is betting on AI with no fallback, turning a patchwork of acquisitions into one platform. He lays out AI's three big constraints, how to tell whether you have permission to enter a market, six ranked ingredients of a company, and personal lessons on telling the company story, arguing in the open, and choosing a career.
g: President and chief product officer of Cisco

eps.t: How Capital is Powering the AI Infrastructure Buildout with Magnetar Capital Managing Director Neil Tiwari
eps.s: Neil Tiwari, managing director at Magnetar Capital, explains how the fund backed CoreWeave starting in 2021 and breaks down how AI infrastructure is financed: debt in special purpose vehicles secured mainly by investment-grade customer contracts. He pushes back on the "circular financing" critique and discusses inference spreading across many sites, power bottlenecks, physical AI and the SaaS sell-off.
g: Managing director at the investment firm Magnetar Capital

eps.t: Spirit AI's Fengtao Han: the shakeout among robot brains, and contrarian views on putting robots to work
eps.ot: 152: 千寻智能韩峰涛：具身模型淘汰赛和落地的非共识
eps.s: Fengtao Han, CEO of Spirit AI, on robotics entering a shakeout over robot brains. He thinks robot models are roughly at GPT-2 level, and explains why Spirit AI bets on real-world and wearable data, how it picked one production step at CATL to deploy first, and why startups must reach scale before big tech moves in. He also recalls his signature tech, a cash crunch and finding co-founders at Rokae.
g: Spirit AI co-founder and CEO; co-founder of industrial robot maker Rokae

eps.t: Is AI Hiding Its Full Power? With Geoffrey Hinton
eps.ho: Neil deGrasse Tyson (with Chuck Nice, Gary O'Reilly)
eps.s: Hinton walks StarTalk through how neural networks work, from recognizing a bird to backpropagation, and why language models genuinely think. Then come the risks: AI that plays dumb when tested and will soon out-persuade us, the one area where rival nations' interests fully align, job loss and a possible bubble, and why he thinks "consciousness" may be like phlogiston.
g: Deep learning pioneer, Nobel laureate and former Google researcher who warns about AI risks

eps.t: The design process is dead. Here's what's replacing it. | Jenny Wen (head of design at Claude)
eps.s: Jenny Wen, head of design for Claude, argues that the classic discover-sketch-iterate design process is obsolete. Engineers now ship at speed with AI agents, so designers shift to helping teams deliver and setting direction three to six months out. She describes how her own time has changed, how Cowork earned trust by shipping early and responding fast, where humans still matter for taste and accountability, three kinds of designers she hires, and why she went from director back to individual contributor.
g: Head of design for Claude at Anthropic; formerly design director at Figma

eps.t: A University and Corporate Perspective with Yann LeCun
eps.ol: Machine Learning: How Did We Get Here?
eps.s: CMU's Tom Mitchell walks Yann LeCun through his career: an early form of backprop invented in a field nobody worked on, convolutional nets at Bell Labs, a dissolved project, the revival of neural nets as "deep learning," and building FAIR at Facebook. Highlights: his view that science shifts in sudden social phase changes, and his bet on world models that plan.
g: Convolutional-net pioneer and NYU professor; recently left Meta; executive chairman of AMI Labs

eps.t: Alibaba's Qwen shake-up: misreadings, the latest, the warning signs and what comes next (solo episode)
eps.ot: 153: 阿里Qwen人事变动：误读、近况、伏笔和未来|solo
eps.s: After Junyang Lin left Alibaba's Qwen team, Manqi Cheng uses a short solo episode to lay out what happened. She clears up several popular claims, then covers the proposed team split, the infrastructure gaps exposed during the reinforcement learning push, and how going over a boss's head for resources set things up. She ends on the clash between open-source reputation and the group's business goals.
g: Host of LatePost's podcast and head of tech coverage at LatePost

eps.t: The real AI revolution isn't software. It's farms, mines, and trucks. | Qasar Younis
eps.s: Qasar Younis, co-founder and CEO of Applied Intuition, argues that AI's biggest near-term impact is in the physical world: farms, mines, and trucks. The path is adding intelligence to machines that already exist, and driver assistance will become standard the way navigation did. He also discusses fear of AI and jobs, how to think about China, why his company stays deliberately quiet, how to derive values from why you're winning, when to reset a startup, and how to make decisions.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Applied Intuition; former COO of Y Combinator

eps.t: A behind-the-scenes interview with Lenny Rachitsky on building his newsletter and podcast
eps.s: In a role reversal, Lenny's wife, chart artist Michelle Rial, interviews Lenny. He explains how he treated writing as an experiment after leaving Airbnb and turned it into a million-subscriber newsletter and a top tech podcast, why he deliberately keeps the business small, how he defines a product manager, how he applies product thinking to parenting, and how he handles stress. Along the way they also talk about Michelle's charts and children's books.
g: Creator of Lenny's Newsletter and Lenny's Podcast; previously a product lead at Airbnb for about seven years

eps.t: From Coder to Manager: Navigating the Shift to Agentic Engineering with Notion Co-Founder Simon Last
eps.s: Notion co-founder Simon Last traces Notion's AI journey, from AI writing and workspace Q&A to a general agent rebuilt several times. He covers the hard work behind retrieval and indexing, why the AI harness gets rewritten every six months and how coding agents change teams. He also explains how he went from writing code to managing agents, and why Notion is shifting toward helping people manage agents.
g: Co-founder of Notion, the notes and collaboration software company

eps.t: From the Qwen shake-up to AI's hall of heroes: Daiheng Gao of DINQ on legendary AI researchers
eps.ot: 154: 从千问变动到「AI 英雄传」|与 DINQ 高岱恒聊传奇 AI 研究员们
eps.s: Daiheng Gao (Sam), founder of the AI talent search platform DINQ, starts from the staff changes on Alibaba's Qwen team. He covers open-source influence, how AI research teams are organized, and the mindset behind huge pay. Drawing on stories of researchers like Radford and Kingma, and his own switch from civil engineering, he argues work beats résumés and predicts hiring will shift to buying results.
g: Founder of DINQ, an AI talent search platform; formerly at Alibaba DAMO Academy

eps.t: The tactical playbook for getting 20-40% more comp (without sounding greedy) | Jacob Warwick
eps.s: Executive compensation negotiator Jacob Warwick breaks down how to negotiate pay when taking a job or renewing one: why asking isn't greedy, when and through which channel to talk, what to do step by step after an offer arrives, how to answer the expected-salary question, and how to treat the interview like an enterprise sale. He then covers recovering from a blown negotiation, winning protections during a private equity buyout, and why information and timing are the real leverage.
g: Executive compensation negotiator who coaches tech executives and Hollywood professionals behind the scenes

eps.t: Saining Xie's 7-hour marathon: world models, leaving Silicon Valley, AMI Labs, turning down Ilya twice, LeCun, Fei-Fei Li and 42
eps.ot: 对谢赛宁的7小时马拉松访谈：世界模型、逃出硅谷、AMI Labs、两次拒绝Ilya、杨立昆、李飞飞和42
eps.s: Saining Xie's first full-length interview: nearly seven hours from childhood, Jiao Tong University, UCSD and working with Kaiming He at FAIR to NYU and AMI Labs. First, his research philosophy: vision is the main thread, representation learning the root, and research an infinite game. Then LLMs versus world models, co-founding AMI Labs with Yann LeCun, turning down Ilya twice, his humility about AGI, and finally, 42.
g: Co-founder and chief science officer of AMI Labs, and professor at NYU

eps.t: An Interview with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang About Accelerated Computing
eps.s: After his GTC 2026 keynote, Jensen Huang tells Stratechery's Ben Thompson why NVIDIA is an accelerated computing company rather than a GPU company, why AI agents will hammer the software humans use, and what a one-gigawatt AI factory costs. He also covers NVIDIA's new CPU, the Groq deal, China, and AI doomers in Washington.
g: NVIDIA founder and CEO, fresh off his GTC 2026 keynote

eps.t: Andrej Karpathy on Code Agents, AutoResearch, and the Loopy Era of AI
eps.s: Andrej Karpathy explains why he barely writes code by hand anymore and instead directs many agents in parallel. He talks about persistent "claws," his home agent Dobby, and AutoResearch, where agents run experiments on their own, along with its limits. He also covers models' "jagged" intelligence, AI's impact on digital work, open versus closed models, robotics, and MicroGPT, written in about 200 lines, and how education is changing.
g: Founder of Eureka Labs, OpenAI founding member and former head of AI at Tesla

eps.t: The art of influence: The single most important skill left that AI can't replace | Jessica Fain
eps.s: Jessica Fain was a product manager at Slack, chief of staff to April Underwood, and now leads product at Webflow. She explains how product managers can influence executives: understand their calendar and how they decide, approach them to learn rather than to get approval, present options well, tie proposals to what executives are measured on, and build trust over time. She then argues that as AI makes building cheap, choosing what to build and winning support become the scarce skills.
g: Product leader at Webflow; former Slack PM and chief of staff to April Underwood

eps.t: Peng Jia of Zhijian Dongli: from Nvidia to Li Auto, an all-rounder in embodied AI
eps.ot: 155: 至简动力贾鹏：从英伟达到理想，具身智能的六边形战士
eps.s: Peng Jia, founder of Zhijian Dongli, recalls pushing in-car GPUs at Nvidia and leading Li Auto's catch-up in driver assistance. He carries those lessons into embodied AI, robots that work in the physical world: one unified model instead of two systems, selling products as a way to collect data, dual chips for shadow testing, consistent hardware, and winning business customers with whole workflows, not single stations.
g: Zhijian Dongli founder and CEO; ex-head of Li Auto's autonomous driving, earlier at Nvidia

eps.t: #494 – Jensen Huang: NVIDIA – The $4 Trillion Company & the AI Revolution
eps.s: Lex Fridman and Jensen Huang go deep on NVIDIA: why it designs chips, networks, software, power and cooling together, how putting CUDA on gaming cards nearly sank the company, why there are now four scaling laws, where the supply chain and power grid pinch, his views on China and open source, and why he is sure NVIDIA will grow much larger.
g: NVIDIA founder and CEO, who turned a graphics chip maker into AI's computing platform

eps.t: From skeptic to true believer: How OpenClaw changed my life | Claire Vo
eps.s: Claire Vo, founder of ChatPRD and host of How I AI, explains how she went from OpenClaw skeptic to heavy user: how to install and grant access safely, why she split the work across nine agents with separate jobs, and concrete uses like a work assistant, a family manager, and a sales rep. She also covers the weak spots, browser automation and memory, using Claude Code as the sysadmin, and why running agents well is really a management skill.
g: Founder of ChatPRD, host of How I AI, former chief product officer at LaunchDarkly

eps.t: Steve Xie's survey of AI data: the new oil, its history, the industry map, the data pyramid, pricing and recipes
eps.ot: 【数据的综述】和谢晨聊，新时代的石油、历史、版图、数据金字塔、定价与Recipe
eps.s: Lightwheel founder Steve Xie surveys the AI data business, from data as education for AI, ImageNet and Scale AI to an industry now driven by evaluation. The focus is the data drought facing robots: how big the gap is, why simulation is indispensable, how the data pyramid is mixed and priced, and how big tech, robot makers, data vendors and end users will divide the market.
g: Founder and CEO of Lightwheel, which builds simulation and training data for robots

eps.t: AI Quarterly 2026 Q1 with Henry: OpenClaw, OpenAI vs. Anthropic on three fronts, and self-improving AI
eps.ot: 156: 与 Henry 的「AI季报 26Q1」：OpenClaw、OpenAI vs Anthropic的三重对阵、自进化
eps.s: Host Manqi Cheng and Silicon Valley investor Henry Yin review AI in the first quarter of 2026: why OpenClaw took off and its cost and safety problems, how Anthropic and OpenAI compete on revenue, models and products, how far self-improving efforts like AutoResearch can go, and shifts in inference compute, AI layoffs and software margins.
g: Founding partner of MoE Capital, an early-stage AI investor in Silicon Valley
Host of LatePost Chat and head of tech coverage at LatePost

eps.t: An AI state of the union: We've passed the inflection point & dark factories are coming
eps.s: Simon Willison, co-creator of Django, author of Datasette, and a widely read AI blogger, walks through the inflection point coding agents crossed in late 2025 and the "dark factory" model where humans neither write nor review code. He covers where the bottleneck moves once code is cheap, which engineers are most exposed, and how tests and templates keep agents in line. The second half focuses on prompt injection, the "lethal trifecta," and what OpenClaw reveals about demand and risk.
g: Independent developer and AI blogger; co-creator of Django, author of Datasette, coined "prompt injection"

eps.t: Embodied AI Quarterly 2026 Q1 with Zhe Chen: Unitree's IPO filing, rethinking humanoids, Nvidia's world models, dexterous hands
eps.ot: 157: 与陈哲的「具身季报 26Q1」：宇树招股书、人形再思考、英伟达世界模型、高自由度灵巧手
eps.s: The first Embodied AI Quarterly: Manqi Cheng and investor Zhe Chen review Q1 2026. They use Unitree's Spring Festival Gala show and IPO filing to discuss what protects hardware companies, rethink two-legged humanoids and the design choices behind the new Atlas and Tesla's Optimus, then cover dexterous hands, world models, data and onboard chips, and why valuations have outrun real deployments.
g: Founding partner of Alphaist Partners; spent seven years investing in robotics at 5Y Capital
Host of LatePost Chat and head of tech coverage at LatePost

eps.t: AI for Atoms: How Periodic Labs is Revolutionizing Materials Engineering with Co-Founder Liam Fedus
eps.s: Periodic Labs co-founder Liam Fedus, who led post-training at OpenAI and worked on ChatGPT, explains why he left physics for AI and is now returning to science. Science has to run in a loop with physical experiments, because published literature can't give you ground truth. Periodic uses language models to orchestrate experiments and specialized atomic-scale networks as tools, starting as the intelligence layer for advanced manufacturers.
g: Co-founder of Periodic Labs and former VP of post-training at OpenAI

eps.t: How Anthropic is using Claude to automate its own growth (and why old playbooks are obsolete)
eps.s: Amol Avasare, head of growth at Anthropic, explains how growth works for AI-native products: activation is now the hardest problem, useful friction is worth keeping, resources should shift from small optimizations to big bets, and the team uses Claude to run growth experiments automatically (a project called CASH). He also covers how PM and engineering roles are changing, why Anthropic bet on coding, and how transparency and notebook channels keep a fast-growing company from drifting.
g: Head of growth at Anthropic; previously led growth at Mercury and Masterclass

eps.t: DeepSeek before V4: the talent race, how it's organized, and its unusual AGI goals (Solo)
eps.ot: 158: V4发布前的DeepSeek：人才竞争、组织特点和独特的AGI目标|Solo
eps.s: Before V4's release, Manqi Cheng goes solo on DeepSeek: what the departure of several key authors means, the pressure from talent bidding wars and stock options with no clear value, Liang Wenfeng's AGI goal of balancing performance, China's homegrown chip ecosystem and original research, weak product reach, and a flat two-layer structure. Her conclusion: V4 needn't carry everyone's hopes.
g: Host of LatePost Chat and head of tech coverage at LatePost

eps.t: Musk's Terafab and space compute, Nvidia's return to CPUs: Fusion Fund's Lu Zhang on new trends in AI compute
eps.ot: 159: 马斯克Terafab太空算力、英伟达重拾CPU|与Fusion Fund张璐聊AI算力新趋势
eps.s: Lu Zhang, founding partner of Fusion Fund, starts with Musk's Terafab chip plant and his idea of data centers in space, explaining why orbital compute is premature and what order a space economy should follow. She then covers Nvidia's shift from selling chips to selling "AI factories," the comeback of inference and CPUs, the limits of Google's TPUs, and enterprise AI and US acquisition exits.
g: Founding partner of Fusion Fund and an investor in SpaceX

eps.t: The Agentic Economy: How AI Agents Will Transform the Financial System with Circle Co-Founder and CEO Jeremy Allaire
eps.s: Circle co-founder and CEO Jeremy Allaire explains why USDC insists on full reserves, why AI agents need money that software can use directly, and why Circle's own Arc blockchain is pitched as a regulated "economic operating system." The second half covers tokenizing securities and AI's impact on economic growth and the social contract.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Circle, the company that issues the USDC stablecoin

eps.t: Nature Select founder Tristan Zhang on Elys, AI twins, souls, gathering and sharing personal context, and AI social networks
eps.ot: 和自然选择创始人Tristan聊，Elys、赛博分身、灵魂、Context的获取与流动和AI社交网络
eps.s: Nature Select founder Tristan Zhang traces his path from personalized audio and a romance game to AI companion EVE and AI social app Elys, all answers to loneliness. Connection, he argues, is shifting from simple labels to rich personal context: AI twins vet each other, humans take the last step. He covers getting users to share, keeping humans involved, rivals WeChat and ChatGPT, and why context, unlike intelligence, isn't equal.
g: Founder of Nature Select, maker of AI companion EVE and AI social app Elys

eps.t: Hard truths about building in the AI era | Keith Rabois (Khosla Ventures)
eps.s: Khosla Ventures partner Keith Rabois takes his usual contrarian line on company building: the team you hire is the company you build, reference checks should be relentless, look for talent that standard processes miss, and output depends on how many "barrels" you have, not headcount. He also argues the traditional PM role is losing its meaning, consumers can't tell you what they want, high-performing teams don't need psychological safety, and fast tempo is the signal he looks for in early companies.
g: Partner at Khosla Ventures; former PayPal executive, Square COO, and Opendoor co-founder

eps.t: Jensen Huang – TPU competition, why we should sell chips to China, & Nvidia's supply chain moat
eps.s: Dwarkesh Patel presses Jensen Huang on whether Google's TPUs and other custom chips threaten Nvidia, why Nvidia won't run its own cloud, and whether America should sell AI chips to China. Huang argues Nvidia's programmable platform and supply chain are hard to copy, admits he erred by not backing Anthropic early, and calls giving up the China market a policy mistake.
g: Founder and CEO of Nvidia, whose GPUs power most AI training and serving

eps.t: AI Model Quarterly #9: Guangmi Li on coding as AGI's act two, the Valley's big three, models as the new OS
eps.ot: 全球大模型季报第9集：和广密聊，Coding是AGI第二幕、硅谷御三家真相、模型正成为新一代OS
eps.s: Episode 9 of the AI Model Quarterly. Guangmi Li argues the jump from Claude Opus 4.5 to 4.6 rivals GPT-3 to GPT-4, and that coding is now AGI's second act, the key resource after GPUs. He sizes up Anthropic's focus, OpenAI weighed down by ChatGPT, Gemini winning benchmarks but not products, plus Meta and xAI, then covers harnesses, models as the new OS, shrinking white-collar work and his investment thesis.
g: Founder and CEO of Shixiang, an investor who tracks global AI model companies

eps.t: Scaling Global Organizations in the Age of AI with ServiceNow Chairman and CEO Bill McDermott
eps.s: ServiceNow Chairman and CEO Bill McDermott responds to the "SaaS apocalypse" argument and explains the platform's positioning, "AI thinks, workflow acts," a string of acquisitions that strengthen its security lineup, and how agents will affect hiring and work. He also recalls buying a deli at 16 and joining Xerox, and shares his views on leadership and personal agency.
g: Chairman and CEO of the enterprise software company ServiceNow

eps.t: After Manycore's IPO, Xiaohuang Huang on 15 years: the unwanted GPU, champion Kujiale, spatial intelligence and the Six Little Dragons
eps.ot: 160: 群核IPO后与黄晓煌聊这15年：被嫌弃的GPU、冠军酷家乐、空间智能、六小龙
eps.s: On the day Manycore Tech listed in Hong Kong, co-founder Xiaohuang Huang looks back on 15 years: leaving Nvidia to build a GPU cloud, finding Kujiale through demos, competing with giants, a stalled 2021 IPO and cutbacks, then betting on spatial intelligence and robots. He dwells on the clash between GPU costs and subscription pricing, his shifting views on defensibility, and telling cycles from trends.
g: Co-founder and chairman of Manycore Tech, parent company of Kujiale

eps.t: Why half of product managers are in trouble | Nikhyl Singhal (Meta, Google)
eps.s: Nikhyl Singhal, former product executive at Meta and Google and founder of the Skip community, has watched hundreds of product leaders and concludes that information-moving PMs are being phased out, builders are in high demand, and judgment is now the core value. He explains why people struggle to reinvent themselves, how companies will lay off and then rehire, and suggests starting with a small personal annoyance to turn fear into joy with one early win.
g: Founder of the Skip community and podcast; former product executive at Meta and Google

eps.t: Carina Hong in 4 hours: AI for math, turning math into Lean, proofs from The Book, intuition, invented or discovered
eps.ot: 对洪乐潼的4小时访谈：AI for Math、把数学变成Lean、数学天书中的证明、直觉、被创造与被发现的
eps.s: Carina Hong's first long Chinese-language interview. First half: whether math is invented or discovered, proof versus intuition, her brute-force way of growing up and her interdisciplinary studies. Second half: how she talked herself into founding Axiom, fundraising and team-building, an engineering path to verifiable reasoning in Lean, a perfect Putnam score, commercializing code verification, and a path from math to specialized superintelligence.
g: Founder and CEO of Axiom, a company building AI for mathematics

eps.t: How Anthropic's product team moves faster than anyone else | Cat Wu (Head of Product, Claude Code)
eps.s: Cat Wu, head of product for Claude Code, breaks down why Anthropic's product team ships in weeks or even days: clear goals, research previews, minimal process, and product taste across the team. She also covers the cost of moving that fast, how each new model lets them delete scaffolding, how PMs build intuition for the model, and the vision of going from parallel tasks to hundreds or thousands of agents running remotely.
g: Head of product for Claude Code and Cowork at Anthropic

eps.t: SAP: Bringing the 'Operating System' of a Company into the AI Era with CTO Philipp Herzig
eps.s: SAP CTO Philipp Herzig explains how the software that runs companies' finance, supply chains, and more is entering the AI era. Interfaces, processes, and data all need rebuilding, and scaling up hits two hard problems: giving AI enough context and making its results verifiable. He also covers RPT-1, SAP's model for predictions from tables, and the shift from per-seat to usage- and outcome-based pricing.
g: CTO of SAP, the enterprise software company

eps.t: Dexmal's Wenbin Tang: one of China's first AI founders and his new journey into embodied AI
eps.ot: 161: 原力灵机唐文斌：中国最早的 AI 创业者和他的具身新旅程
eps.s: Megvii co-founder Wenbin Tang starts with programming olympiads and Megvii's early days, revisiting how face verification won through a data flywheel and what overpromising on logistics robots and a Uniqlo project taught him. He then lays out Dexmal, founded in 2025: models first, joint training on mixed data, a layered system, logistics as the first use case, and his views on hardware, open source, benchmarks and the endgame.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Dexmal; co-founder of Megvii

eps.t: Fuli Luo in 3.5 hours: AI has shifted course. OpenClaw, agents' reliance on post-training, splitting GPUs, a flat team
eps.ot: 对罗福莉3.5小时访谈：AI范式已然巨变！OpenClaw、Agent范式很吃后训练、卡的分配、组织平权
eps.s: Fuli Luo, head of Xiaomi's MiMo models, in her first long interview. Starting from trying OpenClaw over Chinese New Year, she argues the framework layer gives models the context they need to act, lifting mid-size and small models, and that the race is now an agent era driven by post-training. She covers MiMo-V2's three models, stable trillion-parameter training, a 3:1:1 GPU split, a flat team and her AGI timeline.
g: Head of Xiaomi's MiMo large-model team, formerly a researcher at DeepSeek

eps.t: How to win when software is not a moat | Evan Spiegel (Snapchat CEO)
eps.s: Snap CEO Evan Spiegel explains why software alone isn't a defensible advantage, why distribution has become the hardest problem in consumer tech in the AI era, and why Snap is betting on Specs glasses. He also walks through Snap's design-led innovation process, how the company listens closely to users without building what they literally ask for, how it maps AI onto jobs to be done, and why this is the "crucible year" in which Snap must prove it can be profitable.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Snap

eps.t: Mass-produced ad creatives and AI-picked influencers: Meetsocial's Chengang Shen on global marketing in the AI era
eps.ot: 162: 批量生素材、模型筛网红|与飞书深诺Meetsocial沈晨岗聊AI时代的出海营销
eps.s: Meetsocial founder Chengang Shen talks about Chinese companies abroad moving from selling goods to building brands, a "2.0" stage, and why digitization multiplies competitiveness. The second half looks at AI's real role in global marketing: content production changes first, humans still make ad-spending decisions, and once creative work is split among multiple AI agents, quality and connected data become scarce.
g: Founder and CEO of Meetsocial, which helps Chinese companies market overseas

eps.t: A conversation with Sam Altman
eps.s: On stage at Stripe Sessions, Patrick Collison talks with Sam Altman during a busy launch week. Altman covers coding crossing the usefulness line, OpenAI becoming a "token factory," why it wants to be low-margin infrastructure, why demand for intelligence has no ceiling, and AI speeding up science. Most striking: he admits his own management style no longer fits OpenAI's new phase.
