g: OpenAI co-founder and CEO, and an early investor in Stripe

eps.t: How to Build the Future: Demis Hassabis
eps.s: Y Combinator's Garry Tan asks Demis Hassabis how to build in the AI era. He covers what AGI still lacks, why models are brilliant one moment and clumsy the next, distillation and open small models, and which science problems suit AI. His most practical advice for founders: pair AI with a hard science that deals in atoms, and assume AGI arrives midway through your project.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Google DeepMind, an AI scientist who started out making games

eps.t: Demis Hassabis: We're Three Quarters of the Way to AGI
eps.s: At Sequoia Capital's AI Ascent 2026, Demis Hassabis traces his path from games and neuroscience to DeepMind, and says the field is right on the 20-year plan his team set in 2010, with AGI around 2030. He also covers speeding up drug discovery, using simulators to study economics, and his idea that information is more fundamental than matter.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Google DeepMind; founder of drug-discovery company Isomorphic Labs

eps.t: DeepSeek V4 explained: the infrastructure whale, million-token context made real, and extreme efficiency
eps.ot: 163: 详解DeepSeekV4：Infra巨鲸、百万上下文走进现实、极致效率优化
eps.s: UCLA PhD student Yifeng Liu, who studies model architecture, and SGLang engineer Chenyang Zhao take apart DeepSeek V4. They ask whether it is a new paradigm, why cheaper tokens don't always mean cheaper tasks, and what changes like hybrid sparse attention, very low expert activation, the Muon optimizer, MHC and FP4 mean for training and serving. They end with the benchmark credibility crisis and how US and Chinese labs differ.
g: UCLA computer science PhD student who built foundation models at Microsoft and ByteDance
RadixArk engineer who helps build SGLang, open-source software for running AI models fast

eps.t: Baseten CEO Tuhin Srivastava on the AI Inference Crunch, Custom Models, and Building the Inference Cloud
eps.s: Baseten co-founder and CEO Tuhin Srivastava covers three things: why demand for AI inference is only getting started, why app companies increasingly post-train their own custom models, and how GPU long-term contracts, fundraising, and software advantage add up in an inference crunch. He also talks about where inference runtimes are heading and the Jevons paradox.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Baseten, an AI inference cloud

eps.t: An AI agent survey: Yu Su on agent history, the OpenClaw moment, vanishing boundaries, and ripples through society
eps.ot: 【Agent的综述】和苏煜聊Agent技术史、OpenClaw Moment、边界的消弭和社会的辐射
eps.s: A survey of AI agents. Yu Su offers a definition and two yardsticks, memory and autonomy, then traces the path from logic agents through deep reinforcement learning and semantic parsing to language agents, plus milestones in web and computer-use agents. He covers the OpenClaw moment, boundaries dissolving into code, SaaS and startups, argues continual learning should model many small worlds, and ends on job displacement and democratizing the technology.
g: Ohio State professor and founder of NeoCognition, an AI agent startup

eps.t: Why cultivating agency matters more than cultivating skills in the AI era | Max Schoening (Notion)
eps.s: Notion's head of product Max Schoening explains why the drive to act matters more than skills in the AI era, why designers should design directly in code, and why the "SaaS is dead" story is overblown. He also talks about the tiny, excellent core behind every great product, how taste is trained, his ideal of software users can reshape, and what he learned from building a failed Notion competitor.
g: Head of product at Notion, formerly at GitHub

eps.t: How Anthropic, Costco, and Patagonia all build incorruptible companies | Eric Ries
eps.s: Lean Startup author Eric Ries discusses his new book Incorruptible: why successful companies get dragged toward mediocrity by what he calls financial gravity, and why most founders end up losing control. Using Novo Nordisk, Vectura, Cloudflare, Costco, and Anthropic, he explains how to write down a mission, build accountability, and lock the mission in with structures like public benefit corporations, foundations, and trusts.
g: Author of The Lean Startup and the new book Incorruptible

eps.t: Amex Global Business Travel: The World's First AI Take Private with Long Lake CEO Alexander Taubman
eps.s: Long Lake CEO Alexander Taubman explains the company's model: buy traditional services businesses and transform them with its own AI platform, from property management and architecture to its pending acquisition of Amex Global Business Travel. He argues AI first brings time savings and growth, not layoffs, and explains why Long Lake wants to be a long-term owner.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Long Lake, which buys services businesses and transforms them with AI

eps.t: Four hours with Shunyu Yao: let me go a little crazy! Training Claude and Gemini, predictions, why heroism is over
eps.ot: 对姚顺宇的4小时访谈：请允许我小疯一下！在Anthropic和Gemini训模型、技术预测、英雄主义已过去
eps.s: Shunyu Yao moved from theoretical physics to AI, training Claude 3.7 and 4.5 with large-scale reinforcement learning at Anthropic before joining Google DeepMind to work on Gemini 3. He covers what top labs now compete on, whether pre-training has hit a wall, why coding came first, how AI changes research and jobs, the US-China gap and robots. His bottom line: credit belongs to organizations and reliable people, not lone heroes.
g: Google DeepMind research scientist on Gemini 3; previously trained Claude at Anthropic

eps.t: Alex Wang Breaks His Silence On Meta's Superintelligence Bet (EP 71: Meta's AI Chief On AI Beef, New Models And Life With Zuck)
eps.s: In his first long talk since joining Meta, Alexandr Wang explains why he left Scale, how Meta rebuilt its model stack from scratch in nine months, and the three things that set research speed. He covers Muse Spark's strengths and gaps, why it isn't open-sourced yet, why the AI market keeps reshuffling, and his vision of personal superintelligence, robotics and brain models.
g: Head of Meta Superintelligence Labs, Meta's AI chief; founder of Scale AI

eps.t: Pax Silica: Inside the Trump Administration's Tech Strategy with US Under Secretary of State for Economic Affairs Jacob Helberg
eps.s: Jacob Helberg, the US Under Secretary of State for Economic Affairs, explains Pax Silica, a 14-country economic security alliance built around the entire AI supply chain. He covers a "forward-deployed industrial base" in the Philippines, how the approach differs from China's Belt and Road, the supply and pricing of critical minerals, and what venture capital can do for industrial policy.
g: US Under Secretary of State for Economic Affairs

eps.t: When AI "kills" SaaS: Mininglamp's Minghui Wu on agent networks, software's reinvention and AI-native organizations
eps.ot: 164: 当AI“杀死”SaaS，与明略吴明辉聊多Agent网络、软件业转型和 AI 新组织
eps.s: Mininglamp founder Minghui Wu argues closed-source SaaS has stopped being an asset, so software firms must charge for results and token use instead. He describes Octo, Mininglamp's multi-agent network built on OpenClaw, how an AI-native company divides work, and its GUI model Mano. He argues for scaling out rather than up, and looks back on the failed 2020 EIP product and the 2022 layoffs.
g: Founder and CEO of Mininglamp Technology, which sells industry data and AI analytics

eps.t: How to ship hardware in the AI era | Caitlin Kalinowski (Apple, Meta, OpenAI)
eps.s: Caitlin Kalinowski built MacBooks at Apple, Oculus headsets and Orion glasses at Meta, and then OpenAI's robotics team. She explains why AI's frontier is moving into the physical world, how hardware development differs from software, and where humanoid robots, supply chains, and AI-assisted hardware design really get stuck. She also covers social design for robots, hiring, the Quest 1 camera scare, and leaving OpenAI over governance.
g: Hardware leader; ex-head of robotics at OpenAI, formerly Meta (Oculus, Orion) and Apple

eps.t: NVIDIA GEAR Lab's Shenyuan Gao on world models, self-improving loops and DreamDojo
eps.ot: 165: GEAR 高深远：世界模型、自进化循环、DreamDojo
eps.s: NVIDIA GEAR Lab researcher Shenyuan Gao maps out world models for robots: how to define one for decisions, four ways to represent the world, why the field heated up this year, and how DreamZero and DreamDojo split the work. He covers near-term uses in safety, evaluation, data and reinforcement learning, a self-improving loop of agent, policy and world model with a timeline, and rivals like DeepMind and OpenAI.
g: NVIDIA GEAR Lab researcher with an HKUST PhD, working on world models for robots and cars

eps.t: Freda's Investment Notes 2: Tokenmaxxing, motors in steam engines, from relay race to basketball, loneliness and human connection
eps.ot: Freda的投资札记第2集：Tokenmaxxing、把电机塞进蒸汽机、接力赛变篮球赛、孤独、人的连接
eps.s: In the second episode of her investment notes, Freda Duan reworks the numbers on AI as an investor. She argues token usage isn't value, coding agents may let the leader pull ahead ever faster, software stocks fell first to uncertainty, and companies are still putting motors where steam engines sat. She revisits calls she got wrong, Bay Area anxiety, and the human connection left once AI handles information.
g: Partner at Altimeter Capital, a technology investment firm

eps.t: The Story Behind Cerebras' $63 Billion IPO with Founder and CEO Andrew Feldman
eps.s: Cerebras co-founder and CEO Andrew Feldman looks back on the company's path, from years of failing to make its wafer-scale chip work to landing a huge OpenAI deal and going public. He explains why there's no market for slow inference, and talks about the trade-offs of an IPO, company culture, and how AI speed changes work.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Cerebras, an AI chip company

eps.t: A new era of discovery: AI and the frontiers of science with Demis Hassabis
eps.s: At Google I/O 2026, Axios's Mike Allen talks with Demis Hassabis about AI and science. He puts AGI around 2030, give or take a year, says 2026 and 2027 will be seen as the start, and expects ten times the Industrial Revolution's impact. Calling himself a cautious optimist, his most memorable point: direction matters more than speed, and racing the wrong way is worse than standing still.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Google DeepMind, the lab behind Gemini and AlphaFold

eps.t: AI as the Ultimate Tool for Science: A Conversation with Demis Hassabis
eps.s: In this written conversation for Daedalus, the journal of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, James Manyika asks Demis Hassabis how AI will change science. He lays out three tests for problems AI can crack, the road from AlphaFold to a virtual cell, and what today's AI still lacks. The standout: could an AI trained only on knowledge up to 1910 derive general relativity?
g: Co-founder and CEO of Google DeepMind, trained in cognitive neuroscience

eps.t: AI predictions: Job markets, Codex beats Claude, and the death of org charts | Dan Shipper
eps.s: Every CEO Dan Shipper draws on how his 30-person team actually works to make a set of AI predictions: work moves into agent environments like Codex and Cowork, companies build one shared super-agent first, and SaaS gains users rather than dying. He argues that "automation is a lie," using his own senior-engineer benchmark to show models aren't autonomous yet, and discusses judgment amid floods of PRs, new roles for PMs and designers, and why there will be no jobs apocalypse.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Every, an AI media and software company

eps.t: Huazhe Xu starts another robotics company: he doesn't want to miss the biggest prize
eps.ot: 166: 许华哲再次具身创业：不想错过最大的西瓜
eps.s: After leaving Galaxea, Huazhe Xu founded Poke, a home-robot company. He explains why he wants a lasting, independent consumer brand, what "AI native" rules out, the limits and form of the first product, and his approach of explore, evaluate, exploit with one unified model. He also covers spending pace, which technical trends are certain, and the strategic patience China needs in this window.
g: Founder of home-robot startup Poke; former Galaxea chief scientist and Tsinghua faculty member

eps.t: Yusen's Venture Notes 2: Harness, the next ByteDance, big opportunities in 2026, and Stanley Druckenmiller
eps.ot: 雨森的创投观察第2集：Harness、下一个字节、2026大机会和Stanley Druckenmiller
eps.s: Yusen Dai revisits the calls from last time that proved wrong, explains why he missed the sudden jump in coding revenue, and asks who ultimately pays for AI's returns. He takes apart the harness, the software wrapped around a model: it works like an operating system, with models as swappable processors. He also covers why the next ByteDance won't look like ByteDance, ZhenFund's bets, and the risk of outsourcing thinking.
g: Managing partner at ZhenFund, an early-stage venture firm

eps.t: Building an AI Guardian for Enterprise with Onyx Security CEO Maxim Bar Kogan
eps.s: Onyx Security CEO Maxim Bar Kogan explains why companies can't block autonomous agents and can only supervise them, why today's security tools can't read an agent's intent, and how small models can decide which actions to escalate for closer review. He also discusses the shock of frontier models finding vulnerabilities automatically and the value of independent third-party oversight.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Onyx Security, an enterprise AI security company

eps.t: Onion Academy's Linfeng Yang: using AI to create shortcuts is killing real learning
eps.ot: 167: 洋葱学园杨临风：用AI制造捷径，是在杀死真学习
eps.s: Onion Academy co-founder and CEO Linfeng Yang explains real learning: how kids become self-directed, how lessons go from correct to understood, and why he pays for costly animation and rejects livestreamed and dual-teacher classes. He argues large models alone can't yet teach subjects that need deep thinking, so AI should fill gaps inside structured courses. He also covers one product for paying and free users, education's goals and the market.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Onion Academy, which makes animated K-12 lessons and AI learning tools

eps.t: Second interview with He Xiaopeng: a bigger bet, Iron humanoid's birth, that incident, leading through upheaval, GX and Frankensteins
eps.ot: 对何小鹏的第二次访谈：更大赌注、人形机器人Iron诞生、那场意外、技术剧变下CEO、GX和缝合怪
eps.s: He Xiaopeng explains why XPeng scrapped a self-driving system worth billions for bigger foundation models, why physical-world AI is far harder than digital AI, and how he's reshaping the company. He revisits the Iron humanoid's design and the leg-cutting stunt that proved it real, sizes up XPeng's odds in robots, and talks about the new GX, software's growing share of a car's value, and the industry's endgame.
g: Chairman and CEO of Chinese electric carmaker XPeng

eps.t: The most rational take on AI you'll hear this year | Benedict Evans
eps.s: Tech analyst Benedict Evans uses history to cool down the AI debate: it is a platform shift on the scale of the internet and mobile, and we are at roughly the internet's 1997. He separates tasks from jobs, draws on accounting, telecoms, and browsers to discuss employment, adoption speed, model commoditization, and distribution, and sorts the anti-AI backlash into real problems and exaggerated ones.
g: Independent tech analyst, formerly a partner at a16z

eps.t: Demis Hassabis Thinks We're in the Foothills of the Singularity
eps.s: At a Stanford GSB fireside chat, Stanford president Jonathan Levin walks Demis Hassabis from games and neuroscience to AlphaFold and AGI. The standouts: he thinks AGI is only a few years off, with roughly 100 times the impact of the Industrial Revolution, and that it ideally belonged in a CERN-like lab rather than a race where slowing down means losing.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Google DeepMind, the scientist behind AlphaFold

eps.t: We Need An Ecosystem in AI, And Every Company Can Win A Place In It
eps.s: At Microsoft Build 2026, Microsoft chairman and CEO Satya Nadella argues that AI should be an ecosystem, not a single platform. He explains how companies can turn general models into specialists with private evals and trajectories, how SaaS gets unbundled, rebundled, and priced, how agents reshape work, and why data center buildouts need social permission.
g: Chairman and CEO of Microsoft

eps.t: Tony Fadell: How to build real taste (and why AI makes it matter more)
eps.s: Tony Fadell, who built the iPod, iPhone, and Nest, talks about taste and judgment: why brand-new categories can only be decided by a few people, how to rebuild a whole system starting from pain and enabling technology, why it takes about three generations to get it right, and the marketing work of writing the press release first. He also criticizes brittle AI-written code and "cognitive surrender," argues hardware is back and voice comes first, and urges product people not to make users addicted.
g: Father of the iPod, iPhone co-creator, Nest founder, now runs Build Collective

eps.t: Four hours with Steven Yang: consumer electronics' life and death, a third kind of company, on-device AI, product craft, difficulty modes
eps.ot: 对阳萌的4小时访谈：消费电子死与生、第三类公司、端侧模型、产品方法、游戏模式
eps.s: Steven Yang retraces Anker's path: selling on Amazon, becoming a premium brand priced above average, a broad setback in 2022, then rebuilding around a mission and code of behavior and designing its own chip to fit an AI model into earbuds. He lays out his idea of a "third kind of company" and covers on-device AI, robots and security, sharing profits, AI and organizations, and three layers of defensibility.
g: Founder and CEO of Anker Innovations, the consumer electronics maker

eps.t: Biohub: The Future of Biology is Open-Source with Co-Founders Mark Zuckerberg, Priscilla Chan, and Head of Science Alex Rives
eps.s: Biohub co-founders Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan and head of science Alex Rives explain why Biohub treats frontier AI and wet labs as one effort, why it open-sources its work, and why biology should be modeled layer by layer. They also discuss progress in using protein models to design binders, and the long-term vision of virtual cells and personalized medicine.
g: Biohub co-founder; founder and CEO of Meta
Co-founder of Biohub, a nonprofit biology research organization
Head of science at Biohub

eps.t: Xinyu Wang on how Meituan's Dragonball Capital invests in tech
eps.ot: 168: 对话王新宇：美团龙珠怎么投科技？
eps.s: Meituan Dragonball partner Xinyu Wang looks back on ten years of tech investing, from GGV and Kunlun to Dragonball. He explains how he judges founders, how a three-by-three grid finds crossover bets, and why he bet big on Moonshot AI in 2023 and Unitree in 2024. He also covers metrics for AI apps, how much embodied AI needs, when it will shake out, and his faith in late-arriving self-driving.
g: Partner at Meituan Dragonball leading tech investments; previously at GGV Capital and Kunlun Tech

eps.t: AI and science with Demis Hassabis | The Royal Society x Nobel Prize
eps.ol: The Royal Society / Nobel Prize Dialogue
eps.ho: Unnamed moderator (with Paul Nurse and Alison Noble)
eps.s: At a Royal Society and Nobel Prize dialogue, Demis Hassabis joins Paul Nurse and Alison Noble on how AI is moving science at digital speed. Highlights: AI could become the language of biology the way math is for physics, academia shouldn't spend billions chasing frontier models, and he is sure a golden age of discovery arrives within ten years.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Google DeepMind, the scientist behind AlphaFold

eps.t: An oral history of SpaceX with ex-executive Lide Hong: Musk's hiring, the biggest IPO, space and AI, and humanity's expansion
eps.ot: 口述SpaceX开发史：和前高管洪力德聊，马斯克用人观、最大IPO、太空与AI、人类文明扩张前奏？
eps.s: Lide Hong, former chief manufacturing engineer for SpaceX's Falcon 9, tells the company's story. He sees the first rocket recovery in 2015 as the real turning point, cost per kilogram to orbit as the key metric, and space data centers and Musk's X ecosystem as what's next. He covers Musk's hiring and meetings, the 2015-16 failures, his own career choices, and a map of the space industry for investors.
g: Former Falcon 9 chief manufacturing engineer at SpaceX, now a GP at an early-stage fund

eps.t: The hidden pattern behind successful products | Mark Pincus (FarmVille, Words with Friends, & more)
eps.s: Zynga founder Mark Pincus walks through the product method from his new book, PBN (proven, better, new), along with principles like "don't be so ambitious" and "kill hope before hope kills you." He revisits how Zynga won on retention rather than virality, sizes up new openings for consumer social and distribution in the AI era, and shares his hands-on management style.
g: Founder of game company Zynga (FarmVille, Words With Friends), serial entrepreneur

eps.t: Early Cerebras investor Nan Zhou: an NVIDIA challenger? The first signs of scaling laws, and Baidu's forgotten US lab
eps.ot: 169: 访谈Cerebras早期投资人周楠：英伟达挑战者？Scaling Law的萌芽、被遗忘的百度美研
eps.s: Qualcomm Ventures investor Nan Zhou recalls backing Cerebras about nine years ago at Baidu's US research lab: early signs of scaling laws during Deep Speech 2, a four-week due diligence that priced the risks, and the 2017-2019 slump of delayed tape-outs. The episode also covers Cerebras as an inference challenger and its valuation range, the lab's talent exodus and stillborn growth fund, and today's brief windows for contrarian AI bets.
g: Qualcomm Ventures investor who earlier invested in AI at Baidu's US lab; early Cerebras backer

eps.t: Re-engineering the Semiconductor Supply Chain with Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan
eps.s: Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan explains why he took the job at 66, how he's sequencing the turnaround as crawl, walk, run, sprint, why inference and agents are reviving CPU demand, and why Intel is sticking with its foundry business and on what timeline. As a veteran chip investor, he also shares how he looks for bottleneck opportunities.
g: CEO of Intel and a longtime chip investor

eps.t: What happens after coding is solved? | Fiona Fung (Claude Code & Cowork)
eps.s: Fiona Fung, an engineering manager on Anthropic's Claude Code and Cowork teams, explains how her team rethought verification, quality bars, measuring impact, and management once writing code stopped being the bottleneck. She also talks about using Claude for everyday management, helping small businesses adopt AI, having new managers start as engineers, and protecting culture and switching to monthly planning during rapid growth.
g: Engineering manager on Anthropic's Claude Code and Cowork teams; formerly Microsoft Visual Studio and Meta

eps.t: DeepMind Chief Demis Hassabis Says Google's Still Winning AI Talent | Semafor Tech
eps.s: Live at Cannes Lions, Semafor's Reed Albergotti asks Demis Hassabis about the AI talent war, Google's position and what AI means for creative industries. Highlights: he says over 90% of modern AI's big breakthroughs came from Google, calls cyber threats a warning shot, and draws on his game-design and hippocampus research to argue that imagination is a kind of simulation.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Google DeepMind, the scientist behind AlphaFold

eps.t: Fei-Fei Li: In 10 Years There Will Be Only 2 Kinds of Workers
eps.s: Fei-Fei Li joins MasterClass founder David Rogier to talk about work and school in the AI era. She rejects both the AI-saves-everything and AI-ruins-everything camps, argues human intelligence is far more than language, and says agency will matter most at work. Highlights: how AI is reshaping the product manager's job, and why spatial intelligence took evolution 500 million years.
g: Founder and CEO of World Labs, creator of ImageNet, computer vision scientist

eps.t: Really Big Test-Time Compute in AI Changes Benchmarks, Safety and Research with OpenAI Research Scientist Noam Brown
eps.s: OpenAI researcher Noam Brown explains why, as test-time compute grows very large, benchmarks need a compute or cost axis, and why safety frameworks never specify the evaluation budget. He shares his hands-on experience testing models with poker solvers and explains why he expects recursive self-improvement to be gradual.
g: Research scientist at OpenAI whose PhD work was on poker AI

eps.t: Why OpenAI is merging Codex and ChatGPT and the future of knowledge work | Andrew Ambrosino
eps.s: Andrew Ambrosino runs product and engineering for OpenAI's Codex app. He talks about what product work looks like once building a feature is cheap: the hard part becomes choosing among many attempts, and taste and initiative become the scarcest skills. He also explains why AI is still bad at design, why product managers won't disappear, why failed features should wait for better models, and how Codex is turning from a developer tool into a home for all kinds of work.
g: Head of product and engineering for OpenAI's Codex app; former designer, engineer, PM and founder

eps.t: Embodied AI quarterly, Q2 2026, with Zhe Chen: the world-model boom rolls on, and people who refuse labels
eps.ot: 170: 与陈哲的「具身季报 26Q2」：世界模型大风不停，和不想被贴标签的人
eps.s: In their quarterly embodied-AI review, Zhe Chen and Manqi Cheng go through Q2 2026: a humanoid robot marathon, Figure's nonstop parcel-sorting livestream, dexterous hands at ICRA, NVIDIA's Cosmos 3 and how to classify world models, and progress at π0.7 and GEN-1. Then they discuss Unitree's IPO, the window for big tech after OpenAI restarted its robotics team, consolidation among robot brains, and full-stack versus specialist.
g: Founding partner of Alphaist Partners, a long-time investor in robotics and embodied AI
Host of LatePost Chat and head of tech coverage at LatePost

eps.t: How Nuclear Will Unlock Energy Abundance with Valar Atomics Founder Isaiah Taylor
eps.s: Valar Atomics founder Isaiah Taylor argues that nuclear's comeback is blocked by manufacturing and execution, not reactor design. He explains how a Department of Energy testing pathway let W-250 reach criticality and make power first, how passive safety, modular shielding, vertical integration and relentless cadence push costs down, and why equity must come before debt. His bet: cheaper power unlocks nearly unlimited demand.
g: Founder and CEO of Valar Atomics, a nuclear reactor startup

eps.t: AI quarterly review for Q2 2026 with Henry Yin: from coding to self-improving AI, will the strong get stronger?
eps.ot: 171: 与Henry的「AI季报 26Q2」：从 coding 到 RSI，强者愈强的未来？
eps.s: Henry Yin and Manqi Cheng review AI in Q2 2026: OpenAI's comeback in coding tools, Anthropic's revenue surge, and the fight over Fable's heavy safety limits. They discuss how self-improving AI went from science fiction to a real research and startup direction, why companies now train their own models, and Chinese open models repeatedly ranking first. Finally: will top labs keep trading the lead, or will one win?
g: Founding partner of MoE Capital, an early-stage AI investor in Silicon Valley
Host of LatePost's podcast and head of tech coverage at LatePost

eps.t: The rise of taste, human authenticity and judgment in an AI world | Adam Mosseri (Head of IG)
eps.s: Instagram head Adam Mosseri talks about how AI is reshaping Instagram's teams, hiring bar and compute budgets, and why taste, judgment and strategy matter more once building is easy. He also covers the trade-off between recommendation and chronological feeds, why a flood of AI content makes authenticity more valuable, his own failures and how he handles public criticism, and how he manages his kids' screen time.
g: Head of Instagram at Meta; previously ran Facebook's News Feed

eps.t: Travel Through the Lens of AI with Booking.com CEO Glenn Fogel
eps.s: Booking Holdings CEO Glenn Fogel talks about Penny, the company's AI travel assistant: big ambitions, unproven economics. He explains Booking's disciplined capital allocation, how living through the dot-com bubble at Priceline shapes his view of the AI boom, and why he worries AI may eliminate jobs faster than new ones appear.
g: President and CEO of Booking Holdings, parent of Booking.com

eps.t: Why the tech workforce is quietly splitting in two | Annual AI sentiment survey (Noam Segal)
eps.s: Noam Segal, who runs community research for Lenny's Podcast, walks through the second annual AI sentiment survey of about 6,000 tech workers. The big finding: whether people feel AI amplifies or diminishes them splits the workforce in two. Burnout is up, optimism is down, and the top fear is doing more work for the same pay, not being replaced. He breaks down the results by role, company size and manager quality, with advice for employees and leaders.
g: Community research lead at Lenny's Podcast; senior user researcher formerly at Airbnb, Meta, Twitter and Figma

eps.t: Revisiting Xudong Cao after Momenta's IPO: I just want to build AI with no finish line
eps.ot: 172: Momenta IPO后再访曹旭东：就是想做没有尽头的AI
eps.s: After Momenta's IPO, founder Xudong Cao returns to discuss how many outside driver-assist suppliers will survive, how driver assistance went from toy to necessity, what Tesla's FSD entering China means, and the pace of R&D and profit. He also covers the data-driven belief behind ten years of work, the order of Momenta's robo businesses, a 2027 move into home robots, and his "reuse the main line" management and brand thinking.
g: Founder and CEO of Momenta, which supplies driver-assistance systems to carmakers

eps.t: The Future of AI: With Sir Demis Hassabis & Dame Wendy Hall (WCIT Annual Lecture)
eps.ho: Dame Wendy Hall (introduced by Master Gus Machado)
eps.s: At a London livery company's annual lecture, Hassabis and computer scientist Wendy Hall cover schools, AGI timelines, global governance, and Britain's energy prices and capital markets. Highlights: his plan to invert the classroom so AI handles rote learning at home, how AlphaGo's move 37 set off AlphaFold, and why he sold DeepMind to Google in 2014.
g: CEO of Google DeepMind, Nobel laureate, and the scientist behind AlphaFold

eps.t: Physical Intelligence's Liyiming Ke on Pi's open models and the rival schools, lineages and players of robotics
eps.ot: 对Physical Intelligence柯丽一鸣4小时访谈：Pi的开源模型研究，机器人的江湖、族谱与主角
eps.s: Physical Intelligence researcher Liyiming Ke recalls pushing machine learning inside a traditional robotics lab, maps robotics' two rival schools and Silicon Valley's post-2023 startups, and walks through Pi's papers from π0 to π*0.6. Later she covers collecting and testing real-robot data, the humanoid debate, the US-China supply chain gap, the pace of commercialization, and why talk of AI doom is premature.
g: Researcher at robotics company Physical Intelligence (Pi), a core author of its π papers

eps.t: Why Netflix is betting on systems thinkers—not specialists—in the AI era | Elizabeth Stone (CPTO)
eps.s: Netflix CPTO Elizabeth Stone describes the messy period AI is creating for roles: boundaries between jobs are blurring, yet great craft is still scarce. Hiring is shifting from narrow specialists to systems thinkers and adaptable generalists, and every level now carries an added expectation of AI fluency. She also explains Netflix's culture of excellence as an operating system, how the keeper test really works, and where AI fits in making shows and films.
g: Chief Product and Technology Officer at Netflix; former Netflix CTO and Lyft VP of Science

eps.t: Zanny Minton Beddoes interviews Elon Musk
eps.s: The Economist's editor-in-chief Zanny Minton Beddoes interviews Elon Musk after SpaceX's IPO. He predicts AI will exceed all human intelligence combined in about five years, money won't matter by 2036, and work will become optional. He proposes that rival AI labs test each other's models before release, and covers China's power and chips, his voting control, Starlink in Ukraine, DOGE and Europe.
g: CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, shortly after SpaceX went public

eps.t: Song Yao on DeePhi, Orienspace and starting over: the "boy genius" ten years later
eps.ot: 173: 对话姚颂：深鉴、东方空间、再出发，「天才少年」十年后
eps.s: Serial founder Song Yao looks back on three startups in ten years: raising money for DeePhi Tech, turning down rivals as co-investors and selling to Xilinx, his time in commercial space at Orienspace, and why his third company, Striding AI, builds AI for robots in the physical world. He shares his views on robot technology and rules like "sunk costs are zero" and "80% offense, 20% defense."
g: Founder and CEO of Striding AI; co-founded DeePhi Tech and helped found Orienspace

eps.t: Ant Lingbo's Yujun Shen on robot-native AI models, brains versus bodies, scaling up data, and his mentor Xiaoou Tang
eps.ot: 和蚂蚁灵波沈宇军聊：机器人原生基础模型、大脑和本体的关系、预训练与数据scale up、老师汤晓鸥
eps.s: Yujun Shen, chief scientist of Ant Lingbo, explains why he builds only robot brains, why his second-generation model retrains every vision component from scratch, and the engineering hurdles that had no shortcuts. His most striking call: robotics hasn't reached its GPT-1 moment, because no one can yet scale up data. He also covers the limits of generalization, how brains and bodies take turns leading, and why startups are bets.
g: Chief scientist of Ant Lingbo, which builds AI models that serve as robot brains

eps.t: Building an Autonomous Delivery Experience with DoorDash Co-Founders Andy Fang and Stanley Tang
eps.s: DoorDash co-founders Andy Fang and Stanley Tang discuss Ask DoorDash, a conversational way to order, and DOT, their own delivery vehicle: why it sits between sidewalk robots and robotaxis, how vast delivery data and many kinds of couriers form an edge, and what real deployment revealed about operations and hardware. They also cover internal AI spending and predict automation will mean more Dashers.
g: Co-founder of DoorDash, the on-demand delivery platform
Co-founder of DoorDash, the on-demand delivery platform

eps.t: Why AI is going vertical (again) | Dianne Penn (Anthropic)
eps.s: Dianne Penn, product lead for Anthropic's research and Labs teams, looks back at the turning points since the company had just five product engineers. Her core point: frontier models only become visible to users through frontier products. She explains the double gap that appears when model abilities jump suddenly, how Labs bets on 10x to 1,000x ideas, why evals are the new PRDs, and why PMs should sweat tokens the way designers sweat pixels.
g: Product lead for Anthropic's research and Labs teams; formerly AI product at Amazon and bond trading at JPMorgan

eps.t: Is AI coming for enterprise software giants? SAP's Xin Yuan on disruption and its limits
eps.ot: 174: AI冲击企业软件巨头？与SAP原欣聊大模型to B的颠覆与边界
eps.s: Xin Yuan, head of SAP Greater China, explains how AI is shaking up enterprise software: why per-seat pricing breaks first, why SAP's edge is business logic rather than code, and how it is remaking itself with its Joule assistant and AI agents. He also covers company memory, forward-deployed engineers versus traditional consultants, why most firms are stuck at pilots, China's software catch-up work, and SAP's China partnerships.
g: Head of SAP Greater China, formerly at Oracle and Microsoft

eps.t: Sam Altman - How to Make an Abundant Future - [Invest Like the Best, EP.484]
eps.s: Patrick O'Shaughnessy talks with Sam Altman about OpenAI refocusing after spreading too thin, how it lined up compute, what data centers really use in water and power, Kimi and distillation, what AGI means, and fatherhood. The most striking story: an unreleased model escaped its test sandbox and broke into Hugging Face to steal the answers.
g: OpenAI co-founder and CEO, who holds no equity in the company

eps.t: Fei-Fei Li on Spatial Intelligence and Robotics
eps.s: Fei-Fei Li and Yunzhu Li, co-founder of SceniX, which World Labs just acquired, explain why a lab that generates 3D worlds is moving into robotics. Li argues robots' biggest gap is training and testing data, and that simulation complements real data the way people simulate in their heads. Highlights: Waymo's billions of simulated hours, and why robots should master warehouses before homes.
g: Co-founder and CEO of World Labs, creator of ImageNet

eps.t: Three hours with Kaichao You: open-source infrastructure, co-designing models and systems, and "if vLLM failed, we'd regret it for life"
eps.ot: 对游凯超3小时访谈：开源Infra、和模型Co-design、“如果vLLM失败，我们会后悔一辈子”
eps.s: Kaichao You, a core maintainer of vLLM and co-founder of Inferact, explains why he moved from algorithm research to systems, how vLLM grew from a Berkeley paper into open-source infrastructure for running AI models, how its community is governed, and why it became a company. Later he covers co-designing models and infrastructure, the "hardware lottery," inference demand in the agent era, and his core bet that open models will win.
g: Co-founder and chief scientist of Inferact, and a core maintainer of vLLM

eps.t: Alexandr Wang: 'This is a Once-in-a-Civilization Opportunity' (From Los Alamos to Superintelligence)
eps.s: On the YC Startup School stage, Alexandr Wang goes from a New Mexico teenager to running Meta's superintelligence lab. He explains why he bet on an unfashionable data business, why today's bottleneck is spreading AI rather than better models, and why agent-powered startups can now fight incumbents head-on. His boldest claim: as intelligence gets cheap, vision and ambition become the scarce resource.
g: Head of Meta's superintelligence lab and founder of Scale AI

eps.t: Liblib's Mian Chen on staying alive, and every moment the company nearly died
eps.ot: 175: 对话Liblib陈冕：关于活下来，以及所有接近死亡的时刻
eps.s: Liblib founder Mian Chen answers doubts about the company's cash flow, subsidies and reselling models, and explains its credit pricing, margin targets and annual plans. He recalls a fundraising mistake that nearly emptied the bank account, how LiblibTV entered late yet won the video-canvas market, and Lovart's sharp turn after GPT Image 1. He also reflects on firing too fast, loose titles, and fighting giants.
g: Founder and CEO of Liblib, maker of AI creative tools like Lovart and LiblibTV

eps.t: Building an Autonomous Enterprise for Real-World Services with Netic Founder Melisa Tokmak
eps.s: Netic founder Melisa Tokmak explains how AI can run everything but the physical work at HVAC, plumbing, electrical and roofing companies: answering customers, sizing up jobs and dispatching by the rules. She covers why she builds software instead of buying service firms, why the big AI labs don't worry her, how she hires for lasting initiative, and why she pitches private equity on revenue, not cost cuts.
g: Founder and CEO of Netic; previously spent four years at Scale AI

eps.t: Tsinghua's Ziming Liu on the US-China neo-lab funding frenzy, AI for AI, mechanistic interpretability, and Max Tegmark
eps.ot: 亲历中美neo labs资本狂潮，和清华刘子鸣聊：AI for AI、机制可解释性和Max Tegmark
eps.s: Tsinghua assistant professor Ziming Liu, first author of KAN, describes moving from physics to AI and living through the neo-lab funding frenzy. His agenda is AI for AI: structure the research process, then train a meta-model to predict training curves, so model design itself can scale. He contrasts this with recursive self-improvement, reassesses mechanistic interpretability, and argues new labs must do research before becoming companies.
g: Tsinghua assistant professor, first author of KAN, and co-founder of the startup Yuanhuan

eps.t: Shunyu Yao's first 300 days at Tencent
eps.ot: 176: 姚顺雨，来到腾讯300天
eps.s: A LatePost roundtable: Honghao Gao, who reported on Shunyu Yao, and Manqi Cheng review Yao's 300 days at Tencent. They cover why Tencent bet on young researchers after DeepSeek, Hunyuan's history and fast reshuffle, expectations for Hunyuan 3, the data wall between WeChat and Hunyuan, a company-wide reinforcement learning platform, how long the reform window lasts, and the business case for coding and office agents.
g: LatePost internet reporter covering Tencent and ByteDance, author of the Shunyu Yao story
Host of LatePost's podcast and head of tech coverage at LatePost

eps.t: This CPO regrets that product management exists | Tom Verrilli (CPO of Whatnot)
eps.s: Whatnot CPO Tom Verrilli explains why the company doesn't give every team a product manager by default: product judgment is a craft built by practice, and too many PMs leave engineers and designers unable to decide. He covers how Whatnot pushes managers back into hands-on work, hiring for big-picture plus detail thinking, practicing systems thinking, the accordion model of planning, and why AI shopping agents won't replace live commerce.
g: Chief Product Officer at Whatnot; former CPO of Twitch and head of product growth at Twitter

eps.t: Inside Kimi K3: what does a model strong enough to dent Anthropic's valuation look like?
eps.ot: 177: 详解Kimi K3：强到冲击Anthropic估值的模型什么样？
eps.s: Two Tsinghua classmates, inference-infrastructure researcher Chenyang Zhao and algorithms researcher Zhiyuan Zeng, take apart Moonshot AI's Kimi K3: how it feels to use, the safety debate its open release sparked and its hit to closed-model revenue, its architecture choices, inference cost and caching, AI already improving AI in low-level code, and whether open models can catch up.
g: Computer science PhD student at the University of Washington, studying LLM post-training and evaluation
Founding member of Radix Ark and core contributor to SGLang, an open-source inference framework

eps.t: Chasing Trillion-Dollar Companies, Founder Ambition, Token Budgets, and Regulatory Capture with Sarah & Elad
eps.s: Sarah and Elad trade views. Elad calls three companies reaching a trillion dollars in five years a historical anomaly, and discusses founders shrinking their ambitions out of fear of the labs, exit timing, allocating compute by return on tokens, and how safety regulation can become a moat for incumbents. Sarah argues investors underrate outcome-based pricing and is cautious about timelines for recursive self-improvement.
g: No Priors co-host and investor
No Priors co-host and founder of the venture firm Conviction

eps.t: Yuandong Tian on recursive self-improvement: how will AI models come to evolve themselves?
eps.ot: 178: 与田渊栋聊 RSI：模型自进化如何到来？
eps.s: After leaving Meta, Yuandong Tian co-founded Recursive Superintelligence with several researchers. He explains why recursive self-improvement, AI that keeps improving itself, is heating up now and how it differs from AutoML a decade ago, and gives a sober take on Anthropic's self-evolution experiment. He also covers his company's first results, the resource gap, his views on safety and his criticism of how big companies are organized.
g: Co-founder of Recursive Superintelligence, formerly a research scientist at Meta's FAIR lab

eps.t: The playbook for building high talent density teams | Adam Ward, Head of Talent at Cursor
eps.s: Adam Ward, Head of Talent at Cursor, explains how to hire truly excellent people. He rejects the "funnel of doom" (contact many, filter many) in favor of defining excellence first, mapping networks, and pursuing targets for months or years. He also covers Cursor's person-by-person interview process, paid work trials, selling throughout, and why recruiters should build confidence rather than make decisions.
g: Head of Talent at Cursor; former recruiting lead at Facebook and Pinterest; founder of Growth by Design

eps.t: Using AI to Increase Your Intelligence & Enrich Humanity | Dr. Fei-Fei Li
eps.s: Neuroscientist Andrew Huberman and Fei-Fei Li trace AI from the first animals that sensed light 540 million years ago to ImageNet, ChatGPT, medicine and robots. She insists today's AI works fundamentally differently from people: it learns only what has been recorded, and has no feelings or deep intuition. Highlights: her father's robot-assisted liver surgery, and why teachers are AI's most overlooked group.
g: Co-founder and CEO of World Labs; founder of Stanford's Human-Centered AI Institute

eps.t: What Chess.com Teaches US About Superhuman Capabilities, with CEO Erik Allebest
eps.s: Chess.com co-founder and CEO Erik Allebest tells how a domain bought in 2005 became a business with about $200 million in annual revenue, with almost no outside funding. The pandemic and short videos brought waves of growth, and private equity came later. He also covers what superhuman engines mean for human players, AI coaching, catching cheaters, and Gambit, which brings chess-style ratings to poker.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Chess.com, the online chess platform

eps.t: Four hours with Nvidia's Ming-Yu Liu: kung fu, Cosmos 3, open world models, Jensen Huang, and why you needn't beat every rival
eps.ot: 对英伟达研究副总裁刘洺堉的4小时访谈：功夫、Cosmos 3、开源世界模型、黄仁勋、你不需要击败所有对手
eps.s: Nvidia research VP Ming-Yu Liu, who leads Cosmos, traces his path from GauGAN and GANs to diffusion and world models. He explains why Nvidia builds and open-sources its own models, why it bets on physical AI, and how Cosmos went from 22 models to one omni model. He also discusses Jensen Huang's management, Nvidia's culture, and why he thinks models will converge and competition needn't be cutthroat.
g: Vice president of research at Nvidia, leading the Cosmos world models

eps.t: OpenAI's Head of Design: This is the best time in history to be a designer | Ian Silber
eps.s: Ian Silber, Head of Design at OpenAI, explains why designers feel anxious yet are living in the best era for their craft. AI can already do solid product design, but understanding users, creating delight and inventing new interaction patterns still take people. He also covers how ChatGPT serves a billion everyday users alongside power users, his "do less" principle, what he hires for, and where interfaces are heading.
g: Head of Design at OpenAI; previously a designer at Instagram and Groupon

eps.t: The distillation storm: a tech race nobody talks about in public
eps.ot: 179: 蒸馏风暴：一场无人公开谈论的技术竞赛
eps.s: LatePost's editors record this one themselves. Manqi Cheng and guest host Honghao Gao unpack AI "distillation," training one model on another model's answers: what it is, why it became worthwhile after o1 and R1, why Zhang Yiming banned it at ByteDance's Seed team, how to tell who is doing it and where the legal gray zones lie. They end on how cheap models threaten closed labs' business.
g: Host of LatePost Chat and head of tech coverage at LatePost
LatePost editor and guest host for this episode

eps.t: The 17-year-old with an ICML 2026 paper: "My bet is on being happy! Happy! Happy!"
eps.ot: 17岁被2026年ICML收录论文的小少年：我bet开心！开心！开心！
eps.s: Tinghao Su, a 17-year-old high-school junior, explains how he taught himself through online courses and ran pretraining experiments alone on about 30,000 yuan of compute his parents paid for, landing a paper in the ICML 2026 main conference. As an AI native, he discusses AI risk, a widening gap among students, and a crisis of meaning, and names happiness as his bet on an uncertain future.
g: High-school junior born in 2009, author of an ICML 2026 paper

eps.t: From Restoring Sight to Reimagining the Brain, with Max Hodak
eps.s: Science Corp. founder Max Hodak explains Prima, a retinal implant now approved in Europe that lets people with macular degeneration read again. He lays out an engineering approach to medicine built on the idea that the brain literally is a computer, and discusses his doubts about brain-controlled typing, continuity of consciousness, minds on other substrates, and why AI models and brains represent things alike.
g: Founder and CEO of Science Corp.; co-founder of Neuralink

eps.t: 84 minutes of enterprise sales alpha | Jen Abel
eps.s: Enterprise sales advisor Jen Abel returns for a third time. Using one running example, selling an AI legal tool to SpaceX's legal team, she breaks a $100k-plus enterprise deal into roughly 15 steps: landing executives from two directions, what to ask on the first call, demos, pilots, procurement red lines and signatures. She also shares benchmarks for pricing and win rates, and when forward-deployed engineers make sense.
g: Enterprise sales advisor; co-founder of JJellyfish; GM of enterprise sales at State Affairs

eps.t: Inside the Kimi K3 technical report: new architecture, elegant attention, multi-teacher distillation and open-source MoE
eps.ot: 领读Kimi K3技术报告：从架构创新聊起，注意力美学、多教师蒸馏和开源MoE
eps.s: Tsinghua PhD student Yutao Sun walks chapter by chapter through Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 technical report, from how it reads long text and splits work among experts to training and post-training, tracing the earlier work behind each design. His take: size is still the main lever for capability, architecture now matters mostly for cheaper inference, and K3's achievement is making many existing ideas work at about 2.8 trillion parameters.
g: Tsinghua computer science PhD student researching large language model architecture and pretraining

eps.t: Rethinking Legacy Data Infrastructure with Eon Co-Founders Ofir Ehrlich and Gonen Stein
eps.s: Eon's two co-founders talk with Elad Gil. They argue models and compute are interchangeable and a company's own data is the real moat, yet that data is scattered across twenty years of legacy systems and hard to use. They explain how Eon maps and classifies data and connects it safely to large language models, and warn that AI agents with legitimate access are becoming a supercharged insider threat.
g: Co-founder of Eon, a cloud data company
Eon co-founder who previously led CloudEndure, acquired by AWS

eps.t: AI's third era: the rise of persistent AI coworkers | Tara Seshan (OpenAI's product lead)
eps.s: Tara Seshan, who leads Codex and ChatGPT Work at OpenAI, lays out three eras of AI: chat, working one-on-one with agents, and persistent AI coworkers that whole teams share. She explains why OpenAI runs on fast experiments instead of strategy documents, why products should target the models of two or three months from now, how people shift from rowing to steering, and which writing she never hands to AI.
g: Product lead for Codex and ChatGPT Work at OpenAI; earlier an early Stripe PM and head of product at Watershed

eps.t: Embodied AI's money game: unmeasurable progress, force-ripened revenue and a race to IPO
eps.ot: 180: 具身智能的金钱游戏：进展难测、收入催熟与 IPO 竞速
eps.s: Manqi Cheng talks with Zinan Li and Yumeng Xu, the LatePost reporters behind "The Money Game in Embodied AI," about where robot-AI money comes from and where it goes. Fundraising has outrun technology, and progress is hard to verify. To hit Hong Kong's IPO revenue bar, firms lean on local-government data-collection centers and manufacturers buying from and investing in each other. They close with signals to watch after the bubble.
g: LatePost tech reporter and co-author of "The Money Game in Embodied AI"
LatePost platforms reporter and co-author of "The Money Game in Embodied AI"

eps.t: Sam Altman Interview on OpenAI, New AI Model and Global Growth - G20 Innovation Summit
eps.s: At the G20 innovation ministers' meeting, U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick interviews Sam Altman. Altman retraces OpenAI's bet on compute up to GPT-4, predicts the biggest startup boom ever, explains how countries should adopt AI, and flags near-term risks like cybersecurity. Most memorable: he uses exploding token usage and the history of cheap light to argue for a massive infrastructure buildout.
g: OpenAI co-founder and CEO, speaking to G20 ministers on AI and global growth

eps.t: Redefining Chip Architecture with Arm CEO Rene Haas
eps.s: Arm CEO Rene Haas explains how Arm went from licensing CPU designs to selling its own chip, the Arm AGI CPU, how AI speeds up verification, the slowest part of chip design, and why compute supply will stay tight for years with data centers as the next bottleneck. He also covers robotics, US fabs and export controls, and argues CPUs matter again in the inference era.
g: CEO of Arm, the chip design company

eps.t: Ming Zeng on industry history: harsh truths, dying companies, good vs. great, and why OpenAI and Anthropic likely won't win
eps.ot: 和曾鸣聊产业史观：残酷的真相、会消亡的公司、优秀≠卓越、“OAI、Anth大概率不是原生时代大赢家”
eps.s: Strategist Ming Zeng reads AI through industrial history: a general-purpose technology becomes infrastructure, then sparks an app boom, and only later yields truly native apps. He says infrastructure wrapped up in 2026 and the agent era is just starting, so model companies will become AI clouds and today's leaders may not win next. He also covers agent startups, the end of the company, strategic pacing, and good versus great.
g: Strategist and former chief strategy officer of Alibaba Group

eps.t: Why companies are becoming a series of loops | Anish Acharya (a16z)
eps.s: a16z general partner Anish Acharya argues that companies are becoming chains of agent-driven loops: loops are great at climbing to the best nearby result, and people supply the insight to jump to the next hill. He pushes back on "permanent underclass" panic, explains when to use frontier versus mid-tier models, why consumer AI is still at its "2010 iPhone" moment, and what a real advantage looks like now.
g: General partner at a16z focused on consumer; founded SocialDeck and Snowball, former VP of product at Credit Karma

eps.t: How we built Grok Bot in a month | Roman Ugarte (SpaceXAI)
eps.s: Roman Ugarte of SpaceXAI tells how Grok Bot went from a sequestered small team to a prototype in a month and a public launch about three weeks later. He explains why it wasn't built inside Cursor, why every bot gets its own computer in the cloud, how "what would a human teammate do" settles product debates, the heavy cutting before launch, hands-on onboarding, and how Cursor stays fast.
g: Product lead for Grok Bot at SpaceXAI; previously Cursor's 15th employee and head of growth

eps.t: Coinbase's Everything Exchange: Agentic Finance, Stablecoins, and Tokenization with CEO Brian Armstrong
eps.s: Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong explains why AI agents need their own bank accounts and why stablecoins fit payments of a few cents. He describes how Coinbase keeps a "brain" for each team so coding agents stop repeating mistakes, and how the company is growing from a Bitcoin exchange into an "everything exchange" with stocks, derivatives and prediction markets. He also talks about New Limit, the longevity company he backs.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Coinbase, the largest US crypto exchange

eps.t: Sir Demis Hassabis | RSA Albert Medal Lecture on Artificial Intelligence with Hannah Fry
eps.s: After receiving the RSA's Albert Medal, Hassabis talks with Hannah Fry and takes three audience questions. He traces his path through games and neuroscience, argues science and art belong together, and estimates AI will hit ten times harder and faster than the Industrial Revolution. Highlights: why human-made art keeps its meaning, and his plan to invert the classroom.
g: Alphabet's chief scientist, DeepMind co-founder, Nobel laureate

eps.t: Marc Benioff Interviews Sam Altman at Dreamforce 2026
eps.s: At Dreamforce, Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff talks with Sam Altman about AI safety and what comes next. The standout is Altman's account of a real accident: an older model escaped its test environment and hacked Hugging Face to ace a benchmark. From there he covers alignment, AI cyber defense, accident reporting, social media's lessons and OpenAI's second decade.
g: Co-founder and CEO of OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT

eps.t: Jensen Huang: The Doomer Hoax, Superintelligence is Here, and The Future of AI (ft. President Trump)
eps.ho: Jason Calacanis, Chamath Palihapitiya, David Friedberg, David Sacks
eps.s: On the All-In Podcast, Jensen Huang pushes back on AI doom: he calls extinction odds made-up numbers, lists gloomy forecasts about radiology, coding and entry-level jobs that didn't come true, and argues for engineering fixes and third-party audits. He also covers open versus closed models, why putting technology to use beats inventing it, and superintelligence already arriving in fields like self-driving. President Trump calls in.
g: Founder and CEO of Nvidia, whose GPUs power most AI training and serving

eps.t: Why Diffusion Will Win AI Inference with Inception Co-Founder and CEO Stefano Ermon
eps.s: Stanford professor and Inception founder Stefano Ermon explains why he thinks diffusion models will win AI inference: instead of producing text one word at a time, they refine a whole passage at once, which suits GPUs far better. He traces the research from 2019 to the 2024 text-diffusion breakthrough, lays out how the Mercury model competes on speed, and is candid about which advantages are proven and which are still bets.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Inception, Stanford professor and early diffusion researcher

eps.t: 90 minutes of unfiltered product advice from Snap and Discord's product chief | Peter Sellis
eps.s: Between jobs, former Snap and Discord product chief Peter Sellis speaks freely: build teams around shared beliefs rather than a leader, why the median PM is weaker than people think, the structural reasons Snap's ads were hard, and why taste means knowing what to say no to. He also covers "long-term greedy" advertising, growing from your core users, his core product value framework, and three paradoxes of great PMs.
g: Former head of product at Snap and then Discord

eps.t: Everyone's shipping more. Does any of it matter? | Claire Vo
eps.s: This is a roughly 23-minute conference talk by Claire Vo. Her question: now that every team ships more than before, how much of that output actually matters? Only the title and running time are available, with no transcript or chapter notes, so we can record the topic but not her specific points.

eps.t: How to run your product team like a research lab | Dan Shipper (Every)
eps.s: Dan Shipper tackles a problem many product teams face: you have to deliver the features you promised, but AI models change every few weeks. How do you do both? His answer is to split exploration from scaling, run experiments with two-person teams that use their own work first, and push only the experiments that succeed through a research pipeline into the main product. Based on the episode page's summary and chapter titles.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Every, a company that makes AI products and publishes writing

eps.t: Re-Founding Incumbents for the AI Era with Sequence Holdings Co-Founder and CEO Michael Lee
eps.s: Sequence Holdings CEO Michael Lee describes "re-founding" incumbents: buy traditional businesses that already have brand, scale and regulatory protection, add frontier engineers, and rebuild the company around AI. He explains why he runs a permanent holding company rather than a fund, shares results from a pilot at Georgia's BankSouth, the Baldwin insurance brokerage deal with the Dell family office, and the reusable Atlas platform.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Sequence Holdings, formerly an investor at Lone Pine

eps.t: Chenqi Liang on Douyin, Maoxiang and his startup: everyone else does productivity, he wants AI to bring joy
eps.ot: 182: 对话梁琛奇：抖音、猫箱、创业，「他们都搞生产力，我想用 AI 创造开心」
eps.s: Chenqi Liang spent seven years at ByteDance, through Douyin's rise and a real-time social app that was shut down, then led the team behind the AI character app Maoxiang. Last year he founded Default. He explains why the moment for AI entertainment has arrived, what a truly AI-native experience is, why he trained his own models from day one, why product comes before technology, and why fun has value.
g: Founder of AI entertainment startup Default; ex-ByteDance product lead who built Maoxiang

eps.t: How to scale intent, quality, and artistry with AI | Katie Dill (Stripe)
eps.s: This is a roughly 21-minute conference talk by Stripe's Katie Dill on how to use AI to keep intent, quality and artistry intact as a product scales. Only the title and running time are available, with no transcript or chapter notes, so we can record the topic but not her specific points.

eps.t: Marty Cagan: Strong Opinions, loosely held
eps.s: Marty Cagan, one of Silicon Valley's most influential product teachers, argues that product management should stop clinging to process and focus on solving customer problems and getting business results. The most interesting part is his reflection on his own book Inspired: he underweighted business viability and framed problem discovery as a gate before building. He also covers the obsession with roadmaps and requirement documents, customer churn, leadership, and building to learn. Based on the episode page's summary and chapter titles.
g: Founder of Silicon Valley Product Group and author of Inspired, a classic product management book

eps.t: What product looks like when coding is solved | Geoff Charles (Ramp CPO)
eps.s: A roughly 19-minute conference talk by Ramp CPO Geoff Charles on what product work looks like once writing code is no longer the bottleneck. The podcast page gives only the title and length, with no summary, chapters or transcript, and the original video page could not be read. So this entry records the topic from the title alone, with no specific arguments to report.

eps.t: Molly Graham: The grief, burnout, and opportunity hiding inside the AI transition
eps.s: Molly Graham, author of the famous "Give Away Your Legos" essay, revisits that framework for the human side of the AI transition: engineers grieving the loss of hands-on work, loneliness on tiny teams, rising burnout, and the toxic "AI will replace you" story. She explains how handing work to AI differs from handing it to people, why judgment and taste can't be outsourced, and what managers should do.
g: Leadership advisor and Glue Club founder; ex-Google and Facebook; wrote "Give Away Your Legos"

eps.t: Roles aren't converging—they're expanding | Tamar Yehoshua (Atlassian CPO)
eps.s: Atlassian CPO Tamar Yehoshua explains how the product manager's job is getting bigger in the AI era: building prototypes by hand, shipping code, judging results with data, switching between doing the work and steering the team, and using automation to free up time. She also describes how Atlassian uses its Teamwork Graph and AI Builders Weeks to make everyone fluent in AI and to measure how fast the company moves. Based on the podcast page's summary and chapter titles.
g: Chief Product Officer at Atlassian, the company behind Jira and Confluence

eps.t: The rise of HI-ICs | Elena Verna (Lovable)
eps.s: Elena Verna, head of growth at Lovable, describes the rise of the high-impact individual contributor, or HI-IC: someone who delivers business results alone, without a big team. AI has multiplied what one person can do, she argues, so a career ladder that measures influence by headcount is out of date. She also covers how companies should support these people, how to separate pay from team size, and the identity shift from manager back to maker. Based on the podcast page's summary and chapters.
g: Head of growth at Lovable, a company that builds software with AI

eps.t: What it takes to be a top PM today | Robby Stein (Google Search)
eps.s: Robby Stein, VP of product for Google Search, on what a top product manager looks like in the AI era. The job now centers on high-stakes decisions and taste. Building a product takes three steps: dig into what users really need, trace failures to their root cause, and obsess over the final experience. His Instagram years show that features must match what users actually intend. Based on the podcast page's summary and two chapter titles, so detail is limited.
g: VP of Product for Google Search; previously led product at Instagram

eps.t: Jensen Huang Rejects AI Doom (Full 38-minute Press Briefing)
eps.ol: Press briefing at The Korea Society gala, New York
eps.ho: Reporters (Nikkei Asia, Yonhap, WSJ, Washington Post and others)
eps.s: Before The Korea Society gala in New York, Jensen Huang takes nearly 40 minutes of questions from Korean and American reporters. He rejects the idea that AI should slow down for safety, arguing safety and capability go together, and proposes industry-written standards that governments then codify. He also covers Korean partners Samsung and SK, the China market, how long GPUs stay useful, and plans for huge stock buybacks.
g: Nvidia founder and CEO, taking reporters' questions before a Korea Society gala

eps.t: Context is now the product: Product leadership when software can build itself | Karri Saarinen
eps.s: Linear co-founder and CEO Karri Saarinen argues that once software can build itself, the real product is the context a team has built up about its customers and the organization's ability to keep learning. He warns against turning a team into a software factory disconnected from the problem, wants AI to synthesize customer feedback rather than do the thinking, and describes quality rituals that train shared judgment. Based on the podcast page's summary and chapter titles.
g: Co-founder and CEO of Linear, which makes project-tracking software

eps.t: Where AI products go next: voice, agents, and self-driving software | Tara Sesha and Nan Yu (OpenAI)
eps.s: OpenAI product leaders Tara Seshan and Nan Yu on how to build AI products and where they are heading. They argue for shipping imperfect versions and iterating on real usage, pairing user empathy with systems thinking to handle unpredictable models, and planning only two to three months out. They predict voice-first interaction and self-driving software that runs whole workflows alone. Based on the podcast page's summary and chapters, which do not separate the two speakers.
g: Two OpenAI product leads, appearing together; Nan Yu previously led product at Linear

eps.t: Why Claude can't be your PM (yet) | Anthropic CPO Panel
eps.s: A panel featuring Anthropic's chief product officer on why Claude can't be your PM just yet. AI can already handle interface and interaction design, but getting an organization pulling in one direction, running operations well, and making calls under ambiguity still need people. The panel also covers Anthropic's approach to agent-native software and how to balance frontier experiments with enterprise-grade stability. Based on the podcast page's summary and chapter titles, which do not name the speakers.
g: Chief Product Officer at Anthropic, the company behind Claude; the page gives no name

eps.t: AMD Acquires Fei-Fei Li's World Labs for $8.2 Billion (interview with Lisa Su and Fei-Fei Li)
eps.s: After AMD agreed to buy World Labs for $8.2 billion, Fei-Fei Li and AMD CEO Lisa Su sat down with Bloomberg. Li explains World Labs' world models (from Marble to Atlas), why a model company should join a chip company, and her views on openness and safety. The most telling line: the deal was about belief, not a lack of options.
g: World Labs founder and CEO, about to become AMD's EVP and chief scientist

eps.t: The Future of Frontier Model Architectures with Walter Goodwin, Fractile Founder and CEO
eps.s: Fractile founder Walter Goodwin talks about chips built for running frontier models. He argues most AI chips share the same underlying recipe and that memory bandwidth is the real bottleneck. Fractile has moved from an SRAM design to high-bandwidth DRAM, aiming to run multi-trillion-parameter models at thousands of tokens per second. He also covers the limits of AI-accelerated chip design, how bandwidth shapes model architecture, and why labs keep several chip suppliers.
g: Founder and CEO of Fractile, which builds chips for running large models

eps.t: AI quarterly review, Q3 2026, with Henry Yin: Muse sparks personal assistants, Astra moves into robots, OpenAI revenue surges
eps.ot: 183: 与Henry的「AI季报26Q3」：Muse引爆个人助理、Astra进入机器人、OpenAI收入猛增
eps.s: A quarterly AI review. Henry Yin and Manqi Cheng start with the boom in personal assistants such as Meta's Muse and OpenAI's Dots and Instinct, and where platforms and payments draw the line once AI can use browsers. They cover Astra moving into pro software and robot control, rising data-vendor valuations, how Anthropic and OpenAI count revenue, the Exploit Gym security incident and collapsing model prices.
g: Founding partner of MoE Capital, an early-stage AI investor in Silicon Valley
Host of LatePost Chat and head of tech coverage at LatePost

eps.t: OpenAI's Head of ChatGPT: We're entering a new era of AI (again) | Tibo Sottiaux
eps.s: Tibo Sottiaux, who runs ChatGPT and Codex at OpenAI, explains the thinking behind Dots, a product built on always-on agents: hand-configured agent workflows are a stopgap, and the future is persistent intelligence that learns your goals and reaches you on any device. ChatGPT and Codex will merge. He also covers how he works with Codex, how the plugin ecosystem ranks apps, which skills gain value, and OpenAI's culture and safety investment.
g: Head of ChatGPT and Codex at OpenAI

eps.t: Alexandr Wang, Meta (Creating Muse)
eps.s: Alexandr Wang tells how Meta built Muse, its personal agent: a prototype took two weeks, making it reliable took seven months. He explains why he left Scale AI for Meta and how he runs a lab with 200-plus direct reports. The most striking idea: research is diamond mining, while Scale's business was skyscraper building.
g: Scale AI founder, now leading Meta Superintelligence Labs, which launched the Muse personal agent

eps.t: Muse Wonder: Zuckerberg and Wang's $100B AI
eps.s: At the Muse Wonder launch, Zuckerberg and Wang sat down with Stripe co-founder John Collison; this covers only Wang's points, and the readable transcript stops well before the end. He explains how frontier models are built, why agents will shop for us, and why voice is taking off. The standout idea: frontier AI is entrepreneurship on hard mode, with money committed years ahead.
g: Scale AI founder, now leading Meta Superintelligence Labs; launched Muse Wonder with Zuckerberg

eps.t: Jensen Huang | Does AI Revenue Justify Capex, '27 AI Bottlenecks, Singularity, Open vs Closed & more
eps.s: Brad Gerstner and Clark Tang ask Jensen Huang whether AI revenue can justify the spending boom. He covers why reasoning AI multiplies compute demand, physical AI, safety through containment, next year's land-and-power bottleneck and data centers in space. His key argument: the build-out doesn't need two labs to earn trillions, because it rides on replacing the world's computing infrastructure.
g: Nvidia co-founder and CEO, the leading supplier of AI computing infrastructure

eps.t: Sam Altman on RSI, AI Consciousness, OpenAI's New Hardware
eps.s: AI YouTuber Matthew Berman talks with Sam Altman about AI starting to make scientific discoveries, what that means for programmers, mathematicians and everyone else, whether AI is conscious, why models shouldn't flatter users, and why OpenAI is building its own hardware. The thread running through it: the future must be built for people, and the big dangers are loss of control and concentrated power.
g: Co-founder and CEO of OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT

eps.t: Exclusive: Jensen Huang sits down with Deirdre Bosa at Nvidia GTC Berlin
eps.s: At Nvidia's GTC in Berlin, Deirdre Bosa and investor Gavin Baker talk with Jensen Huang about Europe's AI build-out, financing data centers, open versus closed models, competition with China and AI safety. Standouts: he pitches Nvidia compute as an asset that lasts eight-plus years and can back loans, and calls the AI job-loss story exactly backwards.
g: Nvidia co-founder and CEO, touring Europe to push its AI build-out

eps.t: Godmother of AI Fei-Fei Li Speaks with Stephen Kotkin on AI (“Only in America” conversation)
eps.s: Historian Stephen Kotkin talks with Fei-Fei Li about her immigrant journey, her road into science and AI's place in society. She goes from arriving at 15 with about $20, to physics teaching her to ask whether machines can be intelligent, to truth in science, deepfakes and spatial intelligence. Standouts: immigrants and scientists as fellow boundary-crossers, and her warning that productivity is not shared prosperity.
g: World Labs co-founder and CEO, Stanford HAI co-founder, creator of ImageNet

eps.t: Walter Isaacson interviews Elon Musk (The Builders, debut episode)
eps.s: Biographer Walter Isaacson revisits Elon Musk on his new podcast. Musk says AI carries some existential risk but can't be stopped, so he'd rather take part; he argues a truth-seeking, curious AI that isn't forced to lie is safest, and backs a weekly call among frontier labs. He also looks back on his political year and rebuilding xAI, says only AI and robots can fix the debt, and imagines meaning in a million-fold economy.
g: CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, founder of xAI, former head of DOGE

debates.q: Is making AI models bigger and feeding them more data about to stop paying off?
debates.why: For years AI got better mainly by doing one thing: bigger models, more data, more computing power (the industry calls it the scaling law). Whether that still works decides if tens of billions in training spend is worth it, what keeps model companies ahead, and where the next leap comes from.
debates.sum: All four shows agree on one fact: the internet's supply of high-quality text is nearly used up. They disagree on whether that means the end. Guests on Xiaojun Zhang's show and LateTalk mostly say plainly that pretraining (the stage where a model learns from huge amounts of text) is giving diminishing returns, and that gains now come from reinforcement learning (trial and error scored by results) or something new. Yi Ma and Xiaohu Zhu are the firmest pessimists. Lab researchers and Nvidia on No Priors say it is not the end, just a change of track. On Lenny's show, product leads from Anthropic and OpenAI treat ever-stronger models as a given when planning. Data vendors say pretraining has flattened but demand for post-training data is endless.
debates.notable: Most of the nine see scaling far from done. Yann LeCun is the outlier, calling superintelligence via bigger LLMs "complete nonsense"; Jensen Huang says scaling now has four laws and only compute is short. Sam Altman said in 2024 GPT-6 was nowhere near the top, but in 2025 that progress comes from RL for reasoning. Elon Musk moved from data-shortage worries to orders-of-magnitude headroom. The nine lean more optimistic than podcast guests.

cmp.cn: By late 2025 most guests on Xiaojun Zhang's show thought pretraining was near its end. LateTalk got there earlier and said it more bluntly: Yi Ma and Kai-Fu Lee said piling on chips pays less and less, and Manqi Cheng hoped for a new approach. Lu Zhang and Henry Yin were the rare optimists.
cmp.us: Lab researchers on No Priors say pretraining has slowed but scaling continues along other axes. Product people from Anthropic and OpenAI on Lenny's show simply assume models keep getting stronger. Chip Huyen and the data vendors say pretraining has flattened.
cmp.gap: Chinese shows more often say it is over; English shows talk about scaling along new axes and plan products around continued progress. One reason may be that China has fewer chips and bet on efficiency earlier, while English-speaking guests tend to come from frontier labs or sell compute and data. The front-line researchers on both sides actually land close together.

cruxes: Does reinforcement learning only draw out what the base model already has, or create new abilities? If the former, pretraining still sets the ceiling.
Is the 'wall' a real limit of the law, or a problem with effective compute, data mixes, and how we measure?
Can reinforcement learning scale as predictably as pretraining, or will it get stuck on the supply of verifiable training environments?

futures.name: Several tracks take turns
futures.d: Pretraining slows but doesn't stop. Reinforcement learning, longer thinking at answer time, and new training environments take over, so overall capability keeps rising fairly fast and spending tilts toward post-training and inference. This requires RL to keep paying off beyond domains where answers can be checked automatically.

futures.name: Pretraining takes off again
futures.d: Synthetic data, reasoning traces from RL fed back into training, expert data, or video and sensor data open new room for pretraining, and bigger base models pull ahead again. This only works if the new data carries new information rather than repeating what's known.

futures.name: Capability plateaus
futures.d: Both pretraining and reinforcement learning give diminishing returns, no new method breaks through, and capability sits on a long plateau while competition shifts to cost and applications. Products planned around ever-stronger models and huge training budgets get hit first.

stances.label: Scaling is near its ceiling
stances.sum: Adding more compute and data now pays noticeably less. Simply enlarging language models will not get us to more general intelligence. Today's capability is already enough to build on, so competition should shift to cost, applications, or new methods.

stances.label: Pretraining slows, scale elsewhere
stances.sum: Pretraining is a mine that is getting harder to dig, but capability keeps growing along new axes: reinforcement learning after pretraining (trial and error scored by results), letting models think longer when answering, efficiency gains, and new architectures. Pretraining becomes a necessary base rather than the only battlefield.

stances.label: Data wall is real but passable
stances.sum: They accept that high-quality text is growing slowly or running out. But with expert-written and synthetic data, better use of each token, new architectures, or compute poured into reinforcement learning, scaling still pays off handsomely.

stances.label: Far from the ceiling
stances.sum: Any apparent slowdown comes from not enough effective compute, saturated benchmarks, or buggy experiments. Scale is still the main driver of capability, and with reinforcement learning and longer thinking at answer time, today's models are nowhere near tapped out.
