debates.q: What will make AI smarter next: more of the current recipe, or a brand-new approach?
debates.why: The easy gains from pretraining (learning from huge amounts of text) are slowing. Betting on the right next step decides who stays ahead, and where new labs and investors should put their money.
debates.sum: All four shows agree the workhorse today is pretraining plus reinforcement learning (learn from massive text, then improve through trial and error scored by results). Front-line researchers and data vendors mostly think this recipe is enough; the hard part is designing rewards and training environments. The split is over what comes next. Xiaojun Zhang's show, by late 2025, leaned toward online learning and memory stored inside the model's weights. LateTalk and No Priors spent 2026 debating AI training AI, and most judged it would be gradual. Lenny's show stayed close to product and data and rarely discussed new paradigms. Those betting on world models and new architectures are mostly people founding companies to build them.
axis: New approach: online learning, world models, AI training AI
debates.notable: Most of the nine doubt today's recipe suffices. Yann LeCun calls LLMs largely obsolete within five years; Fei-Fei Li bets on spatial intelligence, founding World Labs. Alexandr Wang says reasoning plus RL is enough. Demis Hassabis says continual learning is missing. Jensen Huang said in 2023 AI shouldn't learn on the job, but in 2026 that Transformers aren't universal. Podcast guests' top pick is the current recipe; the nine lean toward a new paradigm.

cmp.cn: By late 2025 Xiaojun Zhang's show leaned toward online learning and memory. In 2026 LateTalk buzzed about AI improving itself: Yuandong Tian and Manqi Cheng moved from 'we need a new paradigm' to self-evolution, while Chenyang Zhao and Zhiyuan Zeng called it gradual.
cmp.us: Lab researchers on No Priors stress reinforcement learning and inference-time compute, and debate recursive self-improvement. Lenny's guests are mostly data vendors and product people who think RL plus good evaluation is enough; only a few, like Fei-Fei Li, raise new paradigms.
cmp.gap: All shows are cautious about AI improving itself. Chinese shows care more about online learning, interpretable 'white-box' systems, and new architectures; English shows discuss the next step through rewards, evaluation, and environments, Lenny's most of all. That tracks who gets invited: data vendors and product people in English, researchers and founders in Chinese.

cruxes: Can reinforcement learning spread from math and code to open-ended tasks, or does it only work where rewards are clear?
Can AI-run research compound, or will research taste, evaluation, and experiment time keep it slow?
Must intelligence be learned from perception, action, and experiment beyond language and the internet?
agree: Pretraining plus reinforcement learning is proven and remains the main engine for now.
Environments, tasks, and rewards have replaced labeled data as the scarce resource.
AI helping train AI is already visible, but outside verifiable domains progress is gradual.

futures.name: Bootstrapping through code
futures.d: The pretraining-plus-RL recipe speeds up research itself through coding agents, and AI helping train AI becomes routine at frontier labs. It pays off first in verifiable steps like GPU kernels and evaluations; limited by research taste and evaluation, the pace is more likely gradual.

futures.name: Online learning breaks through
futures.d: Merging training with use and storing memory in the weights make real progress, so models keep improving while deployed and the user-data flywheel works again. Product competition shifts to who gets more context and reliable feedback.

futures.name: A new architecture starts fresh
futures.d: World models, spatial intelligence, white-box systems, or non-autoregressive approaches like diffusion clearly win on robotics, physical tasks, or reasoning efficiency, and show a scalable curve. LLMs become the interface layer, and research and talent migrate in large numbers.

stances.label: The current recipe is enough
stances.sum: Pretraining plus reinforcement learning plus more thinking at answer time is proven. Teaching a model new behavior mostly means spelling out the task, the environment, and the reward. The next step is extending this to longer, harder tasks.

stances.label: AI training AI, grown from today's recipe
stances.sum: No need to start over: let today's models help build environments, run experiments, and train the next generation. Some say this loop already runs via coding agents; more people warn that research taste, evaluation, and verification will keep it gradual.

stances.label: Online learning and memory come next
stances.sum: Models freeze the moment training ends and can't learn from use. The next paradigm should merge training and inference, store memory in the model's weights, or keep models updating in realistic environments with real feedback.

stances.label: Leave LLMs, start fresh
stances.sum: The LLM path is locked in by language's limits and by what happens to suit today's hardware, and it converged too early. Start instead from world models that predict the results of actions, spatial intelligence, interpretable white-box systems, new architectures, or new ways of generating.

debates.q: Does AI intelligence grow out of language, or is language just a crutch?
debates.why: Whether language is the backbone of intelligence decides if physical AI, like robots and self-driving cars, should be built on large language models or on a separate vision-based foundation. That shapes the technical choices carmakers and robotics companies are making right now.
debates.sum: Guests on all four shows mostly line up by the field they work in. People building video, spatial, self-driving, and robotics systems tend to call language a crutch, or say it must merge with perception and action. People building language models and digital agents (AI that works inside a computer on your behalf) see language as the core. The robotics guests LateTalk recently added mostly land in the middle, favoring one model trained jointly on language, vision, and action. Lenny's show barely discusses the nature of intelligence; it treats natural language and code as the universal interface for humans directing AI and AI operating the world, a view some LateTalk guests share.
axis: Language is the core of intelligence
debates.notable: Yann LeCun sees language as a crutch: LLMs resemble the brain's speech area, and a four-year-old sees as much visual data as all training text. Geoffrey Hinton counters that good autocomplete requires real understanding; Liang Wenfeng guesses human intelligence may essentially be language. Demis Hassabis and Elon Musk sit mid-way. Fei-Fei Li called language lossy in mid-2025, then complementary to spatial intelligence by late 2025. Like podcast guests, most sit mid-way, though more take extremes.

cmp.cn: Xiaojun Zhang's show is sharply split: Shunyu Yao sees language as the core, while Saining Xie and Xianming Liu call it a crutch. LateTalk's robotics guests mostly favor unified models or joint training, and some see coding as an agent's hands and feet.
cmp.us: No Priors hosts both Noam Shazeer's language-is-the-core view and the vision camp of the Sora team and Fei-Fei Li. Lenny's show rarely touches the nature of intelligence and mostly treats natural language and code as the universal interface for driving software.
cmp.gap: Chinese shows argue mostly over self-driving and robotics architectures, including a production car that dropped the language module; English shows, Lenny's especially, look at language through the product interface. That reflects who gets invited, robotics and driving people in Chinese and product people on Lenny, not opposite views of language.

cruxes: Can the process and physical structure that language leaves out be recovered with scale and data like video and 3D?
Should robots bolt an action module onto a vision-language model, or build their own physical foundation model from pretraining?
Can code become the universal way to control the physical world, or does it only work for digital tasks?
agree: Language models really do compress a great deal of world knowledge; they aren't parrots.
Action and spatial information in the physical world can't be captured by language alone.
Code gives models the ability to act in the digital world.

futures.name: Two tracks, separate roads
futures.d: Digital agents keep language and code at their core, while physical AI builds on vision, action, and world models, with language reduced to an interface for instructions, coordination, and explanation. The two tracks evolve separately.

futures.name: One omni model unifies everything
futures.d: Language, video, audio, and action train together in one model and reinforce each other, so 'which is the core' stops mattering. This requires merging understanding with generation and solving the compute limits of real-time control.

futures.name: Vision takes over
futures.d: World models built on video, 3D, and action show stronger general learning than LLMs and absorb language into themselves. LLMs become interface tools, and research and capital shift accordingly.

stances.label: Language is a crutch
stances.sum: Language is a highly compressed version of human experience, efficient to learn from but stripped of process and physical structure. Physical intelligence should be built on vision, video, space, or the machine's own actions; language is at most an interface.

stances.label: Language must merge with perception and action
stances.sum: Language brings common sense and reasoning, but it isn't enough on its own: action must be learned from the machine's own experience, and vision from interaction. The endgame is either one model uniting vision, language, and action, or language coordinating while specialized models execute.

stances.label: Language and code are the universal interface
stances.sum: No need to argue whether language equals intelligence. Natural language and code have already become the universal interface for people directing AI, and for AI operating software and even machines. Being able to code gives AI hands and feet in the digital world.

stances.label: Language is the core of intelligence
stances.sum: Language can represent almost anything and is the axis linking knowledge, reasoning, and action. Predicting the next word is itself enough to distill intelligence; other modalities are mostly supplements or interfaces.

m: He says most human knowledge isn't in language; a text-only model got even a simple falling-paper question backwards.
He sees language as a coarse, low-information description of reality; much human thinking happens without words.
Physical knowledge like body movement and object contact is almost absent from language but can be learned from video.
Generating realistic video requires understanding the world; Sora is a path toward a world simulator.

debates.q: What is holding AI back most right now: chips and power, data, or algorithms?
debates.why: Knowing where the bottleneck is decides whether money should go to chips and power plants, data and training environments, or algorithms and talent. It also explains where China and the US each are strong and weak in the AI race.
debates.sum: The answers swing with field and timing. When the topic is scaling compute, chips, the power grid, permits, and the inference demand from agents (AI that does tasks on its own) come up again and again as hard limits, most often on No Priors. Language-model people point to expert data, reward signals, and evaluation. Robotics guests on three shows all cry out for data. Lenny's show adds a new voice: writing code is no longer the bottleneck, which has moved to human verification, judgment, and giving AI enough context. Some LateTalk guests add that adoption inside organizations is the slowest step.
debates.notable: Most of the nine name compute and power. Elon Musk sees the bottleneck shifting from chips to electricity, with gas turbines sold out; Jensen Huang says next year's shortage is land, power and buildings, even plumbers. Yann LeCun dissents: the next AI needs scientific breakthroughs, not more infrastructure. Alexandr Wang kept shifting: data in 2023-24, compute and power from 2025, adoption in mid-2026. The nine lean even more toward compute than podcast guests.

cmp.cn: Xiaojun Zhang's show stressed power and chips in 2024, then turned to the data wall. LateTalk's robotics guests repeatedly flagged the data gap, and some said China's compute trails the top labs by an order of magnitude, so efficiency is the only play.
cmp.us: On No Priors, chip, cloud, and policy guests focus on the grid and permitting. On Lenny's show, data vendors say expert evaluation is scarce, and product people from Anthropic and OpenAI say the bottleneck has moved to human review and judgment.
cmp.gap: English shows locate the bottleneck in US grid permits and the speed of human verification; Chinese shows talk about chip shortages, efficiency, and robot data. Each reflects local weaknesses and who gets invited. And on both sides, many who cry data or compute shortage are companies that sell data or compute.

cruxes: Can synthetic data, RL-generated data, and data flowing back from deployment get around the data wall? If so, the constraint returns to compute and power.
Will agent inference demand keep growing faster than energy efficiency, chips, and the grid expand?
After AI output explodes, can verification and judgment be handed to AI reviewers, or do humans stay the long-term rate limiter?
agree: In robotics and biology, the number-one bottleneck is data.
Bottlenecks rotate by stage; solve one and the next appears.
Expert feedback, reward signals, and evaluation are becoming the new scarce resources.

futures.name: Inference demand brings back the power limit
futures.d: Multi-step agent reasoning multiplies token demand, so GPUs, memory, power, grid permits, and community consent set the pace of expansion, and inference efficiency and energy infrastructure gain value. This assumes agent usage keeps growing fast.

futures.name: Verification becomes the rate limiter
futures.d: Model output keeps exploding, but human review, acceptance, and decisions can't keep up, so productivity gains stall on verification and organizational adoption. Self-verifying agents, AI reviewers, and new collaboration workflows become the main investment targets. This assumes model capability is no longer the main shortfall.

futures.name: Data and reward engineering break the wall
futures.d: RL environments, expert feedback, synthetic data, simulation, and data flowing back from deployment reach industrial scale, easing the data limit for language models. Robotics and biology accumulate enough diverse data, and progress comes down mostly to data engineering.

stances.label: Compute and power are the hard limit
stances.sum: Intelligence is roughly electricity plus chips: wafers, packaging, memory, the grid, and permits set the pace of expansion. Nominal chip counts overstate usable capacity, agent-driven inference demand grows faster than supply, and efficiency and capital spending become limits in their own right.

stances.label: Data, rewards, and evaluation
stances.sum: High-quality data has nearly stopped growing and piling on chips pays less. Progress now depends on expert data, reliable rewards and evaluation, verifiable training environments, and squeezing more out of every token.

stances.label: Robotics and science lack data
stances.sum: Robotics and biology have no free data or feedback. Real-world collection is expensive and lacks variety, and the data volume trails language by orders of magnitude. Internet data can't supply the outcomes of actions or cause and effect; compute is no longer the main constraint.

stances.label: People and context are the bottleneck
stances.sum: Models are already smart enough. Value is stuck on missing context, human review and decisions, and how fast organizations understand and adopt. The more AI produces, the more people become the rate-limiting step.

Cheaper models bring AI to more industries, so total GPU demand goes up.

debates.q: Will free, open-source AI models catch up with or beat closed ones like OpenAI's?
debates.why: Open-source models publish their weights (the trained parameters) for anyone to download and run; closed models are only available through paid access. Whether open models catch up decides if model companies can earn monopoly profits, what costs app builders face, and how the US-China AI race plays out.
debates.sum: Most guests across the four shows say the gap is shrinking: after DeepSeek, open models were judged to be only months behind, and matching a given capability got far cheaper. But catching up is not the same as winning. On Xiaojun Zhang's show some argue for 'recursive leadership': leaders use AI to speed up their own R&D and pull further ahead. Several LateTalk guests in 2026 added that closed labs' unreleased internal models still lead by half a generation and hold the training environments and real user data. On Lenny's show, those discussing open source are mostly model users who treat it as a cost option chosen task by task. Open-source champions tend to be beneficiaries, or argue from policy and self-reliance.
axis: Open models catch up or win
debates.notable: The ends are far apart: Yann LeCun says open platforms win like Linux and Liang Wenfeng calls closed-source leads fleeting, while Geoffrey Hinton likens weights to nuclear material. Jensen Huang, Elon Musk and Demis Hassabis see open models a year behind or caught up; Sam Altman and Fei-Fei Li expect coexistence. Alexandr Wang said in 2024 open models cap model-layer value; in 2026, that top models must clear safety first. As spread as podcast guests.

cmp.cn: After DeepSeek, Xiaojun Zhang's show shifted to a catching-up narrative, with Xiaohu Zhu and Yi Ma most bullish on open source. On LateTalk in 2026, Zhiyuan Zeng, Chenyang Zhao, Manqi Cheng, and others stressed closed labs' faster iteration and recursive lead.
cmp.us: Most on No Priors think models are converging with a gap of about six months; the open-source champions are mostly policy officials and beneficiaries. Lenny's show rarely asks who wins, and looks at models through application choices and whether they become a commodity.
cmp.gap: Chinese shows see open source as how Chinese models break through restrictions and build an ecosystem, and discussed recursive leadership earlier. On English shows some treat open weights as a strategic asset against Chinese models, while Lenny's guests are mostly model users. Lenny's discussion of this is concentrated after 2025.

cruxes: Can leaders compound their lead by using AI to build AI, or will spreading know-how and falling costs pull the gap back to months?
Can open weights catch up with the RL environments, real user data, and unreleased internal models that closed labs hold?
Will support for open source on policy and ecosystem grounds be reversed by safety regulation, export controls, and anti-distillation measures?
agree: After DeepSeek, the gaps between open and closed, and between China and the US, clearly narrowed.
The cost of matching a given capability is falling fast, and models are converging.
Open source's value isn't just performance; it's also ecosystem, trust, and self-reliance.

futures.name: Closed leads, open follows close
futures.d: The closed frontier stays months ahead while open models follow at a fraction of the cost and cover most needs. App builders mix both by task, and competition shifts to products, workflows, and distribution. This assumes know-how keeps spreading at its current pace.

futures.name: Recursive leadership widens the gap
futures.d: Labs that put AI to work on their own research compound their lead, keep RL environments, real data, and internal models in-house, and iterate much faster than chasers. Add supply cutoffs, export controls, and anti-distillation measures, and the gap between open and frontier widens again, leaving an oligopoly at the model layer.

futures.name: Open source becomes default infrastructure
futures.d: Open models fully catch up on performance and ecosystem, and policy protects open weights as a strategic asset. Model APIs become low-margin like utilities, and closed vendors can only profit from products and proprietary data.

stances.label: Closed labs compound their lead
stances.sum: Large models can't be crowdsourced like traditional open-source software. Talent and capital concentrate at the top, and training costs exceed what venture capital can bear. Closed labs hold unreleased models, training environments, and real user data, and leaders use AI to speed up their own research, so the gap may keep widening.

stances.label: A catch-up and ecosystem play
stances.sum: Open source is how companies that aren't yet ahead, or for whom models aren't the core business, extend their reach, shorten feedback loops, and win developers and trust. It narrows the gap, but the frontier stays months ahead. How much to open depends on how the company makes money.

stances.label: The gap shrinks, models converge
stances.sum: Talent and know-how spread fast, and models hold no long-term secrets. Capability that's six to twelve months behind can be matched cheaply, and costs fall sharply every year. Once capabilities converge, value moves to products, distribution, and data.

stances.label: Open source should and will win
stances.sum: Leaders spend huge sums for small gains, and once open source catches up cheaply it forms an Android-style ecosystem. Openness speeds the research loop and lowers barriers, and is seen as the foundation of software freedom, resistance to censorship, and industrial self-reliance.

m: Large models can't be built by many contributors like traditional software, so open source will fall further behind.

debates.q: Is AI coding the main road to general intelligence, or just a very lucrative application?
debates.why: Coding is the first agent use case (AI that does tasks on its own) to earn real money at scale. If it is truly the main road to general intelligence, then money, talent, and the competitive map will all reorganize around it.
debates.sum: All four shows agree coding is the first agent use case to take off. The mainstream view on both Chinese shows in 2026 is that it is the backbone, or 'second act,' of the road to AGI. Manqi Cheng and Yusen Chen on LateTalk say an AI that can code has hands and feet in the digital world. On Lenny's show, the coding product leads at OpenAI and Anthropic likewise expect it to expand from writing code to all computer work. Tool makers like Cursor and Cognition stress instead that there will be more engineers, with humans still steering. The skeptics focus on two points: coding leads because its answers can be checked, and models lack research taste.
debates.notable: Of the five weighing in, Sam Altman rates coding highest, though he shifted: in 2024 AI could only do tasks; from 2025, writing software lets it get complex things done on a computer. Jensen Huang and Yann LeCun see a tool: engineering is more than typing; coding assistants aren't yet reliable. Demis Hassabis and Liang Wenfeng stress code is verifiable, so self-improvement may start there. As with podcast guests, "productivity tool" is the commonest view.

cmp.cn: In 2026 Xiaojun Zhang's show mostly saw coding as the backbone of AGI. LateTalk had its own 'coding is hands and feet' camp, but Yuandong Tian, Chenyang Zhao, and Honghao Gao pushed back on research taste, verifiability, and the business case.
cmp.us: No Priors is more divided. On Lenny's show, the labs' coding leads see it as the starting point for all computer work, while tool makers like Cursor and Cognition stress that humans stay in charge.
cmp.gap: The mainstream views converge, and 'coding expands to all computer work' appears on both sides after late 2025. The difference is who is optimistic: in English, mostly product leads at labs that sell coding agents; in Chinese, mostly investors and journalists. Chinese skepticism comes mainly from researchers.

cruxes: Does coding lead because code is the universal interface to the digital world, or because it happens to have clear rewards and easy verification?
Can the long-task skills learned in coding transfer to fuzzy white-collar work without dedicated training?
Can AI-accelerated research become a recursive advantage, or will it stall on research taste, evaluation, and time?
agree: Coding is the first agent use case to truly take off and earn real money.
Coding leads because answers can be checked, rewards are clear, and environments are plentiful.
Writing code is no longer the bottleneck; deciding what to build and verifying it are the new limits.

futures.name: Coding drives recursive R&D
futures.d: If leading labs keep using coding agents to speed up research, coding becomes the entry point for AI training AI and the leaders' edge compounds. This assumes research taste and evaluation don't become the new bottleneck; Noam Brown and Yuandong Tian both warn progress may be gradual or hit plateaus.

futures.name: Coding agents become the OS for work
futures.d: Environments like Claude Code and Codex grow from coding into the home base where white-collar workers launch, delegate, and automate work, with coding ability as the foundation of general agents. The bottleneck shifts to verification, trust, and context in knowledge work.

futures.name: Valuable, but bounded
futures.d: Coding becomes the largest agent market, but moving to non-coding tasks still depends on dedicated training, context, and evaluation. Once code is cheap, coding tools compete on price and brand and may become ordinary subscription software; people still set direction and review code.

stances.label: The universal interface to the digital world
stances.sum: Code can describe most tasks in the digital world; it is how agents operate computers and how they bootstrap themselves. Claude Code and Codex are expanding from writing code to all computer work, and leaders can use AI to build AI.

stances.label: Source of capability, research accelerator
stances.sum: Because code can be checked, coding is where reasoning ability comes from and the labs' research flywheel: AI-written code is already speeding up model development. But the self-improvement loop still runs in months, and non-coding tasks still need dedicated training.

stances.label: The surest productivity tool
stances.sum: Coding is today's surest productivity tool with the strongest willingness to pay, but people still set direction and review code. Once code is cheap, the bottleneck moves to judging what to build, reviewing, and maintaining, and the number of engineers may not fall.

stances.label: A special case that's easy to verify
stances.sum: Coding leads because answers can be checked and environments are easy to build. Research and knowledge work are hard to verify and lack rewards, and models lack research taste, so self-improvement is more likely gradual and the road to AGI still needs a new paradigm.

m: Working backward from AGI: a system that builds its next version must be able to code and run experiments.
Coding is the most general training environment; code gives models hands to reshape the digital world.

If it can code it can operate a computer; Claude Code is already the strongest general-purpose agent.

AI is already speeding up AI research; surpassing humans in most fields around 2028 is quite likely.

Coding leads thanks to clear rewards, abundant environments, and consensus on good code; models write 90% of his code.

She relays lab expectations that coding gets solved and mild self-improvement appears, but the 'turning point' has been promised for five years.

He sees coding as today's most promising field, with programmers about three times faster, though AI still does tasks, not jobs.
Devin multiplies engineers' output but doesn't decide what to build, so there will be more engineers.
He lists coding among today's surest application markets, alongside search, video, and robotics.

Agents are like peer programmers with humans steering, and programming languages remain the layer where things are verified.

He says LLMs are most useful as coding assistants, but still too unreliable to trust every day.

Engineers become designers of logic, taste gains value, and demand for software only grows.

Code is cheap and AI can go 90% of the way, but top-level design still depends on people.
He worries coding tools may turn into an ordinary SaaS business: slow growth, no winner-take-all, limited upside.
He says engineering is more than typing code; much work comes after the typing, and AI is creating software jobs.
He says math and coding suit AI self-improvement because answers are checkable, but the messy real world is far harder to verify.
Coding RL needs environments and tests built project by project; the next wall is environments and feedback, requiring autonomous online learning.
Frontier models' intelligence is uneven; the easier a task is to verify, the better they do.
RL has no scaling law of its own yet; outside math and code it's hard to build environments that can't be gamed.
Self-evolution only suits quickly verifiable tasks; the block on the road to self-improvement is research taste.
Code was disrupted first because it's easiest to verify; essays and legal documents are hard to check.
Models lack research taste; they can speed up algorithms but not invent new ones, so takeoff will be gradual.
Self-improvement by diligent coding agents isn't smart enough; research lacks a structured corpus like code.
Self-improvement already runs in verifier-rich areas like GPU kernels, but large-codebase development is hard to evaluate and will slow.
Self-improvement is far bigger than coding; coding agents are just executors, and research taste is what's missing.
Knowledge work can't run tests like code, so AI must lay out its process and evidence for people to see.

debates.q: Will AI models end up like electricity, basically the same no matter who supplies them?
debates.why: If the gap between models keeps widening, value and capital concentrate in a few labs. If models become interchangeable, then the advantages rivals can't copy have to be found in data, workflows, and distribution instead.
debates.sum: Most guests think the big models will grow more alike, and any lead lasts only months. The two English shows lean this way most: what sets companies apart, they say, is how the product is built and delivered. Edwin Chen and Anish Acharya on Lenny's show add that models will have different 'personalities' without becoming identical. A minority expects the gap to widen, mostly on the Chinese shows: Guangmi Li, Ming Zeng, and Manqi Cheng of LateTalk argue that AI is already helping build the next AI, so leaders will pull away faster. Several LateTalk researchers sit in between: it depends on whose training environments iterate faster, and progress may hit plateaus.
debates.notable: Most of the nine expect commoditization: Jensen Huang likens closed models to bottled water when water is free; Sam Altman sees intelligence becoming interchangeable; Liang Wenfeng says leads can't be held; only teams last. Demis Hassabis dissents: inventing is harder than fast-following, and only Google spans chips to products. Alexandr Wang said in 2024 intelligence would be like utilities; in 2026, that compute-rich firms build what others can't. Like podcast guests, most see convergence.

cmp.cn: On Xiaojun Zhang's show the converge and diverge camps are evenly matched. Most on LateTalk expect rotating leadership or open source closing in, but Manqi Cheng and Chenyang Zhao see the gap possibly widening through self-improvement and training environments.
cmp.us: Convergence is the mainstream view on No Priors. Lenny's guests are mostly app companies that use models; they talk about swapping models, interfaces, and distribution. Edwin Chen and others propose differentiation rather than commoditization, and almost no one argues for a generational gap.
cmp.gap: The idea that AI building AI opens a generational gap caught on only in the Chinese shows; English guests barely echoed it. Chinese guests tend to watch the US leaders from a chaser's seat and worry about distillation and supply cutoffs, while English guests are mostly app companies that mix several models and benefit the more interchangeable models are.

cruxes: Can the compounding from AI working on its own R&D outrun the spread caused by moving talent, distillation, and open source?
Does differentiation happen in the model itself, including post-training choices, or in data, context, workflows, and distribution?
Whoever cracks the next paradigm first, such as online learning, decides whether rotating leadership gets broken.
agree: Public data and algorithms themselves are hard to monopolize for long.
Competing at the frontier demands enormous capital, compute, and talent.
Prices for equivalent capability are falling fast, and selling API access alone is getting harder.

futures.name: A two-tier oligopoly
futures.d: Two or three frontier labs take turns leading, open source and the second tier trail by months, and everyone else drops out of the general-model race. For the leaders the model is a durable advantage; for everyone else it's closer to a commodity, and the leaders differ by their post-training choices.

futures.name: Compounding opens a generational gap
futures.d: If the loop of AI training AI keeps accelerating, leaders iterate far faster than chasers and the open-source gap grows past a year. This view currently comes mainly from the two Chinese shows, with English shows skeptical; Yuandong Tian also warns of plateaus.

futures.name: Models become pure utilities
futures.d: If know-how spreads and costs fall faster than compounding, cheap good-enough models cover most tasks, companies swap models at will, and value settles in workflows and distribution. Model companies get squeezed like telecom carriers and are forced to integrate downstream.

stances.label: They converge
stances.sum: Collapsing costs, open source and distillation (training a weaker model on a stronger one's output), and moving talent mean a lead lasts only months. Cheap, good-enough models cover most tasks, models can be swapped anytime, and the difference shifts to workflows and distribution.

stances.label: Rotating leads, different strengths
stances.sum: The few frontier labs can't pull apart while using the same recipe, so the ranking rotates. Choices in post-training give each model a different 'shape,' complementary rather than identical. Open source trails by months. The entry bar is high, but the lasting advantage is shallow.

stances.label: Scale and systems are the real barrier
stances.sum: Compute, years of engineering, enterprise data, and training environments that can keep producing the next generation form the real barrier. The capital required keeps the frontier to a few players, and those who fall behind rarely get back in.

stances.label: Compounding opens a generational gap
stances.sum: Leaders can use stronger AI to build the next generation, and with organizational advantages on top, the gap keeps widening, ending in winner-take-all or a small oligopoly.

m: Specialized hardware is getting cheap and small models are catching up, so the core technology is quickly becoming a commodity.
A model is not a product, let alone an advantage rivals can't copy.
Waiting for the next model beats fine-tuning; with good evals in place, Ramp can switch to a cheaper model within a day.
He notes inference prices fell about 100x in two years; intelligence may become a utility with little difference between providers.
With more entrants, differentiated training gets harder and early advantages get copied.
Leaders spend 10x for a 10-20% gain, and open source catches up within a year at a tenth of the cost.
Base-model capabilities will converge; what separates players is industry-specific data and training compute.
Models converge and differentiation moves up to workflows; he mixes several models inside Copilot.
DeepSeek proves the secret sauce isn't deep; open source catching closed is only a matter of time.
He thinks models will be like transistors, cheap and everywhere, and off the frontier they quickly become interchangeable.
He says DeepSeek shows good ideas come from everywhere, so no one can monopolize model technology.
Inference cost for equivalent capability fell 180x in 18 months; capabilities and product forms are both converging.
Everyone runs the same kind of model; the difference is interface and workflow, and a better interface tripled adoption.
He says open Llama disrupted exactly three companies and expects market pressure to make foundation models open and free.
Once models converge, the difference lies in private data; public data is quickly matched through distillation.
Models hold no long-term secrets; Chinese open source can hold the gap to 6 to 12 months.
Foundation models become commodities within two to four years; research buys only a 6-to-12-month lead.
Token costs may fall a billionfold in a decade, so teams six to twelve months behind can keep pace.
Once benchmarks converge, a pure model company risks being commoditized like Cisco; the underlying engine is replaceable.
Model capability is available to everyone; what's scarce is context, the background information a model works with.
If no model wins outright, margins get squeezed as in telecom, and distribution becomes the real advantage.
Heavily used models leak their capabilities through their output tokens, leaving iteration speed as the only edge.
He expects intelligence itself to become an interchangeable commodity; the durable edge is compute scale plus product.
No company in history has monopolized a technology for long; model capabilities will converge.
Switching models and compute costs almost nothing; your own data is the most valuable asset.
Cheap, good-enough models are crushing closed-model pricing; most tasks don't need the strongest model.
He likens closed models to bottled water: the water itself is free, a commodity like electricity, used where it fits.
He says open models are near the frontier, and specialized fields like law or manufacturing don't need frontier general intelligence.
Open and closed will coexist for a long time, with the lead changing hands often by task.
China will have a second major model, and the US won't have only OpenAI.
She expected open source to reach GPT-3.5 level within a year, with leading labs still about a generation ahead.
He thinks with OpenAI showing the way and papers and code public, no player can build a crushing lead soon.
Cloud providers hedge across models and enterprises want several, so a single dominant model is unlikely.
He thinks OpenAI cannot lead forever; model leads are hard to keep, and only the team and innovative culture can't be copied.
He thinks the race goes to the most training compute and fastest progress, yet leaders stay only months to a year ahead.
API prices fell about 200x, pushing model companies toward lock-in, yet predictions of commoditization keep failing.
Price cuts are dumping, not commoditization; models haven't become interchangeable.
DeepSeek R1 turned o1's puzzle into an open playbook, but US giants still lead in compute by 10 to 100x.
Open source cut innovation costs a hundredfold, but closed labs spending 100x more are still more likely to lead.
Everyone's pretraining data is similar; differences come mainly from post-training, and base-model progress is slowing.
Under one recipe know-how moves fast; the top labs take turns leading, with a shallow edge but a high bar to entry.
He once expected commoditization, but now thinks values and training objectives will make models diverge.
Both sides have a point: the frontier costs billions, yet within a year several peers appear.
Open source's lag has shrunk from about 18 months to 6 to 8, and it will always trail by a few months.
An agile team with a trillion-parameter base could catch today's top model in two or three months.
None of the three big labs fears being left behind for good; small benchmark gaps are mostly noise.
The gap among leaders hasn't opened; whoever releases last looks strongest.
Codex caught up by following Claude Code's path; the two are in a horse race.
Recursive self-improvement will be gradual; research taste and time are the bottlenecks.
Frontier labs will take turns leading, unless one of them gets recursive self-improvement going first.
Closed labs' best internal models still lead by half a generation to one; open source is unlikely to pass them this year.
Whoever reaches self-improvement first can pull away, but progress is more likely an S-curve with plateaus.
Models have different shapes and complement each other; a bit more intelligence can cost 100x more.
He sees no single winner: execution swings, distillation spreads capability, and labs push models in different directions.
The barrier is compute, long accumulation, and repeated trial-and-error experiments; even Google can't skip it.
Replicating GPT-4 is the ticket to the finals; only three have done it, and a year's delay slashes the value.
Good algorithmic ideas spread fast and can't be a barrier; engineering capability built up over years is what's scarce.
Strong models spread faster than expected, but capital requirements will keep the frontier to a few players.
There's no secret recipe; the barrier is getting the base model, behavior data, and agent RL system all to the limit at once.
Closed giants still dominate in resources, compute, and talent, and enterprise data becomes a flywheel.
Frontier models depend on capital spending and depreciate fast; only hyperscale companies can sustain them.
He says inventing is harder than fast-following; Google caught up through top talent, compute and its merged research culture.
Latecomers rarely break into the top three; if the model is weak, users don't stay.
Model companies will shrink from hundreds to a handful; once the model is trained, the product is mostly done.
He says the lead depends on top talent, fastest powered-up chips and unique data; xAI's edge is X's real-time data.
He expects the industry to stratify, since compute-rich companies can build models that compute-poor ones cannot.
He says only Google spans chips, data centers, cloud, frontier models and billion-user products; a few major players will remain.
He estimates maybe 90% or more of modern AI's big breakthroughs came from Google, with the broadest research team.
Weights are a one-time output; the environments and verification that keep producing the next generation are the real advantage.
The general foundation-model war is over; he doubts a second company can get a ticket.
Whoever first builds overwhelming AGI becomes the ultimate monopoly, and he feels OpenAI's lead is growing.
Without the best coding model the gap keeps growing; Anthropic may dominate the hardest tasks.
She used to assume the top spot rotates, but now doubts it: leaders can use better AI to build the next generation.
Once self-improvement kicks in, acceleration keeps rising, and a few months' gap may never be closed.
Large models training large models compound intelligence, and the gap grows like a black hole.

debates.q: Who captures the money in the end, model makers or app builders? Will models swallow the apps?
debates.why: Where the value lands decides whether startups should build models, apps, or the tooling in between. It also decides whether model companies become the next platform, the way Windows and iOS once did.
debates.sum: Taken together, the four shows lean toward app builders keeping the value, while all agree that thin wrappers around a model get overrun by the next release. Founders and investors on the two English shows mostly defend 'wrappers,' pointing to workflows, domain knowledge, and distribution; those who say model and product are one tend to work at OpenAI or Anthropic. On Xiaojun Zhang's show the debate escalated to whether the model is the operating system or the harness around it (the tools, memory, and workflow wrapped around an AI) is. LateTalk mostly sits in the middle: map out what model companies will inevitably build themselves, then find product-market fit with off-the-shelf models before deciding whether to train your own.
axis: Model makers take most of the value
App builders keep most of the value
debates.notable: More of the nine expect value to stay in apps: Liang Wenfeng says DeepSeek builds only base models, leaving apps to others; Jensen Huang says the money is made in applications. Elon Musk dissents: phones will lack an OS or apps within five or six years. Sam Altman swung: mid-2025, OpenAI wouldn't do everything; that autumn, opposing vertical integration had been wrong; 2026, it won't take it all. Like podcast guests, about half back apps.

cmp.cn: Xiaojun Zhang's show has two camps facing off. LateTalk mostly sits in the middle: apps have room but must watch for model companies moving in. Kerui Min and Ling Xia map where apps get swallowed, and Mian Chen lived through a new model gutting his product.
cmp.us: No Priors and Lenny mostly side with the application layer; Ben Horowitz, Bret Taylor, and others push back on the 'wrapper' label. Those who argue model and product are one are mostly OpenAI and Anthropic employees.
cmp.gap: English shows lean toward apps partly because their guests are app founders and their investors; the 'models swallow apps' view there comes from lab employees, while in Chinese it comes from model-company founders and investors. Chinese guests add an extra worry: supply cutoffs and the cost of training their own.

cruxes: Can the memory, skills, and signals accumulated in harnesses and workflows be distilled into the model or copied by the model maker?
How fast model capability spills over: too slow and apps have nothing to cash in; too fast and apps get overrun.
The cost asymmetry: apps pay the model maker's margin, while model companies can subsidize their own products.
agree: Thin wrappers that are just an interface or a prompt get overrun by the next model.
Long-tail, complex, know-how-heavy use cases are beyond model companies' reach.
Apps that get big enough end up training or deeply customizing their own models.

futures.name: Model makers take it all
futures.d: Leading model companies build their own products in high-value areas like coding, office work, and assistants, squeezing third parties with their API margin and the ability to iterate model and harness together. Independent apps retreat to small markets the model companies don't want.

futures.name: The harness layer stands on its own
futures.d: Memory, skills, and workflow signals accumulate in harnesses and apps, and users swap the underlying model at will. Open and mid-tier models handle most tasks through good frameworks, and value accumulates in apps and agent networks.

futures.name: General gateways plus vertical layers
futures.d: A few general agents become the first thing users open each day, dispatching many vertical players that bring domain know-how and enterprise software. Value layers between the gateway and the verticals rather than one swallowing the other, provided AGI doesn't fully arrive in the short term.

stances.label: Model makers move in and swallow apps
stances.sum: An app's ceiling is set by the model underneath. Model companies earn the API margin and can iterate the model and its harness together, so they move up into high-value areas like coding and eat the scaffolding built around them. General agents may even bypass apps entirely.

stances.label: Integrate downward to survive
stances.sum: Relying on a third party's model rarely builds a durable edge; new models erode old accumulation, and supply can be cut off. Either stay out of the giants' range, train your own where the model is the product, or find product-market fit with off-the-shelf models first and integrate downward later.

stances.label: Apps and workflows keep the value
stances.sum: Model makers can't build every application; the long tail, domain knowledge, enterprise software, and workflows all need an ecosystem. 'Wrapper' is an underrated label: the same model with a better interface pulls ahead, and the model itself becomes the swappable part.

m: Chasing only near-term product fit leaves you flattened by the next leap in the underlying tech; grow users and the model together.
Platforms tend to absorb the most valuable features built on top of them, though Veeva is a counterexample.
The endgame is a general agent like a remote coworker, the same one writing code and booking travel.
Model companies' generalization will take about 80% of a job's generic work, leaving long-tail specialist work to vertical players.
Products with many users, delivered online, and heavily dependent on the base model will sooner or later be built by model companies.
He estimates about ninety percent of progress comes from the core general model; products must anticipate next year's model abilities.
Frontier labs are integrating vertically, and startups on someone else's model pay that supplier's margin.
Once general agents generalize to long-tail tools, many single-domain agents become redundant.
Model companies will move in to harvest; the window apps have to themselves has shrunk from nearly two years to months.
The model is the product: about a third of ChatGPT's retention gains came from model improvements.
He now says opposing vertical integration was wrong; OpenAI ties infrastructure, research and product together, like the iPhone.
He expects phones in five or six years to have no OS or apps, with AI generating what you want.
Codex took off because research and product iterated the model, API, and harness together.
Models will absorb scaffolding like vector databases, but most startups fail because customers don't care.
Many apps shouldn't exist; vendors just need to expose APIs and let agents handle cross-system intelligence.
Model makers must move up into products; the layer that owns users is harder to replace than the engine below.
The leading model will become an operating system spanning devices, like Windows and iOS.
The durable advantages mostly sit with the model; Manus and OpenClaw both ended up gravitating toward model companies.
He sees model makers gaining ever more economic and product power.
A frontier model needs a frontier product to be seen; Opus 4.5 and Claude Code made each other.
He says AI product design happens mostly in training; differences between products come down to training methods, data and evals.
The field moves too fast; depending on someone else's model hands over your fate, so build the full stack.
General models belong to the giants; startups should go where the domain is deep and the data barrier is high.
The winners will mostly be integrated companies that pick a core use case and train their own models.
OpenAI will build the general assistant; founders should pick vertical use cases and reach the frontier through fine-tuning.
He thinks companies with their own language and expertise must train or fine-tune their own models; small accuracy gaps matter.
Don't just wrap a chat box: build in-house where you have a data edge and buy commodity capabilities from partners.
There's almost no room to start up within the giants' range; find the spots they can't reach.
A killer app that wants to stay ahead must integrate down to the model, even to inference chips.
When model quality is the product's core, off-the-shelf won't hold; audio, video, and image models must be trained in-house.
Even the strongest general model can't take over medicine; without medical data and training it can't practice.
Every magic moment in Cursor involves in-house models built to patch the big models' weaknesses.
Sora 2's gains came from integrating product and model, generating complete narratives end to end.
Apps that don't understand the foundation get overrun; app companies just haven't trained their own models yet.
Specialized models get absorbed by general ones, but apps can compete sideways and train once they have product-market fit.
Model companies and data-owning platforms both make money; AI apps stuck in between get squeezed from both sides.
He advises founders to pair AI with atom-based deep science: hard to copy and safe from the next big-model update.
Relying on closed frontier models risks a cutoff, and whether training your own keeps paying off remains to be seen.
GPT Image 1 wiped out a year of his team's workflow work, so he pivoted to context plus agents.
Validate demand with a product built from off-the-shelf models first, then decide whether to invest heavily in training.
The 'wrapper' critique underrates the application layer; a few strong companies emerge every year.
Copilot-style assistance is where the value is, and no company has ever built every application on its own platform.
He thinks app barriers keep falling; open models let small apps use AI cheaply, so entrants have chances for decades.
Capital favors the model layer and underrates apps, yet some apps have already closed the loop and turned a profit.
The super app most likely won't come from today's model companies; leading infrastructure providers earn big returns.
The opportunity in generative AI is in apps; start with business customers and monetize right away by replacing labor.
'GPT wrapper' is a wrong-headed insult; about two-thirds of YC's AI companies build at the application layer.
He wants a division of labor: DeepSeek builds foundation models, while other companies build products for businesses and consumers.
Value flows to Nvidia for now and will later shift to applications that solve business problems.
He thinks renting out models is likely a mediocre business; the good money is in chips, cloud and applications.
AI's value distribution is upside down; profits should flow back from chips to applications.
He envisions a free, open global foundation model on which companies build and sell products, as on Linux.
In three years there will be no model companies except OpenAI; the winners will be AI-first applications.
Models are good enough; 2025 is the year apps take off, and startup model companies should pivot fast.
The wrapper evolves with the model and absorbs its gains; long-tail industries and dirty work need an ecosystem.
Template wrappers get swallowed; community, proprietary data, and workflows are what stick.
OpenAI can't cover every use case; industry data and custom models are the founders' turf.
The same model with a different interface tripled adoption; the value is in the application layer.
The wrapper is the environment that shapes model behavior; super agents and know-how-driven vertical players will coexist.
General agents will consolidate, but general models won't eat vertical domains, provided AGI doesn't arrive within five years.
Domain knowledge, sales relationships, and new interaction forms can keep startups from being crushed by the giants.
Competition has shifted from whose model is best to workflows and products.
He thinks models far outrun today's products and OpenAI won't build everything, leaving startups plenty of room.
He thinks no single model will swallow the economy; companies win by turning their own data and environments into models.
The model is just the engine; in the agent era, context and environment matter more.
GPT wrappers are underrated: they use general models to build affordable versions of expensive services.
Don't build foundation models; agent applications that sell business outcomes have better margins.
He disagrees that models swallow apps: new interaction and continuously overflowing model capability both matter.
Labs will go after coding and consumers first; the thick enterprise-software layer is a durable advantage.
The application layer is far stickier than people think; calling it a wrapper is like calling Salesforce a database wrapper.
Models are like smart new hires; thin wrappers get absorbed, while those who own workflows and authoritative data endure.
Labs charging into coding is worrying, but their supposed distribution advantage may not hold.
Model companies only need to define the interface; the dirty integration work and fragmented app markets are left to others.
A vertical agent's edge is interface, context, and domain experience, not an exclusive model.
Go deep on the full workflow and pick the right model for each step, and even a wrapper can be durable and profitable.
He sees AI as a five-layer cake, with the money ultimately made in the top layer: applications in finance, healthcare, manufacturing.
Polish the framework with a top model, then swap in a mid-tier or domestic one; it still works, but top models set the ceiling.
He says OpenAI doesn't want to eat every business; it would rather be low-margin infrastructure that customers build on.
The harness is the OS and the model is a swappable processor; agent network effects resist model companies moving in.
Apps hold workflow signals labs can't get; find product-market fit with the best model, then post-train.
If models become commodities, value flows to the application layer, as it did in telecom.
Expecting AGI to solve vertical problems is lazy; you have to build all three layers: model, orchestration, and product.
He worries labs entering scares top founders into niches, when more markets can be won on product and distribution.
Models won't swallow everything, just as General Electric succeeded on appliances, not power generation.

debates.q: What keeps an AI app from being copied? Does 'more users make it smarter' really happen?
debates.why: 'More users, more data, better product' was the core competitive logic of the mobile-internet era. Whether that flywheel still works for AI apps decides if app companies can hold their ground over the long run.
debates.sum: All four shows are rewriting what 'flywheel' means: from training user data back into the model, to private signals inside workflows, context (the background information a model works with), and memory. Xiaojun Zhang's show started demystifying the data flywheel in 2025. LateTalk is more practical, with backers for brand, teaching experience, company memory, and real user feedback. No Priors mostly affirms the value of proprietary data and workflow signals. Lenny's guests more often say the durable edge lies in context, stickiness, and distribution, and is usually discovered after the fact.
axis: There is basically no data flywheel
Private data flywheels are the core edge
debates.notable: Only three weigh in, split between Alexandr Wang and Yann LeCun. Wang says about 99.9% of data is private and more users make models better; LeCun said in 2023 that data moats matter less than thought, since small models fine-tune efficiently. Sam Altman sits between: ChatGPT had no moat at first and built one through brand, memory and connections. Like most podcast guests, two of three back workflow or private data.

cmp.cn: Xiaojun Zhang's show mostly debunks the flywheel. LateTalk's founders care more about brand, teaching experience, and company memory, while Wenbin Tang and Chenqi Liang still back a 'usage generates data' flywheel.
cmp.us: No Priors stresses proprietary data and workflow signals. Lenny's guests more often locate the edge in context, stickiness, and distribution, and Hamilton Helmer and Michael Truell warn the flywheel is usually overrated.
cmp.gap: Both sides are converging on context and workflows. English shows trust distribution more and see the edge as discovered after the fact, in line with a growth and investing view; Chinese shows have more vertical and hardware founders who stress brand, industry experience, and real user feedback.

cruxes: Can app companies train their own models and get reward signals aligned with product value, turning data into real capability?
Once online learning breaks through, does the flywheel belong to the model company with the most interactions, or to the apps?
Can workflow signals and private context hold out long-term against distillation and model companies' built-in memory?
agree: Data flowing back from users rarely improves the model directly; fine-tuning often loses to switching models.
What's valuable is a small amount of high-quality expert data or feedback that exceeds the model's level.
Memory, context, and workflows are becoming the main source of stickiness.

futures.name: Memory becomes the switching cost
futures.d: The memory, skills, evaluations, business rules, and configurations users and organizations build up inside a product become the main stickiness. Swapping the model is easy; swapping the product is hard. First movers hold their share this way rather than through a training-data flywheel.

futures.name: Online learning absorbs the flywheel
futures.d: If models can update their weights directly from interaction, the model company with the most interactions gets the first real data flywheel, and the context advantage apps have built up is largely absorbed.

futures.name: Vertical homegrown-data edge
futures.d: In fields with continuous private feedback, such as medical records, driving, entertainment, and enterprise processes, filtered homegrown data trains specialized models and forms real local flywheels. General-purpose products still rely mainly on perception, memory, and distribution.

stances.label: No general flywheel yet
stances.sum: User feedback is too noisy. Capability gains come from defining goals, building evaluations, and scaling the base model, not from data flowing back from users. Customers rarely fine-tune, and waiting for the next model usually pays better. Outside coding, no app has formed a real data flywheel.

stances.label: Perception, taste, and distribution
stances.sum: Model APIs are easy to swap; what lasts is how users perceive you, your brand, taste, and distribution, plus experience built through repeated trial and error. Any feature without network effects can be copied by labs or giants within two or three years.

stances.label: Context, memory, and workflows
stances.sum: The bottleneck is getting context. Systems of record, business rules, team and company memory, and the traces of decisions and failures turn a model's lead into stickiness. Skills accumulated in the harness (the tools, memory, and workflow around an AI) are hard to distill away, and that is the new barrier.

stances.label: Private, homegrown data
stances.sum: Everyone has public data. Company data that can't be scraped or bought, data generated inside the product, and real user feedback, filtered and trained back into the system, are the edge nobody can copy.

m: He thinks data moats matter less than assumed: efficiently fine-tuned small models do well without huge proprietary datasets.
Off-the-shelf models already understand security; claiming an edge from fine-tuning is mostly a story.
Model companies don't yet have the network effects or data flywheels of the internet era.
Data-scale advantages and flywheels are usually overrated; most effects aren't big enough to count as an edge.
Fine-tuning pays less than waiting for a stronger model, so he built evaluations to switch models fast.
Nearly all customers moved from fine-tuning to prompts with examples; the fine-tuning feature went unused.
More users don't make a stronger model; capability comes from defining goals and evaluations, not user feedback.
The biggest lesson of two years: data flowing back from users is mostly useless; the edge lies in user perception and workflows.
The loop where user data feeds back into base intelligence hasn't really formed.
Scaling by compute works too well and user feedback is too noisy, so no data flywheel has appeared yet.
There is an implicit network effect from data feeding back, but no explicit two-sided network has grown yet.
Outside agentic coding, he hasn't seen an AI-native app form a data flywheel.
The value of user data volume is easily overrated; the edge is the full loop from writing code to deploying it.
Their edge is a browser-based development environment and community built over years, not a GPT wrapper.
Model APIs are easy to swap; how users perceive you outlasts model performance.
Anyone can plug in a model; the hard part is turning an AI toy into a lasting brand.
Models and product forms are both converging, so competition shifts to distribution.

debates.q: What happens to the companies building AI models in the end, and will they ever make money?
debates.why: Each new generation of models costs several times more to train than the last. Whether model companies can turn a technical lead into profit decides whether the money poured into AI ever comes back. If it doesn't, the whole investment chain from chips to apps is in trouble.
debates.sum: By 2026 all four shows leaned bullish on the leading US labs, but they still disagree about who keeps the profit. Investors on Xiaojun Zhang's show are mostly skeptical of companies that only sell tokens (model usage). Late Post Talk is cautious: every answer costs compute, capex is being planned around aggressive growth, and coding may be the only big use case. Lab employees and investors on No Priors and Lenny talk about revenue growing tenfold a year, the fastest in history. Benedict Evans points to telecom: without a winner-take-all outcome, value flows to the layer above and model makers earn thin margins.
axis: Hard to profit, end up as infrastructure
Become the most profitable companies ever
debates.notable: The four who weigh in mostly doubt big profits: Liang Wenfeng says DeepSeek prices at cost for thin margins; Yann LeCun expects base models to become free; Alexandr Wang calls renting models a mediocre business. Sam Altman shifted most: in 2024, spending $50 billion a year was fine if it created far more value; by 2026, near-zero switching costs made high margins unlikely. Podcast guests' top pick, an "intelligence tax" monopoly, has no takers here.

cmp.cn: Xiaojun Zhang's show splits sharply into bulls and bears. Late Post Talk is cautious and fairly neutral: it accepts that Anthropic's revenue is soaring but keeps asking about per-call costs, capex and whether coding demand will saturate. Yang You is the exception, defending high profits.
cmp.us: No Priors turned bullish in 2026. On Lenny, the optimists are mainly Anthropic's growth lead and Eric Ries, while Benedict Evans and Bret Taylor warn that margins will get squeezed.
cmp.gap: Both sides agree the top US labs are growing fast; they differ on whether it lasts and who keeps the profit. The English-show bulls are mostly lab employees or their investors. The Chinese-show bears reason from China's market, where prices are low and exits are narrow. By 2026 Late Post Talk is mostly watching how the two US labs report their numbers.

cruxes: Does the value of AI replacing labor go to model companies charging for results, or get eaten by price wars, compute pricing and customers?
When does training-cost growth slow, and can a lead last long enough to support high-margin pricing?
Will model companies win the AI-native app era, or stop at infrastructure like refineries and telecom carriers?
agree: The real market is labor and white-collar budgets, not software or ad spend
Training and compute costs explode every generation, so only giants can fund them
Top labs are growing revenue faster than any tech giant before them

futures.name: A few leaders turn profitable
futures.d: Two or three leading labs approach break-even first on coding and enterprise agent revenue. The rest get acquired, pivot, or attach themselves to cloud providers. The industry becomes an oligopoly, not a field where everyone profits.

futures.name: Intelligence-tax giants emerge
futures.d: If agents replace white-collar and service work at scale and the leaders keep their lead, top labs can charge for results and grow into multi-trillion-dollar companies bigger than the last generation of giants.

futures.name: Returns lag, valuations fall
futures.d: If customers can't turn tokens into profit, prices fall faster than usage grows, and capex is planned for even faster growth, model-company valuations could drop sharply within a year or two before recovering as long-term value shows up.

stances.label: A utility with thin margins
stances.sum: Models are unlikely to become a technical monopoly. Price cuts, open source and good-enough models turn model access into a utility like power or water, and every answer still costs compute. Without a winner-take-all outcome, margins get squeezed as in telecom and the value flows to the apps on top.

stances.label: Depend on giants or go niche
stances.sum: Model companies look more like research labs or oil refineries: the money and the pricing power sit with big tech and cloud providers, and their compute assets depreciate fast. Second-tier players retreat to niche enterprise markets or get absorbed. The end state is a few AI clouds, which may not be the winners of the AI-native app era.

stances.label: Burning cash for the future, unproven
stances.sum: Revenue is growing fast, but prices are collapsing and capex is ballooning at the same time. Some treat revenue as just a way to buy more compute, and each unit of business may already pay off. But if spending is planned around even faster growth, the risk gets passed down the chain.

stances.label: An intelligence tax, a super monopoly
stances.sum: Whoever first builds a leading AGI (AI that can do most human work) could become the strongest monopoly in history. Revenue won't just come from subscriptions and ads; the bigger pool is the payroll budget for white-collar and service work. The top labs are already growing faster than any previous tech giant.

debates.q: Will today's tech giants keep winning in the AI era, or will newcomers take over?
debates.why: It decides who ends up with the value AI creates. Either incumbents like Google, ByteDance and SAP keep their grip through resources and distribution, or new companies rewrite the map the way Google once displaced Yahoo.
debates.sum: Across the four shows it's an even split. Nearly everyone agrees the model layer goes to big tech and a handful of labs; the fight is over apps and enterprise software. Investors on Xiaojun Zhang's show talk about the big players' reach, what they can build in-house. Late Post Talk leans toward the giants and keeps estimating when they'll go all-in on robots or video. No Priors moved from "80% of value goes to incumbents" to "the labs are the new incumbents." On Lenny, AI upstarts and SaaS executives talk past each other, arguing whether distribution still counts as a durable edge. And the word "giant" keeps shifting: yesterday's challengers are becoming today's incumbents.
debates.notable: Liang Wenfeng and Yann LeCun back newcomers: legacy businesses become baggage, and AI assistants will replace search, rattling Google. Demis Hassabis backs incumbents: Google's full stack and talent make it a big winner. Alexandr Wang said in July 2026 that agent-savvy startups beat slow incumbents, then in October that consumer AI is Meta's home turf. Sam Altman went from startups almost always winning to praising Google. Podcast guests split evenly; the nine lean newcomer.

cmp.cn: Xiaojun Zhang's show is evenly split. Late Post Talk leans toward the giants and often estimates when they'll go all-in on robots and video, though researchers like Yuandong Tian argue this AI wave actually works against big companies.
cmp.us: No Priors shifted from "80% of value goes to incumbents" to "the labs are the new incumbents." Lenny has both camps: investors talk about breaking through with product, while SaaS and platform executives stress their data, business rules and distribution.
cmp.gap: On the Chinese shows the giants are ByteDance, Alibaba, Tencent, plus phone and car makers, and the question is their reach and timing. On the English shows the giants are enterprise software firms and labs, and the fight is over whether SaaS survives, who acquires whom, and whether distribution still matters. Both agree the model layer concentrates. The English sample has more incumbent executives, so their views come with a business interest.

cruxes: Can the new product be ten times better? If not, distribution, data and bundling win; if so, users move
Can giants go all-in without stumbling, or are they inherently held back by legacy, hierarchy and risk aversion?
Can incumbents remake themselves like Intercom, or does it take an outside owner or an acquisition?
agree: The model layer's barrier is so high only giants and a few labs fit
Giants fall short on organization, execution and risk appetite, not resources
Challengers are becoming incumbents as labs expand into apps

futures.name: Few model makers, new app generation
futures.d: Models and cloud are dominated by giants like Google and a few top labs. New companies build the agent front doors and the rebuilt categories, while today's giants share value as AI clouds. This requires AI-native products to differ enough from existing ones.

futures.name: Giants hold through integration
futures.d: Once models converge and products look alike, giants with chips, cloud, cash flow, data and distribution hold most consumers and enterprises through bundling. Startups get acquired or tied up, surviving only in gaps the giants don't bother with.

futures.name: A tenfold gap rewrites the map
futures.d: If a new approach lets one company deliver a ten-times better experience, users and enterprise budgets move en masse and old advantages fail for a while. But the lead has to last, and several guests think talent and know-how spread too fast for that.

stances.label: Outsiders topple the giants
stances.sum: Giants don't lack resources; they lack fresh organizations, appetite for risk and urgency. Legacy businesses, old tech stacks and hierarchy become baggage. A challenger with a ten-times better experience, deep industry know-how or a new way of interacting can break through the incumbents' distribution.

stances.label: The giants hold more chips
stances.sum: Models need huge capital, dense top talent and long time horizons. Incumbents have the data, the business rules, the distribution and the bundles, so they can quickly copy any feature that works. Most startups end up tied to a giant, acquired, or racing to reach scale before the giants move in.

stances.label: Layer by layer, execution decides
stances.sum: Winning isn't about being old or new. The model layer goes to the giants; in apps it depends on whether a category gets rebuilt. What matters is whether incumbents go all-in on remaking themselves, integrate vertically and acquire. Google fought back with its full stack, and SaaS won't necessarily go to zero.
