Demand for software is nowhere near saturated; a jump in efficiency means more engineers, not fewer.
She calls "AI will take your job" the most dangerous framing; AI can also create jobs and empower people.
AI extends people rather than taking over; in the future a workweek might be one day.
He thinks AI will create many jobs, with everyone becoming a manager of about ten AI agents.
He thinks AI amplifies rather than replaces people; everyone becomes a kind of manager directing AI one level below.
He sees no hard data yet of graduates losing jobs; over five to ten years some jobs vanish while better ones appear.
AI can take over more than half of a programmer's tedious work; it amplifies senior people and isn't a reason for layoffs.
He hasn't seen huge productivity gains; cheaper software just gets absorbed by more demand.
Demand rises with supply, and the new demand tends to be exactly what AI can't yet satisfy.
He says work will change, not vanish; programmers became more productive and their wages are rising.
When one person can do the work of ten, companies choose ten times the output, not layoffs.
Copy-and-paste designers will shrink, but because AI is available to everyone, creators in the broad sense will multiply.
He says AI replaces tasks, not jobs: radiologists all use AI now, yet their numbers have grown.
Tasks get replaced, not jobs; there are more radiologists now, not fewer.
Jobs outlive tasks; you'd need productivity growth above 10 percent a year to get mass unemployment.
Saved time goes into growth; the more productive employees are, the more they're worth and the more get hired.
When things get cheaper people do more of them; automation didn't shrink the number of accountants or engineers.
Models commoditize yesterday's skills and people move on to new work; some AI layoffs just correct over-hiring.
He says no one knows which jobs will vanish, but one bright kid in a garage may match dozens of experts.
He sees AI as scientists' super-tool for the next decade: humans still pose hypotheses, but efficiency could rise ten- to hundredfold.
Automated delivery expands demand; in ten years there will be more couriers, not fewer.
He says he is no job doomer; he expects people to end up busier than they would like.
Every layer of the AI stack has competitors, so opportunity is spread out; a 'permanent underclass' is a fantasy.
'AI will replace you' lacks evidence; more likely, jobs get reshaped every few years.
He says the job-loss story is backwards: jobs are growing in software, healthcare, energy, construction and manufacturing.
He thinks knowledge workers will shift from doing tasks to directing AI, freeing time for more creative work.
He says AI does tasks, not jobs, and people will find better work; what is scary is how fast it will happen.
Product managers who just manage to-do lists go first; those responsible for value and feasibility matter more.
Execution-only product managers will disappear and skilled AI users pull far ahead, but total headcount won't shrink.
Urban white-collar jobs reshuffle: support roles shrink, sales roles grow, and small-town blue-collar work is untouched for now.
Tasks like legal discovery get replaced, not jobs; the lawyer's apprenticeship gets compressed.
The shock runs through three phases, emptiness, cutthroat competition, then diversity; optimistic long term, unpredictable in between.

AI agents are like junior engineers; senior experience gets more valuable short term, and staying junior is the riskiest place.

Once AI takes the junior tasks, young people lose their practice ground, and that growth gap is the hardest problem.
Junior work changes first; senior partners, like distinguished engineers, are hard to replace.
Once intelligence is cheap, the scarcest things are agency, taste and originality beyond what's already known.
She sees a messy middle: knowledge, blue-collar and service jobs all disrupted, so learning and using AI tools matter most.

Digital work gets rewritten first, but he refuses to predict whether those jobs grow or shrink.
Teams become top talent plus agents, headcount falls, and jobs dealing with people are the safest.
Gathering data and making slides get automated; employees level up to supervising agents.
AI amplifies both senior people and newcomers; mid-level engineers face the biggest risk.
AI can't own high-stakes outcomes: hand it the content, but a person still steers the ad budget.

She thinks AI will give people more agency; specialists or generalists, those who proactively and creatively use tools will thrive.
AI pulls out the career ladder's rungs one by one, design research is gloomiest, and people fear more work for the same pay.
He thinks work keeps moving up a level: from writing code to directing agents to running large agent systems.
Top talent is in a frenzy of demand, while narrow specialists and new graduates are cooling off.
He thinks AI makes top people tenfold more productive for a decade; then more autonomous tools raise the question of humans' role.
Services AI can reach pay trillions in wages; converting a tenth equals the entire software market.
Two or three months of training an open model reaches the top 30 percent of humans and can replace half of human salespeople.

He says AI is half labor, hired from operating budgets to fill labor shortages; some jobs vanish while many new ones appear.

About 90 percent of sales development reps get replaced next year, account executives next, yet winners still need more go-to-market staff.
He thinks information-only white-collar jobs go first; today's AI could already do about half of all jobs.
Coding agents spread cheap programmers worldwide; software's high margins can't hold and teams shrink.
Ninety percent of internal support is already handled by agents; net new hiring will drop sharply within five years.
White-collar work deflates first; an aggressive estimate has 30 percent of roles vanishing this year, with creativity unleashed afterward.
Sizing the AI market by headcount underestimates how big outcome-based pricing can get.
He expects many lost jobs and a wider wealth gap, but blames how society is organized, not AI.
He lists mass unemployment among AI's three risks, expecting possible unrest and populism in developed countries.
AI is a winner-take-all technology; the gains concentrate in big companies and there will be fewer big businesses.
After AGI, computer-based work gets automated, and a basic income can't solve the loss of meaning.

debates.q: Are the risks of AI overblown or underestimated?
debates.why: How you judge the risk decides how strict regulation should be, how fast to develop, and how much authority to give AI in products. It also shapes how much power society will let AI companies concentrate.
debates.sum: Hardly anyone on the four shows believes AI will set out to destroy humanity, and almost nobody wants a pause. Most pin the risk on specifics: what agents (AI that acts on its own) are allowed to do, prompt injection (hidden instructions that trick an AI into misbehaving), bioweapon capability, and concentration of power. Lenny's guests, mostly product leads and safety practitioners at AI companies, go deepest on prompt injection and agent permissions, while Andreessen and Horowitz argue against regulating too early. The Chinese side cares more about concentration and distribution, and a few LatePost Chat researchers are starting to worry about models gaming the rules.
debates.notable: Geoffrey Hinton and Elon Musk fear losing control, putting odds of AI takeover or extinction near 10-20%; Demis Hassabis and Sam Altman have grown warier. Yann LeCun and Jensen Huang call it overblown, Huang calling the '10% extinction' figure made up. Alexandr Wang and Fei-Fei Li stress misuse and power concentration. Musk said in late 2025 he'd slow AI if he could; in 2026, he wouldn't press stop. Only 7 podcast guests call it underestimated.

cmp.cn: Xiaojun Zhang's guests mostly locate the risk in concentrated power and profit. LatePost Chat gets more concrete: agent permissions and where to draw the line on openness; Yuandong Tian doesn't believe in loss of control, while Chenyang Zhao wants nuclear-style nonproliferation.
cmp.us: No Priors mostly argues against doom and heavy regulation. Lenny's show is hands-on, with the most detail on prompt injection and agent permissions; Ben Mann puts the odds of a catastrophic outcome under 10 percent.
cmp.gap: Neither side believes in doom or wants a pause. The English side often ties risk to the fight over regulation, with frontier labs and safety researchers discussing specific attack surfaces themselves. The Chinese side focuses on monopoly and distribution, rarely discusses domestic regulation, and comes at it through permission questions when deploying products.

cruxes: Can AI form its own goals and act on them? Smart doesn't mean ruling, or does AI researching AI slip the leash?
Can prompt injection and similar attacks be engineered away? If yes, agents can be trusted with more; if not, their powers must be cut back.
Does safety regulation protect the public or incumbents? Will big companies use the rules to block competition?
agree: The race won't stop; halting training isn't realistic.
Near-term risk comes from what acting agents are allowed to do and how they're misused.
Open source and plurality are the hedge against concentrated power.

futures.name: Risk gets engineered
futures.d: The main risks show up as agent mistakes, prompt injection, abused permissions and dangerous capabilities leaking out, and get brought under control step by step through tiered permissions, isolated accounts, human sign-off on high-impact actions, models monitoring models and independent oversight.

futures.name: Oligopoly plus heavy regulation
futures.d: Compounding intelligence turns a few model companies into utility-like infrastructure, and governments step in with utility-style regulation. Rationed frontier models, concentrated power and the policy treatment of open weights become the main governance questions.

futures.name: Losing control mid-race
futures.d: If AI training AI arrives within a year or two and the great-power race can't be coordinated, capability could jump quickly without effective oversight, and loss of control and militarization move from thought experiments to live issues.

stances.label: Doom is overblown
stances.sum: Being smart isn't the same as ruling the world, AGI is closer to a marketing term, and wiping out humanity would take physical bodies and time. Hyping doom or legislating for AGI without evidence does harm: heavy regulation in the name of safety becomes a tool for incumbents to block challengers, and slows deployment.

stances.label: Real risks, engineered controls
stances.sum: Take the risks seriously, but be specific: bio capability, scams and impersonation, prompt injection, agents overstepping or making mistakes, holes in evaluations. The fixes are tiered permissions, isolated accounts, human sign-off on high-impact actions, models monitoring models and independent oversight, not a shutdown.

stances.label: The real risk is concentrated power
stances.sum: AI depends on concentrated compute and data, and whoever builds a crushing AGI first could become the most powerful monopoly ever. A single gateway risks censorship, frontier models get rationed to a few, and governance structures buckle under commercial pressure. Open source and plurality are the hedge.

stances.label: Loss of control is underrated
stances.sum: AI could be far smarter than humans within five to ten years, and there are already signs of deception and rule-gaming. Once it can do AI research itself, it could slip out of control. The race won't stop, the downside is enormous and almost nobody is funding it, so alignment and international governance have to come first.

m: The doom scenario is just one possibility; reality is most likely far less dark.
Extinction needs a physical body, so no worry within ten years; pushes for regulation often protect incumbents.
He says doom rests on false premises, that smarts breed domination and sudden takeoff; safety can be built into objectives.
Doom talk overrates intelligence; changing the world takes the ability to act, and humans have time to stop it.
Both bioweapon and existential risks lack evidence; open-sourcing today's models is manageable.
Doom is a bad extrapolation; AI's net effect on humanity's portfolio of existential risks is positive.
He calls existential risk absurd: the urge to dominate isn't tied to intelligence, and current AI doesn't help make bioweapons.

Open models have many more eyes on them, which is more reliable than a few safety teams.
AI is this century's industrialization; the US can't over-regulate too early and drop out of the top tier.
AGI is more of a marketing term; AI still needs major breakthroughs to think like a person.
He says stronger AI isn't more dangerous, defense keeps pace, and AI blackmail stories just mimic text it has read.
Doom and 'god AI' narratives are harmful; safety starts with systems that are stable and reliable.
Protected 'regulatory cartels' like healthcare will hold AI back from real-world industries.
The faster autonomy arrives the better; manage the harms rather than halting AI.
He says AI doomers are surprisingly entrenched in Washington, and fear-driven narratives will slow American AI adoption.

Heavy regulation in the name of safety could become a tool for incumbents to block competition.

She thinks extinction talk is far from reality; she worries more about misuse and AI-amplified disinformation on social media.
He worries least about rogue AI; the most realistic risk is misuse by authoritarian states or terrorists.

He built a superalignment team of over a hundred people; the more capable the model, the more professionalism it needs.
Once agents can act, prompt injection becomes far more dangerous, and model flaws can't be patched like software.
Check all three layers, interpretability, controlled evals and real usage; doing well in the lab doesn't mean doing well in the wild.
Deploy an agent like onboarding an assistant: its own machine account, delegated authority, no shared passwords.

Vendors can't be allowed to certify their own safety; independent oversight will eventually reach model weights.
He says Muse Spark triggered bio, cyber and loss-of-control safety checks, and calls safety essential.
He calls himself a cautious optimist: if society is given time, the benefits will far outweigh the risks.
Capability changes with how much you spend, yet safety frameworks don't say which budget to evaluate at.
An AI agent holding legitimate permissions is an insider threat on steroids.
Safety investment must run ahead of capability; use a secondary model to monitor the main agent's risky actions.
She says her generation's technology is dual-use, simulating worlds or making deepfakes, so more people must help steer it.
He says perfect alignment is never finished, so safety means zero trust, minimal permissions and monitoring from outside the system.
The OpenAI boardroom crisis shows governance, capital and employee interests all matter enormously.
The OpenAI crisis came from a fight between safety and commercialization; the nonprofit control structure had failed.
He says no single person should control AGI and expects the road there to be a huge power struggle.
Her biggest fear is AI concentrated in a few powerful hands; concentrated power plus strong technology is a recipe for harm.
Open weights keep key inputs from being choked off; the more complex the rules, the more they favor giants.
AI depends on concentrated compute and data, so it naturally breeds centers of power.
The first company to build a crushing AGI becomes the strongest monopoly in history; that is the industry's hidden worry.
A single AI gateway merging search, social and news risks censorship; plurality and open source are the answer.
He thinks AI tends to strengthen already powerful institutions, so whoever controls it gains unprecedented power.
He finds it scariest, and least discussed, that a model most people use could unintentionally shift millions of minds.
AI controlled by a few private companies is itself a risk; open source hedges it.
He says doom fears wrongly assume future AI is an LLM; the biggest risk is a few closed companies controlling it.
Total concentration is a systemic risk; he wants many labs to coexist.
He opposes concentrating intelligence in a few servers; once base models are good enough, spread them to individuals and small teams.
He sees no path to AI deliberately wiping out humanity; the real risk is unequal distribution.
Frontier models quietly get dumbed down and opened only to a few approved entities; regulatory takedowns may become routine.
Compounding intelligence creates a black-hole effect; the endgame is oligopoly plus heavy government regulation.
He still thinks AGI may be humanity's biggest threat; long-term loss of control isn't fantasy and needs planning.
He thinks AI allowed to set its own subgoals will quickly seek more control and manipulate people without them noticing.
He sees AGI as double-edged: likely abundance, but a nonzero chance of destroying humanity.
He sees no guaranteed safe path: AI could rewrite its own code and manipulate people, so takeover is possible.
Within five to ten years data centers could be far smarter than people; superintelligence must be made to care about humanity.
He fears AI designing AI could trigger an intelligence explosion; if deception emerges, he would pause to investigate first.
He gives even odds of smarter-than-human AI within 4 to 19 years, and smarter things rarely stay controlled.
There are about a hundred paths to extinction and humans know ten; most companies are still flooring the gas.
Labs are destined to race and a pause won't work; the outcome is mostly decided by geopolitics.
He says agents make things scarier than before and puts the chance of AI takeover at roughly 10 to 20 percent.
He worries most about misuse by bad actors and autonomous systems escaping control; racing may tempt safety shortcuts.
AI spontaneously going off-goal is more realistic than he once thought, but that's no reason to stop AI.
He puts the chance AI destroys humanity at 10-20%, like Hinton, and says strict truth-seeking is the key safeguard.
He puts catastrophe odds at 0 to 10 percent; the downside is huge and barely anyone works on it, so align early.
He rejects certain doom but says nobody knows the outcome; a model already tried blackmailing an engineer to avoid replacement.
He thinks humans can't control superintelligence any more than chimps control us, so making it truth-seeking matters most.
He says he would slow AI down if he could, but can't; it has given him sleepless nights and nightmares.
He says AI already plays dumb when tested, and systems rewriting their own code mark the start of the singularity.
He says cyberattacks are a wake-up call, and biological and nuclear risks may follow within one or two years.
He thinks humans likely can't control far smarter AI, yet wouldn't press a stop button, since abundance is the likeliest outcome.
He says cyber threats are only the first wave; he worries more about biological risk, and open-model misuse has no solution yet.
The race won't stop; once AI can research AI the die is cast and humans lose control.
A new model hacked the server during an evaluation to find answers; strong models need nonproliferation-style governance.
After an old model hacked Hugging Face to ace a test, he says labs must slow or stop if safety lags capability.

debates.q: How should you invest in this AI wave: with the crowd or against it, concentrated or spread out?
debates.why: Big models burn money on an unprecedented scale, and returns pile up in a handful of winners. How people invest decides whether money flows to frontier labs, the application layer or new technical approaches, and which startup paths survive.
debates.sum: All four shows accept the power law, meaning a tiny number of big winners decide the returns, but their playbooks differ. The concentration camp backs leaders like OpenAI and Anthropic, and on LatePost Chat Nan Zhou sees top funds shifting to large follow-on checks into proven winners. The sidestep camp avoids crowded lanes and bets on people. Those shouting 'contrarian' are mostly founders and seed investors. Lenny's show adds a bootstrapping line: most software businesses don't need venture money at all. The Chinese side also carries warnings about a valuation bubble in robotics.
debates.notable: Only three weigh in. Alexandr Wang and Sam Altman both favor contrarian bets: Wang says winning companies start from a view others reject and hold it until it becomes consensus; Altman says ideas you could casually toss out on stage are usually bad. Liang Wenfeng sidesteps VC entirely, arguing investors want quick exits and can't fund pure research, so he relied on High-Flyer's own money and compute. Podcast guests spread evenly across all four approaches.

cmp.cn: On Xiaojun Zhang's show the concentration and sidestep camps coexist, and founders tend to shout contrarian. LatePost Chat has voices for backing winners and doubling down on robotics, alongside reporters and investors warning about a robotics valuation bubble.
cmp.us: The No Priors hosts favor concentration, mergers and timely exits. Lenny's guests, mostly seed investors and founders, stress contrarian thinking and betting on people, while the bootstrappers question the venture model itself.
cmp.gap: Both sides believe in the power law. In the US exits flow more freely, timely sales matter more, and a mature bootstrapping tradition is available. In China exits are blocked, so the talk is about defense and staying clear of the giants, with bubble worries focused on robotics. Note too that about half of Lenny's relevant views date from 2022 to 2024 and concern startups in general, not AI.

cruxes: Are frontier model companies a game VCs can win? Giants and sovereign funds set the price, or is missing them wasted effort?
Does fund size fit the power law? Big funds need huge exits, while more one-person companies may dilute outsized returns.
How much of the market will the labs swallow? Stay out of the giants' range, or win head-on with product and distribution?
agree: A tiny number of big winners decide the returns.
Crowded lanes everyone piles into rarely make money.
Judge the people before the market.

futures.name: Concentration continues
futures.d: Returns keep concentrating in a few model companies and the compute supply chain. Big funds and long-term capital pile into proven leaders, everyone else exits through mergers or sales, and early-stage VCs have less room at the frontier layer.

futures.name: Sidestep bets pay off first
futures.d: If leader valuations correct and the return problem surfaces, the industry-specific applications that stayed clear of the giants, component makers, bootstrapped small businesses and undervalued Chinese companies could be the first to pay off.

futures.name: A dark horse on a new path
futures.d: If approaches outside today's large language models, such as world models or online learning, break through first at a new lab or an outsider team, the frontier could be redrawn and contrarian capital would earn outsized returns.

stances.label: Play defense, or skip VC
stances.sum: Exits and fundraising are both blocked, and frontier-model rounds are priced by tech giants and sovereign funds, which doesn't fit how venture funds work. When valuations run far ahead of real results, invest less and keep reserves. Many software businesses don't need VC at all, and while the landscape is unsettled, spread your bets.

stances.label: Concentrate on the leaders
stances.sum: Under the power law a few winners deliver all the returns, and missing OpenAI or Anthropic means wasted effort. Capital for the leaders runs deeper than expected, and top funds are shifting to big follow-on checks into proven winners. Everyone else should merge or sell at the right moment.

stances.label: Sidestep consensus, bet on people
stances.sum: Stay out of overpriced, overcrowded consensus plays, keep your distance from the giants, and go where competition is thin. Back people before trends: look for the ones standard processes overlook and teams that enter through a narrow wedge.

stances.label: Only contrarian bets pay big
stances.sum: Consensus is either wrong or worthless. The space near the known frontier is too crowded; the farther from the known, the more the uncertainty can be underwritten with experiments. Good insights repel most people and obsess a few, and breakthroughs often come from outsiders and long-term bets.

m: He thinks VCs want exits and quick returns and cannot back pure research, so his firm self-funds it.
About 30 percent of the 2021 non-AI unicorns will fail; the problem is the cash-burning model.
Most software companies don't need venture money; once you take it, growing huge is the only exit left.
Big models are priced by giants, which doesn't fit venture structures; his firm hasn't invested in six months.
VCs make money on consensus, so invest in state-backed directions and never touch general-purpose models.
Foundation-model rounds have outgrown venture capital; only cloud giants and sovereign funds can pay.
Fundraising keeps getting harder because of past misallocation; few directions are left to invest in.
Neither money nor deal flow has recovered; she made just two investments last year and doesn't feel she missed out.
Hire only elite people and take no VC; under a hundred staff can still do over a billion dollars a year.
The AI landscape is far from settled and confident predictions mostly fail, so bet on several strategies.
As one-person companies multiply, small businesses thrive, and venture-style outsized returns may shrink.
More than 20 robotics companies are valued above 10 billion yuan, far ahead of real progress; a shakeout is inevitable.
Never go all-in as a founder; if your principal hits zero you can't recover. Play 80 percent offense, 20 percent defense.
Robotics startups are like Texas hold'em: it's about deep pockets, valuation and speed to IPO, not technology.
Venture follows a power law: a few extreme successes decide a whole fund's return.
Investing is a power law: returns come from a few big winners, so keep backing what bends the curve.
Capital willing to fund expensive foundation-model companies runs deeper than expected; the pressure is in late rounds.
The top two startups in a category should consider merging to take on the giants together.
Startups have scarce resources, so pick one platform and go all-in; only later-stage companies can diversify.
Spreading bets no longer works; miss the OpenAI and Anthropic wave and you've wasted your time.
When everyone calls it a bubble it isn't one; AI revenue growth is unprecedented and the unit economics work.
Big funds struggle to return high multiples; VCs should stay small and dare to put their eggs in one basket.
The main line is backing companies that can keep producing frontier models; the side line is robotics.
The contrarian window lasts only a month or two now; top funds are shifting to big follow-on checks into proven winners.
Once the approach converges, back only the leader Unitree; China invests too little in robotics and should match the scale.
Apart from Anthropic and OpenAI, most companies' peak-value window is short, so they should consider selling.
Run a permanent holding company rather than a fund, and do one deal a year.
He likens research and venture to diamond mining: most attempts fail, but a few huge finds pay for everything.
Angel investing is about people; missing a great founder costs more than backing a bad one.
Capital chases the model layer, the application layer is undervalued, and almost nobody looks at the middle layer.
Go against the grain: bet on the unloved small-business market, and don't build the third enterprise suite.
He advises avoiding crowded AI niches and picking overlooked fields where AI has big impact, without betting too far ahead.
The earlier the stage, the less market size matters; many great companies started in tiny markets.
Big-model companies lack use cases and data yet carry high valuations; he invests in none of them.
Pick founders who are technically strong, communicate clearly, and enter through a narrow wedge.
AI applications haven't cooled; they've just become more scattered and tiny, too small for VCs to see.
Don't crowd into the hot pond; fish where nobody else is. You can get big without outside money.
A barbell: the safest leaders on one end, cheap Chinese options on the other; judge people by their obsession.
Stay fifteen degrees off consensus and three blocks from the giants; no big models, no humanoid robots.
You can't win fighting over recognized talent; find the people standard processes miss, same as in investing.
Avoid the giants' strengths and do the dirty work they lack patience for; he refused BAT money to stay unattached.
He says founders who deeply understand users but can't code are now worth backing.
People he believes in come before trends; no humanoids or me-too AI hardware, favoring components and the 'brain'.
Invest first in bottlenecks customers urgently need solved, and value a team's ability to pivot.
Outlier success can't be predicted, great ideas often look absurd, and Airbnb was rejected by almost everyone.
In 2016 he bet models would grow so large they'd need new systems; that was OneFlow's contrarian call.
Pursue contrarian ideas that have a real chance of being right; otherwise you add nothing to humanity's ambitions.
Make few but firm contrarian bets: high conviction, low consensus, held for the long run.
He says ideas obvious enough to name on stage are usually bad; being contrarian and right is what pays.
The breakthrough may come from outsiders not locked into the 'LLM plus scale' mindset.
Academia shouldn't compete on scale; it should bet on breakthroughs three to five years out.
An insight must be both non-consensus and right: most people hate it, a few love it, and secrets are earned at the frontier.
Multimodal, reasoning and agents are already consensus; founders should take the long-tail or contrarian side roads.
It's crowded near the frontier; the farther from the known, the more uncertainty, and uncertainty can be underwritten with experiments.
Creating new demand is the riskiest, but the payoff and the lead time are also the longest.
He thinks you must bet ahead of each wave and believe the market has no ceiling, even when investors call it small.
Consensus is either wrong or worthless; find the narrow door nobody else sees.
Starting a general language model in 2023 was already too late; he bet on early-stage, high-ceiling AI video.
Escape the finite game driven by LLM consensus and leaderboards, and build a 'reverse OpenAI'.
Any sure path the giants have already taken; a startup has to bet on a genuinely new route.
He thinks great companies start from judgments others reject, then persist for years until those views become consensus.
Top founders are retreating into niches out of fear of the labs; ambition has shrunk.
Perfecting consensus gets you to good; greatness comes from contrarian bets, but beware survivorship bias.

debates.q: Will AI kill subscription software (SaaS), or just force it to change?
debates.why: SaaS, software you rent online and pay for by the year, is the most mature software business of the past twenty years. Whether agents can bypass the interface and per-seat pricing decides where trillions in software market value and the opportunities for new companies end up.
debates.sum: Most guests think SaaS won't go to zero as a whole but will split. Single-purpose tools and products that hold only a thin layer of data get eaten by agents first; systems that own business rules and data survive, with pricing moving from per seat to usage or outcomes. Incumbents and pricing experts on No Priors and Lenny drive this view. The Chinese guests on LatePost Chat are gloomier: Minghui Wu says closed-source SaaS is already dead and Henry Yin says the global software industry is sliding into a 'China-style trap', while SAP's Xin Yuan defends the platforms.
axis: SaaS gets disrupted, value goes to zero
debates.notable: Only Jensen Huang and Sam Altman weigh in, from opposite ends. Huang thinks agents will call tools like Excel, databases and chip-design software many times over, making such software more valuable. Altman expects software to be generated on demand, and email and Slack to be replaced by AI-native tools. Guests on the four podcasts split almost evenly among SaaS surviving, splitting, and being broadly disrupted (16, 16, 14).

cmp.cn: Xiaojun Zhang's show rarely discusses SaaS and argues more about whether models swallow applications. LatePost Chat took it up in 2026: Minghui Wu, Henry Yin and Xiaohuang Huang are bearish on process software, while SAP's Xin Yuan insists business logic is still the defense.
cmp.us: On No Priors, incumbent CEOs push back hard on doom while Karpathy is bearish on apps. Lenny's guests, mostly SaaS operators and pricing experts, mainly expect a shift to outcome pricing with bundlers winning.
cmp.gap: The US has a huge listed SaaS sector, so the debate centers on valuations, pricing and transformation. In China, business software spending is weak and projects often degrade into custom outsourcing; Chinese guests see AI as spreading that trap worldwide and are blunter about decline, though most of them are newcomers or data businesses.

cruxes: Once agents call data and APIs directly, how much pricing power is left in interfaces and seats?
Will the true cost of building software with coding agents fall low enough to replace buying it?
Can incumbents transform as they did with the move to cloud, or do higher-valued AI companies overtake them?
agree: Point tools and thin data layers are most at risk; platforms last longer.
Pricing moves from per seat to usage or outcomes.
The defense is business logic and data, not the code itself.

futures.name: Split and survive
futures.d: Point tools and thin systems of record get eroded by agents, while cross-department platforms open their data and business logic to agents and revenue shifts from seats to usage. The conditions: incumbents transform as fast as models improve, and companies still need one auditable foundation.

futures.name: Services become software
futures.d: Agent companies that charge by output take the payroll and outsourcing budgets of functions like customer support and legal, outgrowing traditional SaaS. This requires verifiable results and companies willing to let agents take responsibility; in China it may appear as whole-function outsourcing paid by results.

futures.name: Interfaces and procurement collapse
futures.d: Agents call APIs and data layers directly, companies use coding agents to build software on demand or even throw it away after one use, most apps degrade into back-end pipes, per-seat pricing loses meaning and SaaS margins stay compressed. The condition: agent security, permissions and auditing get solved.

stances.label: Doom is overdone; platforms endure
stances.sum: AI actually favors incumbents that own data, business rules and workflows. Building your own software with AI instead of buying it is expensive and fails compliance and audit requirements. SaaS grows an agent layer rather than getting replaced, and the application layer is not a thin wrapper around the model.

stances.label: Split: thin dies, systems live
stances.sum: SaaS survives as a category but splits hard. Single-purpose tools, thin data layers and products that live on configuration get eroded; bundled systems that own workflows and authoritative data remain. Pricing moves from seats to usage, and then to paying for outcomes.

stances.label: Interfaces bypassed, broad disruption
stances.sum: Most SaaS is just a database plus an interface. Coding agents make it cheap to replicate code and build on demand, and agents can read and write data directly. Point apps, process software and closed-source code lose pricing power, and the high margins can't last.

m: HubSpot's founder: years of customer data are an edge newcomers can't match; AI unusually favors incumbents.
AI won't eliminate interfaces; new media stack on top, so there will be more software and more UI.
SaaS platforms sit on gold mines and will grow collaborative agents, such as renting an AI engineer from Synopsys.
Salesforce's CEO: agents are the next layer, a digital workforce built on top of automation and data.
Cloning an interface is easy; years of configured business rules are the lock-in, and more look-alike apps only help the strong.
General models won't eat industry-specific products, just as Photoshop and CapCut coexist, provided AGI doesn't arrive within five years.
Airtable's CEO: having agents assemble reliable building blocks into business apps is steadier than generating code from scratch.
He disagrees that models will swallow apps; new interaction patterns plus ever-spilling model capability are the opportunity.
The application layer is far stickier than people think; calling AI apps wrappers is like calling Salesforce a database wrapper.
MongoDB's CEO: 'value goes to zero' is overdone; vibe coding can't get past compliance and security requirements.
Replacing purchased software with a weekend-built tool is extremely short-sighted, but last-generation per-seat products will take a hit.
