He is sure agents will heavily use human tools like Excel and databases, so those tools must be accelerated too.
ServiceNow's CEO: rebuilding an app with a large model costs about 10 times more, and cross-department systems of record are hard to copy.
He expects multiplying agents to call tools like Excel and chip-design software far more, making tool makers more valuable.
Data models and business logic remain stable; unbundle them and repackage them for agents.
When compute is scarce, companies spend tokens on their core business, not on replacing cheap SaaS.
Models won't swallow everything, just as General Electric succeeded on appliances rather than on generating power.
Intercom's chief product officer: almost every workflow-based business software is on a path to being replaced or enhanced by AI.
Software history cycles between unbundling and bundling; the LLM era will rebundle around shared data.
Companies will still buy rather than build, but pricing must be by outcome; a product weakened by one model release is too thin.
The big opportunity is replacing labor; thin-data systems of record get eroded first among small and mid-sized customers.
Data flywheels are mostly useless; an app's defense shifts to user habit and recognition, and owning the customer's entire workflow.
SaaS has unbundled as far as it can and is turning to bundling; AI favors horizontal tools where information is concentrated.
Patching old software is pointless; Chinese industry-specific agents should take a cut of results, not charge per seat.
Price by attribution and autonomy: copilots charge per seat, and only attributable, autonomous work charges per outcome.
Agents complete measurable work directly, so the whole market shifts to outcome-based pricing.
Intercom's CEO: Fin charges only for tickets it resolves, anchoring price to value.
Configuration-heavy legacy SaaS doesn't fit the AI era; charging by output can eat into services budgets.
About half of apps may become mere pipes that agents call; systems of record and workflows are what last.
Rippling's chief product officer: point SaaS and middle-layer AI companies get squeezed from both sides; bundlers with data win.
Budgets flow to AI products with clear returns and traditional SaaS lacks leads, but he sees it as a passing wave.
SAP's CTO: interface, process and data layers all get rebuilt; pricing goes from seats to usage to outcomes.
SAP: the deadliest blow is per-seat pricing failing; the defense is business logic and an auditable foundation of trust.
AI can write integrations automatically, tearing open the advantage ERP and Salesforce built on integrations.
Most SaaS is a database plus an interface; in future the data belongs to users and interfaces get generated on demand.
Microsoft plus OpenAI could swallow lots of feature-level SaaS; only those with complex workflows and data have a chance.
Brex's CEO: AI merges data from every system into one real-time layer, making traditional ERP unnecessary.
The cost of building software has collapsed; one-size-fits-all SaaS doesn't fit, and small businesses already build their own back-office tools.
Salesforce is expensive and hard to use; a CRM that just adds an AI column to old tables will die.
He sees AI that handles hours-long tasks as a junior employee, and says on-demand generated software will definitely happen.
He expects email and Slack to give way to AI-native tools where agents do the work and involve humans only when needed.
Rising AI valuations become acquisition currency, while incumbents' buying power shrinks.
With development cost near zero, software gets built for a single task and thrown away afterward.
A home agent replaced 6 of his apps; many apps shouldn't exist at all, and vendors just need to open APIs.
Coding agents push the global software industry into a 'China-style trap'; SaaS can't hold 80 to 90 percent margins.
Models become the operating system of an automated economy; SaaS, consulting and IT outsourcing are hit first.
Manycore: process SaaS getting replaced is a trend, not a cycle; the closer to the physical world, the safer.
Software lost first to rising discount rates, then to agent replacement; interface-based point tools are the most fragile.
Closed-source SaaS is dead; sell outcomes instead. Mininglamp's data supply-chain business is less exposed.

debates.q: When will AI for science and AI drug discovery actually deliver?
debates.why: AI for science is seen as one of AI's biggest long-term payoffs. How fast it delivers decides whether money should go to models, data or wet labs (real biology and chemistry experiments), and tests whether AI can produce new knowledge rather than just repeat old knowledge.
debates.sum: Guests across the four shows broadly agree that math and code, where answers can be checked automatically, will deliver first. Biomedicine is where they split most: on No Priors, molecule-design teams like Chai report big jumps in hit rates, while Daphne Koller, Biohub and others stress the bottlenecks in data and clinical trials. LatePost Chat adds a frontline view from DP Technology: generate data from physical principles and build a platform. Yuandong Tian and Yitang Zhang think groundbreaking discoveries still lack research taste. Lenny barely touches the topic.
axis: Slow and long; stuck at experiments and trials
debates.notable: Most are upbeat: Jensen Huang, Geoffrey Hinton and Alexandr Wang see breakthroughs close. Yann LeCun and Fei-Fei Li are cautious: LeCun says LLMs only retrieve known facts; Li says a model fed astronomy data wouldn't derive F=ma. Demis Hassabis expects decade-long drug R&D cut to weeks, yet says AI can't pose good questions. Sam Altman went from 'big breakthroughs need slow experiments' (2025) to 'AI is finding new knowledge' (2026). Podcast guests are more split.

cmp.cn: Xiaojun Zhang's show mostly views it from a distance, through the lens of the road to AGI. LatePost Chat has DP Technology's frontline experience, pragmatic and leaning optimistic; Wang Xiaochuan bets on medicine, while Yitang Zhang and Yuandong Tian doubt AI can do groundbreaking research.
cmp.us: No Priors hosts a steady stream of biology and science founders, mixing optimism and caution. Lenny barely covers it, apart from Andreessen on medical licensing as a barrier and Eric Simons on verifiable fields going first.
cmp.gap: The English side gets as granular as hit rates and datasets, with a fundraising story attached. The Chinese frontline comes from molecular simulation and platform companies, talking about accurate computation and generating data, and 'medicine' there usually means clinical services rather than new drugs. Lenny's product-and-growth focus keeps it largely absent.

cruxes: Can the jump in design hit rates turn into higher clinical success rates?
Can virtual cells and physics surrogate models get accurate enough to replace most wet-lab experiments?
Do major discoveries need new theory and research taste, or is large-scale search within the known enough?
agree: Math and algorithms, where answers check automatically, benefit first.
Missing data has to be generated by experiments or from physical principles.
Faster design doesn't mean drugs reach the market faster.

futures.name: Math pays off first
futures.d: Math, algorithms and formal verification keep producing new results and find commercial use first in verifying code and chips, while other fields borrow the 'search plus verify' method. The condition: the cost of automated formalization and verification keeps falling.

futures.name: Fast design, slow trials
futures.d: AI-designed antibodies, proteins and materials flood into preclinical and early validation and R&D costs fall, but the number of approved new drugs changes little in the short term. The gains show up first as higher R&D efficiency and failures surfacing earlier.

futures.name: Closed-loop labs take off
futures.d: Autonomous labs, physics surrogate models and virtual cells form a fast feedback loop, models propose and test their own hypotheses in materials and biology, and major discoveries emerge that aren't human-led. This requires much higher simulation accuracy and experimental capacity that can scale.

stances.label: Stuck on data, trials and theory
stances.sum: Most biological data has to be generated slowly through experiments, and model accuracy is still low. Even if design speeds up, clinical trials, regulators and the pace of biology itself set the speed of new drugs. Groundbreaking theoretical problems have almost no training examples and still depend on human abstraction and taste. The payoff is ten-plus years away.

stances.label: Verifiable fields break through first
stances.sum: Math, algorithms and code, where answers can be checked cheaply and automatically, produce new results first. Physics and chemistry can generate data from first principles (the basic laws of physics) and train surrogate models. Biology needs simulators, experiment loops and data feedback, conquered field by field. Progress is spiky, not uniform.

stances.label: Biomedical breakthroughs are near
stances.sum: The design end has already jumped by orders of magnitude: hit rates for antibodies and mini-proteins have soared, and protein and cell models are near their GPT-3 moment. Biology is turning from a science of discovery into a science of engineering, and medicine is reinforcement learning's next frontier.

m: Faster R&D is limited by regulation and by biology's own pace; Alzheimer's, for instance, requires years of follow-up.
Healthcare's near-term opportunity is operations, not new drugs; the hard parts are mouse-to-human translation and approval.
The bottleneck is clinical reality; she wants to see AI-discovered drugs succeed more often in trials first.
AI has essentially solved protein folding, but the productivity payoff will take about ten years to show.
He predicts AI agents won't write a paper accepted at a top venue like NeurIPS within five or even ten years.
He ranks biological intelligence, connecting brain and body, last, at about 20 years out.
Cell models are limited by data, not compute; today's best models are only at about 10 percent.
A virtual cell has to be accurate enough; 10 percent accuracy is just simulating noise, though it can help narrow targets.
He thinks LLMs only retrieve existing knowledge; they can't pose questions or solve new problems, so they can't invent.
AI doing research only looks expert to outsiders; its sample efficiency trails humans by orders of magnitude, a 10-to-20-year gap.
AI will advance math, but contest problems differ from open research; the Riemann hypothesis won't fall without humans.
The near-term value is compressing R&D workflows; he hasn't yet seen a pharma R&D process truly transformed.
She guesses a model fed astronomy data wouldn't derive F=ma: deep learning fits patterns but doesn't grasp causal laws.
AI might diagnose better than doctors but can't get a license; protected industries like healthcare will slow adoption.
Biological data can't be bought or scraped; new ways to generate it must be invented, on a 10-to-15-year timeline.
Even after founding a company he thinks groundbreaking scientific problems have almost no examples; taste and abstraction are what's missing.
She finds AI for science exciting but warns data-poor areas need caution; global liver-surgery cases may not suffice for training.
He says AI excels at searching huge spaces toward clear goals but can't yet pose good questions, science's hardest part.
AlphaProof can't yet build theories; problems like the Riemann hypothesis need new mathematics.
Machine-verifiable fields can scale massively, and formal proofs can also be used to verify code.
AI's unique value is scientific discovery moving toward autonomous experiments, but phase 3 trials remain the bottleneck.
Code can be checked automatically, so large models will improve at programming far faster than in fields like law.
Chemistry and biology data must come from physical experiments, which leaves room for specialized model companies.
Science is fundamentally search: humans write the goal and hard constraints, and AI produces code that can be reviewed.
Math and computer science benefit first because evaluation is nearly free; biology and chemistry can scale with simulators.
Verifiable fields will have their 'Lee Sedol moment'; after the Olympiad gold, discovering small theorems is close.
He says AI still can't choose the right questions, but a virtual cell could speed biology experiments about a hundredfold.
He bets AI will make a major scientific discovery by end-2027, but big breakthroughs still need slow, messy new experiments.
DP Technology's CEO: quantum mechanics at the micro level is barely used; where data is missing, generate it from physics equations.
AI surrogate models speed computation a millionfold; by around 2030 he expects several drugs and materials developed by AI.
Physics, materials or math will produce stunning results, but claims that 'science is solved' will overshoot.
Science must loop with physical experiments; intelligence is spiky, and each field needs its own data feedback loop.
A perfect Putnam score is an AlphaGo-style signal; the supply of mathematics goes from scarce to abundant.
Math, code and theoretical science get automated first because they're objective, but there's no Einstein-level discovery yet.
He says AI suits problems with vast possibilities, data or simulators and clear objectives, but can't yet propose meaningful conjectures.
An Erdős conjecture was disproved at low cost; the scientific capability of today's models is largely untapped.
Drugs are the next batch of 'impossible problems'; language models can already model proteins and chemicals.
DNA is a language not designed for human brains; AI will surpass experts in biology faster than in English.
He says AI already reads medical images about as well as radiologists and is good at designing drugs.
Medicine is the scenario that matters most; he envisions AI supplying a million doctors.
He hopes biology follows chip design into computer-aided design, since models can already represent genes, proteins and cells.
Reinforcement learning suits fields with clear right and wrong; medicine is next, and the goal is a digital doctor.
It's dawn for biology; stop speculating about three to five years, build a super-strong small team and start now.
Medicine is the jewel in the large-model crown; the next era turns life into mathematics.
He thinks AI does in minutes biology work that took a PhD five years; cancer cures may come in our lifetime.
AI for science is closer than robotics; protein and virtual-cell models could take off in 2026 to 2027.
He expects AI to pose its own scientific problems within five to ten years and cut drug development to months.
He thinks models may have intuitions humans lack, especially in biology, making scientific breakthroughs worth expecting.
Antibody design hit rates rose from about 0.1 percent to nearly 20 percent; the AI drug-discovery startup window is one or two years.
Mini-protein design now succeeds nearly 70 percent of the time; biology will get its own CAD software.
He says AI already out-diagnoses doctors, will help design drugs and materials, and will eventually propose new theories.
He aims to move 99% of drug exploration into computers, believing within years it can shrink decade-long development to weeks.
Big data plus big models move biology from a science of discovery to a science of engineering.
Programmable biology might make one drug per person real, though he admits that's more optimism than certainty.
He is very sure the next decade brings a golden age of scientific discovery, with AI now speeding discovery itself.
He says AI already beats humans in specific domains like protein synthesis and virtual drug screening.
He says AI is starting to discover important knowledge; methods proven in math will extend to biology, medicine and materials.

debates.q: Should governments let the AI race run, or step in and control it?
debates.why: How tightly governments regulate, whether chips can be exported, and whether the state spends money to back the industry all decide how fast the AI race runs and who leads it. They also set the daily conditions that open-source projects, startups and Chinese teams have to live with.
debates.sum: Most guests on No Priors and Lenny oppose broad AI laws. Their reasoning: complex rules are only affordable for big companies, so regulation ends up protecting incumbents from new rivals. They want governments to clear bottlenecks like power and permits first, and to police harmful uses rather than research itself. The two a16z founders are the most adamant. After 2025 the conversation shifted from whether to legislate to how nations compete and how to control chips. Anthropic-linked guests like Ben Mann still insist frontier risks are real. The two Chinese shows rarely debate this head-on. Their guests mostly speak as the regulated side, describing how US restrictions on China hit them, or discuss the side effects of local governments investing in AI. Yi Ma argues for regulating uses, not the technology.
debates.notable: Geoffrey Hinton and Demis Hassabis favor firmer oversight: Hinton wants about a third of compute mandated for safety research; Hassabis wants an empowered outside body testing models. Yann LeCun would regulate products, not research; Jensen Huang prefers existing agencies. Fei-Fei Li, Elon Musk and Alexandr Wang sit between. Sam Altman shifted most: licensing (2023), 'most regulation does more harm than good' (2025), a 'speed limit' on self-improving AI (2026). Podcast guests lean lighter.

cmp.cn: Xiaojun Zhang's show has only scattered views: Kevin Kelly opposes chip bans, and Ming Zeng predicts AI will eventually be heavily regulated. Wanchan Liao talks more about how US restrictions hurt Chinese companies and the side effects of local governments funding compute and data centers. Yi Ma wants rules on applications, not on the technology.
cmp.us: No Priors brings on government officials and incumbents, and the mainstream view there is less regulation and more building. On Lenny, the two a16z founders are the fiercest opponents of regulation. Anthropic's Ben Mann is the minority voice, stressing that AI must be made to share human goals ahead of time.
cmp.gap: Guests on the English shows take part in the policy debate directly; some are officials, some are lobbyists. The Chinese shows rarely comment on China's own AI rules and speak instead as the regulated side or as participants in industrial policy. Likely reasons: different room for public debate, different guest mixes, and the fact that in China the government usually shows up as an investor and a customer.

cruxes: Are open source and light regulation a strategic asset, or a weapon handed to rivals and abusers?
Do export controls slow rivals down, or push them to build their own and invite retaliation like rare-earth bans?
State stakes, subsidies and local investment drives expand the government's role. Is that heavy intervention, and does it work?
agree: Complex rules favor giants, and openly downloadable models deserve protection
Compute buildout is stuck on power and permits, not money
The risks are real, but halting or pausing AI is not the answer

futures.name: Few rules, lots of building
futures.d: The US keeps a light touch on AI research, with federal rules overriding state laws, and pours policy effort into energy permits, data centers and exporting the American tech stack to allies. This holds as long as no major AI accident turns public opinion.

futures.name: Targeted controls tighten
futures.d: Chips get tracked to their end use, manufacturing equipment is tightly controlled, dangerous capabilities such as biology are released in tiers, and third-party testing becomes routine, while research itself stays fairly free. The trigger would be credible evidence of misuse, a chip-smuggling case, or a model visibly going off course on its own.

futures.name: Regulated like a utility
futures.d: The model market shrinks to a handful of players, public pressure over job losses and power bills rises, and governments regulate entry and pricing the way they do for water and electricity, with antitrust stepping in. Unlikely, but high impact if it happens.

stances.label: Regulate less, build first
stances.sum: It is too early to legislate. The push for regulation usually comes from incumbents wanting to block rivals, or from fear. Governments should clear energy and permitting bottlenecks, protect open source, and use existing laws for harms that have actually appeared. Export bans and investment limits hurt everyone over time, including the country imposing them.

stances.label: Regulate capabilities, keep it open
stances.sum: This group accepts rules in principle but rejects limits set by compute size or calls to halt research. Regulate what a model can do and where it is used, not the technology itself. Use antitrust to stop a few firms from controlling key inputs. Protect openly downloadable model weights. And data centers should win local community consent first.

stances.label: State leads industry and supply chain
stances.sum: AI is a contest of national power, so governments should get involved in supply chains and demand: use industrial policy to rebuild domestic manufacturing, organize allies, and pay to support the industry. But export controls need restraint, and state-led investment can fall behind the pace of technology.

stances.label: Frontier capabilities need strict control
stances.sum: Frontier AI already touches national and public security. Models above a compute threshold should be registered and tested, chips should be trackable, dangerous capabilities should not be released freely, and oversight must be independent rather than left to the sellers. The endgame may be utility-style regulation, like power and water.

m: AI should not be broadly regulated; he only backs export controls on top chips and limits on autonomous weapons.
He opposes pausing AI research, calling such limits obscurantism, like the Ottoman ban on printing.
The industry's rush to embrace regulation is naive; nuclear permitting stalled for decades and is the cautionary tale.
US limits on investing in China are drawn by use case and judged subjectively; AI is hit hardest, and Metaso's business suffered.
Technology naturally crosses borders; chip bans help in the short run but hurt every country over time.
You cannot know how to regulate a technology before you see it; he criticizes regulate-first thinking and the EU AI Act.
Antitrust has closed off selling startups to big tech, leaving investors in large models with too few exits.
Existing laws can handle today's AI; we should not legislate for AGI based on theory.
He argues the AI diffusion rule is completely wrong; America should spread its tech worldwide fast to keep its lead.
White House adviser: simplify permits, restart nuclear power, and set federal rules so state laws do not strangle open source.
Energy is stuck on permits, not capital; policymakers should not rush to regulate AI before they understand it.
AI is this century's industrialization; the US must stay in the top tier and cannot over-regulate too early.
He thinks most regulation does more harm than good; only far-superhuman models warrant very strict safety testing.
Scaring governments with job losses and god-like AI is harmful; companies lobbying to restrict rivals have conflicted motives.
Protected cartels like doctors, hospitals and government will resist AI entering real-world industries.
He says doomer fear has swayed Washington and some use regulation against rivals; US tech should keep competing in China.
US data centers are stuck on siting, power and permits; space, which needs no permits, may be a way out.
Heavy regulation in the name of safety becomes a shield for incumbents; tech as a whole should be lightly regulated.
Legislation is premature but the fear is legitimate; industry should help build a framework before extreme bans appear.
He opposes a pause; government should mainly require disclosure, punishing unlabeled AI fakes like counterfeit money.
Opposes caps on model size; regulate capabilities the way the FDA approves drugs, testing as you go.
Intelligence is now something nations race for; regulators should watch for capability jumps, not data centers.
The 10^26 compute threshold is arbitrary; regulate capabilities directly. Banning open source is regulatory capture.
She says regulation needn't start over: update existing rules like healthcare's, and fund university research with public money.
He favors light early regulation focused on FDA-style model testing by independent testers, with companies joining voluntarily.
He wants an independent referee watching leading AI labs, but finds real-world regulation often absurd and slowing useful work.
He opposes one AI super-regulator, wanting existing agencies like the FAA and FDA to add AI rules in their own domains.
Regulate applications, not the technology; over-regulation breeds monopoly. Comparing AI to the atomic bomb is absurd.
FTC chair: pursue antitrust actively, support open-weight models, and recognize that complex rules favor giants.
He wants rules for specific products, not research; he opposes compute thresholds and wants government compute for academia.
She wants policy grounded in science, not sci-fi: regulate AI applications that touch people, not halt upstream research.
Thinks extinction risk is underrated but opposes pausing training; that would be like holding back water with a rubber band.
A single AI gateway risks censorship; hedge it with many competing companies and open source.
He now thinks his licensing-agency idea was off, but very advanced models still need external safety testing.
AI drifting off course on its own is more real than thought, but he opposes stopping AI and backs moderate regulation.
Data centers need community consent; within 12 to 18 months residents must see benefits in power bills and jobs.
He sees the race as a prisoner's dilemma needing government involvement, but regulation must be light, agile and keep pace.
He favors industry self-policing: rivals test new models a week or two before release; government steps in only for ignored dangers.
She favors layered governance: industry self-policing, ethics review and use-based laws, with the FDA overseeing AI in biology.
He says AI can't be stopped; Europe should borrow America's ambition and shape it by its own values, not just fear it.
He wants industry to draft and publish AI safety standards first, then have governments turn them into global rules.
The early chip industry grew on government purchases, but real innovation is hard to force by policy; leave room for freedom.
Governments wanting their own AI is real demand, but compute centers built for local investment drives may fall behind hardware upgrades.
In the chip export-control debate he prioritizes ensuring America wins, seeing Taiwan's chip fabs as a key risk.
He says the AI race depends on who controls chip fabs, so building chips in America is vital to national security.
Protective tariffs only make sense alongside active industrial policy such as investing in skills.
Tech companies quitting defense projects is rarely right; staying in the room makes the process more precise.
He proposes a national AI data reserve and energy dominance, and urges government to adopt AI boldly.
Export services and model access first, then GPUs, and strictly control manufacturing tools; a total cutoff invites rare-earth retaliation.
Opportunities in industries like electric vehicles come from long-term national investment; they are national opportunities at heart.
He backs industrial policy: fix energy first, bring manufacturing home, and keep the most advanced tech from adversaries.
A 14-nation economic security alliance should cover the whole AI supply chain, organized by companies rather than governments.
Intel CEO: welcomes government taking a stake; advanced chip manufacturing should be treated as infrastructure.
Export controls are an endless game with no winner, but he supports building more fabs for security.
IPO revenue thresholds push data-collection centers funded by local governments; when the data does not sell, they fold.
Models above a compute threshold should be registered and tested by international teams; AI in ads must be labeled.
He proposes a new agency licensing AI above a capability threshold, with pre-release safety tests and independent audits.
He says he urged pausing AI development and signed the open letter, partly as a favor, never expecting a real pause.
He argues superhuman AI is too weighty for one company; governments and academia must weigh in, and safety institutes need red-team access.
The stronger the model, the riskier it is to release; the best models need not all be published, as a matter of company self-restraint.
Chips should be licensed and tracked to end use; expert-level virology capabilities should be available only to businesses.
He wants governments to force companies to spend about a third of their compute on safety research.
He calls for strongly regulated capitalism, regulation of outrage-driven feeds, and ideally a working world government.
Anthropic: the chance of a very bad outcome may be around 10 percent; align AI early and tell legislators the truth.
Labs cannot be allowed to certify their own safety; independent oversight will eventually extend to inspecting model weights.
He says big companies shouldn't grade their own homework on guardrails; international standards and certification are needed.
He calls for empowered new bodies to test models independently, plus enforceable laws banning harmful deepfakes and mandating watermarks.
Intelligence compounds like interest, leading to oligopoly; the endgame looks like utilities, a few AI clouds under strict regulation.
He argues the world needs a speed limit on AI self-improvement, calling a power-seeking race toward it very dangerous.

debates.q: Will Nvidia keep dominating AI chips on its own?
debates.why: Computing power is the single biggest cost of building AI. Whether Nvidia keeps the market to itself decides how expensive AI is, who captures the profit, and how secure the supply is. For Chinese teams who cannot buy the chips, it also shapes which technical path they take.
debates.sum: Most guests think Nvidia will keep dominating model training thanks to its full package: the chips, the networking that links them, and the CUDA software ecosystem. Lingjie Xu and Lu Zhang on Wanchan Liao agree, and see Huawei's SuperPod and Google's TPU as limited threats for now. The split comes with inference (the computing done when a model answers) and agents (AI that does tasks on its own). AWS, Arm, Intel, Cerebras and the makers of on-device chips all expect Nvidia's share to be carved up. Keep in mind that most of the people predicting this sell chips themselves. Lenny's show barely touches chips.
debates.notable: Jensen Huang and Liang Wenfeng see Nvidia staying on top: Huang says it's cheapest on total cost, and a poorly designed chip isn't worth having even free; Liang says Nvidia rests on a Western tech ecosystem Chinese chips lack. Elon Musk backs Tesla's chips but shifted: in 2024 he put Dojo 2 at B200 level; by 2025 he said Dojo can't match Nvidia for training. Podcast guests mostly see one leader plus others.

cmp.cn: Xiaojun Zhang's show looks at it through software ecosystems and how models fit the hardware. Wanchan Liao adds the systems view: Lingjie Xu and Lu Zhang think Nvidia is hard to dislodge for two or three years, Nan Zhou sees Cerebras breaking through only in inference, and they discuss Huawei's SuperPod directly.
cmp.us: On No Priors, Nvidia and analyst Dylan Patel make the case for its system-wide edge, while AMD, AWS, Arm, Intel and Cerebras each explain how share will be split. Lenny barely covers chips; only a Cisco executive stresses the importance of networking.
cmp.gap: Both sides agree Nvidia is hard to beat in cloud training. On the English shows, the challenge mostly comes from the challengers themselves. The Chinese shows bring Huawei and domestic chips into the discussion, but their concern is system capability and whether the chips can be bought at all, not whether they replace Nvidia globally. Lenny focuses on product, so the topic is mostly absent.

cruxes: Will models keep adapting to GPUs, or will inference, long context and sparsity force new hardware?
Are cloud providers' and Chinese chips real replacements for Nvidia, or just price leverage and backup supply?
In the inference and agent era, how much value can CPUs, memory bandwidth and on-device compute take?
agree: Nvidia's edge is the combination of chips, networking and software
Inference and agent workloads will change what kinds of chips are needed
Competition has moved from single chips to interconnect and whole-system design

futures.name: One leader, several seconds
futures.d: Nvidia keeps training and most inference. Cloud providers' own chips, AMD and Chinese chips handle some internal or restricted-market workloads, mainly to diversify supply and push prices down. This holds as long as Nvidia keeps up its yearly cadence of system-level upgrades.

futures.name: Inference splits off
futures.d: Once agents and inference become the main workloads, servers carry more CPUs, low-latency inference chips and on-device chips win a meaningful share, and value spreads from training GPUs to inference systems.

futures.name: An architecture switch
futures.d: A new model architecture wins, either extremely sparse (using only a small slice of parameters at a time) or dependent on very high bandwidth, so today's GPUs are no longer the best fit and new chip designs leap a generation. This requires the new architecture to match transformers in quality. Unlikely, but high impact.

stances.label: A system-wide edge nobody can copy
stances.sum: Nvidia owns the GPUs, the networking between them, and twenty years of software ecosystem, and it designs the whole data center as one product. Rivals' paper advantages get eaten up by manufacturing process, memory, system capability and shipping delays. Rising demand only strengthens the incumbent.

stances.label: Models adapt to the hardware
stances.sum: Whether a model architecture wins depends a lot on whether it won the hardware lottery. Transformers succeeded because their matrix math happens to suit GPUs, and new methods are actively adapting to GPUs too. As long as models keep bending toward existing hardware, the incumbent only gets stronger.

stances.label: One leader plus several seconds
stances.sum: Chip markets have always had one leader and a strong second supplier. Cloud providers' own chips, AMD, Cerebras and Chinese chips will spread out supply and push prices down, and value will flow to networking, inference infrastructure and applications. But Nvidia stays number one.

stances.label: New workloads need new chips
stances.sum: GPUs were never built for transformers or for inference. Once inference, agents (AI that does tasks on its own) and devices like phones and earbuds become the main workloads, specialized designs such as fast inference chips, CPUs and compute-in-memory will take a big share. Tweaking existing architectures cannot deliver order-of-magnitude gains.

m: Every chip has been CUDA-compatible, even though there were almost no paying customers for the first ten years.
High-end training and inference chips are almost all Nvidia's, and they depend on a few foundries like TSMC.
AI is plural, not singular; chips and platforms matter just as much, and Nvidia may matter more than OpenAI.
He sees Nvidia's edge as a web, not a moat: every accelerator stays CUDA-compatible, with about 300 million in use.
He thinks Nvidia's lead rests on the whole Western tech community and industry ecosystem, which Chinese chipmakers lack.
Co-designing hardware and software beats Moore's law; the whole data center is the unit of computing.
A stable architecture plus the CUDA ecosystem forms a self-reinforcing network, making the hardware ever harder to replace.
Cheaper models are nowhere near a reason to short Nvidia; when unit costs fall, total GPU demand rises.
DeepSeek's cost cuts are still on the normal trend line; Nvidia's roughly 20 percent plunge over it was an overreaction.
Interconnect is the second barrier after CUDA; Huawei's SuperPod has limited impact and will not weaken Nvidia for two or three years.
He says chips are only part of a gigawatt AI factory's cost; with a weak architecture, even free chips aren't cheap enough.
Nvidia is a three-headed dragon; startup chips' paper advantages get offset, and specialized chips often bet on the wrong workload.
Nvidia has gone from selling chips to selling whole AI factories; TPU's edge stays inside Google and will not threaten GPUs soon.
He says Nvidia wins on total cost of ownership; custom chips carry about 65% margins too, so customers save little.
Nvidia research VP: build and open-source models ourselves so the product does not become an interchangeable commodity.
Transformers won the hardware lottery; the architecture hitched itself to the GPU.
Hardware is the final judge of algorithms; algorithms must respect the memory hierarchy, and vendors will not adapt to you.
New compute is getting more specialized, but usually it is the model that moves toward the hardware, not the reverse.
Token-by-token inference is limited by memory bandwidth, so he bets on parallel diffusion models that suit GPUs better.
Google Cloud: TPUs and GPUs are largely interchangeable; what is scarce is people who can tune TPUs.
Every computing wave has had a clear number one and number two; Nvidia will not monopolize.
AMD CTO: opposes closed software stacks; open-source ROCm gives customers a choice.
Nvidia's edge is system-wide, but chip markets usually settle into one leader plus a second supplier.
In the short run Jensen Huang sits higher; Nvidia will back many AI labs to sell more chips.
AWS CEO: in-house Trainium chips diversify supply, and value will shift from Nvidia to applications.
Nvidia makes the most money, but its edge will be tested as the focus shifts from training to inference.
Nvidia's share is near its peak; nations building their own AI open new markets but also bring new competition.
Nvidia takes over 80 percent of the profit; in the long run the profit pool moves to models and applications.
In infrastructure, whoever runs models at the lowest cost and latency is extremely valuable.
Google's hardware-software co-design made Gemini possible, but he is cautious about TPU challenging CUDA.
Competition is now about coordinating everything from chips to apps; Google and Alibaba rely on owning the whole stack.
Cisco: GPUs are only useful linked into clusters, so networking and power are the constraints (Cisco's own business).
Early Cerebras investor: it challenges in inference, it does not replace; OpenAI ordered to diversify supply.
AI chip recipes are similar across vendors; cloud providers build their own mainly to push prices down and keep several suppliers.
GPUs are not the best fit for transformers; hardware and model architecture should be explored together.
He thinks Tesla's own inference chip beats suppliers', and its Dojo 2 training system will reach B200 class.
Nvidia is hard to shake in the cloud, but cars and robots need dedicated chips and entirely new computing architectures.
He concedes training stays on Nvidia, but says Tesla's AI5 for cars and robots beats Nvidia two- to threefold per watt.
Cerebras CEO: new workloads need purpose-built architecture; he claims inference 15 to 20 times faster than GPUs.
Intel CEO: inference and agents will move the CPU-to-GPU ratio from 1:8 toward 1:1.
Running a full model in earbuds means breaking the split between memory and compute; Anker built its own compute-in-memory chip.
Arm CEO: CPUs matter again in the inference era; small devices cannot fit a 50-watt GPU.

debates.q: With AI, will product managers be replaced or become more important?
debates.why: AI has made writing code and building prototypes cheap, so how many product managers a team needs, how work is divided and who gets hired are all changing. Is the PM a middle layer about to be cut, or the new bottleneck? The answer decides how companies build their teams.
debates.sum: This debate mostly happens on Lenny's show. Most guests expect PMs to split in two: those who shuffle information and manage to-do lists will be replaced by AI, while those who decide what to build, explain why, and guard quality will be in higher demand. Keith Rabois, Julie Zhuo and Mian Chen on Xiaojun Zhang's show go further and say the traditional PM role itself is disappearing. A group of guests who make developer tools argue that product, design and engineering will merge into a single role: the builder. The two Chinese shows rarely treat the PM as a profession and talk instead about how organizations should be restructured.
debates.notable: Only Demis Hassabis and Fei-Fei Li weigh in, and they agree the role is splitting. Hassabis says that with technology changing every year, companies need PMs who truly understand it and can anticipate what models will do; Li says PMs are moving from coordinating to building prototypes with AI themselves, and she only hires those keeping up. Guests on the four podcasts most often say PMs matter more now (14).

cmp.cn: The two Chinese shows rarely debate the PM as a profession. On Xiaojun Zhang's show, Mian Chen says AI has already taken the traditional PM apart, while Shunyu Yao and Ming Zeng argue that good PMs are harder than ever to replace. Wanchan Liao focuses on how people who cannot code can now build products.
cmp.us: Lenny is the main arena. Most guests think execution-focused PMs are out and PMs with judgment are in demand. Keith Rabois and Julie Zhuo go further and say teams should not have PMs at all. No Priors covers it less, leaning toward the view that deciding what to build is the new bottleneck.
cmp.gap: The English shows treat the PM as a standalone profession and discuss ratios to engineers, required skills and hiring. The Chinese shows talk more about organizations: the unit of work shifting from roles to tasks, and people stepping back from execution to review. Likely reasons: Lenny's audience is mostly PMs, the PM career track is more established in Silicon Valley, and the PM title lost its shine in China long ago. Both sides agree the bottleneck is moving to judgment.

cruxes: Is deciding what to build a PM-only skill, or can engineers, designers and even the CEO take it over?
Does dropping dedicated PMs and sharing the job cut coordination and speed things up, or throw away hard-won methods?
Is a PM's leverage in writing code and prototypes by hand, or in building review and evaluation systems?
agree: Chores like organizing information, managing backlogs and writing updates go to AI
Once building is cheap, the bottleneck shifts to deciding what to build and judging quality
Working prototypes are replacing long documents as the way teams collaborate

futures.name: Fewer, stronger PMs
futures.d: The PM-to-engineer ratio falls and engineers handle small projects themselves. The remaining PMs own high-stakes decisions, evaluations, launches and explaining the why, while chores are automated. This assumes engineering output keeps surging and judgment stays hard for models to replace.

futures.name: Functions dissolve into builders
futures.d: Small teams routinely go without a dedicated PM, product judgment spreads across engineers and designers, and builder becomes an official title. This requires AI to reliably lift people past the passing grade in their weak areas, and coordination cost to be the main bottleneck.

futures.name: Judgment gets automated too
futures.d: Models catch up with humans on what to build and whether it is good, PMs and engineers get squeezed together, and value concentrates in a very few people. Most guests currently think taste and insight beyond existing data are hard to verify and hard to train, so this is unlikely.

stances.label: The traditional PM is disappearing
stances.sum: AI gives engineers and designers the product skills they lacked, roadmaps now change weekly, and a dedicated PM becomes a redundant hand-off layer. Small teams move faster without one. What remains are the people who teach the AI and the people who write code.

stances.label: Everyone becomes a builder
stances.sum: The lines between product, design and engineering are collapsing. Anyone can prototype and write code, so your role is defined by where you spend your time. PMs need not vanish, but product is no longer their exclusive job, and the title builder may replace the old function names.

stances.label: A split: executors are out
stances.sum: The PMs who get cut are the ones who only manage backlogs, relay information and run process. PMs who own value, make calls and build things themselves are still in demand. There will be fewer, better PMs, and small projects get handled by engineers wearing the PM hat.

stances.label: PMs matter more than ever
stances.sum: Once building is cheap, the scarce skills are deciding what to build, judging whether it is good, and bringing people along, which is exactly the PM's job. PMs who understand needs and can describe them clearly are also the best at directing AI. So this is a golden age for PMs.

m: He says AI has already taken the traditional PM apart; the only core roles left are those who teach AI and those who code.
Her own small team has no PM; engineers no longer hand off product definition, and the results are better.
Annual roadmaps no longer work; deciding what to build looks more like the CEO's job, and the traditional PM is losing its point.
He expects engineers to become architects plus PMs, leaving implementation to AI agents. His company sells Devin.
Wants to break down the walls between design, product and engineering and communicate with working prototypes. Replit sells that tool.
The engineer's core job becomes deciding what to build, and a PM with an idea can submit the code change themselves.
Layers of hand-offs cannot keep up with AI; you need full-stack builders who own the outcome rather than guard a function.
Role boundaries are collapsing; PMs must become design-savvy prototypers, and everyone must understand the neighboring functions.
While the model's abilities are still unclear, design, product and engineering explore together; specialized skills lose value and taste gains it.
PMs, designers and engineers each think AI lets them do the other two jobs; all three are partly right.
On his team PMs, designers and finance people all write code; the title engineer may give way to builder.
Instagram shrank a 13-person team to a few generalist engineers plus one product person who also covers design and data.
The zero-interest-rate era bred process-only PMs; those who just apply frameworks and wait for promotion will be replaced by AI.
The reckoning for product management has begun; backlog administrators go first, and PMs who truly empower teams matter more.
Pessimistic short term, optimistic long term; communication that merely relays information gets taken over. She builds ChatPRD.
He says people misread Airbnb's Chesky on abolishing PMs; someone still has to wear the marketing, execution and design hats.
Execution-focused PMs will be phased out; those with strategy, creativity and early hands-on AI experience will lead.
OpenAI keeps PMs few and strong, each paired with more engineers, to avoid document sprawl and micromanagement.
He says because AI changes yearly, companies need technically fluent product managers who can anticipate next year's models.
About half of PMs are information couriers and are being phased out, yet openings for builder PMs are the highest in three years.
With engineering output exploding, PMs became scarce; projects under two weeks get an engineer acting as mini-PM.
People step out of hands-on execution and focus on proposing ideas, finding context and judging results.
Roles are merging, but abolishing the product function would throw away accumulated experience and methods.
She says product managers now prototype with AI themselves instead of just coordinating; she only hires those keeping up.
ChatGPT augments PMs rather than replacing them, freeing time from repetitive work to focus on strategy.
Once building gets easy, the bottleneck becomes finding the real problem and articulating it.
The non-developers who use Bolt best are often great PMs; PMs will take the lead on interface work.
Ideas and prototypes are exploding, so you need people with taste to act as editors; process-only PMs will be questioned.
A PM who cannot code worked out the requirements, then used AI coding to ship an app that makes money.
With coding faster, deciding what to build is the new bottleneck; human PMs are still needed for the next year or two.
She calls this a golden age for PMs, with trade-offs and consensus as the bottleneck; she disagrees that the PRD is dead.
The more objective the work, the sooner it gets replaced; good products have no objective yardstick, so great PMs are harder to replace.
Building becomes a commodity; PMs and designers who can both build and judge will win.
The unit of organization shifts from roles to tasks, and he expects PMs to become more important.
After becoming Atlassian's CPO, she says the PM role is expanding, not merging, and shifting toward hands-on building.
PM value is concentrating in high-stakes judgment and taste; just pushing projects along is no longer enough.
AI can take over interface design, but the core duties of aligning people and judging under ambiguity matter more.
Deciding what to build and whether it is good is the PM's job and exactly what the AI era needs; PMs will thrive.

debates.q: Should product decisions follow data and experiments, or instinct and taste?
debates.why: It decides how teams make calls, whether to build an experimentation platform, and whom to hire. AI is pushing both ends at once: experiments are getting cheaper, while the taste to decide what to build is getting scarcer.
debates.sum: Both camps have heavyweights. On the experiment side, Ronny Kohavi and the Duolingo crowd argue that most ideas fail, so everything should be tested. On the taste side, Linear, 37signals and Tony Fadell set no feature metrics and decide by judgment. Most guests sit in between and switch depending on the stage of the product and the size of the audience: instinct proposes hypotheses and sets direction, while data acts as a compass and a risk control. Chinese guests say less, mostly doubting that A/B testing (splitting users into groups to compare results) can do more than small optimizations. AI raises the stakes on both ends: experiments get cheaper, and taste gets scarcer.
debates.notable: Jensen Huang and Demis Hassabis lean on intuition: Huang says no spreadsheet can size a brand-new market, so he trusts written-out reasoning; Hassabis says greatness, in games as in science, comes from intuitive leaps. Sam Altman favors data but says anecdotes are often right. Alexandr Wang sits between: one author's clear view first, then 100-plus evals and A/B tests. Podcast guests are similarly spread, most often 'intuition sets direction, data is the compass.'

cmp.cn: The two Chinese shows say little. Chaoping Ming and Qianchuan Zhang on Xiaojun Zhang's show and Junjie Yan on Wanchan Liao all doubt that A/B testing can do more than optimize. By contrast, founders on Wanchan Liao who sell overseas or on Douyin grow through a steady stream of small experiments.
cmp.us: Lenny has the most material and the sharpest split: Ronny Kohavi and the Duolingo crowd champion experiments, Linear and Tony Fadell rely on taste, and most take the middle. No Priors talks more about evaluating AI products and about humans listening and looking through outputs by hand before launch.
cmp.gap: The English shows have both a mature experimentation culture and a backlash against it. The Chinese shows tend to lump A/B testing together with recommendation-system methods and argue that in the era of large models you must define the goal first. The difference may be that Chinese guests are mostly AI founders rather than growth practitioners. Both sides agree that new categories require judgment.

cruxes: Does A/B testing only find local optimums, or can it compound into big breakthroughs?
When data and instinct clash, which one do you doubt first?
Is taste a gift of the few, or a skill anyone can train and a model might even learn?
agree: For new categories, early stages and small samples, data has no answer
Instinct is worth using, but explain its basis and keep a way to check it

futures.name: Experiments go automatic
futures.d: Experiments on small changes like copy and interface get run end to end by AI agents, and the number of experiments jumps. People set direction, define brand guardrails and decide when to change course. This assumes the models' win rate keeps improving and the tracking and evaluation foundations are solid.

futures.name: Taste becomes the edge
futures.d: Once building and testing are cheap, AI output trends toward average, and a few people with taste decide whether the work stands out. Hiring and org design revolve around whoever owns taste. This requires users to notice quality differences, and markets not to be dominated entirely by distribution advantages.

futures.name: Models learn taste too
futures.d: Models surpass most people in aesthetics and judgment, so product decisions go to model review plus automated experiments, leaving humans to pose questions and take responsibility. Yusen Dai has already withdrawn his claim that taste is what humans will be left with, but most guests still think judgment beyond existing data is hard to train.

stances.label: If you can test it, test it
stances.sum: People are far worse at predicting outcomes than they think, and eight or nine out of ten ideas fail. Growth comes from lots of small experiments compounding over time. Test whatever can be tested, down to button colors and when an animation appears.

stances.label: Instinct must pass the data test
stances.sum: Instinct is valuable, but you have to articulate it, write it down, and check it against data or user feedback. The more diverse the users and the bigger the scale, the more often instinct fails and the more experiments matter.

stances.label: Instinct sets course, data is the compass
stances.sum: Vision and instinct decide where to go; data decides how to get there and helps prove you wrong. When samples are too small, the product is too early or the form is brand new, do not force a test. When data and instinct clash, doubt the data first.

stances.label: Taste and vision decide
stances.sum: Big decisions are judgment calls at heart. New categories and disruptive ideas have no comparable data. Leaning too hard on data is fear of being wrong. A/B tests can only patch the details; real leaps come from a few people with taste making the call.

m: At Microsoft and Airbnb, eight or nine in ten ideas failed; he wants every change tested, and a flat result means no launch.
Feeling sure earns only a low confidence score; only building and testing something counts as high confidence.
Growth is fought inch by inch: improve key steps 1 percent a week, accumulated through many small experiments.
AI products use systematic evaluation to turn anxious guessing into measurable improvement. He sells evaluation tools.
Duolingo's streak feature went through 600-plus experiments in four years, roughly one every two days.
Duolingo has run 16,000 A/B tests, down to when an animation should appear.
Early on Douyin e-commerce he copied first and iterated, rotating products and pitches six or seven times a day to cross-check what worked.
Replace arguments about aesthetics with real traffic data; he runs over a hundred experiments a week.
Anthropic lets Claude run growth experiments end to end, with a win rate about equal to a junior PM's.
Research-based market forecasts go stale fast; strategy emerges from rapid experiments, and testing is what rigor looks like.
He says Meta skips public leaderboards for detailed internal evals; many small 2% gains add up to a magical product.
When the founder is the target user, instinct is reliable; the more diverse the users, the more you need experiments.
Mass consumer products can run on experiments; save user research for ill-defined, high-leverage questions.
He calls product 100 percent a science; an instinct you cannot explain usually means you have not thought it through.
Most changes at Etsy get A/B tested; it is the gold standard, but it should not be the only method.
She does not object to instinct, but unless you write it down you never learn when it was wrong.
Real estate has small samples, so find other ways to build confidence; if all else fails ship on judgment but keep a feedback loop.
AI products are hard to design in a conference room; ship first, then analyze implicit feedback like thumbs up and down.
He says he weighs data over anecdotes, but anecdotes are often right, so he watches both closely.
Instinct is usually right but specific ideas are usually wrong; copy what is proven and bet on just one new thing.
A/B testing is like navigation: it picks the route, not the destination. Instagram Stories was decided first, then iterated.
Growth teams need not A/B test everything; experiments mainly de-risk big changes.
Chasing external metrics like annual recurring revenue hurts the product; care more about what users actually need.
Instinct is a kind of data too, but say whether it comes from experience, your own use or user stories.
Growth hacking and A/B testing at the very earliest stage is a waste; go talk to your first customer.
Industry benchmarks are mostly marketing; before launch you still look through thousands of images by hand to pick a version.
Music has no right answer; Suno relies on team listening sessions and internal review, plus A/B tests.
Treat instinct as a hypothesis generator: propose, debate, find data, then converge.
Shopify ships changes that feel right even when the experiment is neutral; the core product has no KPIs and runs on taste.
Data is a compass, not a GPS; when it clashes badly with instinct, the data is usually wrong.
If you cannot gather a sample in a month, do not test; experimenting on everything paralyzes a team.
A prototype takes a day, so waiting for user feedback becomes the drag; decide fast on data-informed instinct.
Explore a brand-new AI capability broadly by feel first; add evaluations once the use cases settle.
Instinct sets direction and metrics are the dashboard; when the growth curve tops out, go back to first principles.
The staged rollout hit every metric, but users scored it in the forties; he scrapped the plan and accepted a delay.
He wants one clear authorial vision for a product, then polishes it with 100-plus evals and A/B tests.
The jobs-to-be-done framework cannot settle multi-way trade-offs; breakthroughs come from intuition about user psychology plus systems thinking.
Linear runs no A/B tests and sets no feature metrics; once everyone understands customers, decisions go on instinct.

He says spreadsheets can't size a market that doesn't exist yet; decisions start from intuition, tested by written reasoning, not spreadsheets.
The recommendation-system habit of A/B testing to patch cases cannot raise AGI's ceiling; define the goal first, then approach it.
With user-generated content, long-term calls like community culture cannot be proven by short experiments; you need conviction.
CapCut trained his data habit, but data is a rear-view mirror; when they conflict, he picks instinct.

Version 1.0 of a new category has no comparable data; the iPhone keyboard fight was settled by Steve Jobs.

debates.q: Should leaders dig into the details themselves, or hand things off to the team?
debates.why: Management style decides how fast a company moves and whether good people stay. After founder mode, the idea that founders should dig into details themselves, became a buzzword, AI added a new question: should managers start doing hands-on work again?
debates.sum: Lenny is the main arena, and the overall lean is toward digging in: Airbnb's Brian Chesky, Intercom's Eoghan McCabe and Dropbox's Drew Houston all think over-delegating slowed their companies down. After 2025, AI companies also started asking managers to return to hands-on work. Most guests, though, limit digging in to the few areas that decide success or failure. The delegation camp is represented by David Singleton, Geoff Charles, and in China Jingkang Liu and Xiaopeng He. The two Chinese shows rarely use the phrase founder mode and talk more about whether the person in charge should get lost in details, and how flat organizations work.
debates.notable: Jensen Huang and Elon Musk lean hands-on; Liang Wenfeng and Sam Altman lean toward delegating. The widest gap is Huang vs Liang: Huang has about 60 executives reporting directly and gives feedback in public; Liang hands important work to staff and tries not to interfere, believing innovation needs minimal meddling. Alexandr Wang changed most: deciding everything at Scale, then acting as a 'gardener' at Meta. Podcast guests most often back founder mode (16).

cmp.cn: Views on the two Chinese shows are scattered. Jingkang Liu and Xiaopeng He say the person in charge should set the context and stay out of the details. Keke Min, Yuandong Tian and the DeepSeek-style flat organization lean toward getting hands-on. The phrase founder mode barely comes up.
cmp.us: Lenny leans toward digging in: Brian Chesky, Eoghan McCabe and Drew Houston speak from experience, AI companies want managers back on the front line, and David Singleton and others argue for delegation. No Priors has only scattered support for hands-on leadership.
cmp.gap: On the English shows, founder mode reads as a backlash against companies run too much like professional managers; it became a buzzword in 2024, and AI added another reason, that you have to use the tools yourself. The Chinese shows focus on whether the top person should get lost in details and how teams take over. This is a guess; it may just be a difference in who the guests are.

cruxes: Is the founder's instinct the company's scarcest asset, or the bottleneck to scaling?
Should most decisions be made by those closest to the work, or by the one person who sees the whole picture?
Can founder mode be taught and built into the system, or does it only work with the founder present?
agree: Dig into the few details that decide success, and let the team govern the rest
AI changes too fast; managers have to use it themselves

futures.name: Hands-on managers become normal
futures.d: Management layers thin out, managers and executives spend much of their time doing the work, alignment meetings and hierarchy shrink, and senior individual contributors replace layers of management. This assumes AI keeps multiplying individual output and model capabilities keep changing fast.

futures.name: Founder mode gets abused
futures.d: Some founders use founder mode as a reason to pull decisions back to themselves and refuse to learn the CEO craft, creating decision bottlenecks and executive departures. This is more likely when growth slows and the founder's judgment drifts away from the team's.

futures.name: Two-layer organizations spread
futures.d: AI makes information transparent and reporting automatic, the middle layer's job of relaying information disappears, and even larger companies can run like DeepSeek with just the leader and the researchers. The main objection comes from Yang Meng and others, who think middle managers are still needed to compress company context for teams. Unlikely, but high impact.

stances.label: Set the context, let the team run
stances.sum: The bigger the organization, the fewer decisions the leader can take part in, and meddling only stalls everything. The leader's job is to make goals and assumptions clear up front, leave solutions to the people closest to the work, and veto only on big irreversible risks.

stances.label: Dig in only where it counts
stances.sum: Delegating and digging in are not either-or. Founders should know when to go deep and when to return to the cockpit: go pixel-level only in the few areas that decide success, and let the team govern the rest. Lead a new executive closely at first, and let go once they prove they know better than you.

stances.label: Managers go back to hands-on work
stances.sum: Models change every month, and you can no longer judge from screenshots and reports. Managers need to ship with AI themselves, read code and run data. Senior people doing the work directly is faster than layers of management, so alignment meetings and hierarchy shrink.

stances.label: Founder mode: own the details
stances.sum: Digging into details is not micromanagement. Over-delegating blurs goals and slows things down. Founders must keep up the pressure and inject energy, and the key decisions should be made by the CEO alone, who then owns the consequences.

During model launches she personally owns one or two workstreams to keep her sense of progress fresh.

debates.q: Does growth come mainly from users spreading the word, or from sales, channels and paid ads?
debates.why: How a company grows decides whether money goes to building or to sales and ads, and how the team is organized. Now that AI has made building products cheap, the biggest split among founders is whether getting the product in front of users has become the real bottleneck.
debates.sum: Across the four shows it is a tug of war. Lenny's growth guests (Elena Verna, Rahul Vohra, Drew Houston) argue that lasting growth comes from word of mouth and loops built into the product, and that paid acquisition can only amplify it. Enterprise sales people and No Priors insist that big business deals still need humans to sell them. After 2025, with AI making products cheap to build, the view that distribution is the bottleneck grew louder, yet AI apps like Gamma, Lovable and Hailuo mostly grew on word of mouth. Chinese guests are the firmest opponents of buying traffic, though Wanchan Liao also features operators who grow through channels and paid placement.
debates.notable: Only Alexandr Wang weighs in: he thinks Meta's traffic alone isn't enough, and Muse has to spread by word of mouth through instantly recognizable screenshots shared in group chats. That matches the most common view among guests on the four podcasts (30): growth comes from word of mouth and product loops.

cmp.cn: The two Chinese shows are the firmest against buying traffic: Junjie Yan, Kai-Fu Lee, Fangbo Tao and Yusen Dai all think relying on ads means the product itself is wrong. Wanchan Liao also features channel and paid-placement operators like Renjie Guo and Eric. Xiaojun Zhang's show barely mentions enterprise sales.
cmp.us: Before 2024, Lenny leaned toward product-led growth and word of mouth; after 2025 the distribution-is-king view rose, and B2B guests mostly urge adding sales early. No Priors leans toward distribution and enterprise sales, noting that so-called vibe sales, AI doing the selling, has not happened.
cmp.gap: Both sides treat the product as the foundation but push back against different things. Chinese guests are reckoning with the mobile-internet playbook of paid traffic, subsidies and e-commerce channels. English-speaking guests argue over product-led growth versus enterprise sales and platform distribution. This may come down to who the guests are (Chinese shows feature AI app and consumer founders, English shows feature B2B software people) rather than a national difference.

cruxes: Once products look alike, can word of mouth still beat the giants' ready-made entry points and distribution?
In enterprise AI, where users and buyers differ, can bottom-up adoption reach big deals?
Is word of mouth an engine you can design and engineer, or a hope strategy you can only wait for?
agree: Buying traffic before product-market fit only magnifies the leaks and gets pricier
Big enterprise deals still need humans to sell; pure self-serve has a ceiling
Every channel and growth loop decays, so never bet on just one

futures.name: Giants' entry points harvest AI apps
futures.d: Models and product forms keep converging, Google and Meta stuff AI into their existing entry points, and ChatGPT becomes a new distribution platform. Independent apps either lock in distribution before being copied or rent traffic on someone else's platform. This assumes no new 10x leap in experience.

futures.name: Product-led plus sales becomes standard
futures.d: AI companies typically start with free credits and self-serve, then send salespeople and forward-deployed engineers into large enterprises, while go-to-market engineers use AI agents to shrink the sales headcount. This holds as long as enterprise purchasing still requires security reviews and change management.

futures.name: Magical experiences spread again
futures.d: If model capability keeps jumping, each leap produces products with a 10x better experience that vault over distribution barriers within months through social sharing and word of mouth, temporarily erasing the edge of ads and entry points. If capability plateaus, this fades fast. Unlikely, but high impact.

stances.label: Word of mouth and product loops
stances.sum: Lasting growth comes from users recommending the product on their own and from loops built into it, where using the product brings in new users. Paid ads and referral rewards can only amplify existing word of mouth. Depending on bought traffic usually means the product does not work yet, and it hides retention problems.

stances.label: Product first, then add sales and marketing
stances.sum: The product delivers the value and reaches people first, but self-serve credit cards and organic spread both have ceilings. Big enterprise deals need salespeople to find the budget holders, and consumer brands need content and brand to amplify. Which engine to pick depends on whether the user and the buyer are the same person. Most companies end up hybrids.

stances.label: Enterprise needs humans to sell
stances.sum: In enterprise settings, where users and buyers differ and deals must pass security, compliance and change management, self-serve never reaches big contracts. Founders must sell themselves and build enterprise sales and forward-deployed engineers early. AI made code cheap, but it did not make selling cheap.

stances.label: Distribution and traffic are king
stances.sum: When products converge and software gets cheap, distribution is what is scarce. Grab the entry points and channels before the giants copy you, spend on ads, and ride platform tailwinds. Word of mouth cannot be counted on, and every new platform redistributes traffic.
